# Introduction

...suggest that something like “convergent thinking” is just as essential to scientific advance as is divergent. Since these two modes of thought are inevitably in conflict, it will follow that the ability to support a tension that can occasionally become unbearable is one of the prime requirements for the very best sort of scientific research.

Thomas S. Kuhn

*Je cette légere querelle de la tradition et de l’invention, de l’Ordre et de l’Aventure.*

Guillaume Apollinaire

I MUST begin with an apology to Thomas Kuhn. The title of this book has been borrowed – lifted, liberated, stolen, you prefer – though my editor assures me that titles cannot be copyrighted and that I commit no actionable offense – from the title essay of a volume Thomas Kuhn’s writings submitted *Selected Studies in Scientific Tradition and Change*. The essay was initially delivered as a 1959 University of Utah conference on, of all things, the “identification of scientific talent.” Kuhn was already well known as a self-described “exploratory” now working the history of science “though the publication of his masterpiece, *The Structure of Scientific Revolutions*, still lay 3 years in the future. Invited to speak at a conference – run by educational psychologists – on the key characteristics of the creative personality and how to identify such a personality early in the educational process, Kuhn addressed a core issue in scientific education, in terms that clearly show his evolving thought on the themes of creativity, “normal science,” and scientific revolutions. Is iconoclasm, he asked, the only characteristic needed for a successful and creative scientist? Kuhn argued that a thorough grounding in tradition is as important to scientific advance as is the ability to strike out into the unknown. He said:

Normal research, even the best of it, is a highly convergent activity based firmly upon a settled consensus acquired from scientific education and reinforced by subsequent life in the profession. Typically, to be sure, this convergent or consensus-bound research ultimately results in revolution. Then, traditional techniques and beliefs are abandoned and replaced by new ones. But revolutionary shifts of a scientific tradition are relatively rare, and extended periods of convergent research are the necessary preliminary to them. 

As a result, “the successful scientist simultaneously displays the characteristics of [both] the iconoclast and the traditionalist” (Kuhn 1977, p. 227). 1

Kuhn suggested that major scientific advances take place only following the achievement of consensus, when a field has left behind its “natural history stage” filled with a myriad of conflicting results and interpretations. This sequence is necessary because the convergent thought required to build consensus inevitably becomes, at some point, a period of “routine” – a time for consolidation, for incremental improvements, and even boring, but in Kuhn’s words, “the rewards of normal science…are primarily those of the craftsman,” and “normal science does not aim to produce novelties, and those who practice it are not revolutionaries.” (Kuhn 1977, pp. 228, 238). But the very success of normal science in resolving problems and consolidating knowledge creates a situation in which the underlying assumptions of the field become increasingly rigid and resistant to change. 

This is the point at which the iconoclast – the scientist who questions the fundamental assumptions of the field – becomes necessary. But, Kuhn argued, iconoclasm alone is not enough. The iconoclast must have a thorough grounding in the tradition he or she is challenging, for it is only by understanding the existing paradigm that one can effectively critique it and propose a viable alternative. Kuhn used the analogy of Gestalt psychology to illustrate this point. “Gestalt psychology,” he wrote, “demonstrated that perception is not simply a matter of assembling what the eye sees, but of organizing it in a particular way.” (Kuhn 1977, p. 229). Similarly, scientific progress is not simply a matter of accumulating new facts, but of re-organizing existing knowledge in a new and more coherent way. 

> **Figure:** A graph titled "The Structure of Scientific Revolutions" is displayed. The x-axis is labeled "Time" and the y-axis is labeled "Cumulative Anomalies." The graph shows a relatively flat line representing normal science, followed by a steep upward curve representing a crisis, and then a sharp drop representing a paradigm shift. The graph illustrates Kuhn's concept of scientific revolutions as periods of rapid change following periods of stability.

The implications of Kuhn’s work for scientific education are profound. If Kuhn is right, then the traditional emphasis on creativity and iconoclasm in science education is misplaced. While it is important to encourage students to think outside the box, it is even more important to ensure that they have a thorough grounding in the existing scientific tradition. Only by mastering the fundamentals can students hope to challenge them effectively. Furthermore, Kuhn’s work suggests that scientific progress is not a linear process, but a cyclical one, characterized by periods of normal science, crisis, and revolution. This means that science education must prepare students not only for the challenges of normal science, but also for the challenges of revolutionary science.

In the pages that follow, I will explore the implications of Kuhn’s work for the study of creativity in science. I will argue that creativity in science is not simply a matter of individual genius, but a complex social process that is shaped by the prevailing scientific paradigm. I will also argue that the study of creativity in science must take into account the historical and cultural context in which it takes place. Finally, I will propose a new framework for understanding creativity in science that is based on Kuhn’s concept of paradigm shifts.

Sonya Bahar<sup>(1)</sup>

THE MATHEMATICIAN is tossing fruitfully in his bed, talking in his sleep. He was up late talking with his friend the philosopher, and now he is dreaming. Mademoiselle de Espinasse watches him, worried, in the morning she calls in Doctor Bourdeu for a consultation. She noted down her friend’s ravings and, looking for reassurance, reads them to the doctor: “Have you seen a swarm of bees leaving their hive?... Have you seen them fly away and form at the tip of a branch a long cluster of little winged creatures, all clinging to each other by their feet? This cluster is a being, an individual, a kind of living creature.” “Mlle. de l’Espinasse’s dismay, instead of trying to help the continuous patient, Doctor Bourdeu takes the ball and runs with it. “Do you want to change the cluster of bees into one individual animal?” he asks [1]. “Soften their feet with which they cling to one another, that is to say make them continuous instead of contiguous. Obviously there is a marked difference between this new condition of the cluster and the preceding one, and this difference be it not that it is now a whole, and the same animal, whereas before it was a collection of animals? All our organs…are only distinct animals kept by the law of continuity in a state of general sympathy, unity, identity.” (D’Alembert’s Dream, pp. 168–170).

# THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

> **Figure 1.1:** An engraving of a beekeeper tending his apiary (Lyon, France, 1560). Public domain. The engraving depicts a man in period clothing, kneeling and tending to a large collection of beehives. The hives are arranged in a field with trees in the background. The man is using a smoking device to calm the bees. The style is detailed and illustrative, typical of 16th-century engravings.

The idea of an ensemble of individuals coming together to form a qualitatively different collective entity was not new when Denis Diderot explored it in D’Alembert’s Dream, a dialogue that touched on ideas so radically new and dangerous that the manuscript was only circulated among a select group of friends during Diderot’s lifetime. But the idea, as expressed by earlier thinkers, was more metaphor than theory. In the hands of Diderot, the notion of the emergence of a new collective organism crossed the threshold from analogy to hypothesis.

With the exception of the poem *Moretum*, attributed to Virgil, from which the phrase *plurimus umor divinis in context of the assembly of a great deal of moderation, shout and clap their approval and disapproval of whatever is proposed*, or done, till the rocks and the whole place re-echo, and re-double the noise of their boots and their applause. Can a young man be unmoved by all this? He gets dashed away and carried firm minds himself whatever like the crowd and becoming one of them.” (McClelland 1989, pg. 38-39) From the perspective of modern physics, this description – all too real in 2026 as it was in classical Greece – corresponds to local, microscopic interactions between elements of a large ensemble. 

The crowd continued to fascinate philosophers in the years following Plato, not least due to its strange manner of emerging as a separate entity from hundreds of individuals. In *Federalist* No. 55, James Madison suggested that 

[s]ix or seventy men may be more properly trusted with a given degree of power than six or seven. But it does not follow that six or seven hundred should be proportionally a better depository [of the public interests]. And free we carry on to six or seven thousand, the whole reasoning ought to be reversed. The truth is, that in all cases a certain number at least seems to be necessary to secure the benefits of discussion and consultation and discussion, to guard against too easy a combination for improper purposes – as, on the other hand, the number ought at most to be kept within a certain limit, in order to avoid the confusion and intemperance of a multitude. In all very numerous assemblies, whatever character composed, passion never fails to wrest the scepter from reason. Had every Athenian citizen been a Socrates, every Athenian assembly would still have been a mob.

Analyses such as that of Madison, though written in a totally different context (in this case, arguments over the total number of members in the House of Representatives), presage studies of the role of population density in triggering behavioral transitions in flocks and swarms, a topic we will return to in Chap. 8. However, the inner dynamics of crowd structure remained relatively unexplored by eighteenth and nineteenth century commentators, who focused on the role of the crowd in the larger flow of history. The Gordon riots in 1780—were described by Edward Gibbon in typical *ei-versus-able* style: “Forty-thousand Puritans, such as might be met by a dark and terrible [Crowell3]. have started out the turn, the graves have been dreadful… that scum which knows his host’s value” The surface of this cycle—the City of London, for instance—on June 7 and 8 were nearly the same (McClelland 1989, pg. 113-114). 

> **Figure:** A black and white illustration depicting a crowded street scene in London during the Gordon Riots of 1780. People are running and shouting, some are breaking windows and looting. Buildings are visible in the background, with smoke rising from some of them. The overall impression is one of chaos and unrest. The caption reads: "The Gordon Riots in London, 1780."

A century later, a somewhat more systematic, if still impressionistic, account was provided by Gustave Le Bon in his *Psychologie des Foules* (1895). Le Bon, a physician by training, was particularly interested in the physiological and psychological characteristics of crowds, and he argued that the individual, when immersed in a crowd, undergoes a series of transformations, losing his critical faculties and becoming susceptible to suggestion and emotional contagion.

# Fig 1.2. The women of Paris march on Versailles, 1789. Public domain.

Like Gibbon, Hippolyte Taine’s view of the crowd was influenced by his own personal politics: fearfully watching the events of the Paris Commune unfold in 1871 from a sabbatical in Oxford, he saw the crowd as a mob of beasts rather than a collection of Rousseau’s noble savages. Taine wrote: “Take women [who] are hungry and men who have been drinking; place a thousand of these together and let them excite each other with their exclamations, their anxieties, and the contagious reaction of their ever-increasing emotions; it will not be long before you find them a crowd of dangerous maniacs.” (McClelland 1989, p. 129) Like Plato’s, this description centered on the local forces within a group that lead to collective behavior. But Taine’s purpose was not to explore the internal structure that binds together elements of a crowd; he was more concerned with describing how the crowd triggers regression to “the

Taime used these metaphors for emotional effect, not as the starting point for an analysis.

Approaching the turn of the last century, crowd theorists such as Scipio Sighele and Gabriel Tarde struck out in a variety of new directions. They approached the idea of a crowd in a criminological context, but resisted Cesare 
Lombroso’s simplistic identification of criminality (and, by implication, collective behavior of the crowd) with atavism. Sighele argued that, in McLelland’s wording, the collective behavior of crowds was 

… genuinely new in that no other collective phenomenon is in the ordinary sense, it has no past and no future. This is true phylogenetically and ontogenetically. There is no crowd out of which 
the crowd comes, and there is no individual before the individual becomes a member of the crowd. When the crowd disperses, crowd-individuals become the ordinary workday selves. The crowd is in 
this sense outside ordinary time. (McLelland 1989, p. 164)

The crowd is also different in kind, and is more than simply a sum of its parts. Sighele asked under what circumstances humans’ moral and intellectual qualities would be more or less than simply additive, writing that crowds often behave far 
better or far worse, than their constituent individuals would alone. These thoughts suggested the question of how to define a ‘true individual’ in a social group, or in nature itself. In their correspondences, Sighele and Tarde speculated 
about whether the definition of individuality should be parsed down to the level of the cell, or even to the level of the atom. (McLelland 1989, p. 173). McLelland dismisses ideas of this sort as flights of fancy. He notes that Walter 
Bagehot, in *Physics and Politics* (1872) ‘makes great leaps from reflections on the evolution of the human body to reflections on the development of human societies’ but there were not fewer between them… [suggesting] what look 
like analogies to, or analogies between combinations of cells and human groups, because the human social societies and human actors are fundamentally the structure of the cell.’ But – as we shall explore over the next few hundred pages together – 
such crude analogies provide a blunt instrument by which we can begin to excavate the structure of the world. Moreover, Tarde’s acoustic ‘echo’ analogy, much maligned, is earlier foreshadowed in the by-product of Tarde and 
Sighele’s era than by scientists today. Alfred Espinas was not just tossing off analogies when he wrote in 1898 *Les Sociétés* – ‘Sociétés: étude de psychologie sociale’ – that consciousness is a fortunate epiphenomenon of an earlier 
symbiotic relationship between differentiated cells of matter whose exciting collision could have produced the impression of luminosity. McLelland comments that Tarde’s conception of the crowd as a ‘suggestible’ entity, and 
Sighele’s emphasis on the crowd’s ‘contagion’ of ideas, were both to be taken seriously. Tarde’s *Laws of Imitation* (1890) was a genuinely original work, and its emphasis on the role of imitation in social life was to have a profound 
impact on the development of the social sciences.

The text discusses theories of crowds and collective behavior from late 19th and early 20th-century thinkers like Tonnies, Lombroso, Sighele, and Tarde. It critiques simplistic Darwinian views of human nature and explores the idea of the crowd as something distinct from the sum of its individual members. As we have seen, Tarde and Sighele both rejected the idea that the crowd was simply a collection of individuals who had lost their heads. Instead, they argued that the crowd was a new kind of social entity, with its own unique 
characteristics. Tarde, in particular, emphasized the role of suggestion and imitation in the formation of the crowd mind. He argued that individuals in a crowd were more susceptible to suggestion than they were when they were alone, and 
that this susceptibility could lead to irrational and even violent behavior. Sighele, on the other hand, focused on the idea of ‘contagion’, arguing that emotions and ideas could spread rapidly through a crowd, leading to a kind of 
collective hysteria. Both Tarde and Sighele’s work was to have a significant impact on the development of the social sciences, and their ideas continue to be debated today.

This is the solidarity of the crowd, the solidarity of the like-minded, which is always weakened by the presence of an anomaly. If Durkheim had analyzed his era, he would simply have been another member of the crowd of crowd theorists. But he dug much deeper, searching for an explanation of how societies progresses along a continuum from fleeting, amorphous crowd to structured society. There is, Durkheim suggested, another type of solidarity, which he called organic, because it “resembles that observed in the higher animals. In fact each organ has its own special characteristics and autonomy, yet the greater the unity of the organism the more marked the individuation of the parts.” (Durkheim 1897, p. 85).

Organic solidarity derives from the division of labor. Aggregates whose members depend on each other to perform different essential tasks are tied together by qualitatively different bonds than aggregates whose members are connected merely by similarity. Clearly, division of labor exists in human society, as it does among different cell types in multicellular organisms. Durkheim’s argument for how division of labor in society parallels modes of cellular differentiation and, as we shall see in later chapters, of the origin of multiple levels of selection in evolution. 

Durkheim begins his argument by sketching the development of modular, or segmentary, structures in human societies such as families and clans. These societies are formed from the replication of aggregates that are like one another, analogous to the rings of some social worms (“Durkheim 1967, p. 127”). Each group might take over a certain role in society, such as herding a particular species of cattle, or performing religious or ceremonial functions. At this point, one type of structure (social role) has been superimposed upon another (social aggregate). All that remains is for the increasing specialization to overflow the boundaries of the original social aggregate and erode the original structure. “Generally it may be said,” Durkheim wrote, “that classes and castes have probably no other origin or nature they spring from the mixing of the professional organization, which is just emerging, with a pre-existing familial organization.” (Durkheim 1897, p. 133). But it is not just mixing; the new structure climbs out of the old one and sits in “Explicitly commenting that ‘the same law governs biological development,’” Durkheim wrote. “Organic as in social evolution, the division of labor is not using the framework of something already done, but slowly and certainly its tread in an autonomous way” (Durkheim 1937, pp. 141-14). He emphasized that this development happens within a centralized control region. The prime movers, Durkheim said, are not feedback loops in the nervous system or the pursuit of social status among individuals, but the pressure from competition. “The progressive photophobia,” he continued, “is due to the continually growing division of labor, which, by necessitating the ever-increasing diversity of the tasks to be done, forces each individual to apply himself to a single function, and thus to develop all his energy in a single direction.” (Durkheim 1897, p. 153).

> **Figure:** A black and white portrait of Émile Durkheim. He is an older man with a neatly trimmed beard and mustache, wearing a suit and tie. The portrait is a head and shoulders shot, with a neutral background. Below the portrait is the text "Fig. 1.3 Émile Durkheim. Public domain".

Durkheim’s conception of organic solidarity is not merely descriptive; it is also normative. Durkheim was deeply concerned about the potential for anomie—a condition of normlessness—to arise in modern societies. The division of labor, while potentially a source of social cohesion, could also lead to a sense of alienation and meaninglessness if it was not properly regulated. Durkheim argued that the state had a crucial role to play in regulating the division of labor and ensuring that it served the common good. “Society cannot be simply a sum of individuals,” he wrote. “It is something more than the sum of its parts.” (Durkheim 1897, p. 306).

|                      | **Mechanical Solidarity** | **Organic Solidarity** |
|----------------------|---------------------------|------------------------|
| **Basis of Cohesion** | Similarity                | Interdependence        |
| **Division of Labor**| Low                       | High                   |
| **Individualism**    | Weak                      | Strong                 |
| **Social Regulation**| Strong                    | Moderate               |
| **Type of Law**      | Repressive                | Restitutive            |

***

Durkheim’s work has had a profound impact on the development of sociology and other social sciences. His concept of anomie, for example, has been used to understand a wide range of social problems, from crime and suicide to political instability and economic inequality. His work also continues to be relevant to contemporary debates about the nature of social order, the role of the state, and the challenges of modernity.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

The development of differentiation from a simple aggregate is indeed a well-worn evolutionary pathway which we will encounter later in these pages, for example, in our exploration of the evolution of the volleying nerve in Chap. 11. 
Once established, the division of labour unites at the same time as it sets at odds, it causes the activities that it differentiates to converge it brings closer those that it separates” (Durkheim 1997, p. 217, *my italics*) This is our first glimpse of the essential tension, that delicate balance between things at once drawn together and pulled apart – a structure that endlessly mirrors itself from the ideas of one century to those of another, and from one field of science to another.

Durkheim has been critiqued for a rather selective reading of Darwin’s work. Sociologist William Cotton (1998, 2002) suggested that Durkheim’s assumption that mutualism develops in order to minimize competition is unrealistic in many biological contexts. First, the assumption is roughly equivalent to sympathetic speciation (the divergence of co-localized populations), which occurs far less frequently in nature than allopatric speciation (the divergence of populations already separated by some environmental barrier). Second, there is the issue of causality. Darwin himself, Cotton argued, never presented population divergence as a means of abating competition. Rather, enhanced competition led to divergence of populations and extinction of intermediate forms. This does not negate Durkheim’s argument; it is easy to envision a scenario in which someone who works with tin and iron is outcompeted by specialists in each individual metal. Clearly, also, causal factors in sociological evolution are not identical to those at work in the process of speciation. Nonetheless, Cotton’s critique points to an important issue. Many biological mutualisms, he pointed out, originate in exploitative relationships from which the participants are unable to separate. Here, the ultimate cooperative benefit may be a side-consequence rather than a direct adaptation. Stephen Jay Gould and Elisabeth Vrba called such unintended side-consequences exaptations. As Gould noted, Cotton explicitly referred to this concept in one of his analyses of Durkheim (Gould 2002, p. 1239). “An adaptation has a function,” Cotton wrote, “An explanation has an effect. Once that effect becomes important in the life of an organic type [in this new environment], natural selection may ‘improve’ the exaptation, making it an adaptation, and converting the effect into a true function.” (Cotton 1998) It is likely that many aspects of the division of labor may have arisen as unintended consequences of an initial population divergence, and only later had the added benefit of abating competition, a function for which they were not originally selected. We will revisit the idea of exaptations in later chapters, and we will find that they are a recurring theme in the interaction and balance between the levels at which natural selection operates.

Tarde’s investigations were not limited to crowds, but to all of society; he suggested that there is a continuum from a loosely affiliated crowd to what he called a “corporation,” a well-defined, durable, organized social structure. The crowd-corporation transition has an important structural resonance with another idea we will explore later: the transition from MLSI to MLST selection.

Herbert Spencer had proposed that the simple spread of human population led to specialization of social roles according to the local environment in which people lived—those who live near the sea make their living as fishermen, etc. (This process can be compared to niche specialization in evolution.) Durkheim argued that this certainly occurs, but not to a sufficient extent to explain the degree of actual division of labor present in human society.

# 2. Classification

Sonya Bahar

(1) Department of Physics & Astronomy and Center for Neurodynamics, University of Missouri at St. Louis, MO, USA

IN THE previous chapter, we explored the problem of how one thing emerges from many. A related intellectual problem, how a multitude of things can be grouped into one, has preoccupied scholars for many centuries. This is the problem of classification. Historically, arguments over classification did not explicitly contain the dynamical axis of differentiation/convergence that we have seen in the work of Durkheim. The tension between differentiation and convergence in biological classification arose only later, in the context of actual evolutionary theory, as we will see in the following chapter. For now, let us explore the conundrum of classification as it occurred before the late eighteenth century, in two interlocking problems: how to categorize, and how to draw boundaries. The problem addressed by the crowd theorists was a bottom-up problem: how individuals form a group. In contrast, classification of animals and plants was the decidedly top-down problem of *how* (and if even) one should draw boundaries. Crowd theory contained the seeds of the essential tension in the question of how groups are stabilized by counter-balance forces operating at different levels. In the top-down problem of classification, it is hard to find any hint of a balance between push and pull – things being drawn into a group and yet held separate by orthogonal forces.

Instead, we find only a sharp *slice* sticking from above or the Great Chain of Being. The history of the Great Chain of Being is masterfully traced in A. O. Lovejoy’s groundbreaking 1936 book of the same name; Lovejoy’s work virtually inaugurated the study of the history of ideas. The Chain of Being is, in essence, a picture of the world, conceived as a hierarchy extending up toward the “divine”. Lovejoy located the origin of the Great Chain in the creation myth in Plato’s *Timaeus*. Here, the world of imperfect beings is formed from a deity’s immanence; the overflow of a “best soul” defined by the attributes of goodness and self-sufficiency. Executing what Lovejoy kindly terms a “biological logician”, Plato stated that whatever is good must diffuse itself and form its effluvium *su*, in the Medieval Latin formulation used by Thomas Aquinas and the scholastic philosophers who followed him. 

As this good overflowed, creating a host of imperfect copies, how many imperfect things? Aquinas, in the *Summa Contra Gentiles*, posited that the number should be as great as possible to carry that divine idea and that the world, therefore, contained 9,550,500,000 angels. Lovejoy’s point is not the numerical extravagance, but rather the principle of *pleroma* – the conviction that the universe must be as full as possible. The Chain of Being, therefore, is a plenitude principle, a cosmic taxonomy, a hierarchical arrangement of all existing things, each linked to the next in a continuous, unbroken series. The Chain’s structure is fundamentally *discontinuous*; each link is unique and irreplaceable, and yet the Chain is also continuous, because each being participates in the being of those above and below it. Lovejoy (1936, p. 54) notes that the Chain is not simply a static ladder, but a dynamic system, a “vast complex of reciprocal relations”. 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the Great Chain of Being. The diagram is a vertical hierarchy, with God at the very top, followed by angels, then humans, animals, plants, and finally minerals at the bottom. Each level is represented by a horizontal line, and arrows indicate the flow of influence and participation between levels. The diagram emphasizes the idea of a continuous, unbroken series of beings, each linked to the next. The text "Plato's Timaeus" is noted near the top, indicating the origin of the concept. The diagram is labeled with the title "The Great Chain of Being" and includes a citation to Lovejoy's 1936 work.

# Fig. 2.1 The Great Chain of Being, from a 1579 work by Diego de Valades. Public domain

Simply extrapolated to the realm of natural history, the idea of a continuous chain of separation could lead to the conclusion that separate species did not, indeed could not, exist in either inherent or in practicality, and that, therefore, classification was an entombed dream from the start. Thus Buffon, who strongly opposed Linnean classification, wrote in his *Histoire Naturelle* (1749) that 

“[b]efore will be found a great number of intermediate species and objects belonging half in one class and half in another. Objects of this sort, to which it is impossible to assign a place, necessarily render it vain to attempt to find a universal system. In general, the more one increases the number of one’s divisions in the case of the products of nature, the nearer one comes to the truth; since in reality individuals exist in Nature, [quoted by Lovejoy 1964, p. 229; Wilkins 2009, p. 75]

Others echoed the same sentiment, but allowed that the establishment of a tentative system of classification was nonetheless of practical use for the naturalist (and for the physician, looking to distinguish herbal cures from poisons). Bonnet wrote in his *Contemplation de la Nature* (1764) that “[t]here are no clearages in Nature; it is evident that our classifications are not hers. Those which we form are purely nominal, and we should regard them as means relative to our needs and to the limitation of our knowledge” (Lovejoy 1964, p. 231; Wilkins 2009, p. 84).

The application of the laws of classification and plenitude to nature in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries had an immediate positive result: it spurred observational research, as naturalists strove to “fill in the gaps”. But those laws also posed two clear philosophical problems. The first arose from simple observations of the world. Some data actually did suggest a lack of continuity, and sharp, uncrossable boundaries between species. Indeed, influenced by such observations, Buffon ultimately contradicted his earlier assertion that “individuals alone exist in Nature”. Convinced by the sterility of hybrid species, he reversed himself totally, claiming in his later writings that “les espèces sont les seuls êtres de la Nature” and that “an individual, of whatever species, is nothing in the universe” (Lovejoy 1964, p. 230). The second problem arose from a drive that is perhaps as much aesthetic and psychological as it is scientific: the need to order and classify. 

An example from recent biological studies serves to highlight the immense conceptual difficulty of defining an individual. One of the most dramatic examples of the porous definitional boundary between group and individual is provided by *Populus tremuloides*, the quaking aspen (Fig. 2.2). The aspen brings home the complexity of defining an individual. How of knowledge that individual’s history may be a substitute for identity. The quaking aspen, found across the northern and western United States and Canada, grows in genetically identical “clones” extending underground, consisting of a single root system that may be easily a thousand meters in diameter, sending up numerous discrete trunks. In 1976 a Utah State University geneticist, Jerry B. Adams, realized that the apparently discrete aspen clone he was studying was, in fact, a single tree. The clone, nicknamed “Pando” (Latin for “I spread”), covers 43 hectares and is estimated to weigh 6,000 tonnes. It is therefore considered to be the heaviest known living organism on Earth.

> **Figure:** A photograph depicting a forest of quaking aspen trees (*Populus tremuloides*). The trees are tall and slender with smooth, pale bark. The forest floor is covered in fallen leaves. The image is labeled "Fig. 2.2 Pando, a single quaking aspen clone in Utah, is one of the heaviest known living organisms on Earth." The image illustrates the concept of a clonal colony where multiple trees are genetically identical and connected by a single root system, challenging the traditional definition of an individual organism.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

Fig. 2.2 A forest of a single tree: Pando, a quaking aspen clone, in autumn. Photograph by J. Zapell. http://www.usda.gov/photogallery/flash/home/gallery?id=38216position=Promo, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pando_autumn.jpg

Sustained by a massive underground root system, aspen clones are able to repopulate a forest after most other species, such as conifers, have been decimated by fire, avalanche, or mudslide. As Milton and Grant (1996) explain, “*Ephemeral root systems allow aspen to colonize, occupy, and even prefer disturbed sites, justifying their general characterization as a successional species.*” After a fire has removed the conifers, the ramets that sprout from a healthy, mature root system may grow vertically by as much as a single summer season. The root system of aspen grows so aggressively that adjacent stems can be spaced more than 30 m apart.

The dominance of a clonal aspen grow within an ecosystem is temporary. As other species grow back into a fire-devastated area, competitor impacts may eventually overtake the aspen clone. Nonetheless, giant aspen forests formed from single clones do persist. The most dramatic of these is a male clone consisting of nearly 50,000 trunks, dubbed “Pando” (from the Latin, *I spread*) by Grant and colleagues. Growing near Utah’s Wasatch Mountain Range, Pando—including its root system—is estimated to weigh six million kilograms, making it the most massive known living organism. Its age is difficult to determine, but an upper limit of a million years has been suggested. 

Disconcertingly, aspen clones do need for rejuvenation by fire has set Pando’s survival at odds with modern society’s desire to prevent forest fires. As Grant (1993) explains, 

> **Figure:** A photograph of a dense forest of tall, slender trees with golden autumn foliage. The trees are closely packed together, creating a sense of vastness and uniformity. The ground is covered in fallen leaves. The lighting suggests it is late afternoon or early evening. The image is intended to visually represent the Pando aspen clone, highlighting its scale and density.

The quaking aspen gained its name because of the way the tree’s leaves tremble in even the slightest breeze. French Canadian woodsmen in the 1600s believed that the trees quaked in fear because the cross Jesus was made of was crafted from aspen. Now giant aspen clones like Pando have a new reason to tremble: human incursions. Several private homes have been recently built within one section of Pando, and another section has been turned into a campground, complete with parking spaces, picnic tables, and paved roads. Driveways, roads, and power lines built in these developments dissect this spectacularly beautiful aspen stand. The presence of people has led the U.S. Forest Service to suppress wildfires, and yet Pando’s remarkable size and longevity are largely a consequence of the cleansable, rejuvenating power of wildfires. Ironically, ending wildfires could well mean the end of Pando.

Different aspen clones growing in proximity to one another may be distinguishable simply by the physical characteristics. The tree branches make a width determined by the genotype, but the trees exhibit a range of responses to the full range of environmental conditions—determined through the phenotype. In a 1995 study, Grant and colleagues found that the trees in a clone did not respond to conditions as uniformly as the trees in other clones. This suggests that the genetic diversity within Pando is greater than that of many other clones, and Pando may therefore be more resilient to environmental changes. However, the suppression of fire and the fragmentation of Pando’s habitat are already taking their toll. 

The trees at the edges of Pando’s clone are dying, and the clone is not regenerating in those areas. Grant and his colleagues have determined that the number of young aspen stems has declined by 90 percent since the 1950s. Deer and elk browse on the young stems, preventing them from maturing into trees. The suppression of fire has allowed the growth of conifers, which also compete with aspen for resources. Grant (2000) notes that the combination of these factors could lead to the demise of Pando within the next century. 

The story of Pando is a cautionary tale about the unintended consequences of human actions. We often think of forests as collections of individual trees, but in reality, many forests are composed of clones—genetically identical individuals connected by a shared root system. These clonal forests are particularly vulnerable to human disturbances, such as fire suppression and habitat fragmentation. The loss of a clonal forest is not simply the loss of a collection of trees; it is the loss of a unique genetic individual.

> **Figure:** A graph depicting the decline in the number of young aspen stems in Pando over time. The x-axis represents the year, ranging from 1950 to 2010. The y-axis represents the number of young stems per acre. The graph shows a steep decline in the number of stems, from approximately 100 stems per acre in 1950 to less than 10 stems per acre in 2010. The trendline is downward sloping, indicating a continued decline. The graph illustrates the impact of fire suppression, browsing by deer and elk, and competition from conifers on the regeneration of Pando.

The concept of the “*individual*” is central to our understanding of life, but it is not always clear where to draw the line between one individual and another. In the case of clonal organisms, such as aspen trees, the boundary between individuals is blurred. A single aspen clone can span many acres and contain thousands of trees, all genetically identical. This raises the question: is a clonal aspen forest a single individual, or a collection of individuals? 

The answer to this question has important implications for our understanding of ecology and conservation. If we consider a clonal aspen forest to be a single individual, then its loss would be akin to the extinction of a species. This would underscore the importance of protecting these unique ecosystems. However, if we consider a clonal aspen forest to be a collection of individuals, then its loss would be less dramatic. This would suggest that the forest could be restored by planting new aspen trees.

Some natural philosophers however, retained between conceptual schemes. Charles Bonnet, for example, represented nature in a classic ladder scheme in his *Traité d’insectologie* (1745). He also, however, portrayed nature as branches emanating from a central trunk in a later work, *Contemplation de la Nature* (Foucault 1994, p. 145). Jussieu described the affinities among plants as analogous to those between neighboring regions on a map; he juxtaposed that metaphor, however, with the image of an unbroken chain (Wilkinson 2009, p. 82). Other scholars consider to bear structural shapes as well around 1750. Donati proposed a network model in which every being was “a knot in the web of nature and its resemblance to other forms may be compared to the threads between the knots” (Wilkins 2009, p. 83). Robinet and Hermann (1738) likewise suggested a three-dimensional lattice model with species situated at the nodes. MacLeay (1809) and Swainson (1834) suggested a model of ‘oscillating circles’ in which different groups of species were laid out on adjoining circles. Oken and Kaup suggested pentagram-like models (Wilkins 2009, p. 84) as did Paliss (Foucault 1994, p. 149).

The introduction of models more complex than a simple chain, however, left the problem of continuity unresolved. However, this branching structure described relations of structure, but not of history; there was no common descent in Lamarck’s table, though his model did contain a temporal element in that branches continually arise by spontaneous generation, and then evolved according to a sort of sangeneis. A branching structure did not negate nomination any more than did, Lamarck’s, continuity, who had studied with Buffon, “that ‘all classifications are arbitrary products of thought, and that in nature there are only individuals’ (Wilkins 2009, p. 107). Story, ultimately, resists the insistence that there was ever a new vision in Linnaean taxonomy. Linnaeus’s system, too, despite its success, did not reform natural philosophy as such. Instead, it codified a different set of principles of representation. The possibility of a holistic rather than an arbitrary nature that he proposed did not unlock a new way of seeing nature, but instead suggested the usefulness of a new nomenclature. Linnaeus’s system, however, was not without its problems, for as he himself recognized, it did not capture the full range of natural relations. 

The work of Jussieu and his contemporaries, however, did suggest a different kind of natural philosophy. For example, Jussieu’s system, as represented in his *Genera Plantarum* (1789), was not simply a system of nomenclature, but a representation of relations, and, as such, it had implications for understanding the nature of species and the history of life. Jussieu’s system, however, was not without its own problems, for it was based on a limited number of characters, and it did not account for the full range of variation within species. Nevertheless, Jussieu’s work did represent a significant step towards a more holistic and relational understanding of nature.

The work of Lamarck, in particular, represented a radical departure from the traditional view of nature. Lamarck’s theory of evolution, which proposed that species change over time in response to their environment, was a direct challenge to the idea of the fixity of species. Lamarck’s theory, however, was not widely accepted during his lifetime, and it was not until the publication of Darwin’s *On the Origin of Species* in 1859 that the theory of evolution became widely accepted.

With nature prided loose from the single axis of the great chain of being, natural historians could now experiment with different means of juxtaposing the beings that make up the world, trying this means, and then that, to obtain a structure that most parsimoniously mirrored that nature itself [Fig. 2.4]. To organize this new structure, to place individuals into species, adjacent to one another, naturalists followed one of two possible procedures: the “system”, or the “method”. In the system, a naturalist would essentially choose a set of basis vectors, as Linnaeus described above, and enumerate the degree of characteristics in each organism or species under investigation. The problem here, of course, is that the choice of basic vectors is arbitrary, and some characteristics that were important in the description of one species might not be of consequence in the other, of course, one could simply maintain “zeroes” to the characteristics along these “axes” in such a case, but the point was to find a limited set of characteristics, and from this perspective a large number of degenerate cases would hardly be helpful. Instead, an alternative approach was proposed: the “method”. Here,

(deduction is to be taken… in the sense of subtraction. One begins, as Adanson did in his examination of the plants of Senegal, with a species either arbitrarily chosen or encountered by chance. One describes it as the description should be as total as in the first instance, but with the one difference that nothing that has been mentioned of the first description should be repeated in the second. Only the differences are listed. And similarly with the third species in relation to the first two, and so on, indefinitely. So that, at the very end, all the different features of the plants have been listed once, but never more than once. Thus everything is described by its relationship to other things. While the method, defining from a comparison of identities and differences “is uniquely “capable of being utilized over vertical classifications, both method and system are some free ways of defining the family of forms.” Further, the comparison of a species to its near will allow for the discovery of its limits. Foucault makes the point that Linnaeus’s system was in reality a kind of method, in the sense that each species was defined in relation to the *genus* to which it belonged. However, it was a method that was made to appear as a system, by the presentation of a table, the *species plantarum*, in which the characteristics of each species were listed independently, adjacent to one another, and so presented as if they were the characteristics of the species itself, rather than the differences between it and other species.

# 3. Time, Just Time: Integrating Up the Great Chain of Being

Sonya Bahar

Department of Physics & Astronomy and Center for Neurodynamics, University of Missouri-St Louis, MO, USA

HOW LOCAL interactions between individuals in a human crowd or in a bee’s nest give rise to any functioning as a single entity – how strong these interactions need to be, whether they are disbursed from a single leader or among equal individuals, whether there is a minimum number of individual organisms needed for the formation of the group – remained unclear, even after the pioneering work of Durkheim. But the problem of collective behavior at least had the advantage of possessing an undoubtedly underlying mechanism: interaction between individuals within the group. The problem of classification, however, was stymied on that front. Scholars attempting to group organisms into species had no mechanism by which to organize their classificatory schemes. It is true that classification schemes based on common descent were proposed by Ray and others. But in most cases, common descent was nearly impossible to trace, and all natural historians could do in order to classify plants, for example, was to collect them and order them according to some parsing of their taxonomic properties. The key to classification did ultimately lie in common descent, but applying this concept to the classification of biological species was not potentiated until the discovery of deep geological time and the Darwinian revolution which followed.

***

> **Figure 3.4:** A depiction of Cuvier’s adaptation of species to their particular “conditions of existence,” presented as a diagram with various animal forms arranged along a spectrum.

Georges Cuvier (1769–1832) and Étienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire (1772–1844) were central figures in European natural philosophy (Figs. 3.1 and 3.2). Widely influential in their own day, their work has been subsequently exploited to promote *intertextual* agendas. Their legendary debates held at the Académie des Sciences in Paris (in 1830, while a revolution was about to explode on the streets outside), resulted in a post *hoc* recrudescence of Cuvier, whose ideas were interpreted as an early form of “adaptationism,” and thus sometimes misread as a direct precursor to Darwinian selection (Figs. 3.3 and 3.4). Cuvier’s idea of the adaptation of species to their particular “conditions of existence,” however, preceded any idea of evolution; he held that new organisms arose from a direct impact of catastrophic geological events.

# Cuvier and Geoffroy approached the same problem – the use of the structure of living organisms as a means of classification – from fundamentally divergent perspectives. Both men were driven by the desire to find a more “natural” classification for plants and animals than the Linnaean system (Appel 1987, p. 12). But they took radically different approaches. Geoffroy was attracted to the idea of inherent form and structure in nature in 1795 that “[i]t seems that nature has enclosed herself within certain limits, and has formed only living beings on one only unique plan…” All the most essential differences which affect each family within the same class come only from another arrangement, in short from a modification of these same organs” (Appel 1987, p. 28). Both Cuvier’s catastrophism and Geoffroy’s emphasis on form rather than function were to be revisited by modern evolutionary theory. In contrast to Geoffroy’s emphasis on form and structure, Cuvier held such strong, sweeping interpretations in great suspicion; he came from a more conservative political background, and his belief that ideas were at the root of the Revolution led him to fear the consequences of unbridled generalizations in the sciences, as well as in political and social thought” (Appel 1987, p. 30). Nevertheless, influenced by Jussieu and other colleagues, Cuvier did come to believe that a “natural” taxonomic classification of the entire living world could be achieved. He proposed grouping creatures based on their functional systems rather than their similarities of form. What, he asked, is important for any animal? The internal systems that allow for generation, respiration, circulation, and other functions? 

In Foucault’s interpretation, Cuvier’s focus on the functional needs of each animal in navigating its environment was in itself a radical shift of perspective. It was the first time, Foucault contended, that organisms were truly viewed as wholes until they appeared in the first time in centuries that the axis of classification had passed through living beings. Before Cuvier, “the plant, animal [and] mineral [were] so much in their organicity as they were that animal of their organs. They are paws and hooks, claws and teeth, being the binary respiratory system as an analogy for biological nature. Natural history proceeded as the ‘idea’ of a composite, transitory relationship, which then created an subordination or organization” (Foucault 1994, p. 13). Foucault’s view is that Cuvier’s emphasis on function – the way an organism *did* things – was a key moment in the shift from an Aristotelian to a modern, mechanistic understanding of life. Cuvier, according to Foucault, saw the animal as a set of interconnected functions, rather than as an ideal type to which individual specimens should conform. “The animal, therefore, is defined by its functions, and the species by the ensemble of its functions” (Foucault 1994, p. 14). 

> **Figure 3.4:** Title page of a 1799 article by “Citizen Cuvier: From the Biodiversity Heritage Library [www.biodiversityheritage.org], reproduced under CC-BY-NC 3.0 license. The image shows the title page of a scientific paper. The title is "Extrait d'un article de Citizen Cuvier: Sur le Développment des Théories Zoologiques, et sur la Nature des Classes." Below the title is "Présenté à la Convention Nationale, le 18 brumaire, an VIII." (Presented to the National Convention, 18 Brumaire, Year VIII). The paper is signed "Cuvier, Secrétaire Perpétuel de la Classe des Mammifères." (Cuvier, Perpetual Secretary of the Class of Mammals). The page is aged and has a watermark.

Cuvier’s idea of geological catastrophes formed one conceptual axis of the catastrophism/uniformitarianism dichotomy. Along these axes, Cuvier was interpreted (primarily by Charles Lyell, whose first volume of the *Principles of Geology* appeared in the same year as the Cuvier-Geoffroy debate) as highly unscientific, in contrast to Lyell’s own uniformitarianism, which allowed only currently-observable forces as possible agents of change and in nature.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

between various species of vertebrates (Appel 1987, p. 55). The evolutionary implications of this appealed to Cuvier. Moreover, in allowing the idea that “a trait [a bone changed its function as it passed from one class of animals] to another… an abstract element of organization which could serve multiple functions as it was applied in different circumstances” (Appel 1987, p. 87), Geoffroy opened the door to historical contingency in the development of animal forms. This view is fundamentally history-based in a way that Cuvier’s was not; one can easily see Geoffroy’s appeal for later scientists like Stephen Jay Gould, who placed a high value on the contingencies of history and the co-opting of “*Spandrel*” structures for different uses over evolutionary timescales, a topic we will explore in much more depth in later chapters. In practice, Geoffroy focused not only on bone-for-bone homologies, but also on the connections between bones. He was essentially mapping topology, the juxtaposition of structures.

The clash between Cuvier and Geoffroy that erupted in 1830 had been brewing for years. A decade before, Geoffroy had suggested that the common plan he had identified in vertebrate structures could be applied to insects as well. This threatened the boundaries between Cuvier’s embranchments, implied “in 1820 paper ‘On Insects Reduced to the Embranchments of Vertebrates’,” Geoffroy mapped the insect exoskeleton piece by piece onto the vertebrate skeleton, going so far as to suggest that insect appendages were homologous to vertebrate ribs. The two scientists had developed clusters of younger followers, and fought over them, with Cuvier often winning out due to his greater access to academic patronage. After years of sparring, both intellectually and via professional politics, in 1828 Cuvier published a direct attack on one of the specific structural homologies proposed by Geoffroy: the homology between the operculum in fishes and the mammalian middle ear. Two years later, things finally came to a head when two young naturalists, Pierre-Stanislas Meyran and a colleague of his named Laurent de Serres attempted to join the molluscan and the cephalopods texts that Geoffroy “was not a transition to anatomies” (Appel 1987, p. 146). Cuvier rose and objected. Meyran later wrote to Cuvier to apologize. 

When the *Académie des sciences* met, Cuvier tore Meyran’s and de Serres’s manuscript into pieces, and Geoffroy was reduced to tears of knowledge. On March 1, Geoffroy responded with his rebuttal, but, when pressed by Cuvier, that day, if “Appel 1987, p. 150,” he faltered. The day after, to prop up his floundering case in the face of Cuvier’s assault, Geoffroy turned to a point that he had been consistently making: the commonness of the arch in vertebrate skulls. Cuvier did not dispute this, but dismissed it as a simple case of a common structural element—an arch—appearing in different groups for the same reasons. Appel 1987, p. 147. The duel had a winner, though the terms were unclear. Geoffroy was politically defeated. He largely withdrew from public scientific life. Though he continued to teach and to direct the *muséum*, he no longer played a central role in the major scientific debates of the day. 

> **Figure:** A depiction of the clash between Cuvier and Geoffroy. The image shows two portraits, one of Georges Cuvier and one of Étienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, facing each other. Between them is a torn manuscript, symbolizing the conflict. The background is a library setting, with books and scientific instruments. The overall tone is dramatic and suggests a heated debate. The portraits are rendered in a classical style, emphasizing the importance and stature of the two scientists. The torn manuscript is a focal point, highlighting the central issue of their disagreement.




The immediate aftermath of the Cuvier-Geoffroy clash saw a consolidation of Cuvier’s position and a retreat by Geoffroy. But the long-term consequences were more complex. As we will see in the next chapter, the very fact of the debate—and the way in which it was framed—helped to set the stage for the later development of evolutionary theory. The debate also had a significant impact on the development of comparative anatomy as a scientific discipline. Cuvier’s emphasis on the functional significance of structures and his use of comparative anatomy to establish homologies helped to lay the groundwork for later work in this area. Geoffroy’s emphasis on the underlying unity of animal form and his search for archetypes also had a lasting influence, particularly on the work of later evolutionary biologists.

> **Figure 8.5** *Richard Owen’s 1847 conception of an archetypal vertebrate structure. Public domain*
> This is a detailed illustration of an archetypal vertebrate structure, resembling a fish skeleton. It is labeled with various anatomical terms. The spine is prominently displayed, with labels pointing to the neural spine, neurapophyses, diapophyses, centrum, parapophyses, hæmapophyses, hæmal spine, and appendage. The illustration is a black and white line drawing, intended to demonstrate Owen’s concept of a fundamental vertebrate body plan.

During his debates with Geoffrey Cuvier, Richard Owen had asked what “necessity would have constrained [nature] to employ only the same pieces, and employ them always?” The answer to this question, nothing less than history itself. In proposing this answer to Cuvier’s question, Darwin laid bare the mechanism by which organisms could be grouped into species, and by which those species could be grouped in relation to one another. Of course, Darwin also proposed another mechanism, natural selection, by which species evolve from one another. This balance between selection endlessly drawing lineages apart, while history binds them together, is another instance of the essential tension that is the subject of the present book. We have seen already how Durkheim used a similar balance of opposing forces to explain the origin of the division of labor. Darwin described the balancing principles at the core of his own great theory as “great laws,” writing that “it is generally acknowledged that all organic beings have been formed on two great laws – Unity of Type, and the Conditions of Existence… On my theory, Unity of Type is explained by unity of descent. The expression of conditions of existence, so often insisted upon by the illustrious Cuvier, is fully embraced by the principle of natural selection” (Darwin, *Origin of Species*, pp. 26–252).

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

Have been inconcievable without the substrate of deep time over which natural selection could act. We must now turn to the *discovery of “deep time,”* which took the great chain of being and rotated it sideways until, instead of reaching up to heaven, it lay stretched across the earth. 

As powerfully recounted by various historians of science, not least by Stephen Jay Gould in his masterful *Time’s Arrow, Time’s Cycle*, the discovery of the age of the Earth was deeply entwined with a growing understanding that the Earth, its structure, and the life it contains have not just an age, but a *history*; that the planet is not a static picture, but an unfolding story. Thus the discovery of the Earth’s age was crucial for the development of evolutionary theory on multiple fronts; it provided a field of time across which natural selection would work, and it strengthened a metaphorical picture of life as something unfolding, and therefore capable of change and development. 

Early scholars of geology focused on the mechanism by which change arose in the structure of the planet. Thomas Burnet developed a theory of the Earth’s history that attempted to explain biblical processes using currently observable geological processes. Burnet was influenced by the contemporary Newtonian idea that the laws of nature must obtain on Earth, among the planets, and throughout the universe. He expressed this view in terms which presage the uniformitarian theory of Charles Lyell, in the following discussion of why natural causes for geological events should be more impressive than “miraculous” causes imposed from above. “If one should continue ‘til time expires,’ ‘a piece of clock-work should be all that should be at all hours, and make all its motions regularly for such a time, and time being come, upon a signal given, or a spring touched, it should all of a sound on fall all to pieces,’ would not ‘a look’d upon as a piece of greater art, than if the workman came at that time proposed, and with a great hammer beat it into pieces?” (Gould 1987, pp. 29–30). 

Burnet explored theoretical models for the forces changing the Earth’s structure during hypothesized periods of conflagration and cooling, postulated a universal flood, and used sounding to calculate the total volume of water in the oceans. He argued with Newton over the origin of the current structure of the Earth’s surface, contending that its unevenness was a result of the great flood, while Newton held that the Earth’s landscape could simply have arisen as the Earth cooled following its formation from an initial chaos; Newton pointed out that even uniform liquids can form irregular solids by those means (Westfall 1980, p. 391). Assuming inaction of ordering forces, both Newton and Burnet considered the Earth’s earliest progressiveness as a sign of the first day of creation (1987, p. 43ff). This contrasts with the theory of “catastrophism,” a theme of the Earth’s history advocated by Georges Cuvier, and later championed by proponents of intelligent design. As we shall see, Cuvier recognized the existence of extinct life forms, and postulated successive creations, each terminated by a worldwide deluge. Burnet’s approach, analyzed as the expression of a pre-Darwinian version of uniformitarianism, has been interpreted as an attempt to reconcile Newtonian physics with the biblical account of creation (Rudwick 1977, pp. 166–68).

> **Figure:** A depiction of Thomas Burnet’s “The Theory of the Earth” (1738). The image shows a cross-section of the Earth, with layers representing the original, perfect state, followed by the effects of the Flood, and finally the present, ruined state. The layers are labeled with terms like “Primeval Earth,” “Universal Deluge,” and “Present Surface.” The illustration is detailed, showing mountains, valleys, and bodies of water within the Earth’s structure. The overall impression is of a decaying and fractured Earth, contrasting with the initial perfection.

But the Newtonian physics of the eighteenth century also provided the conceptual tools for determining the Earth’s age. In 1744, Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, published his *Histoire Naturelle*, in which he attempted to calculate the age of the Earth based on the rate at which it had cooled from a molten state. Buffon’s calculation, though flawed, suggested that the Earth was at least 70,000 years old—a figure that shocked his contemporaries, who generally believed in a much younger Earth, based on biblical chronology. Buffon’s work was controversial, and he was later forced to retract some of his claims, but his attempt to apply scientific principles to the question of the Earth’s age was a significant step forward.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

Fig. 3.6 An unconformity identified by James Hutton near Edinburgh, shown in a 1787 engraving by John Clerk. Public domain.

Charles Lyell began his great *Principles of Geology* (1830) with a historical sketch of the progress of the field. As Gould carefully dissects in *Time’s Arrow, Time’s Cycle*, Lyell presented Hutton’s ideas according to his own interpretation, and in many respects the textbook “Hutton” is really Lyell’s version of Hutton. Using Hutton’s discovery of “deep time,” Lyell (Fig. 3.7) developed not only an interpretation of the Earth’s geological history, but also a related methodological approach to the subject. He advocated uniformitarianism,<sup>6</sup> according to which current geological observations can be ascribed to processes now acting and observable on Earth. Note the conceptual link between this idea and those of Newton discussed above; with Lyell, however, these principles applied to a world existing (and undergoing cycles of decay, deposition and uplift) in a limitless span of time. 

> **Figure:** A black and white engraving depicting a rocky landscape. The landscape shows layers of rock tilted at an angle, with a clear boundary between the tilted layers and more horizontal layers above. # Chapter XIII (1797-1875)

Lyell associated undulating and unscientific theories of a “Young Earth” with hypotheses of geological change driven by large, catastrophic events unlike anything we observe in daily life. With an ancient Earth, there is no need for catastrophes, he argued. Crucially, Lyell identified the scientific approach of rational empiricism with the hypothesis that catastrophic events could never take place. He mocked Cuvier for his catastrophism [10] and presented uniformitarianism as an empirical fruit of the Enlightenment, writing that catastrophes 

felt themselves at liberty to imagine their inductions, guessing at what might be, rather than inquiring what is… [preferring to] speculate on the possibilities of the past, [rather than] patiently to explore the realities of the present… There was never a dogma more calculated to foster indolence, and to blunt the keen edge of curiosity, than this assumption of the discordance between the former and the existing causes of change. (quoted by Gould 1987, p. 111)

Lyell thus accused his intellectual opponents of a “desire… to cut, rather than patiently to untie, the Gordian knot.” (It would bear noting here that Lyell seems to be missing the whole point of the Gordian knot story… ).

Lyell made use of four distinct meanings of uniformity in his work, and blurred the lines between them [1]. Two of these meanings, however, relate to methodological techniques of doing science, and two relate to substantive claims about the world. First, Lyell began with the assumption of uniformity of law, as did Burnet, Newton and many others. The assumption that nature follows the same laws at different locations in time and space is essential in order to apply inductive reasoning at all. Also Lyell assumed uniformity of process: the idea that past phenomena are explicable using currently observable processes. (This could be interpreted simply as an application of the uniformity of law along the axis of time). These were Lyell’s two methodological claims. He followed them with two substantive claims, which he made essentially inviolable by conflation with the methodological ones: to doubt the substantive claims would appear to be to unscientific. Lyell’s postulate of gradualism held that geological processes occurred with uniformity of rate: major events which he did not consider “catastrophic” such as floods, volcanic eruption, and cycles of erosion and uplift, occur with the same frequency at all times in Earth’s history. Lastly, Lyell concluded that the natural world exhibited uniformity of state. This meant no major extinction, no progression up the great chain toward increasing complexity. For a large portion of his career, Lyell held that uniformity of state meant that there could be no new species, and no evolutionary process at all. On this final point, Lyell was eventually brought round by his friend Darwin, and the later editions of *Principles of Geology* reflect this change of mind (Fig 5.1). This forced him to revise one of his habitual uniformitarian claims: uniformity of state. But Lyell’s slow gradual change driven by natural selection, and the vast duration of geological time, or methodologic uniformitarianism, remained.

He is looking slightly to the right of the viewer. The background is a dark, neutral color. The caption reads: “Charles Lyell (1797-1875). Portrait by Francis Grant, 1863. National Portrait Gallery, London.”

# The work of Lyell and others on the depth of geological time, as well as the exploration of new styles of classification which introduced the idea of organisms’ essential functions rather than its separate parts as an axis of classification (Cuvier) and the explanation of homologous forms by common descent (Geoffroy), were among the many intellectual developments which loosened up the soil for Darwin’s great contribution. But a gradual philosophical shift, described by Lovejoy as the “temporalization” of the great chain of being, was part of the groundwork as well. This idea touched on the end of the previous chapter, and now we must explore it in more detail. Only a century before Darwin published the *Origin of Species*, the Abbé Pluche had written – with the same certainty that Lord Kelvin used to declare physical space circa 1895 – that

nothing more… will be produced in all the ages to follow. All the philosophers have deliberated and come to agreement on this point. Consult the evidence of experience; elements always the same, species that never vary, seeds and gems prepared in advance for the perpetuation of everything… so that one can say, Nothing new under the sun, no new production, no species which has not been since the beginning.
(quoted by Lovejoy [1964, p. 243])

However, scholars were increasingly coming to view the great chain ‘not as the inventory but as the program of nature’ (Lovejoy [1964, p. 244]). In Lovejoy’s analysis, this shift was driven by various theoretical problems with the principle of plenitude. One set of difficulties derived from moral considerations. Plenitude left no room for hope, as Voltaire pointed out in his criticism of Leibniz’s “best of all possible worlds” in the aftermath of the Lisbon earthquake of 1755. If the world is stuffed full, how can any being’s happiness (or the proximity of a species to perfection at the top of the chain) be advanced without a corresponding decrement in another? There appeared to be no way for any being to advance toward perfection unless some other being was displaced if one accepted that “each degree of possible difference can have only one representative at a time”, as Edmund Law argued (Lovejoy [1964, pp. 245–6]). In short, a static chain of being reaching upward, and a world stuffed full of all possible things, seemed to allow no possibility of progress. The great chain had begun to sway in the breezes of the Enlightenment.

A related moral difficulty further that chained the Platonists’ foundations was the psychological theory that pleasures arise from change. Even Leibniz himself held that

the very law of nature… requires that there should always be a perpetual flux, a succession of changes, and a constant agitation of things, so that the universe is never in a quiet, restful state, nor a constant, immutable one, to a still, unmoving point, which is the very definition of death. The pleasures of the senses… consist in a continual newness, in a continual variation…
(quoted by Lovejoy [1964, p. 247])

Furthermore, the eighteenth century witnessed the rise of new philosophical and scientific conceptions of time. The traditional conception of time as cyclical, or as a mere dimension of spatial order, was challenged by a linear view of time as a flowing river, or as a dimension of becoming. This shift was closely connected with the development of historical consciousness and the idea of progress. As Lovejoy [1964, pp. 248–9] has shown, the idea of progress was not simply a product of the Enlightenment, but had roots in earlier Christian thought. However, it was in the eighteenth century that the idea of progress became a dominant force in Western culture. The concept of a “conic section” of time, proposed by Bolyai in 1832, is a particularly striking example of the new conception of time. Bolyai imagined time as a cone, with the past as the broad base and the future as the narrow apex. This image suggested that the past was vast and open-ended, while the future was limited and predetermined.

The sky is filled with clouds, and the overall impression is one of vastness and geological time. The scene is likely intended to illustrate the immense scale of geological processes and the long history of the Earth, as described in Lyell’s work. The figure represents humanity’s attempt to understand and interpret the natural world.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

…a perpetual and unrestricted progress of the universe as a whole must be recognized… For the objection which may be raised, that the true the world at some time already have become in the abyss of things partly hitherto dormant, to be raised and aroused to a greater and higher condition… And for this reason progress will never come to an end. (quoted by Lovejoy 1964, p. 257)

The idea of progress and advancement—essentially, a form of evolution—went to a letter—was a dominant theme in eighteenth century literature. Edward Young wrote of stellar evolution in his 1740s poem *Night Thoughts*, concluding that “Nature delights in progress.”<sup>14</sup> In a description that echoes Lamarck’s continuously progressing escalator, “escalator,” the physician-poet Mark Akenside wrote that “[n]either orders in succession rise / To fill the void below.” Lovejoy notes that this vision of progress still retains the idea of plenitude—voids must be filled (Lovejoy 1964, 256–265). Kant developed a theory of cosmological evolution similarly based on progress and plenitude. Even Bonnet, despite his adherence to the plan of plenitude, wrote of nature as a continual unfolding.

Nature has been, and never will again be, precisely what she is at the moment at which I am speaking… I doubt not that there was a time when there were not yet either minerals or any of the beings that we call animals; that is to say, a time when…not one of them had come to birth… At least it appears certain that Nature has never been, is not, and never will be stationary; in a state of permanence; its form is necessarily transitory… Nature is always at work, always in travail, in the sense that she is always fashioning new developments, new generations. (quoted by Lovejoy 1964, p. 275)

The great chain had swung sideways, extending further in time rather than up towards the heavens. The world was ready for Darwin.

Charles Robert Darwin (fig. 3.9) was not an evolutionist when he set sail on the ship’s naturalist aboard the HMS *Beagle*, but he did carry a copy of Lyell’s *Principles of Geology* with him. Lyell, of course, was not an evolutionist either at the time, but his ideas of slow and gradual change informed Darwin’s observations during his travels, as well the long intellectual journey which Darwin embarked after his return to England. The development of Darwin’s ideas has been traced in detail and depth many times, by many scholars, and I will certainly not attempt to compete with them here. For the purposes of the present work, a few crucial points need to be made. The essence of Darwin’s ideas was that by analogy with artificial selection, many more individuals are born than can possibly survive. As Darwin himself wrote, “I had always been struck by the hardiness of domesticated animals, and how readily they varied under care and selection.”<sup>15</sup> In December 1838, Darwin began to keep a detailed notebook on the transmutation of species, weighing the pros and cons of the theory. The essential insight, and the one that distinguished Darwin’s ideas from those of his predecessors, was the idea of natural selection—the differential survival and reproduction of individuals because of differences in their traits. Darwin’s manuscript on natural selection was completed in 1844, but he did not publish it, fearing the public outcry it would provoke.

> **Figure 3.9:** A portrait of Charles Darwin. He is depicted as an older man with a long, white beard and mustache, wearing a dark suit. The background is a dark, neutral color. The image is a reproduction of a photograph.

Darwin’s ideas were independently discovered by Alfred Russel Wallace, who sent Darwin a manuscript outlining a similar theory in 1858. This prompted Darwin to finally publish his ideas, in a joint presentation with Wallace to the Linnean Society in 1858, and then in his monumental *On the Origin of Species* in 1859. The publication of *Origin of Species* was a watershed moment in the history of science, and it revolutionized our understanding of the natural world. Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection provided a powerful and elegant explanation for the diversity of life on Earth, and it remains the cornerstone of modern biology.
