# Darwin’s Critics and the Ideal of Perfection

Darwin’s critics, including Sir Lysil Hartwell, argued that natural selection could act as a “destroyer,” but not as a creator (Gould 2002, pp. 139–140). Darwin simply cited observable evidence that variability in nature was, in Gould’s phrasing, “small, copious and undirected,” and suggested that future research would ultimately uncover the underlying mechanisms of such variation. “I have, he wrote, ‘hitherto sometimes spoken as if the variations—so common and multifirm with organic beings under domestication, and in a lesser degree with those under nature—were due to chance. This, of course, is a wholly incorrect expression, but it serves to acknowledge plainly our ignorance of the cause of each particular variation’” (Darwin, *Origin of Species*, p. 172). 

For our purposes, there are three critically important aspects of Darwin’s work that relate to the idea of collectivity and classification. We have discussed at length the struggles of philosophers to find a method or system for classifying living organisms. By combining Lyell’s uniformitarianism and Hutton’s deep time with his own idea of natural selection, Darwin proposed not merely a method, but a mechanism, for classification: common descent. Closely related organisms should be grouped more closely together, and closely related species (likewise. Determining the degree of closeness might be easy, or quite difficult, depending on the biological evidence available. If a lineage could be determined, then a meaningful classification was possible, based on tangible shared history.

The radical innovation of Darwin’s approach may be seen by comparison to Lamarck, for whom adaptation was inheritance of acquired characteristics was far less important than the unseen structural driving forces pushing organisms upward toward greater complexity. Darwin completely removed these unseen forces, laying everything at the doorstep of adaptation. As Gould writes, 

>acknowledged Lamarck’s implied claim that small scale adaptation to local environment defines the tractable subject matter of evolution. But he refuted the disabling connotation that adaptation in this mode only diverted the real ‘force of evolution’ into side channels and dead ends. And he revised previous evolutionary thinking in the most radical way—by denying that Lamarck’s ‘real’ force existed at all, by encompassing its supposed results as consequences of the ‘subsidiary’ force accumulated to grade by the simple expedient of relentless action over sufficient time” (Gould 2002, p. 89).

Darwin added another revolutionary idea in introducing natural selection as the mechanism of adaptation by the natural environment. He argued that natural selection accounts for the range of natural diversity observable in the world, given sufficient time. Darwin did not argue that natural selection’s force accounted for the origin of life itself. Indeed, Darwin explicitly acknowledged that the origin of life remained a mystery—a “primeval soup” in which the first forms could have arisen. He did not propose a mechanism for this origin, nor did he speculate about the nature of the initial conditions. Darwin’s theory, in Gould’s assessment, “simply postponed the central problem of evolution to a prior, and perhaps intractable, question” (Gould 2002, p. 90). 

Darwin’s theory also contained an important implication for the study of classification. If all organisms are related by common descent, then the history of life is like a tree, with branches representing different lineages. The task of the systematist is to reconstruct this tree, to determine the relationships between organisms. This is not a simple task, as the tree of life is often very bushy, with many branches and twigs. But it is a task that can be accomplished, in principle, by careful study of the evidence.

> **Figure 3.10.** Darwin’s famous sketch first of an evolutionary tree, drawn in an 1837 notebook, shortly after his return from traveling about the Beagle. Public domain.
>
> The figure is a hand-drawn tree diagram. The trunk is labeled "A". Branches extend from the trunk, splitting and re-splitting into smaller branches. Labels are scattered throughout the diagram, including "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G", "H", "I", "J", "K", "L", "M", "N", and "O". The branches are not evenly distributed; some are longer and thicker than others. The overall impression is of a complex, branching structure representing the diversification of life. The diagram is sketched in black ink on aged, yellowed paper.

Darwin’s approach to classification was not entirely new. Indeed, Linnaeus had already proposed a system of classification based on shared characteristics. But Linnaeus believed that these characteristics reflected God’s plan for creation, not common descent. Darwin, on the other hand, believed that these characteristics were the result of natural selection. This difference in perspective had a profound impact on the study of classification. For Darwin, classification was not merely a matter of describing the existing order of nature, but of reconstructing the history of life.

Darwin’s theory also had important implications for the study of adaptation. Before Darwin, adaptation was often seen as evidence of God’s design. It was argued that organisms were perfectly adapted to their environment because God had created them that way. Darwin, on the other hand, argued that adaptation was the result of natural selection. This meant that organisms were not perfectly adapted to their environment, but merely well enough adapted to survive and reproduce. This was a radical idea, as it challenged the traditional view of nature as a harmonious and purposeful system.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

A high degree the spirit of patriotism, fidelity, obedience, courage, and sympathy, were always ready to aid one another and to sacrifice themselves for the common good, would be victorious over most other tribes; and this would be natural selection (Darwin, *Descent of Man*, pp. 157–158, my italics).

As Gould emphasizes, the “one long argument” Darwin constructed in the *Origin of Species* relies on methods of historical inference to support his conclusion that natural selection and the immensity of time are sufficient cause for evolution. The first method used by Darwin is an extrapolation of Lyell’s uniformitarianism to the biological realm. Accumulation of small change, given sufficient time, can produce radically divergent morphologies. Gould describes this approach as the “worm principle,” in honor of Darwin’s last study, a study of the role of worms in processing the soil of Britain. Taking a physicist’s perspective, we might alternately call this the “definite integral principle,” in analogy to the definite integral as creating something finite by summing infinitesimal parts over some given interval. As he did later in his books, Darwin constructed his argument based on deceptively mundane data. He began the *Origin* with a discussion of artificial selection on domesticated pigeons, and then extrapolated to the process of natural selection acting over an immense reach of time. 

I look at individual differences, though of small interest to the systematist, as of the highest importance for us, as being the first steps toward such slight varieties as are barely thought worth recording in works on natural history. And I look at varieties which are in any degree more distinct and permanent, as steps towards more strongly-marked and permanent varieties; and at the latter, as leading to sub-species, and then to species. The passage from one stage of difference to another may, in many cases, be the simple result of the nature of the organization of the different physical conditions to which it has been exposed; but with respect to the more important and adaptive characters, the passage from one stage of difference to another, may safely be attributed to the cumulative action of natural selection… (Darwin, *Origin of Species*, pp. 77–78).

The second method of historical inference that Darwin employed was to infer history from a series of reefs. Gould refers to this as the “coral reef” principle, in a nod to Darwin’s first book, in which he proposed “a single historical process for the formation of coral atolls by recognizing their configurations of reefs – fringing reefs, barrier reefs, and atolls – as sequential stages in the founding of oceanic islands” (Gould 2002, p. 74). Again taking a physicist’s perspective, we could propose another name, and call this the “Fourier series principle,” since it takes data from the spatial domain and transforms it into an axis of time. Note the metaphorical parallel between these two kinds of chain of rotation of being from a ladder climbing up toward the heavens to a horizontal axis representing the flow of time. As he did with the discussion of worms, Darwin initially investigated the coral reef in a deceptively mundane context. The initial building of the coral reef was, before being extrapolated to the founding of an oceanic island, an inquiry into the ecology of small, polyphic marine animals. Darwin’s description of the formation of atolls is wonderfully clear and accessible. 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating Darwin’s theory of coral reef formation. The diagram shows three stages: (1) a volcanic island surrounded by a fringing reef (a reef directly attached to the shore); (2) the island subsiding, with the reef growing upwards to become a barrier reef (separated from the shore by a lagoon); and (3) the island completely submerged, leaving only a circular atoll (a ring-shaped reef enclosing a lagoon). Arrows indicate the direction of subsidence and reef growth. The diagram is labeled with terms like "Volcanic Island," "Fringing Reef," "Barrier Reef," "Atoll," "Lagoon," and "Subsidence." The overall purpose of the diagram is to visually explain how coral reefs evolve over geological time as islands sink into the ocean.

Darwin writes: “We have seen that a bank of coral grows in a situation where the sea is less than a certain depth, and that a bank of coral grows upwards from the bottom, as long as the sea continues of a sufficient depth; and we have further seen that the sea is generally, though not invariably, clear around coral-banks. Now, if a land which is subsiding slowly, and at the same time is capped by a coral-reef, is examined, we shall find that the reef will grow upwards, so as to keep its summit near the surface of the water… As the land sinks, the reef grows and keeps pace with it; and at last, when the land has subsided completely, a circular reef or atoll is left…” (Darwin 1842, pp. 108–109).

It is important to emphasize that Gould (2002, pp. 183–184) lamark’s evolutionary theory was far subtler than the cliché view most people know from textbooks, with the giraffe lengthening its neck to reach leaves on high branches. While Lamarck did argue for the inheritance of acquired characteristics, an inherent tendency toward increased complexity or perfection – which in series of organisms moving upward along the chain of being through time – was an even more important element of his theory. He also held that new “simple” organisms at the base of the chain would arise by spontaneous generation, resulting in organisms mounting upward along the chain in series of continually renewed “escalators,” some of which were further advanced than others. Gold presents Lamarck’s view as envisioning a hierarchy of causal factors, but one that can also interpret it as a tension between a “pulling apart” (branching) and a drawing together (tendency toward increased complexity or perfection). Interestingly, Lamarck also considered a biologically null model, in which the environment remained constant, presaging twentieth and twenty-first century studies of genetic drift and neutral theory in evolution.

# 4. The Battle of the Parts

Sonya Bahar

(1) Department of Physics & Astronomy and Center for Neurodynamics, University of Missouri at St Louis, MO, USA

<br>
<br>

WHILE DARWIN, Dukheim and others struggled to define a collectivity made up of individual organisms, a group of nineteenth and early twentieth century scholars, inspired by Darwin’s work, explored at a smaller scale, sowing the seeds of a full-fledged hierarchical evolutionary theory. This work was primarily done in Germany, by Ernst Haeckel, Wilhelm Roux, and August Weismann, and was inspired by their studies of embryology. 

Ernst Haeckel (Figs 4.1 and 4.2) is perhaps best known today for the idea (now seen as evocative metaphor rather than scientific fact) that *ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny*. But, in addition to his studies of embryological development (ontogeny) and its relation to evolutionary history (phylogeny), Haeckel suggested a full hierarchical theory of organic structure in his 1866 work *Generelle Morphologie der Organismen*. In what he referred to as the ‘doctrine of organic individuality’, he postulated that organic bodies can occur, and be included in, six structural levels, each of which can be considered as an individual. At the lowest (meaning the smallest, not the least important) level were *plastids*, comprising cells and organelles. The second level contained organs, including not just organs such as liver, lungs and spleen, but also tissues and organ systems. The third level contained symmetrical body parts, which Haeckel called *antimeres*. Fourth came body segments, and fifth what he termed persons, or, in Gould’s phrasing, “vernacular individuals”. Lastly, colonies of persons, which Haeckel termed *cemacuria*. Haeckel emphasized that each of these levels should be considered as a type of individual; the primacy given to the level of persons was simply an accident of our own perspective as persons ourselves. He wrote that

This concept has become so general, and has been so strongly fixed in both scientific and vernacular consciousness, that we must mark it as the major source of the numerous and varied interpretations and debates that prevail on the subject of organic individuality. A decade and a half later, Wilhelm Roux (Fig. 4.3) published a book titled *Der Kampf der Theile im Organismus* (The Struggle of Parts in the Organism), which applied Darwinian natural selection to cells and, most particularly, to organs. In a letter urging George Romanes to review the book for *Nature*, Darwin wrote that, making allowance for his limited ability to read German, the book appeared to be “the most important book on Evolution which has appeared for some time… Roux argues that there is a struggle going on within every organism between the organic molecules, the cells and the organs” (quoted by Gould 2002, p. 210).

# 4. Roux’s Model, Organic Similarity

In Roux’s model, organs metaphorically jostled each other in a struggle to obtain sufficient nutrition from the whole organism. He argued that “the construction of a harmonious and well-designed organism emerges from a struggle among the parts competing for limited nourishment” (Gould 2002, p. 211). Roux was explicitly drawn to this model on the basis of his observations of variability between cells. “No hepatocyte,” he wrote, “is perfectly similar in size or shape to another, yet they all fit together in an efficient organ” (quoted – and translated – by Heams 2012). The second idea that inspired Roux was the idea of the Malthusian mismatch between reproduction rates of organs and resources. “Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace have,” he wrote, “demonstrated that because of geometrical growth of organisms, there must be a… struggle between them, and that due to the continuous variation of all parts within the organism, one could assume that only the best organisms would ‘survive’ ” (quoted by Heams 2012). Roux then fixed his model for intra-organismal struggle from two of the three key premises of Darwinian evolution (later codified, with the inclusion of heritability as the third leg of the tripod, by Lewontin in 1970); variability, competition, and differential survival. Roux only discussed competition between components at the same level (cells with cells, organs with organs). He did not consider cross-level conflict because he would be, in his words, trying to find the “sum of differential equations of different orders” (quoted by Heams 2012). 

There exists a fundamental difference between selection at the organismal level and Roux’s battle of the parts. The results of conflict between cells of the same type are not beyond the lifetime of the containing organism. Limiting the natural selection analogy, even further, victories or defeats in struggles between organs, which do not reproduce at all, cannot be transferred to the offspring of the containing organism, unless one reverts to the idea of acquired characteristics. *Lingua versus Lingua* is “a theory of functional adjustment in development” (Gould 2012, p. 211), not a theory of evolution. Moreover, as Vernon Kellogg wrote in 1907, “This competition chiefly depends on the hazard of position… Not the best qualified by the best situated fibers have vanquished the others by robbing them of food and thus finally triumphing” (quoted by Gould 2002, p. 212). Interestingly, however (and perhaps due to his lack of fluency in German), Darwin himself interpreted Roux’s theory differently, concluding that in Roux’s model, “the best fitted survive. According to Heams (2012), Darwin wrote to Romanes that the theory’s “basis is that every cell that best performs its function is allowed to survive, at the cost including that the best equipped are not killed” . Through the of a Roux-like process consistently with this latter interpretation, the cells more “properly” a tissue, in their competition, would be the ones to reproduce, at the time of reproduction, and bequeath their properties to the next generation. Darwin, however, misread Roux, as he assumed that Roux’s cells were reproducing in a manner inconsistent with the idea of inheritance. This misinterpretation is important because it reveals Darwin’s commitment to the idea that selection only operates on reproducing entities (Gould 2002, p. 212). 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating Roux’s model of organismal development. The diagram depicts a series of cells arranged in a grid-like structure. Some cells are larger and darker, representing “stronger” or more competitive cells, while others are smaller and lighter, representing “weaker” cells. Arrows indicate the direction of competition, with stronger cells encroaching on the space of weaker cells. The overall impression is one of a struggle for resources and dominance among the cells. The text accompanying the figure explains that Roux believed organs developed through a competitive process, with cells vying for limited nourishment.

Roux’s model was not simply a matter of cells competing for space. As he put it, “The cell does not merely *wait* to be molded, but it actively *strives* for form” (quoted by Heams 2012, p. 38). This active striving was not random; it was guided by the “physiological selection” of cells, a concept that Roux borrowed from Herbert Spencer. Roux believed that cells were inherently different and that these differences were the basis for their selective advantage. “The fate of each cell,” he wrote, “is determined by its own inherent properties” (quoted by Heams 2012, p. 39). This emphasis on the inherent properties of cells led Roux to reject the idea that development was simply a matter of external forces acting on a passive organism. Instead, he argued that development was an active, self-organizing process, driven by the internal dynamics of the organism. Roux’s model had a profound influence on the development of experimental embryology. His emphasis on the importance of cell-cell interactions and the active role of cells in development helped to pave the way for the field of developmental biology. However, his model also had its critics. Some scientists argued that Roux’s model was too focused on competition and neglected the importance of cooperation. Others argued that his model was too deterministic and did not allow for the possibility of chance events in development. Despite these criticisms, Roux’s model remains an important contribution to our understanding of development. It is a reminder that development is not simply a matter of genes and environment, but also a matter of the active, self-organizing processes that take place within the organism.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

Fig 4.5 A figure from Weismann’s 1904 *The Evolution Theory* illustrating the fertilization of *Ascaria*s. Note the level of detail in the drawing of the miotic spindles and chromosomes. From author’s collection.

Weismann developed his theory of germinal selection in an attempt to defend strict Darwinian selection from attacks by the philosopher Herbert Spencer. Early in his career, Weismann was a strict adherent of Darwinian selection at the organismal level. However, Spencer raised an argument about the disappearance of vestigial limbs as a challenge to the primacy of natural selection in driving evolutionary change. For example, it would be reasonable to suggest that the ancestor of a whale might benefit from a decrease in the size of its hind limbs, since this would make the animal a more streamlined swimmer. But what would happen when the limbs grew so small that further reduction was to speak, below the threshold of selection? A decrease in the size of a limb with a surface area equal to the smallest fraction of the body’s surface could not conceivably produce a life-or-death advantage to its possessor. Even more, what of the continued decrease in limb size when the limb was so small as to be contained within the animal’s body?<sup>4</sup>

In an 1895 article entitled “The Inadequacy of Natural Selection,” Herbert Spencer proposed that a principle of use and disuse would best explain the disappearance of vestigial organs. Weismann replied with a work entitled “Die Allmacht der Naturzuchtung,” translated as “The All-Sufficiency of Natural Selection.” The choice of the term Allmacht, which can also be rendered as “omnipotence” or more directly, but less flowingly in English, as “all-might,” was a direct rebuttal to Spencer’s charge of inadequacy (Gould 2002, p. 198). Drawing on his idea of the sequestration of germ cells, Weismann wrote that “Nature has carefully enclosed the germ-plasm of cells in a capsule, and it is only yielded up for the formation of daughter-cells, under the most complicated precautionary conditions” (quoted by Gould 2002, p. 201). If the germinal material is sequestered in only a few cells, then it is these cells and these cells alone that transmit evolutionary information to future generations. In immediate consequence of this is that inheritance of acquired characteristics is “null.” From this starting point, Weismann struggled to construct arguments to explain the selective benefit of degeneration. In *Gould’s* interpretation of Weismann’s intellectual journey, “Gould aged as the level that predated Weismann from his panselectionism, and his led him through a chronological series of honorable changes that must be read, in one sense, as a retreat from a former pugnacious insistence on Allmacht, but also represents a complex accommodation to emerging cellular and original views” (Gould 2002, p. 204). Alternatively, as *Sarkar* (2005, p. 77) allows, Weismann’s germ plasm theory should be understood as an attempt to reaffirm the importance of natural selection in the face of Spencer’s challenge. 

From the passage in the 1904 edition, it is apparent that Weismann believed that degeneration, as well as adaptation, is the result of natural selection. He provided, for example, a hypothetical scenario in Weismann 1904, Vol. I, p. 226–229 (Gould 2002, p. 202) to illustrate this point.  A barnacle, attached to a rock in intertidal zone, is buffeted by the waves and currents, and its carapace is constantly damaged. Weismann argued that, if the carapace were to disappear, the barnacle would be better off, and natural selection would favor individuals with reduced carapaces. But, he continued, the disappearance of the carapace is not the result of disuse, but of the fact that individuals with smaller carapaces are more likely to survive and reproduce. 

> **Figure:** A detailed illustration from Weismann’s 1904 *The Evolution Theory* depicting the fertilization of *Ascaria*s (roundworms). The image is a black and white line drawing showing a cross-section of the reproductive system.  Visible are the egg, sperm, and the complex structures within the cells during fertilization, including the miotic spindles and chromosomes. The drawing is highly detailed, showcasing the intricate cellular structures. The figure is labeled with numbers pointing to different parts of the reproductive cells, indicating the stages of fertilization. The overall impression is one of scientific precision and detailed observation.

Weismann’s argument is that the degeneration of the carapace is not a direct response to the environment, but an indirect consequence of selection for individuals that are better able to survive and reproduce in that environment. In other words, the disappearance of the carapace is not the result of disuse, but of selection for individuals with smaller carapaces. This is a subtle but important distinction. Spencer believed that the environment could directly cause changes in organisms, while Weismann believed that the environment could only select for individuals with pre-existing variations. 

This distinction is important because it has implications for our understanding of the inheritance of acquired characteristics. If Spencer were right, then it would be possible for organisms to pass on to their offspring characteristics that they have acquired during their lifetime. But if Weismann were right, then it would not be possible. Only characteristics that are encoded in the germ plasm can be passed on to future generations. This is why Weismann’s theory is often referred to as the “germ plasm theory.”

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

To an extent, Conklin’s criticisms were justified. Weismann’s theory was largely no more than a hypothetical construct. It is worth noting, however, that experimental work being done on nuclear and cytoplasmic material at the time, and thus his concepts of ids, determinants and the rest were not entirely fanciful. Weismann, particularly early in his career, was no mean experimentalist himself (Churchill 2010, and certainly well familiar with the work of Oscar Hertwig, who in 1875 had observed in his studies of sea urchins that fertilized fusion of the cell nuclei of the sperm and the egg. In the same decade, other scientists, exploiting recent advances in light microscopy and the discovery of aniline dyes, observed staining that cell nuclei contained threadlike structures that were segregated from other cellular components during cell division. In 1884, Eduard van Beneden observed the reduction in the number of chromosomes in the parasitic nematode *Ascaris* during the formation of its germ cells; this observation was made during microscopic studies of the formation of polar bodies and their role in cell division. 

The brilliant experiments of Theodor Boveri<sup>5</sup> and others soon to clarify the role of chromosomes in inheritance, providing strong support for Weismann’s theory of the germ-plasm (Bödmer 2008). Thus, while Weismann’s speculative theory was far from a fantasy.

In the mid 1890s, Weismann argued that germinal and organismal selection as working synergistically to account for the disappearance of vestigial organs (Gould 2002, pp. 218-219). A few years later, Weismann expanded his theory to encompass a fuller picture of hierarchical selection, and explicitly considered situations in which the direction of germinal selection could be decoupled from the direction of organismal selection. 

Now that we have made ourselves familiar with the idea of germinal selection we shall attempt to gain clearness as to what it can do, and how far the sphere of its influence extends, and, in particular, how whether it can effect lasting transformations of species without the co-operation of organismal (personal) selection, and what kind of conditions may accrue to it (Weismann 1904, Vol. II, p. 126)

Indeed, the problem of degeneration could be considered as an instance of decoupling of selective levels. On an organ might indeed in some due to organismal (or, in Weismann’s terminology, “personal”) selection alone. But since the organ had shrunk the notice of this selective level, germinal selection completed the job. Thus the two levels worked in the same direction, but with complete independence, at least in the last stage, once personal selection had ceased to operate. “Needless organs,” Weismann wrote in 1909, “are the only ones which are not subject to any personal selection, and therefore the organs in which the germ-plasm has free play, and in which, therefore, the reduction in the number of ids can go on without any impediment.”  For example, the case of the barnacle, in which the loss of the eyes had occurred in both sexes, was to Weismann a clear example of germinal selection at work.

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating Weismann’s theory of germinal selection. The diagram depicts a branching tree representing a lineage of organisms. At each branch point, there are two lines extending downwards: one representing the organismal line (soma) and the other representing the germ-plasm line. The organismal line is shown with various traits, some of which are beneficial and some of which are detrimental. The germ-plasm line is shown with ids, which represent the hereditary units. The diagram illustrates how germinal selection can act independently of organismal selection, leading to the evolution of traits that are not necessarily beneficial to the organism but are beneficial to the germ-plasm. The axes are not explicitly labeled, but the diagram visually represents the flow of heredity and the interplay between organismal and germinal selection. The data is represented by the branching pattern of the tree and the presence or absence of certain traits in the organismal line. The meaning of the diagram is to illustrate Weismann’s theory that germinal selection is a powerful force in evolution, and that it can lead to the evolution of traits that are not necessarily adaptive for the organism.

Weismann’s insistence on the independence of the two levels of selection, and his emphasis on the importance of the germ-plasm, led him to reject the neo-Lamarckian notion of the inheritance of acquired characteristics. “The idea that characters acquired during the lifetime of an individual can be transmitted to its offspring is a very ancient one,” he wrote in 1896. “It is based on the assumption that the body is capable of impressing its modifications on the germ-plasm, and that these modifications are then transmitted to the next generation.” But, Weismann argued, there was no evidence to support this claim. “On the contrary,” he wrote, “all the evidence that we have goes to show that the germ-plasm is protected from the influence of the body, and that it is only through the process of selection that changes can occur in the hereditary constitution of an organism.” 

It is important to note that Weismann was not opposed to the idea of evolution. Quite the contrary, he was one of the most important evolutionary theorists of his time. But he believed that the process of evolution was driven by natural selection acting on the germ-plasm, and not by the inheritance of acquired characteristics. This view put him at odds with many of his contemporaries, but it has been vindicated by modern genetics.

# THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

[the great prominence thus given to the idea of selection has been condemned as one-sided and exaggerated, but the physicist is quite as open to the same reproach when he thinks of gravity as operative not on our earth alone, but dominating the whole cosmos, whether visible or us to it. There is gravity at all must prevail everywhere, that is, wherever material masses exist; thus not only are the vital units which we can perceive, such as individuals and cells, subject to selection, but those units the existence of which we can only deduce theoretically, because they are too minute for our microscopes, are subject to it likewise. (Weismann 1904, vol. I, p. iii).]

Note how this comparison essentially contains *R*ink’s point of omnipotence and omniscient. but from a diametrically opposed emotional (if such a thing can be said to exist in scientific commentary). For all his emphasis on evolutionary hierarchy, it is a supreme irony that Weismann’s “doctrine” was distilled into something quite by the mid-nineteenth century scientists who codified the modern synthesis of evolutionary theory. Weismann’s specific germ-plasm theory was shown to be incorrect, of course, but his idea of the segregation of germinal information in certain cells is certainly correct, since, while most cells contain DNA, only gametes contain the information to create a new genetic individual. This aspect of Weismann’s doctrine has become the one to which his name is primarily attached, and his emphasis on the genetic uniqueness of the individual provided an impetus for a renewed focus on selection at the organismal level. As described by Leo Buss in his groundbreaking book *The Evolution of Individuality*, the reasoning ran as follows: “if variation in the course of ontogeny is not heritable [beyond a short-lived cell lineage that will die with its host organism], the dynamics of cell lineages within the somatic environment are a matter of little direct evolutionary interest” (Buss 1987, p. 3). 

Weismann had envisioned a quite different intellectual legacy, writing in the preface to *The Evolution Theory* that the “extension of the innate principle of selection to all grades of vital units is the characteristic feature of my theories; it is to this idea that these lectures [are] dedicated. It is in this opinion – which gives this book its importance. This idea will endure even if everything else in the book should prove transient” (Weismann 1904, vol. I, p. ix). Indeed, the idea was temporarily eclipsed. The distorted organism-centered perspective Haeckel had warned against opened its jaws and swallowed biology whole. 

As a result of the narrowing focus, *Buss* writes, “[t]he modern synthesis was an intellectual event largely unattended by embryologists” (Buss 1987, p. 3). And in the manner of John Maynard Smith, “[t]he publication of Darwin’s *Origin of Species*, but before the general acceptance of Weismann’s views, problems of development were beyond the horizon” (Smith 1989, p. 2). Concurring, Robbin Holliday offered the exasperation that the general line of attack was to make the process of development unnecessary, even superfluous, and to assume that development was but a “nuisance” to be ignored. The consequence of this evolutionary amnesia was considerable. To understand that the concept of the extended phenotype, pioneered by Richard Dawkins, was not new, one need only consult Weismann, who, in 1893, wrote of the “operative power of the germ-plasm, which is not limited to the organism, but extends to all its products, to all those formations which are due to its activity, and which, coming into operation during the lifetime of the individual, may again influence the germ-plasm” (Weismann 1893, p. 168). The irony is acute: the very concept that was to revolutionize evolutionary biology a century later was present at the birth of modern evolutionary theory, only to be stillborn. 

> **Figure:** A photograph of August Weismann. He is an older man with a full white beard and mustache, wearing a dark suit and tie. The photograph is a portrait, showing him from the chest up. The background is a neutral tone.

***

### A BRIEF HISTORY OF THE EXTENDED SYNTHESIS

It is important to note that the term “extended evolutionary synthesis” (EES) was coined relatively recently, in 2009, by Massimo Pigliucci and Gerd Müller, but the ideas that comprise it have a long history. As we have seen, many of the core concepts were present in the work of Weismann and others in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. However, these ideas were largely marginalized by the dominance of the neo-Darwinian synthesis, which focused primarily on genetic variation and natural selection. 

The re-emergence of these ideas in the early twenty-first century can be attributed to a number of factors, including advances in the fields of developmental biology, epigenetics, and systems biology. These advances have revealed that inheritance is not simply a matter of passing on genes, but also involves the transmission of epigenetic marks, regulatory networks, and other non-genetic factors. 

> **Table:** A table listing the core concepts of the Extended Evolutionary Synthesis (EES) and how they differ from the Modern Evolutionary Synthesis (MES).
>
> | Feature | Modern Evolutionary Synthesis (MES) | Extended Evolutionary Synthesis (EES) |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Primary Focus** | Genetic variation & natural selection | Genetic, epigenetic, developmental, and cultural inheritance |
> | **Inheritance** | Genes only | Genes, epigenetic marks, regulatory networks, niche construction |
> | **Variation** | Random mutations | Random mutations, developmental bias, phenotypic plasticity |
> | **Adaptation** | Primarily genetic | Genetic and non-genetic adaptation |
> | **Role of Development** | Development as implementation of genetic program | Development as a key source of variation and constraint |
> | **Role of Environment** | Selective pressure | Active role in shaping development and inheritance (niche construction) |

***

The EES, therefore, represents a broadening of the neo-Darwinian framework, rather than a rejection of it. It recognizes that evolution is a more complex process than previously thought, and that a complete understanding of evolution requires integrating insights from a variety of disciplines. The EES is not without its critics, some of whom argue that it is simply a repackaging of old ideas, or that it lacks empirical support. However, the EES is gaining increasing acceptance among evolutionary biologists, and is likely to play an important role in shaping the future of evolutionary research.

**HYPOTHESES REGARDING** selection at a level below the organismal, we as have just seen in the work of Haeckel, Roux and Weisemann, and ideas of higher levels, in sociological works such as those of Durkheim, as well as key passages of Darwin’s own writings, set the stage for twentieth century scientists to rigorously explore evolutionary processes at multiple levels. This did not happen. Instead, for much of the twentieth century, evolutionary theory was almost exclusively focused on the organismal level. Selection at the group level was pushed to the margins of discussion and, when it was brought up, often dismissed with ridicule. Stephen Jay Gould recalled suggesting, in the question session after a conference talk in 1973, that the small size of some island-dwelling mammal species in the Pleistocene era might be due to the advantage of large population size, which would render the population more resistant to extinction than larger, broader-sized species. “Are you,” the speaker replied, “really satisfied with a group selectionist argument like that?” Gould waited, but was it. No actual content-based argument was forthcoming (Gould 2002, p. 554).

How and why did the scientific community turn so emphatically away from the interaction, balance, and tension between levels in biological systems? The shift to a nearly exclusive focus on adaptation at the organismal level was codified during period known as the Modern Synthesis, after Julian Huxley’s 1942 book *Evolution, the Modern Synthesis*. 

Sociological reasons have been put forward to explain this shift. Smocoviti (1986) has emphasized that the idea of “synthesis” in the sciences in general was quite popular early in the last century, influenced by the philosophers of the Vienna Circle. Synthesis was seen as a measure of the intellectual maturity of a field and its proponents (Good 2002, p. 503). The catastrophic history of mid-century Europe may also have driven biologists toward a focus on adaptation and “improvement”; tragically, of course, this idea of improvement was also linked to some of the most terrible horrors of the twentieth century. This topic, historic perspective turned the work of the biologists of the Synthesis, as in the sections of R.A. Fisher’s *The Genetical Basis of Natural Selection*, “improvement” to “adaptation”, the arguments laid out in those texts, and the institutional arrangements associated with them.

I'm trying to make creme brûlée." Panel 2 shows a man with a beard looking at the first man with a slightly annoyed expression. A speech bubble reads "Bernard Black." More prosaic reasons have also been suggested. Robert Richards (1987) contends that the intellectual climate in American biology was conservative in the early decades of the twentieth century, and that this prompted a dismissal of group-level selectionism. The American embrace of the gene-centered view of evolution, powerfully articulated by W.D. Hamilton in the 1960s, further cemented the focus on the gene as the primary unit of selection. The shift away from group selectionism was, then, not simply a matter of scientific rigor, but also of sociological and political forces. The Modern Synthesis, for all its successes, may have inadvertently closed off potentially fruitful avenues of inquiry.

Difficulties with defining the “group” and measuring fitness at the group level were, and remain, legitimate concerns. However, the dismissal of group selectionism was often accompanied by a lack of nuance and an unwillingness to consider the possibility of multilevel selection, in which selection operates simultaneously at multiple levels (Goldberg & West 2007; Michod 1999). As we will see in the following sections, multilevel selection is not necessarily equivalent to simple group selection, and can, in fact, help to resolve some of the theoretical difficulties associated with the latter. The recent resurgence of interest in multilevel selection theory (Gardner & Grafen 2007; Szathmáry 2007) suggests that the time may be ripe to revisit this important and often-controversial topic.

But we may confidently predict that when a meeting-point is found, and one of the two sciences is swallowed up, that one will not be biology.” (Smocovitis 1996, pp. 106–107). The modern synthesis defined a clear tradition against which “loci of trouble” such as the problems of collective dynamics in biological systems could stand out and demand attention as the twentieth century drew toward a close.

> **Figure:** A black and white photograph of J.B.S. Haldane. He is a white man with short hair, wearing a suit and tie. He is looking slightly to the left of the frame with a serious expression. The background is a plain, light color.

The Modern Synthesis can be divided into two stages, each marking a decisive turning point in the development of evolutionary theory. In the first stage, the rediscovery of the work of Gregor Mendel was folded into Darwinian theory; as genetics was shown to provide a substrate of variation upon which natural selection could act. The start of the second phase can be traced to the late 1930s and early 1940s, with the publication of key works by Julian Huxley and Theodosius Dobzhansky. In this period, various core subfields of biology, such as paleontology, systematics, cytology, botany and morphology were brought into alignment with the new “synthetic” theory linking Mendel and Darwin. This codification of a body of knowledge sounds like nothing so much as the development of a Kuhnian “well-defined and deeply ingrained” tradition. Yet it was the result, as we shall see, of grappling the perceived attacks on the natural selection in the organizational framework of population genetics—a framework developed by Fisher, Haldane, and Wright.  Moreover, as we shall see, the Mendelian revival was itself the result of a reaction to challenges to Darwinism, and the synthesis was not simply a matter of incorporating Mendelian genetics into Darwinian theory. It was, rather, a complex and often contentious process of realignment, a process that involved the reworking of key concepts in both fields.  The synthesis was not a seamless affair, and the work of key figures such as Sewall Wright was often at odds with that of Fisher and Dobzhansky.  Furthermore, the synthesis was not universally accepted, and there remained a significant minority of biologists who continued to adhere to alternative evolutionary paradigms.  

The synthesis was, however, remarkably successful in establishing a dominant paradigm for evolutionary research for much of the twentieth century.  It provided a unifying framework for understanding the diversity of life, and it generated a wealth of new research.  The synthesis also had a profound impact on other fields, such as agriculture, medicine, and conservation biology.  In recent years, however, the synthesis has come under increasing scrutiny, and there is growing recognition that it is not a complete or perfect theory of evolution.

The emergence of new fields, such as molecular biology and genomics, has revealed new complexities in the evolutionary process that were not anticipated by the synthesis.  These discoveries have led to the development of new evolutionary theories, such as neutral theory and punctuated equilibrium, which challenge some of the core assumptions of the synthesis.  Despite these challenges, the synthesis remains a valuable and important framework for understanding evolution. It has provided a foundation for much of our current knowledge of the evolutionary process, and it continues to inspire new research.

> **Figure 5.1:** Two pioneers of evolution. The young Julian Huxley, being held by his grandfather, Thomas Henry Huxley. *Public domain*

Just as there is no one method of the origin of species, so there is no one type of variation. Different evolutionary agencies differ in intensity and sometimes in different sorts of organisms, partly owing to differences in the environment, partly to differences in way of life, partly to differences in genetic machinery. No single formula can be universally applicable; but the different aspects of evolution must be studied afresh in every group of animals and plants. We are approaching the time when evolution must be studied not only broadly and deductively, but as a comparative subject. (Huxley 1942, p. 46)

There is no arguing, however, that adaptation was the central pillar of Huxley’s synthesis. He described it as “omnipresent,” though he allowed that some adaptive traits could conflict with one another. Adaptation, he said, “cannot but be universal among organisms, and every organism cannot be other than a bundle of adaptations, more or less detailed and efficient, coordinated in greater or lesser degree. On the other hand, adaptations subserving different functions may be mutually destructive” (Huxley 1942, pp. 420–421). Elsewhere he noted that “genes may have their expression altered by modifiers so as entirely to change their selective effect” (Huxley 1942, p. 60). His view of adaptation, and its genetic basis, was quite subtle and multi-layered, even writing a decade before Watson and Crick, and many decades before the birth of epigenetics.

Huxley dealt explicitly with various possible sources of non-adaptive evolutionary trends. He noted that there were limitations on the range of possible variations and, like Haldane, suggested that these limitations might drive orthogenesis, which 

depends on a restriction of the type and quantity of genetic variation. When dominant it prescribes the direction of evolution; when subsidiary it merely limits its possibilities, but we are not yet able to be sure in most cases whether a limitation of variation as actually found in a group is due to a limitation in the supply of mutations or to selection, or to other causes (Huxley 1942, p. 524).

However, Huxley dismissed orthogenesis as a rare phenomenon, noted the lack of any known mechanism behind it, and described the explanation of any phenomenon in terms of orthogenesis as “provisional.” He noted that even if the existence of orthogenesis… be confirmed, it appears to be a rare and exceptional phenomenon, and… we have no liking of any mechanism by which it might be brought about. It is not yet description, not an explanation, indeed. (Huxley 1942, p. 525)

He allowed some room for the possibility of genetic drift, though he felt that natural selection was generally a more important force. He believed that only “relatively unimportant” characters could be altered by random drift, and that such drift was most likely to occur in small, isolated populations. Huxley considered that the concept of drift offered no very satisfactory explanation of evolutionary trends. 

Huxley’s views on the role of chance in evolution were nuanced. He acknowledged the importance of random mutation, but he considered that the direction of evolution was primarily determined by natural selection. He wrote that “the main driving force of evolution… is due to the selective action of the environment” (Huxley 1942, p. 419). However, he also recognized that chance events, such as genetic drift and founder effects, could play a significant role in shaping the course of evolution, particularly in small populations. He saw these chance events as “modifications of the general scheme” rather than as fundamental forces in their own right.

In his discussion of the evolution of behavior, Huxley emphasized the importance of both genetic and environmental factors. He argued that behavior is a complex trait that is influenced by a variety of genes, as well as by learning and experience. He noted that the study of animal behavior could provide valuable insights into the evolutionary processes that shape the nervous system and the brain. He also pointed out that the evolution of behavior is often constrained by the physical and physiological limitations of the organism.

> **Figure 5.2:** A diagram illustrating the concept of “hopeful monsters.” A single generation produces a mutant with a large deviation from the norm, which, if viable and fertile, may found a new species. From Huxley 1942, p. 527.

Huxley was also interested in the possibility of macromutations, or “hopeful monsters,” as he called them. These are large-scale mutations that can produce dramatic changes in phenotype. Huxley argued that macromutations are rare, but that they can play an important role in evolution, particularly in the origin of new species. He suggested that macromutations may be more common in organisms with short generation times and high mutation rates. He also noted that macromutations are more likely to be beneficial in organisms that are living in unstable environments.

This is due to the nature of the evolutionary process, which proceeds by the presentation of numerous small steps, and the subsequent incorporation of some of them in the constitution by selection, or in some cases by Sewall Wright’s “drift.” The improbability of the mutative steps being identical in two isolated groups, even if they are pursuing parallel evolution (i.e., experiencing similar selective drives), is enormously high, so that reproductive incompatibilities will in the long run automatically arise between them. If the direction of selection differs for the two groups, visible divergence will also automatically result, even in the absence of divergence due to drift. (Hulety 1942, p. 259).

In another comment on Hulety, wrote that although “the most frequent mode of geographical differentiation is broadly adaptive, there are many cases in which apparently non-adaptive differentiation has occurred, predominantly or superposed on a general adaptive divergence, or as a correlate of invisible physiological adaptation” (Hulety 1942, p. 242, my italics). He does not mention the possibility of these non-adaptive changes being later co-opted to serve other purposes, but if this next logical step had been made, he could have introduced the concept that Gould and Vrba were to label, decades later, “exaptation” or “preadaptation.”

While Hulety clearly allowed for the possibility of other evolutionary processes such as drift, adaptation was beyond any doubt the central focus of his conception of the modern synthesis. This is an important part of our story because adaptation is more clearly conceptualized at the level of the individual organism. It is therefore no accident that the focus of the modern synthesis on adaptation went hand in hand with a nearly exclusive study of evolution at the organismal level. Even the discussions of drift cited above all refer to traits at the organismal level. 

The increasing focus on adaptation shifted researchers’ views away from selection, drift, or any other process at other levels. As a consequence, it shifted the focus away from possible interactions between levels, and hence away from the dynamic core tensions that form the central theme of this book. For Hull’s references to non-adaptive processes, he gives short shrifts to selections of problems at levels higher than the organismal. In his later chapters, he briefly discussed intergroup vs. intrapopup or interspecific vs. intraspecific selection, in the context of the evolution of altruism in social insects and human societies. He called that natural selection and adaptation can be “for the good of the species as a whole, for the good of the evolving type pursuing a long-range trend, for the good of the group undergoing adaptive radiation.” Simply a fallacy. This might be possible “if there were a way in which selection could be restricted to effects on the species as a species.” But as a matter of fact Hulety’s idea (Hulety 1942, p. 483). Hulety could have hardened his work to demonstrate that only societies like social insects, which have separate reproductive castes, can evolve a bluish altruistic behavior. 

Hulety’s work was incomplete because in his rejection of the possibility of selection at levels above that of the individual, he simply ignored the possibility of selection favoring certain ways in which different levels are organized and interact. He simply could not see that selection could favor certain kinds of hierarchical organization. The modern synthesis, as Hulety expounded it, was a spectacularly successful, but ultimately incomplete, synthesis. It incorporated Mendelism into Darwinism, but it did so at the cost of ignoring the possibility of selection at levels above that of the individual organism.

> **Figure:** A photograph of a man, presumably Sewall Wright, sitting in a chair and looking at the camera. He is wearing a suit and tie. The background is a simple wall. The image is black and white.

The conceptual tension between adaptation and other processes, and between different levels of selection, was not resolved by the modern synthesis. Instead, it was largely ignored. The modern synthesis provided a powerful framework for understanding evolution, but it was a framework that was based on a number of simplifying assumptions, one of which was that adaptation was the primary driver of evolution, and another of which was that selection operated primarily at the level of the individual organism. These assumptions were not necessarily wrong, but they were incomplete. 

The failure to recognize the importance of selection at levels above that of the individual organism had a number of important consequences. One consequence was that it led to a neglect of the study of group selection and multilevel selection. Another consequence was that it led to a neglect of the study of the evolution of social behavior. And a third consequence was that it led to a neglect of the study of the evolution of complex systems.

In the 1960s, a number of biologists began to challenge the assumptions of the modern synthesis. One of these biologists was George C. Williams, who argued that group selection was almost always weaker than individual selection and that it was therefore unlikely to be an important force in evolution. Another biologist was W.D. Hamilton, who developed the theory of kin selection, which explained how altruistic behavior could evolve even in the absence of group selection. And a third biologist was John Maynard Smith, who developed the theory of game theory, which provided a new way of understanding the evolution of social behavior.

These biologists did not reject the modern synthesis entirely, but they did argue that it needed to be revised. They argued that selection could operate at levels above that of the individual organism, and that group selection and multilevel selection could be important forces in evolution. They also argued that the evolution of social behavior was a complex process that could not be understood by simply focusing on the individual organism.

The work of these biologists led to a renewed interest in the study of group selection and multilevel selection. It also led to a renewed interest in the study of the evolution of social behavior. And it led to a renewed interest in the study of the evolution of complex systems.

# Fig. 5.3 Ernst Mayr. From the Archives of the Museum of Comparative Zoology, Ernst Mayr Library, Harvard University

In the first edition of Dobzhansky’s *Genetics and the Origin of Species*, he laid out a programme that allowed for parallelism and macroevolution. He considered the problem of discontinuity between species to be the fundamental problem of evolutionary biology (Gould 2002, p. 232). He urged a shift away from an exclusive focus on population genetics, even though Dobzhansky genetics was his own particular field of study. He wrote that

“[t]he origin of hereditary variations is…only a part of the mechanism of evolution. Mutations and chromosomal changes are constantly arising at a finite rate, presumably in all organisms. But in nature we do not find a single variable population of living things which becomes more and more variable as time goes on; instead, the organic world is segregated into more than a million separate species, each of which possesses its own limited supply of variability which it does not share with the others…The origin of species…constitutes a problem which is logically distinct from that of hereditary variation” (quoted by Gould, p. 2002, p. 533).

Elsewhere, Dobzhansky addressed population-level traits and the degree to which the survival of individual organisms was subsumed beneath the group-level need for high variability: “Evolutionary plasticity can only be purchased at the ruthlessly dear price of continuously sacrificing individuals to death from unfavorable mutations” (quoted by Borello, 2010, p. 4). 

Between the first (1937) and third (1951/1959) editions of the *Origin of Species*, Dobzhansky deleted two chapters that focused on non-adaptive aspects of evolutionary change: a small amount of the material in these chapters was sprinkled throughout the updated text, but most of it was excised (Gould 1980, p. 526). He mentioned the role of small populations, but with far less emphasis than Huxley, who, as we have seen, repeatedly referred to the work of Sewall Wright. Dobzhansky agreed that “much evidence secured by different biological disciplines…attests the existence of phenomena which can not most plausibly be accounted for by genetic drift” (Dobzhansky 1951, p. 176). As an example of such a phenomenon, he cited the distribution of the desert plant *Linanthus polyphyllus* in the Mojave Desert, noting that “as to [its] microgeographic variation, the most reasonable hypothesis is that it is caused by genetic drift” (Dobzhansky 1951, p. 169). His overall conclusion about drift, however, was the rather halfhearted concession that it might have some effect in small populations, but further studies were needed.

In the first edition, there is a lengthy discussion concerning the adjusting role that natural selection plays in evolutionary processes. If genetic drift is operative at all, Dobzhansky seemed to be arguing, at least some aspects of the process are attributable to random events, contradicting the idea of the beneficial, deterministic, nonrandom processes Huxley was emphasizing. In the second edition, this material was considerably reduced. The deletion of the chapters on non-adaptive evolution, the reduced discussion of the role of small populations, and the softening of his stance on genetic drift all combine to suggest a move away from a more pluralistic evolutionary theory and toward a more selectionist one.

> **Figure:** A black and white photograph of Ernst Mayr. He is an older man with white hair, wearing a suit and tie. He is standing in front of a bookcase filled with books. The background is a library or office setting. The photograph is a portrait, focusing on Mayr's face and upper body.

The third edition (1970) contains even less discussion of non-adaptive evolution. The chapter on “The Genetics of Natural Populations” (ch. 8) is almost entirely devoted to selection. The discussion of the role of chance is relegated to a few pages near the end of the chapter (Dobzhansky 1970, pp. 169–172). He still acknowledges the importance of random processes, but he frames them as “episodic” and “fluctuating” and as being of less importance than directional selection (Dobzhansky 1970, p. 170). He writes that “the relative importance of the several factors of evolutionary change is difficult to assess” (Dobzhansky 1970, p. 171), but the overall impression is that he now believes that natural selection is the dominant force in evolution. 

The shift in Dobzhansky’s emphasis between the first and third editions of *Genetics and the Origin of Species* is striking. It reflects, in part, the growing influence of the “modern synthesis,” which emphasized the importance of natural selection as the primary mechanism of evolution. It also reflects Dobzhansky’s own changing views on the subject. While he remained a committed defender of the importance of genetics in evolution, he became increasingly convinced that natural selection was the most important force driving evolutionary change. This shift in emphasis had a significant impact on the field of evolutionary biology, helping to solidify the dominance of the neo-Darwinian perspective.

This is related," he wrote, "to the still vital problem of micro-evolution as opposed to macro-evolution...if the two proved to be basically different, innumerable studies of micro-evolution would become relatively unimportant and would have a minor value to the study of evolution as a whole" (quoted by Gould 2002, p. 529).

In 1944 Simpson proposed the idea of quantum evolution in order to explain macro-evolutionary trends. He suggested that genetic drift might push a small population into an “adaptive peak,” off a local adaptive peak. The population would then be forced to change or die—to develop major new adaptations to enable it to thrive in its new circumstances, or to become extinct. For this reason, Simpson called it a “quantum” phenomenon; it was all or nothing. Simpson’s idea allowed for the same underlying mechanism to drive macroevolutionary trends and small-scale adaptive trends. That mechanism was genetic variation. And yet there was a fundamental difference: natural selection and adaptation were present in the microevolutionary process, but not in the macroevolutionary one. He called his quantum evolution idea “perhaps the most important outcome [of] his investigation, but also the most controversial and hypothetical” (quoted by Gould 2002, p. 529). Elsewhere in *Tempo and Mode*, he emphasized that the quantum evolution idea dethroned selection from its role as sole driver of evolutionary change.

The aspects of tempo and mode that have now been discussed give little support to the extreme dictum that all evolution is primarily adaptive. Selection is a truly creative force and not solely negative in action.3 It is one of the crucial determinants of evolution, although under special circumstances it may be ineffective, and the rise of characters indifferent or even opposed to selection is explicable and does not contradict this usually decisive influence (quoted by Gould 2002, p. 530).

By 1953, Simpson’s view of adaptation had become more dynamic and his definition of quantum evolution had completely changed. He now argued that any advantageous evolutionary trend must have a selective advantage at its inception, thus ruling out the possibility for positive dogmatic “hit-or-miss” on other adaptive features. He now declared that “[g]enetic drift is certainly not involved in all or in most origins of higher categories, even of very high categories such as classes or phyla” (Gould 2002, p. 530). Most strikingly, he now completely redefined quantum evolution as a sort of accelerated selection which while the “continuous maintenance of adaptation,” and note a different sort of evolution from phyletic evolution, or even a distinctly different element of the same thing. Gould (2002, p. 530) wrote, “Indeed my rapid change in such a shift is more rapidly than the usual or even phyletic adaptation can account for it. The two great Mesozoic trends are based on [142-143] ample and impressive evidence. A systematist may not concern himself to evolve the mechanism of these adaptations, but a student of evolution must, and the only consistent explanation is a rapid and quantum rate of adaptation.” As a result, he reasserted the importance of natural selection as the primary driver of evolution, and rejected the idea of non-adaptive, or random, processes playing a significant role in the origin of higher taxa. He concluded that quantum evolution was simply a case of rapid adaptation, and that all evolutionary change, even at the highest levels, was ultimately driven by natural selection. Simpson’s revised view of quantum evolution and adaptation was a significant departure from his earlier ideas, and it reflected a growing consensus among evolutionary biologists that natural selection was the primary force driving evolutionary change.

> **Figure:** A graph titled “Rates of Adaptation” showing two curves. The x-axis is labeled “Time” and the y-axis is labeled “Adaptive Level.” The first curve, labeled “Gradual Adaptation,” is a steadily increasing line. The second curve, labeled “Quantum Adaptation,” is a flat line for a period, then rises sharply. The graph illustrates Simpson’s shift in thinking, from viewing quantum evolution as a non-adaptive process to seeing it as a period of rapid adaptation.

It is also important to note that Simpson’s views on quantum evolution and adaptation were not universally accepted. Some evolutionary biologists, such as George Gaylord Simpson, continued to argue that non-adaptive processes, such as genetic drift, could play a significant role in the origin of higher taxa. However, Simpson’s revised views had a major impact on the field of evolutionary biology, and they helped to solidify the importance of natural selection as the primary driver of evolutionary change. In the end, Simpson’s work on quantum evolution and adaptation helped to shape our understanding of the complex interplay between chance and necessity in the evolutionary process.

By 1957 May had come to the conclusion that 

neutral genes are improbable for physiological reasons… It seems unrealistic to me to assume that the nature of the particular chemical (enzyme or other product) would be without any effect whatsoever on the fitness of the ultimate phenotype. A gene may be selectively neutral when placed on a particular genetic background in a particular temporary physical and biotic environment. However, genetic background as well as environment change continually in natural populations and I consider it therefore exceedingly unlikely that any gene will remain selectively neutral for any length of time. (quoted by Gould 2002, p. 538)

In fact, the idea that a genetic variation might be initially selectively neutral, but could later may take on selective value, is an important concept in current pluralistic evolutionary theory. We will revisit this idea in later chapters in the context of spandrels and exaptations.

During the two decades between the publication of May’s books, some traits that were originally thought to be neutral found to have a selective advantage. This strengthened May’s growing assumption that neutral traits were as rare as to be virtually impossible. “Virtually every case quoted in the past as caused by genetic drift… has, recently been reinterpreted in terms of selection pressures,” he wrote in 1965 (quoted by Gould 2002, p. 538). Moreover, he cited the recently discovered role in copulation of the tarsal claws in some *Drosophila* species and the role of patterns on snail shells previously viewed as “cryptic” in helping the snails evade predation. From these observations, however, he concluded that “selective neutrality can be excluded almost altogether wherever polymorphism or character changes are found in natural populations” (quoted by Gould 2002, p. 538). If the “almost” seems like a fragile concession to pluralism, it did not outweigh May’s certainty of the impossibility of disproving that a trait had selective value. “One can never assert with confidence that a given structure does not have selective significance,” May concluded by Gould 2002, p. 538). One could object that it is possible to show, with statistical rigor, that possessors of a given trait have an approximate equal fitness. The response, however, is that “the experimental conditions are always artificial” (quoted by Gould 2002, p. 538). May’s position—that any detectable polymorphism necessarily reflects a corresponding degree of divergent selection—was consistently maintained throughout his career. 

> **Figure:** A graph depicting the relationship between the number of selectively neutral alleles and the time elapsed. The x-axis represents time in generations, ranging from 0 to 10,000. The y-axis represents the number of selectively neutral alleles, ranging from 0 to 100. Two lines are plotted: a solid line representing the expected number of selectively neutral alleles under the strict neutrality model, and a dashed line representing the observed number of selectively neutral alleles in natural populations. The solid line starts at 0 and increases linearly with time, while the dashed line starts at a higher value and increases at a slower rate. The graph illustrates that the observed number of selectively neutral alleles is consistently lower than the expected number, suggesting that selection plays a role in maintaining genetic variation. The title of the graph is "The Fate of Selectively Neutral Alleles."

In his 1963 book, May acknowledged that “it is, of course, always possible that a character is selectively neutral in a particular environment.” However, he immediately added, “it is exceedingly improbable that it will remain so for long.” He then reiterated his earlier point that “the environment is never constant” and that “selection pressures are always operating.” He concluded that “the assumption that a character is selectively neutral is, therefore, almost certainly false.” (May 1963, p. 184). This position, which Gould (2002, p. 539) aptly described as “a kind of hyper-adaptationism,” was to characterize May’s work for the next two decades. It was a position that would be vigorously challenged by the neutral theory of molecular evolution, which began to emerge in the mid-1960s, largely through the work of Motoo Kimura and Jack King.

# The Essential Tension

A decade later, in their book *The Variation of Animals* Robson and Richards issued a critique that reads like a direct rebuttal of Mary’s faith in the ubiquity of adaptation. 

A survey of the characters which differentiate species [and to a less extent genera] reveals that in the vast majority of cases the specific characters have no known adaptive significance. It may be conceded that in a number of instances structures apparently useless may in the future be found to play an important part in the life of the species; further, many ‘useless’ characters may be correlated with less obvious features which are of real use, but, even allowing for this, the number of apparently useless specific characters is so large that any theory which merely assumes that they are indirectly bound to be a more a matter of predilection than of scientific reasoning. (quoted by Provine, 1986, p. 253)

As both adaptationist viewpoint became increasingly dominant, advocates for nonadaptive change were pushed aside by mid-eighteenth century biology. Yet Wright’s story is far more complex than this. In later years interview with Gould and Provine, Wright argued that he had not advocated a major role for drift in driving evolutionary diversity. In 1957, he wrote “I have never attributed any evolutionary significance to random drift except as a trigger that may release selection toward a higher selective peak through accidental crossing of a threshold” (quoted by Provine 1986, p. 28). As we have seen, quotations from his earlier papers appear to flatly contradict this statement. However, it is true that Wright had never condoned drift as merely a driver of nonadaptive change.

Wright was the first to introduce the idea of an adaptive landscape. In this model, how could a population on a local adaptive peak ever explore the rest of the terrain? Wright’s shifting balance theory, Wright suggested that genetic drift could lead a population from a local peak, allowing the population, now subject to the influence of natural selection, to explore other adaptive peaks. In his 1932 paper he noted that because “species will be shuffled out of low peaks more easily than high ones, [the total population] should gradually drift its way to the higher general regions of the [adaptive landscape] as a whole” (quoted by Provine 1986, p. 235). This Wright conceived of drift as an essential helpmate to natural selection, a source of noise which facilitated exploration of the adaptive landscape (Fig 5.4). As a small increase in temperature can allow a protein to explore its folding landscape. Nonetheless, it was As Provine noted, this idea was not present in Wright’s 1931 work, and thus there is no evidence that his initial ideas of drift were introduced to in order to explain how species explore the adaptive landscape. Nonetheless, it was key aspect of Wright’s work from 1932 onward, and claims of a standalone role for nonadaptive change were increasingly relegated to the sidelines.

> **Figure 5.4:** A diagram illustrating Wright’s adaptive landscape concept. The landscape is depicted as a hilly terrain with multiple peaks representing adaptive optima. A population is shown moving across the landscape, sometimes drifting downhill (representing non-adaptive change) and sometimes climbing uphill (representing adaptive change driven by natural selection). The x and y axes are not explicitly labeled, but represent the genetic composition of the population. The height of the hills represents the fitness of different genotypes. The diagram illustrates how drift can allow a population to escape a local adaptive peak and explore other, potentially higher, peaks.
