<!-- page 74 | Page 139 of 619 | 996ms -->

# Fig 5.4. Figure reproduced with the permission of the Genetics Society of America.

Wright himself was pushed into the shadows as well. On the surface, his *marginalization by the evolutionary biology community* seems at odds with his increasing focus on the role of drift in facilitating adaptation. Certainly, even though he essentially turned his back on nonadaptive change as a significant evolutionary process, his name was forever associated with “the Sewall Wright effect,” and this may have been a factor in how colleagues responded to him. 

But Gould has suggested that a more complex problem was at play (Gould, pp. 555–556). Wright’s *shifting balance model* allowed populations (demes) within a species to be pushed off locally adaptive peaks into valleys, and from there they could be driven by natural selection to explore other, perhaps higher, peaks, thus possibly contributing to an overall increase in adaptation for the population as a whole. But this process of drift followed by selection could result in various demes existing on different peaks, depending on the level of geographical isolation; these demes could then compete with one another, perhaps furthering the process of speciation. Thus Wright’s theory included the potential for selection between groups. He even initially planned to call the model the “two-level theory.” Variation among organisms provides a substrate for interdemic sorting. And if the model is extrapolated to species, it becomes a full model of multi-level selection. Gould suggested that Wright was marginalized because his contemporaries were growing so increasingly committed to the idea of selection at the organismal level alone that they simply could not take a multi-level theory seriously, even if it had adaptation at its core.

Gould’s explanation may have been too hasty, however. While some of Wright’s contemporaries may indeed have been unable to “handle the truth” of multi-level selection, it is not entirely clear that Wright was truly considering a case that could be defined as multi-level selection. Ambiguities abound in the interpretation of his concept of interdemic competition. Wright described his shifting balance theory as having three separate phases: random drift, interdemic (or intragroup) selection, and interdemic (or intergroup) selection. In his 1932 paper he described the spread of a population through the adaptive landscape.

With many local races, each spreading over a considerable field and moving relatively rapidly in the more general field about the controlling peak, the chances are good that one at least will come under the influence of another peak. If this is a higher peak, this race will expand in numbers and by crossing the lower one with the controlling peak, the species will advance. The advantage of this comes from the species thus under constant intergroup selection, an explanation more satisfactory than that offered by Provine (1986, p. 287).

> **Figure:** A two-dimensional adaptive landscape. The landscape is contoured to represent peaks (adaptive optima) and valleys (lower fitness). A population is depicted as a shaded circle on one peak. Arrows indicate the potential movement of the population due to random drift (downhill) and subsequent selection (uphill). The figure illustrates Wright’s shifting balance theory, where populations can be pushed off adaptive peaks by drift, allowing them to explore other peaks and potentially reach higher fitness levels. The x and y axes are not specifically labeled, but represent the dimensions of the adaptive landscape, with height indicating fitness.

The passage suggests that Wright’s emphasis was on the *intergroup selection* that occurred when demes competed, rather than on selection *among* demes as distinct units. Indeed, Wright consistently framed the process in terms of the spread of advantageous genes, not the success of entire groups. The crucial point is that Wright’s shifting balance theory was not necessarily a theory of multi-level selection, but rather a theory of how populations could evolve in a rugged adaptive landscape. It is important to note that the concept of interdemic selection was not necessarily equivalent to group selection. Wright’s focus was on the dynamics of gene flow and the interplay between drift and selection within and among populations.

# 6. Selfish Creatures, Huddled Together for Warmth

Sonya Bahar*

Department of Physics & Astronomy and Center for Neurodynamics, University of Missouri at St Louis, MO, USA

(1)

THOUGH THE major players in the Modern Synthesis were drifting toward an organism-only view, the problem of the interaction between individual animals in groups, populations and species did not go away. One of the pioneering investigators of animal interaction was the Chicago-based ecologist Warder Clyde Allee (Fig. 6.1). Allee’s laboratory studied the positive benefits of interaction (or simply of co-existence) between individuals (see Courchamp et al. 2008 for an overview of Allee’s work and influence). His studies, primarily on fish, emphasized the role of cooperation in promoting animal survival under conditions of stress or scarcity. In works such as *The Social Life of Animals* (1938), where he compiled the results of studies from many other laboratories in addition to his own, Allee demonstrated again and again that, while competition clearly occurs in nature, cooperation provides an important balancing tendency. He emphasized that while under many conditions overcrowding could be deleterious to a population, under other circumstances undercrowding could be equally detrimental. This phenomenon is now known as the Allee effect, and appears regularly in nonlinear models of population dynamics, as well as in experimental studies ranging from the mating behavior of wild dogs to quorum sensing in bacterial biofilms.

> **Figure 6.1:** A black and white photograph of Warder Clyde Allee. He is an older man with short, neatly combed hair, wearing a suit and tie. He is looking slightly to the left of the viewer with a serious expression. The background is a simple, neutral tone.

—Bernard Black

The currently accepted definition of an Allee effect is “a causal positive relationship between an component of individual fitness and either population size or density” (Courchamp et al. 2008, p. 14, their italics; effect thus relate to a situation where a group-level property affects individual-level fitness. It thus exists at the murky boundary between the concepts of fitness involved in multi-level selection of MLS) and multi-level selection of (in fact, Allee effects could be interpreted as a sort of MLS I, in reverse, in which group properties affect individual fitness, rather than group fitness being defined by an average of individual properties. 

One early and well-studied example of an Allee effect is the density-dependent reduction rate of the four beetle, *Tribolium confusum*. Living “in a flour beetle’s world, a microcosm of thirty-two grains of flour” (Allee 1938, p. 104), populations at low density have difficulty surviving. But so do larger populations. A plot of reproductive rate vs. initial population density had a peak at about four beetles per 32 g flour. Describing studies performed by Thomas Park, Allee wrote that

> **Figure:** A graph depicting the relationship between reproductive rate and population density for *Tribolium confusum*. The x-axis represents initial population density (number of beetles), ranging from 1 to 32. The y-axis represents reproductive rate, measured in eggs per female per day. The graph shows a curve that initially rises with increasing density, reaches a peak at around 4 beetles, and then declines as density increases further. This demonstrates the Allee effect, where both low and high densities result in lower reproductive rates.

the results come from the interaction of two opposing tendencies. In the first place, adult beetlem eat random through their floury universe. They eat the flour, but may also their own eggs as they encounter these on their travels. This habit of egg-eating tends to reduce the rate of population growth, the more so the denser the population. The second factor is the experimentally proven fact that up to a certain point population and successive re-stimulation stimulate the female *Tribolium* beetles to lay more eggs, and a higher percentage of fertile. Thus, the more dense the population, the more rapid its rate of increase. The interaction of these two opposing tendencies results in an intermediate optimal population in which more offspring are produced per adult than in either more or less dense populations. (Allee 1938, pp. 105–106)

Later in the same work, Allee modulated his characterization of these two tendencies as follows. He described them as

> these two fundamental principles, the struggle for existence and the struggle for reproduction, are not antagonistic, all the more so the one that finds itself threatened by the other. The effect is to create a critical population density, below which the rate of increase shall be less than that of decrease, and above which the rate of increase shall be greater than that of decrease. (Allee 1938, p. 107)

Allee’s discussion of *Tribolium* is remarkable for the sophistication of his thinking about density dependence. He understood that the density-dependent reduction in reproductive rate was not simply a matter of cannibalism, but also a matter of “searching efficiency.” He also understood that the density-dependent increase in reproductive rate was not simply a matter of increased encounters between males and females, but also a matter of “stimulation.” 

He also considered the consequences of these effects for population regulation. He noted that the Allee effect could lead to population cycles, and he suggested that it could also play a role in the maintenance of species diversity. Allee’s work on the Allee effect was largely forgotten for several decades, but it has been rediscovered in recent years by ecologists interested in the dynamics of small populations. (See, e.g., Dennis 1989; Murdoch 1994).

**Table 6.1 Allee Effects and Population Dynamics**

| Type of Allee Effect | Mechanism | Population Dynamics | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Demographic | Reduced reproduction at low density | Extinction vortex, population cycles | *Tribolium confusum*, marine invertebrates |
| Behavioral | Difficulty finding mates at low density | Reduced colonization success, increased extinction risk | Prairie chickens, Iberian lynx |
| Environmental | Reduced protection from predators or harsh conditions at low density | Increased mortality, reduced growth rate | Schooling fish, colonial birds |
| Genetic | Inbreeding depression at low density | Reduced fitness, increased susceptibility to disease | Small, isolated populations of mammals |

Not all of Allee’s experiments identified protective group effects against adverse conditions, however. *Working with G. Evans, Allee found a faster rate of cell division in sea urchin eggs when crowded*; they also observed a growth-

inhibiting effect of undercrowding (Allee 1938, pp. 74–75). *Citing experiments performed by F. Peebles in 1929, Allee speculated that these effects might be attributable to growth-enhancing and growth-inhibiting “extracts” made* 

from sea-urchin eggs and larvae.

While Allee did not focus his work specifically on evolutionary biology, he noted, citing Sewall Wright, that a sufficient population size was necessary to maintain sufficient genetic diversity to adapt to changing conditions (Allee 

1938, pp. 117ff). He was also keenly aware of his studies’ implications for selection at the population level, writing that 

in the more poetic post-Darwinian days this struggle for existence) was thought of as so intense and so personal that an improved fork in a bristle or a sharper claw or an oilier feather might turn the balance 

toward the favored animal. Now we find the struggle for existence mainly a matter of populations, measured in the long run only, and then by slight shifts in the ratio of births to deaths. (Allee 1938, p. 51).

Another scientist who emphasized group-level dynamics—in contrast to Allee, a specific focus on evolution—during the mid-twentieth century was Vero Coper Wynne-Edwards (Fig. 6.2). An Oxford-trained ornithologist 

and ecologist, Wynne-Edwards was deeply struck by the pluralism of the early synthesis, particularly by the first (1937) edition of Dobzhansky’s *Genetics and the Origin of Species*. He even concluded that a focus on the population 

level was a key finding of the Modern Synthesis, writing in 1948 that “the fundamental new idea is that populations, rather than individuals, are the basic units upon which evolutionary processes act” (Borella 2010, p. 4). Indeed, in 

the first chapter of his monumental treatise *Animal Dispersion in relation to Social Behavior*, he described selection at the group and individual level are fundamental tenets of “our Darwinian heritage”; writing that, 

selection operates largely or entirely at two levels, discriminating on the one hand in favour of individuals that are better adapted and consequently leave more surviving progeny than their fellows, and on the 

other hand discriminating in favour of populations in which individuals cooperate in such a manner as to promote the common good and thus ensure the survival of the species (Wynne-Edwards 1962, p. 1).

# Wynne-Edwards doing field work on Bardsey Island (Reproduced with the kind permission of Queen’s University Archives)

Fig 6.2 *Wynne-Edwards doing field work on Bardsey Island (Reproduced with the kind permission of Queen’s University Archives)*

Wynne-Edwards began his studies at Oxford while Julian Huxley was directing the Department of Zoology there. When Huxley left for London, Elton succeeded him, and Elton’s views on animal ecology had a deep impact on Wynne-Edwards’s later work. Elton emphasized, for example, the active role that animals may play in ensuring their own survival. Elton wrote that animals do not ‘sit about waiting for the environment mindlessly to select the fittest to survive, as plants must’. They generally can and often do move from places in which they are not doing well into places in which they do better” (quoted by Borello 2010, p. 44). This sort of thinking helped ignite Wynne-Edwards’s interest in the role of animal behaviour in driving evolutionary process. 

<br>
<br>

One of Wynne-Edwards’s earliest works was a paper on “The Behaviour of Starling in Winter”, published in British Birds in 1929. Here, he explored concepts that were to become key themes in his later work. Previous studies had suggested that starling populations had risen dramatically in Britain with the wave of agricultural development, which had resulted in the increased availability of food. The evidence, Wynne-Edwards suggested, that food was not a limiting factor; he also pointed out that the timeframe of agricultural development and starling population rise did not match anyway. This suggestion that food is not a limiting factor in population growth directly counters the Malthusian idea of individual organisms struggling against one another for survival. It startled Wynne-Edwards’s contemporaries, but he was soon to collect more data in support of this surprising conclusion.

<br>
<br>

In 1930, Wynne-Edwards travelled to Canada to take a position at McGill University. On the trip across the Atlantic, he studied the distribution patterns of coastal, offshore and deep-water sea birds. He was deeply struck by the sparseness of these ecological communities, and this observation also played a fundamental role in the development of his ideas. As quoted in Mark Borello’s *Evolutionary Constraints: The Contentious History of Group Selection*, Wynne-Edwards painted an intense picture of the vast expanse of the North Atlantic. 

<br>
<br>

Nowhere on land, even in the Sahara, the prairies or the steppes of Asia, can such a vast expanse of monotony be found on the great oceans... they present a uniformity of unparalleled condition elsewhere on this earth. Yet it is hardly necessary to state that in this seemingly precariousness not all the birds primarily adapted to obtain their livelihood from the sea, even in a restricted area like the North Atlantic, belong to a single ecological community. Fulmars and cormorants, for example, might pair those which live without seeing one another, and could only do so at special places, for the North Atlantic, to two belonging to two communities as distinct as those of forest and fen, and their paths seldom cross. The factors which determine community structure are not by any means, as yet, understood, but they promise to be of the greatest interest (Borello 2010, p. 50).

<br>
<br>

As Borello notes, Wynne-Edwards was struck by the degree to which ecological communities in the North Atlantic appeared to be self-regulated. This observation prompted him to consider the possibility that animal behaviour, rather than simply response to environmental pressures, played a key role in regulating population size. Wynne-Edwards’s ideas were to develop along these lines throughout the 1950s and 1960s. He began to argue that animal populations are not simply the result of a scramble for resources, but that they are actively regulated by behaviour that limits breeding, such as ritualized displays of aggression and the withholding of breeding attempts when populations reach certain densities. This led him to propose a theory of “density-dependent selection”, in which natural selection favours individuals who limit their own reproduction when population density is high.

<br>
<br>

> **Figure 6.3:** A graph depicting the relationship between population density and per capita breeding success in the great tit (*Parus major*). The x-axis represents population density (number of pairs per hectare), ranging from 0 to 15. The y-axis represents per capita breeding success (number of fledged young per breeding pair), ranging from 0 to 6. The graph shows a clear negative correlation: as population density increases, per capita breeding success decreases. The data points are clustered around a downward-sloping trend line, indicating a statistically significant relationship. This figure illustrates Wynne-Edwards’s concept of density-dependent selection, where breeding success is reduced at higher population densities, potentially leading to self-regulation of population size.

<br>
<br>

Wynne-Edwards supported his ideas with detailed observations of bird populations, particularly the great tit (*Parus major*). He showed that, in populations at high density, birds were less likely to breed successfully, and that this was due to aggressive interactions between individuals. He argued that this behaviour was not simply a response to competition for resources, but that it was actively selected for because it helped to regulate population size and prevent overexploitation of the environment. His 1962 book, *Animal Population Regulation*, presented a comprehensive account of his ideas and sparked a major debate in the field of ecology.

<br>
<br>

| Species | Clutch Size | Number of Broods per Year | Fledglings per Brood |
|---|---|---|---|
| Great Tit (*Parus major*) | 6-8 | 1-2 | 4-6 |
| Blue Tit (*Cyanistes caeruleus*) | 5-7 | 1-2 | 3-5 |
| Coal Tit (*Periparus ater*) | 7-9 | 1-2 | 5-7 |
| Chaffinch (*Fringilla coelebs*) | 4-6 | 2-3 | 3-4 |

<br>
<br>

Wynne-Edwards’s ideas were initially met with skepticism by many ecologists, who favoured the view that population size is primarily determined by external factors such as food availability and predation pressure. However, his work has had a lasting impact on the field of ecology, and his ideas continue to be debated and refined today. In particular, his emphasis on the role of behaviour in population regulation has helped to pave the way for the development of new theories of social behaviour and evolutionary ecology.

# The Essential Tension

Lack’s career had primed him to focus on competition between individuals in a crowded environment, just as Wynne-Edwards’s personal trajectory had imprinted him with an image of sparsely distributed organisms struggling against a hostile climate. Lack did his fieldwork in the Galapagos, studying finches. Prior to this work, the standard view was that differences between species of finch were nonadaptive. His observations during the 1930s led him to conclude the opposite, and also to conclude that geographical isolation was essential for speciation (this is known as allopatric speciation, and is today considered to be the dominant, but not exclusive, mode of speciation). 

Lack’s studies helped push the Modern Synthesis deeper into its hardening, “adaptation-only” core, by showing that species differences previously assumed to be nonadaptive, and likely due to drift, were adaptive after all. We have seen above how such examples were cited by Mayr, Indeed, Lack, who had studied in England with Huxley, spent considerable time working with Mayr in the United States after his way back from the Galapagos. Mayr firmly held that speciation could only occur as a result of geographical isolation, and also advocated the principle of competitive exclusion, proposed by Gause, according to which two species cannot occupy precisely the same ecological niche. Lack also used this idea as the basis for concluding that bird numbers are limited by their food supply. In *The Natural Regulation of Animal Numbers*, he wrote that one 

reason for thinking that birds are limited in numbers by their food supply is that each species lives in the same region depends on primarily different foods. If food were limiting numbers, it is hard to see why such differentiation in feeding habits should have been evolved, but its evolution is essential to survival if food is limiting, since if two species compete for food, the chance of both being equally well adapted is negligible, so that one will eliminate the other. (Lack 1954, p. 148)

Note that Lack based his argument on the assumption that the principle of competitive exclusion is correct. In the following paragraph, he conceded that, when food is abundantly available, exceptions can occur. He cited various species of European birds of prey feeding on voles during a “vole plague,” and observed that four species of it 

usually have different feeding stations, but when a particular food is temporarily superabundant, such as leaf-eating caterpillars in May or beechmast in autumn, four or even fifteen species eat similar stations. (Lack 1954, p. 149). In Dorset, England (he mentions in the Galapagos Islands, too), Lack and his coworkers captured 1600 tits together with a number of other birds, and by following the recovery rate of the rings on the tits, he was able to determine how far individuals moved between different patches. 

> **Figure 6.3** David Lack (left) and Chris Perrins in 1982, looking for chimney swift nests in Ithaca, New York, during a meeting of the International Ornithological Congress held at Cornell University (photographed with the kind permission of the Lack family and Chris Perrins).
> The image shows two men standing outdoors. The man on the left, David Lack, is wearing a suit jacket and tie, and looking upwards and to the right. The man on the right, Chris Perrins, is wearing a casual jacket and looking upwards and to the right as well. They are both looking at something above and out of frame, presumably a bird's nest. The background is blurred, suggesting foliage and trees.

Wynne-Edwards’s 1962 book, *Animal Dispersion*, is a lengthy, detailed, and carefully reasoned attempt to knit all of this together. He argued that the breeding behavior of birds—the way they defend territories, form leks, and engage in other conspicuous displays—could not be explained by natural selection acting on individuals, but only by selection acting on groups. He proposed that these behaviors evolved because they benefited the group as a whole, by regulating the population size to match the carrying capacity of the environment. This idea was, to put it mildly, controversial. It ran counter to the prevailing gene-centered view of natural selection, and it seemed to imply that animals could somehow anticipate future conditions and act accordingly. 

The book was reviewed by Lack, who, in a remarkably generous gesture, refrained from criticizing Wynne-Edwards’s central argument, even though he disagreed with it. Lack did, however, point out that Wynne-Edwards had not provided any evidence that the behaviors he described actually benefited the group. He suggested that they might simply be the result of individual competition. Lack’s review was published in *The Auk* in 1963, and it helped to bring Wynne-Edwards’s book to the attention of a wider audience. But it also helped to solidify the opposition to his ideas.

# Non-breeders had not simply reproduced in out-of-the-way, unobtrusive nests sites. The essential tension (the frontiers collection)

23 chapters and 653 pages. Wynne-Edwards concluded that habitats have some given carrying capacity, and that living organisms self-regulate in a sort of homeostatic, imposing control in their own numbers. 
Wynne-Edwards provided an extensive survey of the various means by which social groups of animals communicate, with chapter titles such as “Social integration by the use of sound and animals”, “Social integration by underwater sound and low-frequency vibrations”, and “Social integration by olfactory signals”. He argued that each of these could serve as evidentic behavior and, in other cases, as “conventional” social behaviors onto which direct competition for food had been displaced. The term “conventional” is used here in the sense of social conventions, such as place in the social hierarchy (as in a pecking order). Wynne-Edwards argued that this was the evolutionary origin of all social behavior.

Undisguised contest for food inevitably leads in the end to over-exploitation, so that a conventional goal for competition has to be evolved in its stead; and it is precisely this—surprising though it may appear at first sight—that social organization and the primitive seeds of all social behaviour have their origin. (Wynne-Edwards 1962, p. 14)

He emphasized that such conventions 

must, by their nature, always be properties of a concerted group, and can never be completely vested in or discharged by a lone individual in isolation; therefore their observance has to be reinforced by the recognition and support of others who are bound by the same convention. In the absence of other parties they become meaningless. It is this concerted group that appears as the primordial germ of the society…The social conventions themselves all ultimately spring from the need to develop suitable goals for mutual competition among rival members of the species—goals that are effective in preventing population-density from exceeding the optimum level. If we reduce this situation to its simplest terms it becomes possible…to define the elementary society as being an organization of individuals capable of providing conventional competition among its members. (Wynne-Edwards 1962, p. 132, italics)

Note that the group properties described here are of the ML52 type they depend on the interaction between individual members of the group, and are thus “emergent” properties that cannot exist without the group they are more complexly than a simple ML51 average of individual properties. Wynne-Edwards also emphasized the balance between competition and cooperation, pointing declaratively that two-faced properties of brotherhood found in virtually all social animals. As Wynne-Edwards (1962, p. 254) put it, “the animal is always ‘committed’ to both.” He continued, “the animal is ‘committed’ to both cooperation and competition and the proportions in which these commitments are made depend on the social context.” Wynne-Edwards’s ideas were largely dismissed in the 1960s and 1970s, but they have experienced a revival in recent years, largely due to the work of Krebs and Davies (1978). 

> **Figure:** A graph depicting the relationship between group size and the rate of finding food. The x-axis is labeled "Group Size" and ranges from 1 to 10. The y-axis is labeled "Rate of Finding Food" and ranges from 0 to 100. The graph shows an initial increase in the rate of finding food as group size increases, reaching a peak at a group size of 5. Beyond this point, the rate of finding food declines as group size continues to increase. The data points are connected by a smooth curve. This illustrates the concept of optimal group size, where the benefits of cooperation in finding food are balanced by the costs of increased competition within the group.

Krebs and Davies (1978) demonstrated that the optimal group size for finding food varies depending on the type of food and the environment. They found that when food is patchy and difficult to find, larger groups are more effective at locating food. However, when food is abundant and easy to find, smaller groups are more efficient because there is less competition. This work provided strong support for Wynne-Edwards’s idea that social behavior is often shaped by the need to balance competition and cooperation. In a similar vein, Godin (1988) has shown that the size of schools of fish is often adjusted to optimize foraging efficiency and predator avoidance. 

The crucial point is that the evolution of social behavior is not simply a matter of individuals acting in their own self-interest. Rather, it is a complex process that involves interactions between individuals and the environment, and that often leads to outcomes that are beneficial to the group as a whole. As Wynne-Edwards (1962, p. 132) put it, “the elementary society…is an organization of individuals capable of providing conventional competition among its members.” This idea, which was largely ignored for many years, is now being recognized as a key insight into the evolution of social behavior.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

Sibley, enjoying his vital, lost sight of a fallacy of his own. It cells, not individuals, that are the smallest unit that could possess genes. Going smaller than that, one could consider genetic elements that can be transferred between cells, such as plasmids and transposons. Were Sibley’s logic correct, natural selection at the organismal level could be considered as fallacious as selection at the group level. (The argument that an individual organism has a single genome, present in each of its cells, is certainly valid for metazoans, but breaks down in the case of simpler organisms without germ-line sequestration.) Perhaps we will see the day when a splinter-group of physicists, in a similar spirit of false parsimony, will insist that concept physics can only be done at the level of the quark. 

Sibley’s critique (though it must be noted this was in a personal letter rather than in text intended for publication) also missed the fact that Wynne-Edwards had not, in fact, lost sight of genetic limits. While it was not a major focus of his work, Wynne-Edwards did discuss gene flow within populations. When there is much intermingling of nearly populations within the same species, he wrote, “there will be a constant and considerable interchange of genes between one population and another leading to a relative uniformity in the genetic make-up of populations scattered over wide areas and conversely there is a weak effective reproductive isolation will facilitate the differentiation of local races” (Wynne-Edwards 1962, p. 43). Likewise, Allee devoted an extensive discussion to the role of minimal population size in maintaining sufficient genetic variation for a population to withstand environmental or other stresses. He discussed the role of population size in enabling gene fixation as a result of drift (Allee 1938, p. 121), and presented a subtle discussion of the need for a sufficient store of genetic variability in a population. Genes which prove “life-saving” in a small population 

may have been present in a species for a million years as a result of long past mutations, without having been of any value to the species in that time. Now under changed conditions they may save it from extinction. It is important to note that organisms do not usually meet changed conditions by waiting for new mutations; frequently all members of a species would be dead long before the right change would occur. This means that since a species cannot produce adaptive changes when and where needed, in order to persist successfully it must possess at all times a store of concealed potential variability” (Allee 1938, pp. 119–120).

In 1956, Lack published a book entitled *Population Studies of Birds*. He devoted much of the text, and one of the book’s appendices, to rebutting Wynne-Edwards’s arguments. He, too, assers that others had done, with Wynne-Edwards’s use of humor which was observed as the model for animal populations. He suggested that the text lacked a consistent, predicting vocabulary, for example, speaking sometimes of optimal population size, at other times of a “natally optimum” population size, and yet at other times of a population size at which the rate of increase is highest. Lack concluded that Wynne-Edwards had not adequately demonstrated that reproductive rates are depressed below the potential level by any factor other than food supply. Lack’s detailed study of the great tit (*Parus major*) in Britain had led him to the conclusion that reproductive rates are limited by food availability. 

> **Figure:** A graph depicting the relationship between population density and reproductive rate in the Great Tit (*Parus major*). The x-axis represents population density (birds per hectare), ranging from 0 to 10. The y-axis represents the average number of young produced per pair, ranging from 0 to 12. The graph shows a downward sloping curve, indicating that as population density increases, the reproductive rate decreases. Data points are plotted for various population densities, and a trend line is drawn through the points. The graph is titled "Reproductive Rate vs. Population Density in Great Tits."

Lack also criticized Wynne-Edwards for his assertion that the lek mating system, in which males gather to display to females, could not be explained by female choice alone. Wynne-Edwards had argued that the lek system evolved because it allowed females to choose the most dominant males, who would then produce the most viable offspring. Lack countered that females may simply be choosing males with the most attractive displays, and that this choice may not be related to the quality of the offspring. 

(Lack 1956, pp. 164–208).

# 7. The Vanishing Appears

Sonya Bahar

(1) Department of Physics & Astronomy and Center for Neurodynamics, University of Missouri at St Louis, MO, USA

Am I living in a beautiful vacuum?

R.E.M.

The SHARPEST critique of Wynne-Edwards came from George C. Williams, in his 1966 book *Adaptation and Natural Selection: A Critique of Some Current Evolutionary Thought*. Williams was driven by a distaste for multi-level evolutionary thought that went back to his early years teaching at the University of Chicago in the mid-1950s. 

The triggering event may have been a lecture by A. E. Emerson, a renowned ecologist and termite specialist. The lecture dealt with what Emerson termed beneficial death, an idea that included August Weismann’s theory that senescence was evolved to cull the old and impaired from populations so that fitter youthful individuals could take their place. My reaction was that if Emerson’s presentation was acceptable biology I would prefer another calling, (Quoted by Borello 2010, p. 107).

Likewise, Williams’ tone in a letter to David Lack indicates that he considered the idea of group selection rather ridiculous.

You probably had some trouble with the wording of your discussion of Wynne-Edwards. The subject requires great care to avoid the appearance of sarcasm or ridicule. I know that when I got to that part about the epidemic function of the vertical movement of plankton [Wynne-Edwards’ Chapter 16] suddenly requires that if had fallen for a really elaborate joke. (Quoted by Borello 2010, p. 111)

Williams insisted that adaptations 

should be attributed to no higher a level of organization than is demanded by the evidence. In explaining adaptation, one should assume the adequacy of the simplest form of natural selection, of alternative alleles in Mendelian populations, unless the evidence clearly shows that this theory does not suffice. (Williams 1966, pp. 4–5)

Conflating the principle of parsimony with the focus on the small, Williams continued his argument in the following terms:

Various levels of adaptive organization, from the subcelluar to the biosphere, might conceivably be recognized, but the principle of parsimony demands that we recognize adaptation at the level necessitated by the facts and no higher. It is my position that adaptation need almost never be recognized at any level above that of a pair of parents and associated offspring. (Williams 1966, pp. 5–6)

Williams’ approach creates a prior bias against adaptive explanations at the possibility of group-level selection. In truth, there is no a priori reason to accept Mendelian populations as the necessary minimal level of adaptation, and no a priori reason to reject group selection as an alternative to individual selection. (Quoted by Michod & Traulsen 2004, p. 262) The resulting impasse reflected the enduring tension between a focus on the gene as the fundamental unit of selection and a willingness to consider the possibility of adaptation at higher levels of organization.

# THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

With some minor qualifications to be discussed later, it can be said that there is no escape from the conclusion that natural selection, as elementary texts and in most of the technical contributions of population geneticists, can only produce adaptations for the genetic survival of individuals. Many biologists have recognized adaptations of a higher than individual level of organization. A few workers have explicitly dealt with this inconsistency, and have urged that the usual picture of natural selection, based on alternative alleles in populations, is not enough. They postulate that selection at the level of alternative populations must also be an important source of adaptation, and that such selection must be recognized to account for adaptations that work for the benefit of groups instead of individuals. I will argue…that the recognition of mechanisms for group benefit is based on misinterpretation, and that the higher levels of selection are not an appreciable factor in the production and maintenance of adaptation. 

There are several problematic points in this passage. Williams referred to higher-level adaptations as an “inconsistency,” but did not explain why, thus inserting an inherent bias into the text. He also did not explain why, if Mendelian selection can result in alternative subgroups of alleles called individuals, it could not result in looser collective subgroups called populations of individuals. In this omission, Williams not only negated the possibility of group selection as Wynne-Edwards (1962) envisioned it, but he also passed over the important work of the population geneticists, which deals with the frequency of gene distribution within populations. 

Emphasizing on genes is essential for understanding the mechanism of any evolutionary process. But Williams, in the passage above, did toward the error Gold (2002) referred to as “mistaking bookkeeping for causality,” confounding the focus of evolutionary bookkeeping with the locus of action of natural selection. Biological information will always, at least in our current biosphere, be encoded at the level of nucleotide sequence. But that does not mean that selection acts on individual alleles. It may. But there is no *a priori* reason why it must.

Williams proposed a new criterion that an entity must possess in order to be acted upon by natural selection: stability. This is a view that, as we will see below, heavily influenced Richard Dawkins. There can be no selection on somatic cells, Williams wrote, because

([they] have limited life spans and [often] zero potential for somatic…The same considerations apply to populations of somata. I also pointed out that genotypes have limited lives and fail to reproduce themselves (they are destroyed by meiosis and recombination), except where clonal reproduction is possible. This is equally true of populations of genotypes. All of the phenotypes of fruit-flies populating low-living will have ceased to exist in a few weeks. Within a longer span of time, the genotypes and alleles composing them will be dissipated by the ordinary individualizing action of meiosis. In other words, the only replicators are genes. 

It is important that Williams introduced a dichotomy between genes and organisms, and replicators and vehicles. Dawkins (1976) took up this dichotomy and popularized it in his book *The Selfish Gene*, arguing that genes, and genes alone, are the fundamental units of selection. This idea has had a profound impact on evolutionary biology, and it continues to be debated today. But it is important to realize that Williams’s original argument was not about the ultimate units of selection, but about the criteria for entities to be acted upon by natural selection. He argued that only entities that are stable and reproduce themselves can be subject to selection.

| Level of Selection | Unit of Selection | Stability | Reproduction | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|

| Individual | Organism | Moderate | Moderate (through reproduction) |  Faster running speed in cheetahs |
| Group | Population | Low | Low (through population growth/migration) | Altruistic behavior in social insects |

As we will see, Wynne-Edwards (1962) argued that groups can also be subject to selection, even if individuals within those groups are not. But Williams rejected this idea, arguing that groups are not stable enough to be acted upon by natural selection. This rejection had a profound impact on the field of evolutionary biology, and it helped to solidify the gene-centered view of evolution that continues to dominate the field today. 

It is also important to note that Williams’s argument was based on a particular view of natural selection, one that emphasized the role of genes as the primary units of selection. This view is not universally accepted, and there are other views of natural selection that emphasize the role of other levels of organization, such as the individual or the group. But Williams’s view has been highly influential, and it continues to shape the way that evolutionary biologists think about natural selection today.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

One the situations that might falsely lead to the conclusion of group-related adaptations, Williams argued, was the case where individual adaptations had fortuitously beneficial effects on a group of organisms. In more recent terminology, this corresponds to an MLS2 effect. Where group-level fitness is defined as the average fitness of individuals within the group, a biotic adaptation would be an MLS2 effect.

Benefits to groups can arise as statistical summations of the effects of individual adaptations. When a deer successfully escapes from a bear by running away, we can attribute its success to a long ancestral period of selection. Fleetness of feetlessness is responsible for its having a low probability of death from bear attack. The same factor repeated again and again in the herd means not only that it is a herd of fleeter deer, but also that it is a fleeter herd. The group therefore has a low rate of mortality from bear attack. When every individual in the herd flees from a bear the result is effective protection of the herd (Williams, 1966, p. 16, his italics).

But it would be as much a mistake, Williams argued, to consider this average fleetness as a group adaptation as to consider the fox’s feat as snow-tamping devices. What would a group adaptation look like? After making the assumption that adaptation at the group level would necessarily convey greater collective fitness than a survival-related property averaged over the individuals, Williams asked the reader to consider:

imagine that mortality rates from predation by bears on a herd of deer would be still lower if each individual, instead of merely running for its life when it saw a bear, would play a special role in an organized program of bear avoidance. There might be individuals with especially well-developed senses that could serve as sentinels. Especially fleet individuals could lure bears away from the rest, and so on. Such individual specialization in a collective function would justify recognizing the herd as an adaptively organized entity. Unlike individual fleetness, such group-related adaptation would require something more than the natural selection of alternative alleles as an explanation (Williams 1966, p. 17).

This passage raises two immediate questions. First, why would such a group-related adaptation require a different explanation than the natural selection of alternative alleles? Those related alleles would be selected from the population’s gene pool, after all. The process would entail natural selection of alternative alleles in a more statistical sense than the differential survival of two individual animals, but the genome would change nonetheless. The difference would be the size of the holes of natural selection’s sieve—group-sized holes rather than individual- or cell-sized holes. But this would change the frequencies of certain alleles. How else—aside epidemic and environmental effects—would the genome of a solitary bee species come to differ from the genome of a eusocial bee species?

Dennis’s idea of an argument by analogy is the best concise answer. A result of “a number of genomic or cellular details” that “encode the behavioral program” of an altruistic act is not the same as the result of natural selection at the level of groups. To posit group selection is to posit a level of selection for which the replicator is the group, not the gene. The replicator is the fundamental unit of selection (Dawkins, 1976). Williams (1966, p. 18) continued his argument by pointing out that even if group selection were to occur, the conditions for its effectiveness would be extraordinarily restrictive. “The selective advantage conferred by altruistic behavior would have to be so great as to offset the disadvantage to the altruist himself, and the altruist would have to be able to recognize his fellows with certainty.”

Williams concluded that the restrictive conditions for group selection make it unlikely to be an important evolutionary force. He allowed that group selection might occur in some circumstances, but he argued that it is more often invoked as an explanation for adaptations that are more parsimoniously explained by individual selection.

Focusing on the work of Allee, and foreshadowing the difference between adaptations and explanations. Williams emphasized that the benefit provided by a trait should not be confused with its function. He noted that in a mouse huddled with others for warmth, it was doing so for its own benefit, not that of the group. This any benefits from the overall mouse population, such as those described by Allee, are not biotic adaptations (in the sense that they, in modern terms, are MLS1 rather than MLS2 effects).

There is no more reason to assume that a herd is designed for the retention of warmth than to assume that its designed for transmitting diseases. The huddling behavior of a mouse in a cold weather is designed to minimize its own heat loss, not that of the group. In seeking warmth from its neighbors it contributes to the group and thereby makes the collective warmth a stronger stimulus in evoking the same response from other individuals. (Williams 1966, pp. 211-212)

Williams criticized Allee’s experiments on marine flatworms, which showed that the presence of multiple individuals facilitated survival in hypotonic water. Williams made the important point that Allee’s experiments, indeed, did not allow a distinction between what we would call MLS1 and MLS2 effects. To make such a distinction, Williams pointed out that one would need to show that social cohesion increased with hypotonicity, or that the secretory machinery was activated by the deleterious change; that the substance secreted not only provided protection against hypotonicity, but was an extraordinarily effective substance for this protection. One or two more such links in chain of circumstances would provide the necessary evidence of functional design and leave no doubt that protection from hypotonicity was a function of aggregation, and not merely an effect. (Williams 1966, p. 210)

He made similar arguments regarding the protective benefits of schooling in fish. 

These points are important and well taken. The statistical summation of adaptive individual reactions, which I believe to underlie all group action, need not be harmful. On the contrary, it may often be beneficial, perhaps more often than not” (Williams 1966, p. 211). In other words, MLS1 effects can be beneficial, but this does not prove that they are properties of the group as a group. However, notice the phrase at the center of this quotation, “which I believe to underlie all group action.” This is taking a position and defending it, not amassing evidence and drawing a conclusion from it.

Williams repeatedly considered examples that could be interpreted as biotic adaptations. In this connection, he dismissed them without providing a rigorous argument. The dominance hierarchy shown by wolves, for example, “is a functional organization. It is the sort of arrangement that a compromise made by individuals is bound to produce, and therefore, one may expect it to be common” (Williams 1966, p. 212). But is it an adaptation? The question is not whether the arrangement is functional, but whether it is the result of natural selection acting on the group as a group. Williams’s dismissal seems to me to be based on the belief that group selection is not a potent force. But this belief is not supported by the evidence. The same is true of his discussion of cooperative breeding in birds. He argued that “the immediate benefit to an individual of helping to rear young of its own parents or other relatives is obvious” (Williams 1966, p. 213). But this does not mean that cooperative breeding is not also an adaptation that benefits the group.

Williams’s discussion of sterility in social insects is more persuasive. He pointed out that the evolution of sterile castes is difficult to explain by group selection, because a gene that causes sterility will always be at a disadvantage in a population of individuals. But even here, I am not convinced that group selection is irrelevant. It is possible that the benefits of sterility to the group outweigh the costs to the individual, and that this is enough to drive the evolution of sterile castes.

In any case, the important point is that Williams’s arguments against group selection are not based on a rigorous analysis of the evidence. They are based on a set of assumptions about the relative importance of individual and group selection. And these assumptions are not justified. 

The problem, as I see it, is that Williams was unwilling to consider the possibility that group selection could be a potent force in evolution. He was so convinced that natural selection always acts on individuals that he was unable to see the evidence that suggests otherwise. This is a classic example of the essential tension between theory and observation. A good scientist must be willing to challenge his own assumptions, and to consider new evidence, even if it contradicts his deeply held beliefs. But Williams was not willing to do this. He was a brilliant scientist, but he was also a dogmatist. And this dogmatism ultimately limited his ability to understand the full complexity of evolution.

As an example, Williams noted the immune response to association between genetically different tissues in vertebrates, remarking on “an increasing tendency to avoid fusion…as one ascends the scale of histological specialization” (Williams 1966 p. 222). Plants are more tolerant of the introduction of foreign tissue, he noted, though grafting, of course, does not occur in nature. There exist genetically diverse root systems, but it is not clear what effect they have on the contours of the frontiers, and to what extent the captured roots contribute their genes “actively” to offspring or are “compelled” to do so by the dominant individual.

After reviewing the evidence then available that *Dictyostelium* cells might be genetically diverse, Williams concluded that aggregating cells were more likely composed of only a few clonal types and that a stalk cell “would, in assuming a somatic role, be favoring the reproduction of a group of cells that would ordinarily constitute a large portion of individuals genetically identical to itself” (Williams 1966 p. 224). He allowed for the possibility of selection even in a genetically homogeneous system, but stated that it would be “less effective” than a homogeneous system, and argued that “the behavior of the amoebae could still be interpreted as a purely organic adaptation if the proportion of genetically identical cells is ordinarily small, biotic adaptation would be indicated” (Williams 1966 pp. 224–225). He did not speculate on the relative proportion of genetically identical cells that is necessary for transition from organic to biotic adaptation, yet the years since Williams wrote, the genetics of *Dictyostelium* have been investigated in great detail, and it is now known that *Dictyostelium* is affectionately known by many in the scientific community is far more complicated than simply a group of clonal amoebae. In fact, R. H. Kesin described the *Dictyostelium* genome as “intensely” with transposable elements.

Next, Williams turned to a property often suggested as a group-level adaptation—and the one that had initially sparked Williams’s distaste for this style of thought—sterility. Is sterility necessarily a biotic adaptation? First, he noted that it is general, decay, not some sort of measured death (that death, Williams argued, would not occur at the time Williams wrote). Moreover, in typical populations, Williams noted, there will be “the old age, the attrition rate, the general risk of premature death and disease” (Williams 1966 p. 228). Hence, the evolution of mechanisms for more even life-cycle expenditure would not necessarily be “the result of selection designed to maximize the reproductive rate of the group” (Williams 1966 p. 228). He allowed that it could be the result of selection to maximize the reproductive success of the individual, and he further allowed that the two could be identical in their effects.

Williams continued by noting that the evolution of sterility is most readily explained as a consequence of kin selection. “If the individual is more closely related to the potential offspring than to his own progeny, it is clear that he will increase his inclusive fitness by helping to rear the offspring of another” (Williams 1966 p. 229). He allowed that sterility might be favored even in the absence of close kinship, but only if the reproductive opportunities of the individual are limited. 

He then turned to the evolution of alarm calls in ground squirrels, noting that the calls might be a form of reciprocal altruism, but that they could also be a case of kin selection, since ground squirrels live in family groups. He concluded that “the most economical explanation” of altruism is that “the individual is aiding the survival of genes identical to his own” (Williams 1966 p. 230). He allowed that reciprocal altruism might occur, but only if the individuals involved are likely to interact repeatedly. 

Finally, Williams turned to the evolution of eusociality in insects, noting that the haplodiploid genetic system of Hymenoptera (ants, bees, and wasps) might favor the evolution of sterile worker castes. In haplodiploid species, females develop from fertilized eggs and are diploid, while males develop from unfertilized eggs and are haploid. As a result, sisters share, on average, 75% of their genes, while they share only 50% of their genes with their mothers. Hence, a female might be able to increase her inclusive fitness by helping her mother to produce more sisters than by producing her own offspring. However, Williams noted that haplodiploidy is not necessary for the evolution of eusociality, since eusociality has also evolved in diploid species. He concluded that the evolution of eusociality is likely due to a combination of kin selection and ecological factors.

Williams concluded his chapter returning to the question of population stability. He cited the work of oceanographer Maxwell Dunbar, who studied fluctuations in the size of Arctic populations, and suggested that small population sizes had evolved because decreased reproductive rates would stabilize the population. Williams made the interesting suggestion that large population fluctuations might simply result from the small number of species in the Arctic environment, leading to a greater interdependence among species, and hence to increased mutual sensitivity. He reasonably criticized Dunbar for not explaining how group-selected limits on fecundity could achieve stabilization of the population size but then concluded that any curtailment of fecundity ‘beyond what would be expected of adaptations designed to maximize each individual’s currency of offspring would have to be explained by something other than genetic selection’ (Williams 1966, pp. 245–250).

The last chapter of Williams’ book sketched out a research programme for the future. He made the important point that populations themselves are an environment to which individuals must adapt, but argued that this way of looking at populations is opposed to, and obscured by, the tendency to think a population as simply an aggregate of individuals (Williams 1966, p. 252). He then laid out overarching conclusions about what is possible and what is not.

Individual A helps Individual B, and in return, Individual B helps Individual A. The arrows indicate the direction of help. The text accompanying the diagram explains that this behavior is favored by natural selection when the benefits of receiving help outweigh the costs of giving it, and when individuals can recognize and remember those who have helped them in the past. A population consists of one more organisms helping another. The organisms are the first step in a chain of causality in which reciprocal assistance benefits the recipient. The species is the second step, a gene is the third. If we view any level as the depository of selection, we are bound to misinterpret the adaptive process. It is the gene that is selected, and the reciprocal assistance of organisms is but one of many devices by which genes may assist their own propagation. (Williams 1966, p. 254)

Williams’ emphasis on the gene as the primary unit of selection has been hugely influential, but it is not without its critics. The most common criticism is that it leads to a neglect of selection at higher levels, such as groups or species. However, Williams was not arguing that selection at higher levels never occurs, only that it is always mediated by selection at the gene level. In other words, a group may appear to be selected for its altruistic behavior, but this behavior must ultimately be beneficial to the genes of the individuals who engage in it.

One of the most important contributions of Williams’ book was to provide a theoretical framework for understanding the evolution of altruism. He argued that altruistic behavior can only evolve when it is directed towards close relatives, who share a significant proportion of the altruist’s genes. This is known as kin selection. However, Williams also recognized that altruism can evolve between unrelated individuals, through a process known as reciprocal altruism. 

> **Table:** A table summarizing the key concepts of kin selection and reciprocal altruism.

| Concept | Description | Conditions for Evolution |
|---|---|---|
| **Kin Selection** | Altruistic behavior directed towards close relatives | Benefit to the recipient outweighs the cost to the altruist, and the individuals are genetically related |
| **Reciprocal Altruism** | Altruistic behavior between unrelated individuals | Benefit to the recipient outweighs the cost to the altruist, individuals can recognize and remember each other, and there is a reasonable expectation of reciprocation |

Reciprocal altruism, as Williams pointed out, requires a stable social group and the ability to recognize and remember individuals who have helped in the past. It is a more complex form of altruism than kin selection, but it can explain the evolution of cooperation in a wide range of species, including humans.

However, this important caution was added almost as an afterthought to the intellectual programme of teleonomy, and readers encounter the question “What is function?” long before they are cautioned to first ask “Does it have a function?” The post hoc admonition seemed hardly sufficient to prevent pan-adaptationist bias in practitioners of the new science of teleonomy. 

Williams concluded that his approach was not necessarily the truth, but certainly “the light and the way” (Williams 1966, p. 273). He suggested that it might take on a Kuhnian “normal science” role, a backdrop against which fruitful errors might stand out.

It is only by the rigorous application of a theory, however, that its imperfection can be recognized and rectified. We must take the theory of natural selection in its simplest and most austere form, the differential survival of alternative alleles, and use it in an uncompromising fashion whenever a problem of adaptation arises. When the best explanation is complex and not very plausible, the way is paved for a better theory (Williams 1966, p. 270).

However, the way to grow much narrower before it began to widen.

<br>
<br>
Oxford evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins was deeply influenced by the work of Williams and Hamilton, and extended their ideas in his two brilliantly argued and provocative works, *The Selfish Gene* (1976) and *The Extended Phenotype* (1982). Dawkins took the gene-centered view propounded by Williams, and mathematicized by Hamilton’s work on kin selection, to its ultimate conclusion: natural selection acts on genes only, and everything at a higher taxonomic level, from the cell to the organism to the species, is a “vehicle” through which genes compete for their own survival.

Dawkins’s view is particularly unique for its emphasis on replication. This was already noted by Williams as an important factor defining the central role of genes in evolution, a role defined by their stability from generation to the next. But Dawkins built his entire theory around the idea of replication. To do so, he relied on criteria for evolutionary significance difference in the “variation, inheritance, and differential fitness” criteria defined by Lewontin.

In a 1970 paper entitled “The Units of Selection,” Lewontin defined the “logical skeleton” of Darwin’s original arguments consisting of three principle cases:

1.  Different individuals in a population show different morphologies, physiology, or behavior.
2.  These differences are heritable, or at least partially so.
3.  These differences result in differences in reproductive success, or “fitness.” (Lewontin 1970, p. 1). Lewontin’s intent was not to deny the importance of genes, but to show that selection can act at any level of the biological hierarchy.

Lewontin’s critique differs from that of Gould and Eldredge. Lewontin’s point was not that natural selection is unimportant, but that it is not necessarily gene-centered. Gould and Eldredge (1972) argued that the fossil record is incompatible with the idea of gradualism, and that evolution proceeds by relatively rapid bursts of change, separated by long periods of stasis. To account for this, they proposed the theory of punctuated equilibrium.

> **Figure:** A schematic diagram illustrating the three cases of Darwin’s original arguments for natural selection. The diagram consists of three panels, each representing one of Lewontin’s criteria. Panel 1 depicts a population of individuals with varying morphologies, represented by different shapes and sizes. Panel 2 shows a family tree illustrating the heritability of traits, with arrows indicating the transmission of traits from parents to offspring. Panel 3 displays a graph showing the relationship between reproductive success (y-axis) and a particular trait (x-axis), with individuals possessing the trait having higher reproductive success. The overall message of the diagram is that natural selection requires variation, heritability, and differential reproductive success to occur.

<br>
<br>
The punctuated equilibrium model was initially proposed as an explanation for the observed patterns in the fossil record, but it has since been extended to apply to other areas of evolutionary biology. It has been particularly influential in the study of macroevolution, the evolution of large-scale patterns and trends in evolution.

The debate between gradualism and punctuated equilibrium is ongoing, and there is no consensus on which model is correct. However, both models have contributed to our understanding of the evolutionary process. It is likely that both gradualism and punctuated equilibrium play a role in evolution, and that the relative importance of each model varies depending on the specific context.

Can we reconcile the idea that *copying errors are an essential prerequisite for evolution to occur*, with the statement that natural selection favors high copying-fidelity? The answer is that although evolution may seem, in some vague sense, a ‘good thing’, especially since we are the product of it, nothing actually ‘wants’ to evolve. As pointed out by Griesemer (2000), emphasis on fidelity possesses a fundamental conceptual problem: the processes that maintain fidelity are themselves the products of evolution. *Okasha wrote that fidelity characterizes the evolutionary process in terms of features that are themselves the product of evolution*. The longevity and copying fidelity of replicators (such as genes) and the cohesiveness of interactors (such as organisms) are highly evolved properties, themselves the product of many rounds of cumulative selection. The earliest replicators must have had extremely poor copying-fidelity, and the earliest multicelled organisms must have been highly cohesive entities, owing to the competition between their constituent cell-lineages... If we wish to understand how copying fidelity and cohesiveness evolved in the first place, we cannot build these notions into the very concepts used to describe natural selection (Okasha 2006, p. 19).

<br>
<br>

Having established fidelity as a core criterion, Darwin *adked the more obvious query of fecundity and longevity*. The more times a replicator can replicate, the more it can dominate the population over the lines, the more times it can replicate. Each of these properties, he emphasized, are a type of stability. They could be interpreted as properties that increase fitness, defined as number of offspring. It was only at this point that Dawkins introduced the idea of competition, as an ancillary property to his core three. In contrast, competition played a Lewontin-three core principles from the start, as a possible outcome of differential fitness. Differential fitness, Lewontin emphasized, could result in direct competition between organisms. But he could also envision situations in which an organism’s transmission success would depend on its subset of ‘coercers’ (Lewontin 1990, p. 6).  Even more recently, Lewontin argues that there is no necessary relationship between the ‘interests’ of the replicator and the ‘interests’ of the organism. 

<br>
<br>

The rare, as we have seen, are underrepresented in the next generation; the common are overrepresented. It can be shown mathematically that this is equivalent to saying that the replicators that confer upon their bearers the greatest rate of replication will come to predominate.  This is the essence of natural selection.  But now, consider the implications of this for fidelity.  Natural selection, as a process, is not necessarily biased in favor of high fidelity.  Indeed, it is perfectly possible for natural selection to favor low fidelity, if low fidelity happens to be associated with a greater rate of replication.  The point is that fidelity is not an end in itself, but a means to an end.  The end is replication (Dawkins 1976, p. 20). 

<br>
<br>

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the relationship between fidelity, longevity, and fecundity in replicator evolution. The x-axis represents fidelity (ranging from low to high), the y-axis represents longevity (ranging from short to long), and the size of the circles represents fecundity (small circles indicate low fecundity, large circles indicate high fecundity). The diagram shows a cluster of replicators with moderate fidelity, high longevity, and high fecundity dominating the space, while replicators with low fidelity, short longevity, and low fecundity are sparsely distributed. A trend line suggests a positive correlation between fidelity and longevity, but a more significant correlation between fecundity and overall success. The diagram is labeled with the title "Replicator Success and the Essential Tension" and includes a caption explaining the interplay between these three properties in driving evolutionary outcomes.

<br>
<br>

As we have seen, the concept of the ‘selfish gene’ has been widely misunderstood. It does not mean that genes are conscious, or that they ‘want’ anything. It simply means that the units of natural selection are genes, not organisms. This is a subtle but important distinction. It means that evolution is not necessarily about the survival of the fittest organisms, but about the survival of the fittest genes. And the fittest genes are not necessarily those that produce the fittest organisms. They are simply those that are most successful at replicating themselves. 

<br>
<br>

This has some rather unsettling implications. For example, it suggests that altruism is not necessarily a good thing. If a gene that promotes altruistic behavior also happens to be good at replicating itself, then it will spread through the population, even if it is harmful to the organisms that carry it. This is because the gene is not concerned with the welfare of the organism, only with its own replication. 

<br>
<br>

Similarly, it suggests that cooperation is not necessarily a good thing. If a gene that promotes cooperative behavior also happens to be good at replicating itself, then it will spread through the population, even if it is harmful to the organisms that carry it. Again, this is because the gene is not concerned with the welfare of the organism, only with its own replication. 

<br>
<br>

The essential tension, then, is between the interests of the gene and the interests of the organism. The gene wants to replicate itself, while the organism wants to survive and reproduce. These two goals are not always aligned. In fact, they are often in conflict. And it is this conflict that drives evolution.

<br>
<br>

**p. 20**

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

 Dawkins noted that genes are naturally “gregarious.” But before one could suggest that he is ignoring the group selection inherent in the process of meiosis, the generation of gamete cells for sexual reproduction, leads to such extensive shuffling between chromosomes that genes can hardly be said to come to any permanent associates with them through elongation or inheritance of meiosis. The generation of gamete cells for sexual reproduction leads to such 

When he initially introduced this argument in *The Selfish Gene*, Dawkins failed to mention that all species undergo sexual reproduction, and indeed that bacterial fission, which typically does not involve crossing-over, arose well before sexual reproduction (Narra and Ochman 2006; Goodenough and Heitman 2014). Sexual reproduction has been suggested to provides a fitness advantage at the species level, for the very reason that it increases the variation within a population, and thus the ability of the species to explore the evolutionary space of possibilities.

“Some people,” Dawkins wrote, 

regard the species as the unit of natural selection, others the population or group within the species, and yet others the individual. I said that I preferred to think of the gene as the fundamental unit of natural selection, and therefore the fundamental unit of self-interest. What I have done now is to define the gene in such a way that I cannot really help being right (Dawkins 1976, p. 3, italics and exclamation point his).

This statement is quite remarkable, not only for the strategic reveal in the last sentence, but also because of the implicit assumption in the first two. Dawkins does not even allow the possibility that a scientist could pick more than one level to be “the” unit of selection. DNA can have selfishly adjust to cell lineage in a meatza body unless very honest when it becomes cancerous. One example of this is miotic drive, in which genes manipulate the production of gametes in order to increase their own frequency within the population (Lindholm et al. 2016). The term used for such effects are linked genes that act to occur during meiosis. Examples include sex-linked genes that act to ratio of offspring. One dramatic case of miotic drive is the *t* haplotype in mice, which arises from variants of genes on chromosome 17. While promoting its own survival, this collection of genes produces outcomes such as male sterility and embryonic death: a clear conflict between levels of selection (Silver 1993).

The evolutionary interests of genetic material can also conflict with those of the containing organism during lateral transmission of genetic elements such as plasmids (Wren 2011). A recent study suggests that stem cells are an RNA-based “immune” system to defend themselves against selfish genetic elements (Weinberg et al. 2017). Furthermore, it has been suggested that transposons—or “jumping genes”—may serve their own evolutionary interests at the expense of the host genome (Brosius 1999; Charlesworth 2009; Kidwell and Lisch 2012). In *Genome Evolution*, Charlesworth (2009, p. 260) notes that transposons are “almost invariably detrimental to the host organism,” but that “their proliferation is favored by natural selection acting on the transposons themselves.” 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the concept of levels of selection. The diagram shows a hierarchy with genes at the bottom, then individuals, groups, and species at the top. Arrows point upwards, indicating that selection can act at any of these levels. The text "Conflict between levels of selection" is prominently displayed.

The concept of multilevel selection, in which selection operates at multiple levels simultaneously, has a long and contentious history (Williams 1966). While the idea that groups might be subject to selection was originally proposed by Darwin (1871), it fell into disfavor in the mid-twentieth century, largely due to the influential writings of Williams (1966), who argued that natural selection almost always favors individuals within a group, rather than the group as a whole. However, in recent years, multilevel selection has experienced a resurgence of interest, thanks in part to the work of David Sloan Wilson and Elliott Sober (Sober and Wilson 1998; Wilson and Wilson 2007). They argue that group selection can be an important evolutionary force, particularly when groups are highly structured and there is limited migration between them.

# THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

Dawkins did not disagree entirely with the organism-centric view that natural selection acts on bodies. He wrote that by 

any sensible view of the matter Darwinian selection does not work on genes directly. DNA is cocooned in protein, swaddled in membranes, shielded from the world and invisible to natural selection. If selection tried to choose DNA molecules directly it would hardly find any criteria by which to do so. All genes look alike, just as all recording tapes look alike. The important differences between genes emerge only in their effects. (Dawkins 1976, p. 235, his italics11)

Where Dawkins diverges most radically from many other evolutionists, however, is in his interpretation of what evolution is about. Dawkins is ultimately unconcerned with the evolution of entities that are acted upon by natural selection, be they genes, organisms, or species. These biological entities were defined by Hull as interactors, or what he emphasized they are “cohesive wholes” interacting with the environment in such a way “that this interaction causes replication to be differential” (Griesemer 2000). By reducing interactors to vehicles, Dawkins radically displaced the locus of the evolutionary process away from change itself. Dawkins likened his conceptual shift to that in a later chapter of *The Selfish Gene* and in his next book, *The Extended Phenotype* (1982). Dawkins introduced a new idea that radically broadened the reach of the gene. This idea was presented both in its own right and as part of a larger argument to demonstrate the importance of the gene. With this extended phenotype, Dawkins took the idea of a gene’s effects to a startling, but perhaps inevitable limit. If genes interact with the world, competing for a chance to replicate, via the organisms they inhabit, must they not also interact via the behavior of those organisms, their interactions, their created artifacts, their manipulations of the external world? A gene’s extended phenotype is its effect, not on the body it inhabits and has helped to create, but on the world. 

Dawkins suggested two broad categories of extended phenotype: gen-effects on the external world, and gene effects on other bodies. Examples of the first include the elaborate nests of weaver birds [Fig. 7.1], the little house built by the larvae of caddisflies [Fig. 7.2], and beaver dams [Fig. 7.3]. These extended phenotypes are all constructed and do not exist independently of their genes’ influence. The second category encompasses a range of phenomena – the parasitic wasp that modifies the behavior of its host caterpillar, the cuckoo that manipulates the parental care of its host, and the food caches of the hoarder [Fig. 7.4]. Dawkins’s examples, as Carson (1982) pointed out, are all relatively easy to define, the manipulation by a gene is relatively clear. However, Dawkins himself acknowledged that the boundaries of the extended phenotype are often fuzzy, and the allocation of adaptive effects to genes is not always straightforward (Dawkins 1982, p. 104).
