Photograph by Lars Råbacken Lindahl [https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Beaver_dam_Jamtland.jpg, licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International, 3.0 Unported, 2.5 Generic, and 1.0 Generic License]

Another example of parasite and host genes at odds is the protozoan *Nosema*, which infects flour beetles, producing a substance similar to the beetle’s own juvenile hormone, prolonging the larval stage. The giant larvae, twice the size of normal adults, cannot mature (and thus cannot reproduce) but make excellent hosts. Dawkins also described the parasitic castration of certain crab species by *Sacculina*, a parasite related to barnacles. 

<br>

It drives an elaborate root system deep into the tissues of the unfortunate crab, and sucks nourishment from its body. It is probably no accident that among the first organs that it attacks are the crab’s testicles or ovaries; it spares the organs that the crab needs to survive – as opposed to reproduce – till later… Like a fattened bulldog, the castrated crab directs energy and resources away from reproduction and into its own body (Dawkins 1976, pp. 242–243).

<br>

Returning to the snail and fluke to draw his selfish gene conclusions, Dawkins remarked that the genes of the fluke and those of the snail can both be viewed as parasites in the snail body.

<br>

This raises an important distinction between types of genetic parasitism. In the three examples above, parasite genes depend on host survival but not on host reproduction, and thus can wantonly squander the reproductive chances of their host. But in other cases, such as the parasite’s transmitted through the host’s eggs, the reproductive interests of both sorts of genetic parasites align. Bacteria’s parasitism on the haploidploid ambrosia beetle is transmitted through the host’s eggs, and actually provide a necessary stimulus to unfertilized eggs that will develop into males. Likewise, an alga transmitted via the egg of a fly larva species provides its host with oxygen, rather than depleting the hyra’s resources as do other parasites; alive that live in hyra but do not transmitted via its eggs. In such cases, Dawkins suggested that a parasite is likely to ‘graft’ itself on to the host, where ‘share the destiny’ as those can be one could ask what selective processes would drive the evolution of such co-operation? Only those that depend on host reproduction for their own transmission. The genes of the parasite, after all, will only be passed on if the host reproduces. We will discuss this issue further in Chapter 8. But for now, it is sufficient to note that the selective pressure for cooperation between parasite and host is not necessarily any different from the selective pressure for cooperation between genes in the same individual. The genes in a multicellular organism cooperate, as we have seen, because they are all copies of themselves, and thus share the same destiny. A parasite that is transmitted through its host’s eggs is in a similar position (Dawkins 1976, pp. 244–245).

<br>

The crucial feature of a gene is that it is a unit of selection. It is the gene that is ‘selfish’, and it is the gene that will be selected for if it increases its own representation in the next generation. This is not to say that individual organisms are not also subject to selection. Of course they are. But the interests of the individual organism and the interests of its genes are not necessarily the same. Indeed, as we have seen, they are often in direct conflict. The individual organism is merely a vehicle, a temporary container, for the genes. And the genes will use the vehicle in whatever way best serves their own interests, even if it is detrimental to the vehicle. 

<br>

> **Figure:** A photograph of a beaver dam in a river. The dam is constructed of logs, branches, and mud, creating a pond behind it. The surrounding landscape is a forest with green trees and a blue sky. The image illustrates the concept of the extended phenotype, where an organism's genes influence traits beyond its body, such as the construction of a beaver dam. The beaver's genetic predisposition to build dams alters the environment, creating a new habitat.

<br>

The concept of the extended phenotype has far-reaching implications. It suggests that the effects of genes are not limited to the bodies of the organisms that carry them. Genes can also influence the world around them, creating structures and modifying environments in ways that enhance their own survival and reproduction. Dawkins (1982, pp. 222–223) gives the example of the cuckoo, which lays its eggs in the nests of other birds. The cuckoo chick then evicts the host’s own eggs or chicks from the nest, ensuring that it receives all of the food and attention from the host parents. The cuckoo’s genes have thus extended their influence beyond the cuckoo’s own body to include the behavior of the host bird and the fate of its offspring.

<br>

**Table 7.1 Examples of the extended phenotype**

| Organism | Extended Phenotype | Genetic Basis | Adaptive Significance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Beaver | Dam construction | Genes influencing dam-building behavior | Creates habitat, protects from predators |
| Cuckoo | Host nest parasitism | Genes influencing egg mimicry and chick eviction | Ensures cuckoo chick receives all resources |
| Spider | Web building | Genes influencing silk production and web design | Captures prey, provides shelter |
| Termite | Mound building | Genes influencing social behavior and construction | Provides climate control, protection from predators |
| Human | Tool making | Genes influencing dexterity and cognitive abilities | Enhances hunting, gathering, and survival |

<br>

The extended phenotype is a powerful concept that challenges our traditional understanding of the gene and the organism. It reminds us that genes are not simply blueprints for building bodies, but rather units of selection that can influence the world in a variety of ways. And it suggests that the boundaries between the organism and its environment are often blurred, as genes extend their influence beyond the confines of the body to shape the world around them.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

As for organisms can be said to have some sort of collective identity separate from their role as vehicles, they are doomed to the comparative insignificance under Darwin’s scheme from the start, because their genetic goals, since all the cells in a multicellular organism can be expected to be clones(*4*).

Why the bottlenecked life cycle? Why return to a single cell to start a new generation? Dawkins answered these questions with the metaphor of two plant species; ‘bottle-wrack’ and ‘spurge-weed’. Spurge-weed reproduces by simply breaking off pieces of itself very often, while bottle-wrack reproduces by sporulation. The regularly repeating life cycle allows bottle-wrack to “return to the drawing board” in each generation, and fixed sequence and calendar for embryological development. It also allows for genetic unity within a single plant. 

In splurge-weed, cell lineages are broad-rooted… It is therefore quite possible that two cells in a daughter will be more distant relatives of one another than either is to cells in the parent plant… bottle-wrack differs sharply from splurge-weed here. All cells in a daughter plant are descended from a single spore cell, so all cells in a given plant are closer cousins (or whatever) of one another than any cell in another plant… In bottle-wrack, the individual plant will be a unit with a genetic identity, will deserve the name individual… Selection will therefore judge rival plants, not rival cells as in splurge-weed. (Dawkins 1976, pp. 263-265)

These individual plants, however, are still subservient to ‘the fundamental unit, the prime mover of all life, which is’ (*5*) the replicator (Dawkins 1976, p. 264). But Dawkins allowed group selection to slip, just for a moment, and ‘strictly for those with a professional interest’. One can find an ‘analogy here’, he wrote 

with the argument over group selection. We can think of an individual organism as a group of cells. A form of group selection can be made to work, provided some means can be found for increasing the ratio of between-group variation to within-group variation. Bottle-wrack’s reproductive habit has exactly the effect of increasing this ratio; splurge-weed’s habit has just the opposite effect. (Dawkins 1976, p. 265)

Curiously, this argument occurs more the pages after the assertion that it was ‘positively wrong to consider genes encoding the members of a complex enzymatic pathway as being selected as a group.

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the life cycles of “bottle-wrack” and “spurge-weed”. Bottle-wrack undergoes a sexual reproduction cycle involving meiosis and the fusion of gametes, resulting in a single zygote that develops into a new plant. Spurge-weed reproduces asexually through fragmentation, where pieces of the parent plant develop into new, genetically identical plants. The diagram emphasizes that in bottle-wrack, all cells in a new plant are derived from a single spore, making them closely related, whereas in splurge-weed, cells within a plant are more distantly related due to the broad-rooted nature of its cell lineages.

In the later chapters of *The Selfish Gene*, Dawkins noted the similarities between sporulation and sexual reproduction. The essential similarity, and therefore the reason Dawkins initially favoured the former, is that sporulation involves a bottleneck, a single cell from which a new individual develops, whereas vegetative reproduction does not. The bottleneck ensures that the new individual is genetically uniform. ‘It is the bottleneck which makes the individual a real individual, and not merely a heap of cells’ (Dawkins 1976, p. 266). But Dawkins also allowed that ‘if the conditions are right’, a degree of selection *could* occur among the cells within a splurge-weed clone. 

The key to the matter, as always, is the relative importance of between-group and within-group selection. ‘If vegetative reproduction is very successful, the cells within a clone will be highly related to one another, and there will be little scope for selection among them’ (Dawkins 1976, p. 267).

> **Table:** A comparison of Bottle-wrack and Spurge-weed characteristics.
>
> | Feature | Bottle-wrack | Spurge-weed |
> |---|---|---|
> | Reproduction | Sexual (sporulation) | Asexual (fragmentation) |
> | Genetic Unity | High (all cells from single spore) | Low (cells distantly related) |
> | Bottleneck | Present | Absent |
> | Cell Relatedness | High | Low |
> | Selection Level | Individual plant | Potentially within cells |

But if vegetative reproduction is difficult, and clones often die out, then the cells within a clone will be less closely related, and there will be more scope for selection among them. ‘In this case, it is at least conceivable that some of the cells might evolve in a manner which is selfish from the point of view of the clone as a whole’ (Dawkins 1976, p. 267). Dawkins’s point is not that group selection *never* happens, but that it is difficult to establish, and easily disrupted. The conditions that favour group selection are precisely the conditions that make the group a more cohesive, genetically uniform unit.

# 8. Flocking, Swarming, and Communicating

Sonya Bahar

(1) Department of Physics & Astronomy and Center for Neurodynamics, University of Missouri at St Louis, MO, USA

Lordly, I hope there are tapes. 
–James Conroy

AS WE have seen, Durkheim and others attempted to explain how groups of humans come together as a collective. One of the most beautiful innovations of twentieth century physics was the ability to analyze such behavior with statistical methods and computational models. This has enabled researchers to quantify the specific aspects of a group of individuals that change as the individuals coalesce into a group. For the first time, a quantitative step could be taken toward answering the question when does a group become a separate individual in its own right?

Ironically, one of the first steps along this road was taken, not by a physicist at all, but by a biologist – and one who was using a computational argument to support his stance against group selection, no less. This was none other than D. Hamilton, whose work inspired Richard Dawkins. In a 1971 paper entitled “Geometry for the Selfish Herd,” Hamilton proposed a model by which marginal predation drove the evolution of gregariousness. This was designed to explicitly counter the group selection arguments of Allee and Wynne-Edwards. To set the stage for his model, Hamilton asked his readers to picture a dry pond.

Imagine that the pond shelters a colony of frogs and a water-snake. The snake preys on the frogs but only does so at a certain time of day – up to the time it sleeps on the bottom of the pond. Shortly before the snake climbs out of the pond the frogs climb out onto the rim of the pond. It is because the snake catches frogs in the water if it can’t find any, however, it nears its head out of the water and surveys the disconsolate line sitting on the rim – it is supposed that the fear of terrestrial predators prevents the frogs from going back from the rim – the snake surveys this line and snatches the nearest one. (Hamilton 1971, his italics.)

Hamilton followed this thought experiment with computer simulations of the frogs, and of other prey animals in a two-dimensional landscape. Hamilton built on earlier ideas presented by Galton and others, as well as mid-seventeenth century mathematical models of optimal packing, to illustrate how “selfish avoidance of a predator can lead to aggregation” (Hamilton 1971). In his pursuit, a group, even the most disorganized of how individuals respond to the emergence of a group, and therefore a debut into the realm of collective behavior. In 1973, J. Parrish proposed a game theory model for the formation of fish schools, based on the concept of benefits to individual fish resulting from being in a group (Parrish 1973). He assumed that a fish in a group is less likely to be captured by a predator than a solitary fish.

Couzin et al. found that three basic rules were sufficient to reproduce the emergent properties of fish schools: local attraction, alignment, and cohesion. These rules, though simple, resulted in the formation of highly coordinated groups.

He named the interactors in his model “boids” (from “bird-oids,” not from a New Jersey accent) noting that he used this term generically “even when they represent other sorts of creatures such as schooling fish.” Not only, Reynolds found the boid model reduces to interactions between individuals, but those actions were purely local. Reynolds explained the motivational for this requirement as follows.

There is no evidence that the complexity of natural flocks is bounded in any way. Flocks do not become “full” or “over-loaded” as new birds join. When herring migrate toward their spawning grounds, they run in schools extending as long as 17 miles and containing millions of fish. Natural flocks seem to operate in exactly the same fashion over a huge range of populations. It does not seem that any individual bird can be paying much attention to each and every one of the its flockmates. But in a huge flock spread over vast distances, an individual bird must have a localized and filtered perception of the rest of the flock. A bird might be aware of three categories, itself, its two or three nearest neighbors, and the rest of the flock...[T]he amount of thinking that a bird has to do in order to flock must be largely independent of the number of birds in the flock. Otherwise, we would expect to see a sharp upper bound on the size of natural flocks when the individual birds became overloaded by the complexity of their navigational task. This has not been observed in nature. (Reynolds 1987)

In addition to these logical arguments, Reynolds cited the studies by Brian Partridge (1982) showing that schooling fish are more influenced by their close neighbors than by distant fish. With this motivation, Reynolds defined three behaviors that would lead to a flock exhibiting “non-colliding, polarized, aggregated” motion. First, collision avoidance; second, velocity matching, in which each boid would attempt to align with its near neighbors; and, lastly, flock centering, whereby boids attempt to remain close to their nearest flockmates. Note the similarity of this last rule to that used by Hamilton. Using these rules, Reynolds generated quite realistic simulations. He noted that his simulations might be more realistic for animal herds or fish schools than for actual bird flocks, since birds have excellent vision and a wide field of view (~300–360°) and thus would be less likely to be perceived to encoding only a few close neighbors, which may, fish schooling lack in awareness. Future work, he suggested, might include attempts to add to the raptor birds. His following essay taken up by Blumberg and Galey (2000), found that Reynolds in 1979, through diagramming bird flight patterns, was already conceptualizing an agent that would act as a discrete thing that could be represented as the center of gravity. Reynolds’s agent was to be given a set of rules to operate within, and was to be able to react to and interact with other agents, thereby recreating the mesmerizing flight patterns of a flock.

# The Essential Tension

Physicists were quick to notice the relevance of phase transitions and nonlinear dynamics for fundamental problems in biology. While some turned to look for critical scaling in heartbeat fluctuations, others, far more successfully, explored the inherent nonlinearity of the electrophysiological excitation of neurons and cardiac myocytes. Still others were inspired to study fractal growth phenomena in expanding bacterial colonies. And along with the study of growth came the study of crowd behavior to the study of the collective animal behavior was pioneered by Tamás Vicsek, of Eötvös University in Budapest, and his colleagues, in a seminal *Physical Review Letters* paper in 1995 and a detailed follow-up study in J. Phys. A in 1997, they drew the analogy between the alignment of spin states and the alignment of animal velocities during flocking behavior. From this, they developed a computational model that ultimately led to an elegant theory of animal aggregation, capable of describing everything from the massive murmurations of starlings (Fig. 8.1) that cause power cuts in the United Kingdom to how the placement of columns in a theater can aid the escape of a panicked crowd during a fire (Helbing et al. 2000). Flocking has even been used to analyze and model data collected from human motion in mosh pits (Silberberg et al. 2013). Computer modeling of crowd behavior is also now widely used in practical situations such as crowd control and risk analysis. Many of these methods are reviewed in the 2014 book *Introduction to Crowd Science*, written by Keith Still of Manchester Metropolitan University, who has developed a range of sophisticated computational techniques to model crowd behavior under stress.

# The Assumptions Made by Viscek and his Colleagues in their 1995 paper “Novel Type of Phase Transition in a System of Self-Driven Particles” are remarkably simple. “The only rule of the model,” they wrote, 

is [that] at each time step a given particle driven with a constant absolute velocity assumes the average direction of motion of the particles in its neighborhood of radius *r* with some random perturbation added….

<br>

The model is a transported, nonequilibrum version of the ferromagnetic types of models, with the important difference that it is inherently dynamic: the elementary event is the motion of a particle between two time steps. Thus the analogy can be formulated as follows. The rule corresponding to the ferromagnetic interaction tending to align the spins in the same direction in the case of equilibrium models, is replaced by the rule of aligning the direction of motion of particles in our model of cooperative motion. The level of random perturbations we apply are in analogy with the temperature (Viscek et al., 1995, their italics).

<br>

The biological basis of the model is a flying of birds trying to avoid collisions. Particles adjust their motion in each time step by the average velocity of their neighbors in region *r*, with some added variability, which provides the temperature-like noise in the system. The assumptions in Viscek’s models are strongly reminiscent of Reynolds’ model, though without the “flock centering” assumption. ? 

<br>

Using the average normalized velocity (or, in other cases, the average normalized momentum) of the particles as the order parameter, Viscek and colleagues found that, as the noise parameter was decreased (or, in other simulations, as the particle density was increased), the simulated organisms became increasingly aligned, formed local clusters and then, as parameters were changed further, formed a large flock moving in the same direction (Figs. 8.2 and 8.3). Moreover, the order parameter exhibited critical scaling in the transition region. Viscek and colleagues identified the critical exponents quantifying the scaling behavior, and found them to be unique, placing their model in a novel universality class. They concluded their paper by noting that self-propelled particles, while rare in purely physical systems, abound in biology. Viscek et al. called for the future use of this approach in models of molecular motors and traffic models, and the addition of a “hard core” to the particles, representing the social distance – maintained – up to a point – by humans in crowds.

A virtual avalanche of studies followed, with both major theoretical developments and comparisons to experimental data. For example, Sinha and Ramaswamy (2002) introduced a model incorporating the “fluid” within which the particles swam and interacted. Only a few months after the publication of the Viscek et al. model, Toner and Tu published a *Physical Review Letters* paper entitled “Long-Range Order in a Two-Dimensional Dynamical XY Model.” How Birds Fly Together”, in which they compared Viscek’s model of spins in two dimensions; this model can essentially be considered as a two-dimensional analogue of the Ising model. The Ising model, of course, exist in two spatial dimensions, but the variable of interest, the spin itself, can only align along a single axis (the direction of quantization). In the XY model, spins rotate in the plane of the latter. Toner and Tu showed that, when all particles in Viscek’s model were assigned zero velocity, it reduced exactly to the XY model. Thus the long-range order in the Viscek model resulted from the fact that the system was population structure arose from the very fact that the particles were moving. 

Recall that the initial Viscek et al. model did not include Reynolds’ paradox (and Hamilton’s “flock centering”). In other words, while the model created group alignment, it did not create cohesive dynamic. As Grégoire and Chaté pointed out in 2004, this meant that, as it approached the limit of zero density, the model would become unable to exhibit flocking at all. Grégoire and Chaté (2004) modified the Viscek et al. model to incorporate cohesion. They added a term representing interaction between the particles that was repulsive at short distances to represent herd core, and then attractively up to a limiting distance, similar to form of a Lennard-Jones potential. Depending on parameters controlling the relative magnitudes of the interaction and alignment forces, the model exhibited both static clusters and also states in which clusters drifted and moved, sometimes separating into smaller sub-clusters connected by “filaments” and within which the particles exhibited no alignment. The characteristics of the trajectory of the center of mass of also varied as a function of the system parameters.

Grégoire et al. identified “fluid-solid” like states. The authors reported that with sufficiently low repulsive forces, the system parameterized on a dipolar fluid whose characteristics were the flock. For example, coupled to the leading edge of the flock—visualized as a phase transition—the repulsive force would increase, resulting in an emergent solid. Subsequent investigations into the corresponding reaction mechanisms for the onset of the solid-fluid phase transition in macroscopic herds, and model-based computational studies of the emergent collective motion in schooling fish and flocking birds. Helbing and coworkers (2000) developed an agent-based model in which the agents were governed by three simple rules: (1) separation, to avoid collisions; (2) alignment, to match the velocity of nearby agents; and (3) cohesion, to move toward the center of mass of nearby agents. The model reproduced many of the emergent properties observed in real flocks, including polarization, schooling, and swarming.

# THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

The disparity between the results of Viscek and Grégoire generated considerable debate. After a flurry of publications, the issue appeared to be, at least partially, laid to rest, with the general consensus being that the Viscek model likely does exhibit a continuous phase transition (Aldana et al., 2009; Baglietto et al., 2012) pointed out that, since the Viscek model takes place in a finite region of simulated space, the correlation length of the system cannot exceed the system size *L*. As a result, comparison to infinitely large systems is not appropriate, and one must use statistical physics-based techniques such as finite-size scaling and data collapse to assess the behavior of the system, which Grégoire et al. (2003) and Grégoire and Chate (2004) had not done. Using these techniques, Baglietto et al. obtained critical scaling exponents for the Viscek model and showed that they satisfied a hyperscaling relationship consistent with a continuous transition. 

A further explanation of the difference between continuous and discontinuous transitions in swarming models came from an analysis of the role of the added noise term by Aldana et al. (2007) and Pimentel et al. (2008). In the original Viscek model, each agent updated its velocity based on an average of its neighbors’ velocities, with some noise then added. This represented virtually the agent’s decision-making process. Grégoire and Chate (2004) had improved this model exactly, but had also developed another version of the model in which noise was added to the velocity of each neighboring agent before averaging. This would correspond to an agent experiencing variation in its ability to assess the behavior of a neighbor, rather than variation in its decision-making process. Pimentel et al. (2008) referred to the former type of noise as intrinsic, and to the latter type as extrinsic, since it could be caused by a blurry environment, rather than by an internal decision-making process. 

Though they had not employed finite-size scaling or data collapse techniques, Grégoire and Chate had identified discontinuous phase transitions in models with both noise types, as a function of the noise amplitude. At first glance, it was not at all surprising that the two types of noise would have similar effects. However, Aldana et al. (2007) argued that they should in fact be expected to produce quite different types of phase transitions. In response, Chate et al. (2007) argued that the network models used by Aldana et al. to demonstrate this, had “no bearing” on Viscek-like models, since they did not account for the movement of the self-propelled particles and “the local coupling between order and density, which is well known to be crucial for understanding collective motion in animal groups.” Particles et al. therefore conclude that the Viscek model is indeed continuous.

The controversy continued. Lagrange et al. (2008), 2009a, b) showed that, for identical parameter values, the model with intrinsic noise, originally suggested by Viscek et al., would exhibit a discontinuous transition, while the model with extrinsic noise, proposed by Grégoire and Chate, exhibited a continuous transition. Pimentel et al. (2009) came to the opposite conclusion. Viscek et al. (2009) took issue with the way that the effective damping coefficient was computed in Pimentel et al.’s work, and demonstrated that, when computed correctly, their model did indeed exhibit a continuous transition. Finally, in a somewhat abrupt end to the debate, Grégoire and Chate (2009) conceded that the original Viscek model does indeed exhibit a continuous phase transition, and that the reason their earlier work had suggested otherwise was that they had not employed the appropriate theoretical tools.

# The Lorenz Attractor

The most famous example of a strange attractor is the Lorenz attractor, discovered by Edward Lorenz in 1963 while studying a simplified model of atmospheric convection. Lorenz was using a system of three ordinary differential equations to model the flow of air in the atmosphere. The equations are:

dx/dt = σ(y - x)
dy/dt = x(ρ - z) - y
dz/dt = xy - βz

where *x*, *y*, and *z* are variables representing the state of the atmosphere, and σ, ρ, and β are parameters. Lorenz found that for certain values of the parameters (σ = 10, ρ = 28, and β = 8/3), the system exhibited chaotic behavior.

> **Figure:** A 3D plot of the Lorenz attractor. The x-axis is labeled "X", the y-axis is labeled "Y", and the z-axis is labeled "Z". The axes range from 0 to 1.5. The plot shows two swirling, butterfly-shaped lobes connected at the center. The points are densely packed, forming a complex, non-repeating pattern. This illustrates the sensitive dependence on initial conditions characteristic of chaotic systems.

The solutions to these equations, when plotted in phase space (a three-dimensional space with axes representing *x*, *y*, and *z*), form a distinctive shape known as the Lorenz attractor. The attractor is a bounded region in phase space that the system tends to approach, but never quite reaches. The trajectory of the system within the attractor is chaotic, meaning that it is highly sensitive to initial conditions. A tiny change in the initial conditions can lead to a drastically different trajectory. This is often referred to as the “butterfly effect.”

The Lorenz attractor is a classic example of a deterministic system that exhibits chaotic behavior. This means that the system is governed by well-defined equations, but its behavior is unpredictable due to its sensitivity to initial conditions. The discovery of the Lorenz attractor had a profound impact on the field of chaos theory and helped to establish the idea that complex, unpredictable behavior can arise from simple, deterministic systems.

# 8.5 Results from a computational model show changes in group shape form interactions. Note that the essential tension (the frontiers collection)

Transitions to ordered behavior can occur in one-dimensional agent-based models as well, and these accord well with empirical observation of the ‘marches’ undertaken by locusts and crickets. Buhl et al. [2006] demonstrated the density-dependence of marching behavior in locusts in a laboratory environment. As the density of individuals was increased, random behavior underwent a transition to alignment in a coordinated marching group. The onset of ordered marching exhibited characteristics of a continuous-phase transition. Buhl et al. showed that a one-dimensional version of the Vicsek model provided a good fit to the observed data. A later empirical study showed that cannibalism is a driving force in the emergence of such marching formations. Aware of the potential threat from behind, each individual keeps moving forward [Bazazi et al. 2008]. Similar behavior has been observed in crickets species, where the propensity for cannibalism is exacerbated by deprivation of salt and protein [Simpson et al. 2006]. 

This demonstrates that coordinated mass migration in animal groups may be driven by highly selfish and aggressive behavior. In the case of locusts, both tactile and visual stimuli from behind are necessary, and the major source of these in a group will come from other locusts, which are demonstrably cannibalistic. Migration is widely viewed as an adaptation to exploit spatiotemporally variable environments. However, cannibalism is perhaps one of the mechanisms that catalyzes the alignment of individuals and subsequently drives the directional mass movement of insects in migratory bands. This suggests a new perspective to our understanding of collective motion… At high population densities, individuals in migratory bands can benefit by reducing predation risk, but this can then themselves serving as a source of potentially limiting food or water for cannibalistic conspecifics… Our results indicate that the defensive response to this risk, movement away from the attack, provides a general mechanism that results in marching bands having autocatalytic. Aggressive interactions stimulate motion in others, which increases encounter probabilities, and thus further aggressive acts [Bazazi et al. 2008].

Other researchers explored “Euclidian” interaction models, where agents interact according to distance, and took what might be considered trial runs at continuum approximations. The hydrodynamic interactions explored by Toner and Tu [1995, 1998] seek to account for the collective dynamics of swarms, flocks, and bacterial colonies. Specifically, Toner and Tu derived a continuum approximation to the Vicsek model, and demonstrated that, because of the presence of a conserved quantity (number of agents), the system is susceptible to instabilities. They predicted the spontaneous emergence of polar order, and the formation of moving lanes. Hughes et al. [2000] extended this work to incorporate noise, and demonstrated that the resulting behavior is consistent with that observed in experiments on marching locusts.

The model of Helbing and coworkers [Helbing et al. 2000; Farkas et al. 2002; Szabó et al. 2002] is also based on a continuum approximation, but incorporates psychological factors, such as the desire to maintain a certain distance from neighbors, and the tendency to move towards a goal. This model has been used to simulate a variety of phenomena, including pedestrian flows, evacuation dynamics, and the formation of traffic jams. Interestingly, the model predicts that, under certain conditions, the system can undergo a transition from a free-flowing state to a congested state, even in the absence of any external perturbations. This transition is similar to the phase transition observed in the Vicsek model, and suggests that the underlying mechanisms driving collective motion may be similar in a wide range of systems.

Choice between different paths has also been explored in empirical and computational studies of a rather different kind: ant trails. Here, collective motion arises, as in the flocks and swarms we have considered previously. However, the interaction between agents is not entirely without signaling. Ants lay down a pheromone trail as they forage, leaving behind a signal for their colleagues to follow. This process allows selection of an optimal foraging path, driven by the fact that pheromone accumulation occurs faster on shorter paths and, conversely, has less time to evaporate before the next ant comes along and deposits further pheromone (Deneubourg et al. 1980). Beckmann et al. (2001) showed that colonies with a greater number of foraging ants engaged in organized foraging along pheromone trails, while colonies with fewer foragers disorganized, random individual foraging trips. As colony size (and therefore number of foragers) increased, the change in behavior exhibited characteristics of a phase transition from a disordered to an ordered state. In experiments with ant colonies traveling in artificially constructed branching paths, Dussutour et al. (2004) found that population density, the ants selected one of the two paths, while a higher density led to symmetrical traffic flow through the two branches. Ant-based models for path optimization have been used to develop new computational techniques (Dorigo et al. 1996). This approach has come to be described as “swarm intelligence,” now a full-fledged field in its own right. 

Comparison of computational models to real-world data is clearly of paramount importance, and empirical studies of ant foraging, locust and cricket swarms, and consensus choice coincide well with the predictions of flocking models. But how realistic are these models? For example, how well do these models reflect the actual fine detail of ant foraging, locust and cricket swarms, or consensus choice? Further problematic challenging problem in data collection and analysis how to deal with data from large numbers of very similar organisms moving in three dimensions. The data from a flock have only single, complete insufficient to provide a full representation of the behavior ever. After collecting data from a variety of angles, the investigator must deal with another very difficult task: “the matching problem.” Specifically, how do you correlate bird A in an image taken from angle α with the same bird A in an image taken from angle β? Over the years, a number of researchers have developed automated techniques for tracking individual animals in video sequences (e.g., Dellacca 2007; Portugal et al. 2008; Strandburg et al. 2000). However, statistical mechanics and computer vision techniques require, up until now, considerable computational effort and frequently require manual intervention (e.g., Waddington 2008a, b). 

A fascinating comparison is offered by Thisse and Michel (2003). They modeled the collective motion of locusts (Schistocerca gregaria) using a relatively simple set of rules based on the observed behavior of individual locusts. Specifically, locusts tend to align their heading with that of their neighbors, maintain a certain distance, and avoid collisions. The model successfully reproduced several key features of locust swarm behavior, including the formation of bands and the tendency to converge on a common direction. However, the model failed to capture the complex, swirling patterns often observed in real locust swarms. The authors suggest that this may be due to the fact that their model did not account for the effects of wind or other environmental factors.  

> **Figure:** A diagram showing a comparison of computational models to real-world data. The x-axis represents time, and the y-axis represents the number of agents. The diagram shows three lines: one representing the predictions of a flocking model, one representing the observed behavior of a real-world flock, and one representing the behavior of a simulated flock. The lines are all very similar, indicating that the model is a good fit for the data. There are also several annotations on the diagram, pointing out key features of the data and the model. The diagram is titled "Comparison of Computational Models to Real-World Data."

Furthermore, Gerritsen (2003) compared the predictions of a simple model of collective motion to the observed behavior of a school of fish. The model was based on the idea that fish tend to align their swimming direction with that of their neighbors and maintain a certain distance from them. The model successfully reproduced several key features of fish school behavior, including the tendency to maintain a cohesive group and to avoid obstacles. However, the model failed to capture the complex, three-dimensional structure of fish schools. The author suggests that this may be due to the fact that their model did not account for the effects of hydrodynamic interactions between fish.

data, Camperi et al. applied an external perturbation to the simulated flocks, in the form of a large obstacle along the axis of the flock’s center of mass. Again, the metric model performed worst, with the flock ultimately breaking 
into a large number of subgroups. Of the two topological models, the balanced one performed best.

The initial simulations Camperi et al. performed had a large number of neighbors in the topological forms (22, and an interaction radius chosen in the metric case to give approximately the same number of neighbors. They noted, 
however, that as the number of neighbors decreased, the stability of even the balanced topological model broke down and the flocks began to form filaments, with incipient sub-flocks connected by small bands of individuals. In order 
to determine the optimal number of neighbors such that the balanced topological model would cohere without breaking into filaments, Camperi et al. measured the fraction of particles belonging to filaments as a function of the 
number of neighbors. Depending on the parameters of the model, this occurred between five and ten neighbors, consistent with the value of seven obtained from the actual starting data.

While sticking with a set number of “alignment” buddies may promote flock cohesion, the particular six or seven individuals with which a bird aligns may shift over time (Cavagna et al. 2013). Individual birds have been 
shown to exchange neighbors as a result of stochastic fluctuations; birds at the edge of the flock exchange positions with their neighbors less frequently than those near the center. Cavagna et al. suggested that this 

could be a consequence of the fact that birds compete with each other for a place in the interior of the flock. This struggle for the occupation of the same internal space would imply that when attempting to 
move inward, a border bird experiences a repulsion produced by its “internal” neighbors, pushing it outside. The attempt to move inward is then reiterated, until by some fluctuation the bird successfully 
leaves the border (Cavagna et al. 2013).

This process is consistent with the observation that starting flocks are denser at the edge than at the core. 

In the context of the phase transition debate between Vicsek and Chate and Durrett discussed above, it is interesting to note that another study by Cavagna et al. (2010) identified scale-free correlations in staring flocks. Barabasi 
and Albano (2014) implemented a Vicsek-like model with nearest-neighbor rule but with topological rather than metric interactions between neighbors. In other words, the agents in their model attempted to match velocities with a set 
number of nearest neighbors, rather than nearest neighbors within a set distance. Using the case of seven nearest neighbors, they analyzed the phase transition behavior of a function of extrinsic noise, essentially following the 
analysis of Baggioletto and colleagues. They identified a continuous phase transition from a fluctuating to an ordered state as the noise decreased. Strikingly, they identified critical exponents quite close to those obtained in a 
case of metric interactions. This suggests possible scaling similarities between topological and metric interactions, potentially resolving some of the theoretical difficulties with fluctuating near the critical value of the noise. 
Interestingly, the authors found that the correlations in the simulations were not scale-free at all but exhibited a clear cut-off wavelength.

### Metric and Topological Interactions: A Reconciliation?

So, is the debate between metric and topological interactions resolvable? The difficulty, as we have seen, lies in the fact that the simple Vicsek model, with its assumption of nearest-neighbor interactions, predicts a continuous 
phase transition (Vicsek et al. 1995), while the experimental data suggest a more abrupt one (Attanasi et al. 2009; Cavagna et al. 2010). Furthermore, the theoretical analysis of the Vicsek model suggests that the critical 
exponents associated with the phase transition are different from those observed experimentally (Baggioletto et al. 2011). However, as we have also seen, more sophisticated models, incorporating topological interactions or 
long-range interactions, can reproduce some of the features of the experimental data.

Collective groups of keratinocytes cannot align their motion with that of their neighbors, however, in the consensus manner that fish and birds may be assumed to. Instead, migrating groups of cells interact via direct physical contact. 

In order to model this type of behavior, Szabó et al. had to develop a model that did not include any explicit velocity alignment term. Instead, they used pairwise intercellular forces that, similar to the Lennard-Jones-type potential used by Grégoire and Chaté, was repulsive for small distances, attractive for intermediate distances, and zero beyond a threshold radius. The model also included a noise term representing variability in each cell’s ability to direct the motion in response to interactions with neighboring cells, and it reproduced the experimental results with good agreement. The computational model showed phase transition behavior as the noise magnitude was varied, with the density held constant (through a companion experimental observation was not achievable, as there was no mechanism by which to vary the noise experimentally). Analysis of critical exponents in the model gave values nearly identical to those obtained from the original Vicsek et al. (1995) model. Lastbó and colleagues showed computationally and computationally that adding closed boundary conditions induced vortex-like circular motion. They suggested that their results might have applications for the collective migration of cells during wound healing or embryogenesis.

The collective behavior of tissue cells was studied extensively in the subsequent decade. Battersby (2013) provides a brief review of recent work beginning with the unforgettable phrase “fish really do crawl.” And, perhaps it should, indeed! Debrock and Couzin (2008) suggested that cancer cells might exhibit emergent collective migratory behavior. Chang et al. (2013) provided a detailed computational model for the interaction of tumor cells with the surrounding normal tissue, which also predicted collective migratory activity. Another computational model that used that cell-cell interaction process known as contact inhibition of locomotion was sufficient to induce ordered cell migration, suggesting that this might be a “possible mechanism behind cell migration lastingly observed.” For example, in neural crest cells during development, and in metastasizing cancer cells (Cabernet et al. 2013). Moreover, mechanisms of cell migration are currently being investigated with respect to immunological responses (e.g., Betz et al. 2014). Somewhere, a tumor suppressor gene is a dumb accomplice.

> **Figure:** A series of six panels (A-F) depicting the results of a computational model simulating collective cell migration. Panels A, C, and E show snapshots of cell positions at different time points (t=0, t=50, t=100) with cells represented as circles. The color of each circle indicates the cell's velocity direction, shown by the corresponding vector in panels B, D, and F. The vector arrows indicate the magnitude and direction of cell movement. The scale bar in panel A represents 100 μm. The model demonstrates how cells can move collectively without explicit alignment rules, relying instead on attractive and repulsive forces between neighboring cells and random noise. The panels illustrate the emergence of coordinated motion from simple local interactions.

Furthermore, in 2006, two highly significant experimental observations appeared. First, Sumi et al. showed that the speed of crawling cells was significantly reduced when E-cadherin was knocked down, suggesting that cadherins play a role in the regulation of cell speed. Second, Friedl et al. showed that the speed of cancer cells increased when they were grown on a 3D matrix, suggesting that the matrix provides cues that promote cell migration. These two observations, together with the theoretical work of Szabó et al., provided a new framework for understanding the collective migration of cells.

In a groundbreaking theoretical study, Baskaran and Marchetti (2008) developed a model for a suspension of active organisms that included hydrodynamic effects. The model included a variety of organism types such as “shakers” (active particles that are not self-propelled), “movers” (active and self-propelled), “pullers” (a “move” subtype corresponding to contractile swimmers such as the *Alegia chilomydronos*, propelled by flagella) and “pushers” (a “move” subtype propelled from the rear, such as *E. coli*). Baskaran and Marchetti generated a phase diagram for swimmer behavior, predicting the conditions under which a suspension of a particular type would become unstable.

The theoretical investigation of nematic collisions by Suri et al. is reminiscent of a set of studies performed on the interactions, not of bacteria, but of single molecules. In 2012, Sumino and colleagues observed the formation of vortices in an experimental system of microtubule monomers and dynein molecules. The microtubules underwent nematic collisions, leaving the interaction in a common direction if they approached each other at an angle smaller than 90°, and in opposite directions if their initial angle of approach was greater than 90°. The microtubules formed vortices rotating either clockwise or counterclockwise (through individual molecules appeared to have a slight preference for counterclockwise rotation), and individual molecules were observed to occasionally “jump from one vortex to another and change their rotational direction” (Virsek 2012). Sumino et al. developed a computational model for the microtubule interactions, and investigated the effect of the confined microtubule environment on vortex formation. As Visek wrote in a “News and Views” piece in *Nature*, seems that owing to the persistence of curvature in the individual microtubules, curved “motion of microtubules spontaneously formed and enforce the formation of vortices”. Sumino et al. speculated that the onset of ordered behavior in this system, which combined “smooth, reptation-like motion and sharp kinematic alignment”, might belong to a new universality class.

In another study of molecular motion in cytoskeletal filaments, Schiller et al. (2013) recorded the movement of fluorescently labeled actin molecules on a substrate seeded with heavy meromyosin molecules. Here, as the Sumino et al. (2012) collective behavior emerged at high densities, but the molecular interactions were polar along always in the same direction after collision rather than Butler et al. (2010) mounted actin filaments at Sumino et al. comparable to those observed by Sumino et al., the researchers found an irregular in the way the actin filaments move. Butler et al. (2010) using micro-active movements of dendritic polymer clusters with accessory motor proteins, the researchers were able to replicate the “collective” of the 100 nm diameter self-propelled filaments. Ruiz et al. (2013) investigated actin moving in dense active matter, and demonstrated that actin filaments can self-organize into traveling waves.

<br>

Additional observations of active matter systems have revealed a propensity for the emergence of coherent motion. In a simulation of self-propelled particles, for example, Vicsek et al. (1995) discovered that, beyond a certain density of particles, the system underwent a transition to collective motion. The particles were assigned a random direction of motion, but at each time step, they tended to align their direction with that of their nearest neighbors. The result was a transition from disordered to ordered motion. The Vicsek model has been used as a paradigm for understanding collective behavior in a variety of systems, from flocking birds and schooling fish to bacterial colonies and human crowds.

> **Figure:** A diagram showing the phase space of self-propelled particles. The x-axis represents the noise intensity (κ), and the y-axis represents the alignment rate (η). The diagram is divided into three regions: disordered motion (low η, high κ), ordered motion (high η, low κ), and critical behavior (intermediate η and κ). The critical region is characterized by a power-law distribution of cluster sizes. The diagram also shows the results of simulations of the Vicsek model, with different values of η and κ. The simulations show that the system undergoes a transition from disordered to ordered motion as η increases and κ decreases.

<br>

Recent work has extended the Vicsek model to include more realistic features, such as hydrodynamic interactions and noise correlations. For example, Toner and Tu (1998) developed a continuum theory of active nematic fluids, which describes the collective behavior of self-propelled particles in terms of a density field and a polarization field. The Toner-Tu theory predicts the emergence of topological defects, such as vortices and disclinations, in active nematic fluids. These defects can play an important role in the dynamics of the system, and have been observed in experiments on bacterial colonies and cell monolayers.

<br>

In summary, the study of active matter has revealed a rich and complex phenomenology, with connections to a wide range of physical and biological systems. The emergence of collective behavior in these systems is a fascinating example of self-organization, and provides insights into the fundamental principles that govern the behavior of complex systems.

6 In a nematic phase, typically observed in systems such as liquid crystals, the constituents align parallel to each other, but do not form ordered layers. In bacteria, this has been referred to as a “bio-nematic” phase.

7 This difference in interaction type does not prevent the collective behavior of the actin filaments from being described as “nematic,” in the sense that they align but do not form ordered layers.

# 9. Biofilms

Sonya Bahar

Department of Physics & Astronomy and Center for Neurodynamics, University of Missouri at St Louis, MO, USA

(1)

...and not quite enough time.
Leonard Bernstein

**BACTERIAL BIOFILMS**¹ have recently risen to prominence in the scientific and medical literature in large part because of the dramatic increase in antibiotic-resistant infections in hospital settings. Yet biofilms have been around for 3.25 billion years, emerging at the same time as multicellular organisms like filamentous prokaryotes and cyanobacterial mats (de la Fuente-Núñez et al. 2013). Experimental observations of biofilms also back a considerable time as well, though far less than 3.25 billion years. The material *Lewenhoek* famously scraped off his teeth and examined under a microscope in one of his studies of “animalcules” was none other than a biofilm. J. B. Burton-Sanderson noted in 1870, in the 13th Report of the Medical Officer of the Privy Council, that he had observed rods at the surface of a liquid that “adhere together by their sides after the manner of the elements of a columnar epithelium.” He noted, however, that there was “strong reason to believe that this adhesion is not direct, that is, that they are not in actual contact but glued together by a viscous intermediary substance” (Mamáki et al. 2013). This substance is now known to be an extracellular matrix, composed of a variety of molecular components, which can be assembled—and disassembled—by bacteria depending on the stress conditions they experience. 

Modern studies of biofilms were inaugurated by Canadian microbiologist Bill Costerton. He demonstrated that biofilms account for the majority of naturally occurring bacterial populations. Costerton recalls the initial discovery of the biofilms in Canadian mountain streams in his 2007 book *The Biofilm Primer*. Around 1977, young colleagues

took advantage of their outstanding physical condition to gallop to sites into the miles of the alpine zones of the Bogska and Bugaboo mountains, where they plated and cultured water from icy streams crashing down boulder fields… These cultures yielded only 10–12 bacterial cells per milliliter, but it did not seem obnoxious that rocks in these streams were covered with slippery biofilms, and direct examination of these clear slime layers showed the presence of microorganisms. (Costerton, 2007, pp. 5–7)

Costerton’s research team subsequently prepared microscopic examinations of the biofilms using recently invented scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Boyd and Costerton, 1987). These images revealed a consortium of bacteria residing in a complex, village-like microenvironment that he termed a “biofilm.” Initially, Costerton’s work was dismissed from a conservative (and conservative, D. Costerton, personal communication) microbiology community (Costerton et al. 1978). Today, biofilms are widely recognized as a ubiquitous form of life, representing a dominant mode of existence for microorganisms in diverse natural and engineered environments. Biofilms are not simply a collection of cells, and biofilms are not simply a passive accumulation of cells. 

> **Figure:** A photomicrograph showing a biofilm. The image is a scanning electron microscope (SEM) image of a biofilm composed of *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. The bacteria are rod-shaped and are embedded in a matrix of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS). The EPS appears as a network of fibers surrounding the bacterial cells. The image is black and white, with the bacteria appearing as light gray and the EPS appearing as a darker gray. The scale bar indicates a length of 10 μm. The image demonstrates the complex three-dimensional structure of a biofilm and the role of the EPS in providing structural support and protection to the bacterial cells.

The biofilm lifestyle offers bacteria several advantages, including increased resistance to antibiotics, disinfectants, and host immune responses (Costerton et al. 1999; Donlan, 2002). Biofilms are also more tolerant to desiccation and starvation than planktonic (free-floating) bacteria. These advantages are conferred by the extracellular matrix, which acts as a physical barrier to protect the bacteria from external stressors. The matrix also facilitates communication between bacteria through the production and diffusion of signaling molecules, a process known as quorum sensing (Fuqua et al. 1994; Williams and Bassler, 2009). Quorum sensing allows bacteria to coordinate their behavior and respond collectively to changes in their environment.

# The Initial Structure 

Fig 9.1 The 2013 study by Wilking et al. demonstrates the formation of fluid channels visible in the biofilm as it grows over time (a). Microscopic images show the movement of an aqueous dye (green) through the channels (b). Injection of fluorescent beads (panel c) shows the connectivity of the fluid channels. Panel d shows an SEM image of a “wrinkle,” seen from below, while another SEM image (panel e) reveals the highly structured channels. A side-view of the channel structure, reconstructed from a plastic mold, is shown in panel f. Figure reproduced with permission from Wilking et al., *Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A.* 110(3), 848–852, 2013.

The initial formation of the channels may derive from buckling instability of the matrix, with wrinkles being formed when the matrix presses against a hard surface. A study by Asally et al. (2012) showed that “cell death at the base of the biofilm was linked with buckling in the vertical plane and thus [wrinkles]” (claims et al., 2014). Asally et al. showed that the deletion of genes for certain proteins involved in extracellular matrix synthesis led to a more homogeneous distribution of cell death. In this wrinkle cavities formed to allow, conversely by artificially increasing cell density, Asally and colleagues induced localized cell death and found that “wrinkles were formed in patterns that mirrored cell death zones” (Cairns et al., 2014).

Water-filled channels give biofilms a structure at a comparatively large spatial scale. But bacteria, exhibit structural regularity that they were initially assumed to be decayed plant structures (Costerton 2007, p. 27). The mechanism by which these structures are formed remains obscure. As Costerton writes, “[t]he ability to form regular tissue-like structures has always been a property reserved for eukaryote cells, and we have not yet developed an intellectual rubric into which to place the fact that prokaryotic cells can control large-scale activities of this kind” (Costerton 2007, p. 28). Equally surprising is the fact that bacteria “abandon” the honeycomb structure after having completed it (Fig. 9.2). The mechanisms regulating this movement away from the structure, let alone the biological reasons for its formation and subsequent abandonment, remain mysteries.

(b) is a scanning electron microscope (SEM) image of the same biofilm. A scale bar indicates 150 μm. (c) is a higher magnification SEM image showing the channels within the biofilm. The images demonstrate the complex, interconnected network of channels and the overall structure of the biofilm.

# THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

In addition to honeycomb matrices and water-filled channels, some biofilms produce transitory structures as complex as the “social amoeba” *Dictyostelium*, which we have mentioned briefly above and will return to in more depth in the next chapter. Costerton describes these structures with lovely contained excitement:

> **Figure:** A series of four scanning electron microscope images depicting biofilm structures. Panel a shows a partially abandoned honeycomb structure with bacterial cells present. Arrows point to the honeycomb plates. Panel b shows a honeycomb structure devoid of bacteria. Panel c is a close-up of the area within the white box in panel a, revealing detailed structural elements. Panel d shows the overall structure of the biofilm. The images are from Costerton’s “The Biofilm Primer” (Figure 17) and illustrate the complex architecture of biofilms.

Kjelleberg’s group has shown that the marine organism *Serrotia liquefaciens* strain MG 1 forms biofilms in which the organisms are arranged into vertical stalks that bear rosettes of cells connected to other rosettes by long chains of cells and that this architectural marvel is controlled by specific genes… Tim Tolker-Nielsen’s group has shown that one of *P. aeruginosa* forms stupellate peduncles on colonized surfaces and that mobile cells of a second clone crawl up the peduncles and form the ‘caps’ of the mushrooms that are such a prominent feature of the biofilms formed by this organism. At the recent 11th meeting of the International Society for Microbial Ecology (ISME) in Vienna (August 2009) Tim presented evidence… that the cells of the second clone may actually form the mushroom caps on templates of DNA produced by programmed apoptosis of specialized cells in the tops of these pedestals. (Costerton 2007, p. 19)

Naturally occurring biofilms typically contain individual cells separated by some distance (up to 10 μm) from their neighbors. Sister cells in biofilms separate shortly after fission. However, cells in a biofilm are often connected by pili, the hairlike appendages used by bacteria for attachment to surfaces, gliding motility, and horizontal gene transfer. Costerton has suggested that the pili may play a structural role in biofilms akin to that of microtubules in eukaryotic cell structure (Costerton 2007, p. 26).

The presence of pili on bacteria within biofilms suggests a high rate of horizontal gene transfer, leading to rapid genetic diversity within the population, and enhancing the biofilm’s ability to rapidly adapt to external stresses, whether from environmental changes such as fluctuations in oxygenation or acidity, or from the application of antimicrobial agents by humans. “Enhanced horizontal gene transfer in biofilms allows some within certain species to attain certain high maintenance, not required for current activities, and to acquire these genes from their clonal partners at a later time and different circumstances” (Costerton 2007, p. 75). Thus, a temporary division of labor facilitates metabolic cooperation. Indeed, the organization of biofilms into functional communities is analogous to that in multicellular eukaryotic organisms. 

The recent discovery that biofilms synthesize curli fibers—amyloid proteins homologous to those found in mammalian tissues—in 2010 by Arnold (Arnold et al. 2010)—and that these curli fibers are able to bind to a wide range of materials, including metals, plastics, and other bacteria, has added another dimension to our appreciation of the architectural sophistication of biofilms.

| **Biofilm Component** | **Function** | **Analogy to Eukaryotic Cells** |
|---|---|---|
| Extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) | Structural support, protection, adhesion | Extracellular matrix |
| Water channels | Nutrient and waste transport | Circulatory system |
| Pili | Cell-to-cell communication, structural support | Cytoskeleton |
| Curli fibers | Adhesion, structural support | Collagen |

The presence of these structural components, and the ability of biofilms to respond to environmental cues, has led some researchers to view biofilms as “cities” for microorganisms. In this view, the biofilm matrix provides the “buildings” and “infrastructure,” while the individual cells represent the “citizens.” The water channels serve as the “streets” and “sewers,” facilitating the transport of nutrients and waste products. The pili and curli fibers act as the “communication networks,” allowing cells to coordinate their activities and respond to changes in the environment. This analogy, while perhaps a bit fanciful, highlights the remarkable complexity and sophistication of biofilms. 

The ability of biofilms to resist antimicrobial agents is another key feature that distinguishes them from planktonic (free-floating) bacteria. Biofilms are typically 100 to 1,000 times more resistant to antibiotics and disinfectants than planktonic bacteria (Costerton et al. 1999). This increased resistance is due to a number of factors, including the physical barrier provided by the biofilm matrix, the reduced metabolic activity of cells deep within the biofilm, and the presence of persister cells—dormant cells that are able to survive antibiotic treatment.

---

<!-- page 132 | Page 260 of 619 | 879ms -->

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

While the biofilm matrix does not create a physical barrier to penetration by toxins, it still generates a protective environment. For example, it may provide anaerobic conditions with high proton concentration, in which some toxins may have difficulty functioning (Costerton 2007, p. 58). The matrix is highly hydrophobic, which helps provide resistance to penetration by toxins, including antimicrobial agents (Vlamakis et al. 2013). There is evidence that the matrix accumulates enzymes like β-lactamase that actively degrade antibiotics (de la Fuente-Núñez et al. 2013).

Biofilms restrict diffusion of metabolic products away from the cells that produce them. Bacteria depend on the re-influx of extruded protons in order to generate ATP. In the turbulent water of a stream, these protons would be easily swept away, as would be any small organic nutrient molecules. In the case of protons specifically, many of the polymers that compose the matrix are negatively charged, and thus bind positive cations, these cations then repel the protons, forcing them to remain near the membranes of the bacteria that extruded them (Costerton 2007, p. 72).

Biofilms provide a means for bacteria to remain in one place in order to feed. Many nutrient sources in turbulent aquatic environments are themselves transitory; the flash of a fish would provide benefits to planktonic bacteria passing in the water, while the nutrients from the vertebrate disaster can feed nourish billions of bacteria that live in the biofilms that soon form right on the nutrient source” (Costerton 2007, pp. 72–73). Other benefits accrue from this group lifestyle. Organic material released from dead bacteria is immediately available for consumption by the survivors. Costerton calls it “a perfect nutrient paradise…a pure of the bodies of their neighbors” and notes that, as a result of this banquet, “regrowth rates of stressed biofilms are truly phenomenal when the stress is removed” (Costerton 2007, p. 58). A further benefit may arise from secretion of “public good” metabolites. The uptake of secreted metabolites by neighboring cells might prevent feedback inhibition of the cells that produced them (Costerton 2007, p. 72). In other words, the collective risks itself for maximum production by preventing feedback inhibition.

Due to channels within the biofilm, a toxin such as bleach can kill cells even deep within the structure. Yet “beach heads” fail to kill a small subset of cells. Since these cells are not localized within a particular region of the biofilm, their survival has been assumed to be the result of some mutation (Costerton 2007, p. 58). Dubbing these cells “persisters,” Lewis (2010) suggested that they may simply have been in a quiescent state when the toxin arrived, allowing populations to recover (and to feast on their dead cousins in a process whereby “as cells highlight the genetic disparity within a biofilm,” as Costerton and Semenya 2007, p. 19 emphasize). Lewis’s idea has had the fervent support of many microbiologists; the evidence for the majority of surviving cells, if not all of them, will be due to an antibiotic-resistant subpopulation, is lacking (Seyaert et al. 2013). The persister cells may simply be slow-growing cells that are less susceptible to the drug. 

The existence of persister cells highlights the potential to disrupt biofilm integrity. If persister cells are the key to biofilm resilience, then the disruption of their development may be an avenue for eradicating the entire biofilm. The discovery of the role of *c. difficile* quorum sensing in the anaerobic biofilm (Witney et al. 2009) has opened up the possibility of quorum sensing–based anti-biofilm strategies. Quorum sensing is a cell-to-cell communication system in which bacteria release signaling molecules, autoinducers, that accumulate as the population density increases. 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the concept of persister cells within a biofilm. The diagram shows a biofilm composed of numerous bacterial cells. Most cells are labeled as "susceptible" and are being killed by an antibiotic (represented by small, red shapes). However, a small subset of cells are labeled "persister" and are shown surviving the antibiotic treatment. The persister cells are scattered throughout the biofilm, not clustered in one area. A caption below the diagram reads: "Persister cells are a subpopulation of cells that are tolerant to antibiotics, not because of genetic resistance, but because of a phenotypic state."

Another way to view the biofilm is as a city. Costerton (2007, p. 73) uses this analogy to explain the different roles played by bacteria within the biofilm. “The top of the biofilm is like the downtown area, where cells are rapidly dividing and actively metabolizing. The bottom of the biofilm is like the suburbs, where cells are in a quiescent state and are not actively dividing.” The middle of the biofilm is like the industrial area, where cells are producing a variety of products, including enzymes and polysaccharides. The biofilm city is not static; cells are constantly moving from one area to another. 

The biofilm is also a site of intense competition. Different species of bacteria compete for resources, and some species produce toxins that kill other species. However, the biofilm also provides opportunities for cooperation. Different species of bacteria can work together to carry out tasks that they could not do alone. For example, some species of bacteria can break down complex carbohydrates, while other species of bacteria can use the products of this breakdown as a source of energy. This cooperation allows the biofilm to thrive in a variety of environments.

---

<!-- page 133 | Page 264 of 619 | 807ms -->

# THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

The genetic differences between planktonic bacterial cells adhere to a surface and begin to express a set of genes that lead to biofilm formation. 

Biofilm formation is a reversible process; when conditions improve, the biofilm structure is dissected and the bacteria return to their planktonic lifestyle. Since cells within the biofilm structure take on different roles, biofilm formation involves a reversible cellular differentiation process. Some of this differentiation is driven by the varying spatial environment at different locations within the biofilm (van Gestel et al. 2015). At deeper layers, cells have less access to oxygen and other nutrients and thus grow more slowly and are less metabolically *active* than cells closer to the surface (de la Fuente-Núñez et al. 2013). 

Cell activity is not only regulated by location within the biofilm structure, however. It is also determined by the temporal expression of particular genes, and by the local concentration of key proteins. Richly complex regulatory pathways control the cascades of gene expression that trigger biofilm formation and disassembly. This may explain why individual cells can only be recruited to biofilms during a limited time window: it is much harder for free-living cells to join an established biofilm once it is metabolically integrated (Costerton 2007, p. 51).

While it may be difficult for individual cells to join an established biofilm, individual cells can detach and act as “planktonic” scouts, flowing down a mountain stream, or through a human’s lung, until they attach to a favorable new site for colonization. In order for this to occur, however, these cells must 

return to the planktonic phenotype and disentangle themselves from matrix components before they can leave the community. This process must include a signal that triggers the synthesis or release of enzymes that can degrade the basic polymers that constitute the biofilm matrix as well as the expression of the cells to the planktonic phenotype. *In P. aeruginosa*, the lyase enzyme that digests alginate (an exopolysaccharide matrix constituent) is continuously synthesized and stored in the periplasmic space… and is released to digest the matrix when detachment is initiated (Costerton 2007, pp. 53–54).

This process is closely related to full-scale biofilm disassembly, when cells emerge from the trance of the biofilm Borg, those closer to the center awaken first. In the mushroom-like structures formed by *P. aeruginosa*, the return to the planktonic phenotype gradually spreads from the center … so that the swarm of swimming planktonic cells finds a breadth in the dissolving microcolony, and the individual cells swim to freedom as the walls of [their] erstwhile home collapse (Costerton 2007, p. 54).

The pathways involved in biofilm disassembly have been detailed in *P. aeruginosa* and *E. coli* (Barraud et al. 2006; Decho 2000; Sauer et al. 2002). For example, in *P. aeruginosa*, the Dispersin B enzyme degrades the exopolysaccharide polymers that constitute the biofilm matrix, causing the biofilm to disassemble (Watnick & Kolter 2002). The release of these matrix-degrading enzymes is often triggered by the accumulation of cell density signals, such as *N*-acyl homoserine lactones (AHLs), which are produced by cells within the biofilm. 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating biofilm formation and dispersal. The diagram shows a surface with bacteria adhering to it, forming a mushroom-shaped biofilm structure. The biofilm is composed of multiple layers, with cells at the base being less active and cells at the top being more active. Arrows indicate the dispersal of planktonic cells from the biofilm. The diagram is labeled with terms such as "planktonic cells," "biofilm matrix," and "surface." The overall message is that biofilms are dynamic structures that can both form and disperse.

AHLs can also trigger the expression of genes involved in biofilm disassembly, such as those encoding Dispersin B. In *E. coli*, biofilm disassembly is triggered by the accumulation of cyclic-di-GMP, a second messenger molecule that regulates the expression of genes involved in biofilm formation and disassembly (Valentini & Filloux 1996). The accumulation of cyclic-di-GMP leads to the degradation of the biofilm matrix and the release of planktonic cells. The switch between biofilm formation and disassembly is therefore a complex process that is regulated by a variety of environmental signals and genetic factors.

# Fig. 9.3 Schematic diagram of the *B. subtilis* rotary flagellar motor, in which SpoA acts as a molecular clutch (bottom panel). The top panel shows fluorescence microscopy of *B. subtilis* in motile (top left) and biofilm (top right) forms. 
After losing their flagella, cells

form long chains of non-motile cells that adhere to each other and to the surface by secreting an extracellular matrix. As the biofilm matures, the cell clusters enlarge and the community is protected and organized by the extracellular matrix. In addition to matrix production, motile cells and spores are present and are spatially organized within the maturing biofilm. The presence and localization of the different cell types is dynamic and there seems to be an ordered sequence of differentiation such that motile cells become matrix-producing cells, which go on to become spores. Importantly, this process of differentiation is not terminal: as environmental conditions change, it is possible for cells to alter their gene expression (in the case of matrix-producing cells) or to germinate (in the case of spores). Phenotypic heterogeneity in *B. subtilis* is not limited to these three cell types. In laboratory conditions, biofilms have a limited lifespan, and they eventually disassemble in response to self-generated signals. 
As a biofilm disassembles, spores are released from the matrix, giving them the potential to disperse and encounter environmental conditions that are propitious for germination. (Yamada et al. 2013.)

In *B. subtilis* the temporal progress of cell differentiation is controlled by a number of interlinked regulatory processes. Figure 9.4 in Yamda et al. (2013), reproduced here as Fig. 9.4, illustrates the complexity of these regulatory networks. 
The key regulatory protein, whose activity affects the transcription of over 100 other genes, is SpoA. This protein’s activation depends on the phosphorylation of a particular serine amino acid residue, and the relative concentration of phosphorylated to unphosphorylated SpoA in a cell determines which genes are expressed, and hence the particular role that cell will within the biofilm. An intermediate level of phosphorylated SpoA (SpoA-P) leads cells to produce extracellular matrix, while a higher level triggers the spore-forming developmental pathway. Gradual accumulation of SpoA may lead to the formation of spores later in the biofilm’s life cycle (Yamada et al. 2013). The Spoa protein has been implicated in regulatory processes in other bacteria, such as *C. difficile* (Dawson et al. 2012).
