# 11. Multicellularity: Volvox

Sonya Bahar

Department of Physics & Astronomy and Center for Neurodynamics, University of Missouri at St Louis, MO, USA

(1)

On phone:
Bernard Black

VOLVOX MEANS “fierce roller.” These little algae rarely flowed into human consciousness in an encounter with the Dutch microscopist Anton van Leeuwenhoek. “I saw,” he wrote, “that they were not simply round, but their outermost membrane was everywhere beset with many little projecting particles…the little bodies…never still. Their progression was about by a rolling motion…Each of these little round bodies had enclosed within it 5, 6, 7, nay, some even 12, very little round globules, in structure like to the body itself wherein they were contained…While I was keeping watch for a good time, on one of the biggest round bodies…I noticed that in its outermost part an opening appeared, out of which one of the enclosed round globules, having a fine green colour, drop out, and took on the same motion in the water as the body out of which it came…soon after a second globule, and presently a third, drop out of it; and so one after another till they were all out, each took on its proper motion.” (Debell 1960, pp. 257–258, also quoted by Kirk 1998, p. 1)

In the years following Leeuwenhoek’s observations (Fig. 11.1), Volvox was viewed as a prime example of form’s “embodiment.” But what ultimately came to intrigue the scientific community most was the diverse range of forms taken on by the various species of Volvox and its more distant cousins. Some are single cells, while others form colonies of identical cells. Still, others, like those observed by Leeuwenhoek, differentiate into germ and somatic cells.

> **Figure 11.1:** A drawing of *Volvox* as observed by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek. The image depicts several spherical *Volvox* colonies, each composed of numerous smaller cells arranged in a hollow sphere. Small, hair-like projections extend from the surface of the colonies. Some colonies appear to be releasing smaller, individual cells. The background is a dark, undefined space. The drawing is labeled with annotations in Dutch, indicating Leeuwenhoek's observations of the colonies' movement and internal structure.

<!-- page 173 | Page 341 of 619 | 1220ms -->

# Fig. 1.1

An illustration from Leeuwenhoek’s 1700 letter on *Volvox*. Figure 1 shows the glass tube stopped with a cork within which Leeuwenhoek collected water containing *Volvox* (Figure 2)

<br>

August Weismann keenly contemplated the importance of these varied forms in explaining the transition to multicellularity, describing them as “simpler forms in which phyletic transitions are represented” (Kirk 1998, pp. 4–5). In *The Evolution Theory*, Weismann wrote that *Volvox* encapsulated the core question of cell differentiation (Fig. 11.2). “How can a cell by division give rise not only to others like itself, but also to body-cells, which are of quite different structure? This is, in its simplest form, the fundamental problem of all reproduction through gem-cells” (Weismann 1904, Vol. I, p. 259).

<br>

C, D, E, and F show individual cells or smaller groupings of cells, some with flagella visible. The images appear to be line drawings based on microscopic observations.

# Illustrations of *Volvox aureus* from Weismann’s 1904 *The Evolution Theory: From author’s collection*

> **Figure:** A color photomicrograph of *Volvox aureus*. The image shows a roughly spherical colony of green algae. The colony is composed of hundreds of individual cells arranged in a single layer at the surface of a gelatinous matrix. Each cell has flagella extending outwards, giving the colony a fuzzy appearance. The cells are densely packed and appear as small, green dots. The overall structure is reminiscent of a hollow sphere.

*Volvox* is a genus within the class Chlorophyceae, a type of green algae. *Volvox* belongs to the order Volvocales and the family Volvocaceae. We will encounter various genera within the Volvocaceae in this chapter: *Gonium*, *Pandorina*, *Eudorina*, *Pleodorina*, *Volvulina*, and *Volvox* itself (Fig. 11.3) and its cousins are closely related to, and may have descended from, another well-known Chlorophyceae, the bi-flagellated green alga *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii* (Fig. 11.4).

# THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

> **Figure 11.4:** A scanning electron microscope (SEM) image of *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii*. Note their pairs of flagella. Scale bar shown 10 μm. Image released to the public domain by the Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility, Dartmouth College.

The volvocaceans were initially thought to provide a prime example of Darwinian inference of history through a series. Just as *Dictyostelium* passes from single-celled to multicelled within a single life cycle, the volvocaceans were thought to do so within their evolutionary lineage (Fig. 11.5). As David Kirk writes, 

it would be quite satisfying if one could identify a group that…comprise an exact collection of closely related organisms that range in complexity from unicellular forms through colonial forms to multicellular forms – the evolutionary history of which would need to be shed light on the evolutionary origins of multicellularity, and the divergence of organisms within such a group would need to be of such recent origin (in a geological frame of reference) that there is some hope that its various members may still retain within their genomes – unblurred by long sets of genetic drifts – traces of the genetic changes that permitted transitions from one level of organizational complexity to the next (Kirk, 1988, p. 13).

Indeed, ribosomal RNA sequence comparisons in the late 1980s suggested that *Volvox* (center, one of the best-studied *Volvox* species, and *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii* shared a common ancestor only 35 million years ago (Kirk 1988, p. 43). A more recent study from Micho’d’s group pushes the divergence point back significantly further, into the Triassic, about 200 million years ago (Herron et al. 2009, Fig. 11.6). Umen (2014) throws some shade on this result; however, noting that, of all the multiple fossil calibrations used by Herron and colleagues, the only green alga they used, *Proterocladus*, has produced incongruences in other analyses and may not be part of the taxonomic group it was originally identified with. Nonetheless, if correct, the divergence time (proposed by Herron et al. still fall more recent than the appearance of the first filamentous prokaryotes (3.5 billion years ago) and the first multicelled prokaryotes with distinct cell types (2 billion years ago) (Kirk 1998, pp. 8–9), or *Spironema pallidum*, a putative eukaryotic alga dating back 2.1 billion years (Yan and Runnegar 1992).

> **Figure 11.5:** The volvocacean evolutionary grade. From left to right: *Chlamydomonas*, *Pandorina*, *Pleodorina*, *Volvox*, and *Eudorina*.

The tree is unrooted and displays branch lengths proportional to genetic divergence (measured in millions of years ago - MYA, shown on the x-axis). # Fig. 11.6. Chronogram of the volvocine lineage, with reference to the twelve steps proposed by Kirk. Permitted with permission from R.D. Hackett, J.O. Ayward, E.O. Aiyawatt, R. E. Michod, Triassic origin and early radiation of multicellular volvocine algae. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 106(9): 3254–3258, 2009.

The initial picture of the development of multicellularity in the Volvocineae, known as the volvocine lineage hypothesis, envisioned a linear, monopyle developmental sequence. The purported earliest ancestor was a Chlamydomonas-type alga like *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii*, which typically lives a unicellular lifestyle, propelling itself with flagella and reproducing asexually. *C. reinhardtii*, however, are able to resorb their flagella and form a multicellular conglomerate called a palmella (a relatively normal life cycle). This conglomerate is held together by a mixture of secreted glycoproteins called mucilage. 

In order of increasing complexity, the next member of the putative volvocine lineage is the genus *Gonium*. All multicellular members of *Gonium* cells reproduce by multiple fission. After enlarging to 21 times its original volume, a cell rapidly undergoes 7 fission events, producing 2¹ daughters cells in unicellular forms, each of these daughter cells detaches and swims off in *Gonium* and other multicellular species, the 2¹ cells produced by a round of cell division become cemented to one another by extracellular materials before hatching from their mother cell [Kirk 1988, p. 25]. This sort of cluster is called a coenobium. *Gonium* typically forms very small irregularly shaped coenobia, of perhaps eight cells. In the late 1980s, Janko and Babic identified a new *Gonium* species, *G. dispersum*, which could be considered a “missing link” between single-celled and multicellular forms. This species undergoes multiple fission as do other *Gonium* species, but then some – though not all – newly divided cells disperse to live a free-swimming individual lifestyle reminiscent of *Chlamydomonas* [Kirk 1988, pp. 25–26].

Next up in the hypothetical volvocine lineage is *Pandorina*, which forms tightly packed spherical colonies of about 16 cells. These cells are so tightly packed that they take on a key-stone configuration. *Pandorina* colonies show some anterior-posterior polarity, such as a greater size disparity [Kirk 1988, p. 27]. *Gonium* forms some exhibits the differences between cells, but the result of their location in the coenobium. In the case of *Gonium*, this presents in the form of differences in the rotation of the basal bodies. This polarity is however believed to be the precursor of the polarity of *Pandorina* and the volvocine genus. 

Like *Pandorina*, *Eudorina* is composed of a coenobium but forms a more flattened sphere and the periphery of the coenobium, and the cells are arranged in a distinct pattern. Reproduction in *Eudorina* is also by multiple fission. “Each time an ancestor colony divides, the anterior four cells come to serve as the anterior pole of the daughter colony and the posterior four cells serve as the posterior pole” [Kirk 1988, p. 28]. *Eudorina* exhibits a more distinct polarity than *Pandorina*, with anterior cells being larger, and the posterior cells smaller. *Eudorina* also demonstrates the early stages of cellular differentiation, with some cells specializing in reproduction and others in vegetative growth. 

Finally, *Volvox* [Figs. 11.7, 11.8] represents the acme of volvocine multicellularity. Colonies can contain up to 50,000 cells arranged in a hollow sphere, with a defined anterior-posterior axis, cellular differentiation, and specialized reproductive cells. *Volvox* colonies are capable of coordinated movement, and the individual cells are interdependent. The genus *Volvox* comprises several species, including *V. globator* [Kirk 1988, p. 29], *V. carteri* [Kirk 1988, p. 30], and *V. rousseletii* [Kirk 1988, p. 31].

> **Figure:** A chronogram of the volvocine lineage, showing the evolutionary relationships between different genera. The x-axis represents time, with the earliest genera on the left and the most recent on the right. The y-axis represents the level of multicellularity, with unicellular organisms at the bottom and highly multicellular organisms at the top. The diagram shows a branching pattern, with each branch representing a different genus. The length of each branch corresponds to the estimated time since the genus diverged from its ancestor. The diagram also shows the key characteristics of each genus, such as the size and shape of the colony, the degree of cellular differentiation, and the mode of reproduction. The diagram is based on the work of Kirk (1988) and Hackett et al. (2009). The genera included are *Chlamydomonas*, *Gonium*, *Pandorina*, *Eudorina*, and *Volvox*.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

More recently, the genomes of both *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii* and *Volvox carteri* have been sequenced (by Merchant et al. in 2007 and Prochnik et al. in 2010, respectively), providing new data and insights striking similarities between the genomes of *C. reinhardtii* and *V. carteri*. This new data, however, has not resolved fundamental complexity of the volvocine lineage (Umen and Olson 2012). As recently as 2014, Nozaaki et al. identified an entirely new genus in Lake Kamuya. They named it *Colemanosphoera*, after pioneering *Volvox* researcher Annette Coleman.

<br>
<br>

There are clear advantages – predator avoidance, to store nutrients – to a multicellular lifestyle. But the volvocine lineage shows, this lifestyle can be adopted in a variety of ways. A comparison between two canonically different *Volvox* species, *V. rousseletti* and *V. carteri*, helps illuminate the molecular origins of the transition to multicellularity. As cells in *V. rousseletti* grow, they remain connected by cytoplasmic bridges. This gives them a “size-like” shape when viewed from the side (Kirk 1938, p. 53). All developing cells in this species have a pair of flagella. But a few cells grow slightly larger than their neighbors; work in 1953 by Pocock suggests that these cells stop dividing one cycle before their fellows (Kirk 1938, p. 54). These cells – the gonidia – then reabsorb their flagella and divide, while continuing to grow, without breaking their cytoplasmic bridges to the neighbors. After multiple divisions, the gonidia have created an embryonic *V. rousseletti* spheroid. In contrast, *V. carteri* cells break their cytoplasmic bridges at the conclusion of embryogenesis; their gonidia, which never have flagella or eyespots, “put all of their energy into growth, eventually becoming 500–1,000 times larger (in volume) than somatic cells before they begin to divide” (Kirk 1938, p. 54). They then stop growing and undergo a rapid series of cleavages in order to generate an embryonic spheroid.

<br>
<br>

It is not always advantageous in the “time-share” habitat enjoyed by volvocaceans, where seasonally changing conditions of nutrient abundance, and water temperature favor different species in different seasons. These environmental variations help to answer the questions posed by Kirk (among many others): “Chlamydomonas is still found in such environments, why is there also *Volvox*? Alternatively, however, we might also ask: Given that there is now known in such environments, why is there also still *Chlamydomonas*?” (Kirk 1938, p. 52). Nonetheless, there is on the evolution of multicellularity, factored from increasing in size are of particular interest.

<br>
<br>

Wilson’s line is known to help biologists recognize the emergence of coloniality (Wilson 1895). Any organism that can reproduce as a unicellular propagule can reproduce in modes in size and number that facilitate better responses to environmental fluctuations. But as Wilson (1895) also pointed out, this is not enough. Multicellularity requires mechanisms that ensure cells remain associated, and that they do not cheat. By 1950, Gause had demonstrated the importance of population size (Gause 1934). He showed that, in a homogeneous environment, two competitors cannot coexist unless one is a superior competitor, or unless the environment is sufficiently heterogeneous to allow both to persist. Kirk (1938, p. 56) recognized the importance of these ideas to volvocine evolution, noting that “the indefinite prolongation of the cleavage series in *Volvox*…represents a device for increasing the size of the individual and, therefore, its competitive ability.”

<br>
<br>

> **Figure:** A composite image showing the evolutionary relationships within the Volvocales order. The top portion displays a phylogenetic tree constructed using 18S rRNA gene sequences, illustrating the branching order of various species and genera. Key genera like *Chlamydomonas*, *Dunaliella*, *Pandorina*, *Eudorina*, and *Volvox* are labeled. The tree indicates that *Volvox* is closely related to *Eudorina* and *Pandorina*, while *Chlamydomonas* represents a more basal lineage. Below the tree are representative images of different volvocine species, showcasing their morphological diversity. *Chlamydomonas* is depicted as a single-celled, motile organism with two flagella. *Pandorina* is shown as a colony of 8-32 cells arranged in a spherical shape. *Eudorina* is similar to *Pandorina* but with a larger colony size. *Volvox* is illustrated as a large, hollow sphere composed of hundreds or thousands of cells, each with two flagella extending outwards. The image also highlights the presence of gonidia (larger cells responsible for reproduction) within the *Volvox* colony. The bottom right corner includes a scale bar indicating the size of the organisms. The overall purpose of the figure is to visually represent the evolutionary relationships and morphological diversity within the Volvocales order, emphasizing the transition from unicellular to multicellular lifestyles.

<br>
<br>

In 1956, H.S. Levine proposed that the evolution of multicellularity in volvocaceans was driven by the need to achieve a minimal viable size. Larger organisms are less vulnerable to predation, and can store more nutrients. But larger organisms also have a lower surface area-to-volume ratio, which can limit their ability to acquire nutrients. Levine proposed that the volvocine lineage had evolved to optimize this trade-off. More recently, researchers have begun to explore the genetic basis of multicellularity in volvocaceans. A comparative genomic analysis of *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii* and *Volvox carteri* revealed that the evolution of multicellularity was associated with expansions of gene families involved in cell adhesion, cell signaling, and extracellular matrix production (Prochnik et al. 2010). These findings suggest that the evolution of multicellularity in volvocaceans required significant changes in gene regulation and protein function.

<br>
<br>

Furthermore, studies of gene expression in *Volvox carteri* have shown that the expression of many genes involved in development and differentiation is spatially regulated within the colony (Nedelcu et al. 2009). This suggests that the cells within a *Volvox* colony are not all identical, but rather that they adopt different fates and functions. The evolution of multicellularity in volvocaceans is therefore a complex process that involves changes in gene regulation, protein function, and cell-cell communication. It is a process that is still not fully understood, but that is beginning to yield new insights into the origins of multicellular life.

Podock observed that a somatic cell that apparently had become isolated from all others because of an accidental severance of all of its cytoplasmic bridges was larger than all of its neighbors, and she suggested that the increase size may have resulted from its loss ability to export materials through the cytoplasmic-bridge system. (Kirk 1988, p. 65)

The cytoplasmic bridge feeding system is so efficient that *V. russelii* gonidia grow an astounding 5600-fold during development (Kirk 1988, p. 66).

As important as the source-sink hypothesis may be in providing an advantage for the division of labor in Volvox, it only holds under high-nutrient conditions. Fluctuating environmental conditions conceivably favor such a source-sink process, since volvoxaceans with some germ-somatic differentiation would have an advantage at least some of the time. But metabolism is not the only source of evolutionary pressure toward differentiation. Flagella provide a structural constraint favoring division of labor between germ and soma. As Koufopanou and Bell (1993) explain, “cells of Volvox and related genera do not maintain flagella during embryonic cleavage, apparently because their basal bodies move to the mitotic poles and away from the flagellar bases… Sterile tissue (i.e., somatic cells incapable of reproduction) may have evolved to provide functional flagella during embryogenesis.” As Kirk emphasizes, the source-sink model represents a solution to an ecological constraint, while use of somatic cells for motility represents the solution to a cytological constraint. This is a vivid example of what Stephen Jay Gould would have referred to as historical ‘channeling,’ an evolutionary lineage whose innovations are driven by a set of inescapable limitations, as the roots of city trees grow between slabs of pavement.

Green flagellates must be able to execute phototaxis, moving toward the light when needed, but not steering too close in order to avoid the production of toxic photoproducts. A precise relation has been developed between the location of the eyespot and the flagella. This relationship is maintained during cell reproduction by the “same cells cytoplasmic components [in critical parts of the cell] in dividing cell are equally stereotyped manner” (Kirk 1998, p. 91). In *Chlamydomonas*, for example, the eyespot is symmetrically placed, allowing the cell to perceive the direction of incoming light. The flagella are located near the eyespot, but they are asymmetrically. The flagellar stem of the eyespot is linked to its flagellum, and the one flagellum responds differently to incoming light. The two flagella respond differently to incoming light. As a result, when swimming, *Chlamydomonas* performs an asymmetric breaststroke, so that its eyespot moves in a helical path, surveying all 360° of the horizon. (Kirk 1988, p. 74).

However, a Volvox colony, no matter how synchronized, is not a differential light receptor. It is not capable of performing a helical path, surveying the horizon. Flagella in a Volvox colony, for vegetative strains at least, beat with a regular pattern, propelling the entire sphere in a more or less straight line. Differential shading of the colony does not result in a change in direction; no matter what, the colony continues to move forward. But this is not to say that Volvox colonies are incapable of sensing light. Indeed, they can. But they sense light in a different way. 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the difference in flagellar arrangement and movement between *Chlamydomonas* and *Volvox*. The *Chlamydomonas* diagram shows a single cell with a symmetrical eyespot and asymmetrically positioned flagella, demonstrating the helical swimming pattern. The *Volvox* diagram depicts a colony with all flagella beating in unison, resulting in linear movement. The diagrams are labeled with key features like "eyespot," "flagella," and "direction of movement." The purpose of the figure is to visually represent how the different flagellar arrangements contribute to different light-sensing and movement strategies.

The key is that Volvox colonies sense the *gradient* of light, not the absolute intensity of light at any given point. As Kirk (1979, p. 155) explains, “the entire colony acts as a single receptor, and the response is determined by the average intensity of light striking the entire colony.” This is possible because the colony is large enough that different parts of it are exposed to different intensities of light. The colony is therefore able to determine the direction of the light source by comparing the amount of light striking different parts of its surface.

This is a remarkably sophisticated mechanism, and it allows Volvox colonies to move toward the light even in the absence of any differential shading. But it also has a cost. Because the colony is large, it is more vulnerable to predation than a single-celled alga. And because the colony is not capable of performing a helical path, it is less able to avoid obstacles. But these costs are offset by the benefits of colonial life, such as increased efficiency of nutrient uptake and increased resistance to grazing.

# THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

Water-dwelling flagellates cannot simply resorb and hang on. Not only is there no substrate to attach to, but, without flagella, the organisms could not execute phototaxis and would be unable to maintain their position within the water column, potentially depriving themselves of key nutrients during cell division (Kirk 1998, p. 101). Pond-dwelling *Chlamydomonas* species and multicellular volvocaceans up to the size of *Eudorina* solve this problem by decoupling their flagella and body basies. The flagella continue to beat, maintaining cell motility, while the intracellular components execute their well-choreographed cytokinetic dance beneath them (Kirk 1998, p. 101). But flagella can remain decoupled only so long before they begin to beat in an uncoordinated fashion and eventually tear themselves loose from the cell (Kirk 1998, p. 104). This can be avoided by one last creative solution to the flagellation constraint: division of labor .

Division of labor in volvocaceans is facilitated by the fact that green flagellates with cell walls undergo multiple, rather than binary, fission. Indeed, multiple fission appears to be closely coupled to the existence of a cell wall. 

Why these two phenomena are so tightly coupled is not certain. However, a credible working hypothesis is that the flagellation constraint was first resolved (as it is today in *C. reinhardtii*) with loss of motility during division, and thus variants that combined several divisions in one immediate period per day would have survival advantage over ancestral forms that had to become immobile several times per day in order to complete the same number of divisions. In this regard, it may well be significant that most species that lose their flagella while dividing do all of their dividing at night and are motile while the sun is shining… 

Are cells held closely together during multiple fission, a step toward permanent multicellularity could be facilitated by incomplete cytokinesis. Rekall that V. rousseletii maintains cytoplasmic bridges between cells; such bridges are a natural part of cytokinesis. “hold sister cells in a fixed spatial relationship until cell division has begun” (Kirk 1998, p. 102). Such incomplete division was observed in some of the *Gonium dorsum* colonies studied by Bąkło and Jakičič.

It is noteworthy that the walls of adjacent cells in a *G. dorsum* colony are so loosely joined that individual cells frequently break free after hatching. A second known multicellularity very likely involved coalescence of volvents between adjacent cells, as is now seen in the marine colonial volvocacean *Platydomonas pachyrhiza*, in which the cells are connected by a hemidesmosome-like structure (Kirk 1998, p. 103). In either case, the advantage of remaining attached, or even just nearby, is to allow for coordinated cell division. The first step toward multicellularity, then, may well have been the evolution of a mechanism for ensuring that cells divided in synchrony. 

> **Figure:** A photomicrograph showing a colony of *Volvox globator*. The colony is roughly spherical and appears green due to the presence of numerous individual cells embedded within a gelatinous matrix. The cells are arranged in a single layer at the surface of the sphere, each with visible flagella extending outwards. The image also shows a few individual cells and smaller colonies nearby. The scale is not indicated, but the overall impression is of a microscopic organism in a liquid environment.

The multicellular volvocacean *Volvox* provides a particularly compelling case study of the evolution of multicellularity. The genus includes both colonial and solitary species, allowing researchers to directly compare the genomes and phenotypes of closely related multicellular and unicellular organisms. *Volvox* colonies are typically composed of thousands of somatic cells arranged in a hollow sphere, with each cell possessing two flagella that beat in coordination to propel the colony through the water. Reproduction in *Volvox* is also unusual. Colonies produce both asexual and sexual progeny. Asexual reproduction involves the development of daughter colonies within the parent colony, while sexual reproduction involves the formation of eggs and sperm that are released into the environment. 

The evolutionary transition from unicellular to multicellular life in *Volvox* has been accompanied by a number of significant genetic and developmental changes. For example, multicellular *Volvox* species have evolved a suite of genes involved in cell adhesion, cell communication, and programmed cell death, which are not found in their unicellular relatives. In addition, multicellular *Volvox* species exhibit a more complex pattern of gene expression during development, with different cells in the colony expressing different sets of genes.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

In contrast to *nogameris*, Volvox carteri forma wetsteinornis is not only reproductively isolated from *nogameris* in its sexual stage, but produces none of the mutants found in *nogameris*. They have been suggested that the difference may lie in the DNA repair systems of the two strains. 

Volvox carteri *E. nogameris* is typically studied in descendants of the original strains, HK10, which is female in the sexual stage, and HK8, which is male. As adult spheroids, they contain 2,000–4,000 somatic cells and up to 16 gonidia. Their growth cycle occurs once 48 h and is closely regulated by the light-dark cycle, a fact exploited by researchers who wish to synchronize their spheroids to the same life cycle stage. Somatic cells have a polarized structure similar in many respects to *Chlamydomonas*, with basal bodies and the apical end. A striking difference from *Chlamydomonas*, however, is the orientation of the flagella. 

In V. carteri, somatic cells are arrayed along the outer surface of the spheroid. If each performed the breaststroke, they would simply cause the swarm to whirl around. All flagella on one side of the spheroid must beat in the same direction, while those on the other side beat in the opposite direction, in the entire spheroid, rather than a single cell, to do the breaststroke.<sup>6</sup> The arrangement of the basal bodies (Chlamydomonas is not compatible with this. In Volvox, instead of being mutually oriented at 180°, the basal bodies are ordered parallel to one another. This may a physical constraint on the somatic cells that acts as a form of conflict suppression, in the sense of Michod (see Chap. 13). This basal body alignment, somatic cells are incapable of “making it on their own” since, separated from the rest of their galley crew, they could not swim, let alone execute phototaxis. Isolated, they would simply tumble in place.

*Gonidia*, unsurprisingly, are structurally quite different from somatic cells. They lack an eyespot and have rudimentary flagella only at an early stage of development: these are eventually completely resorbed. Gonidia have a radial configuration, with a central nucleus surrounded by large vacuoles. The extracellular matrix that fills the spheroid interior has crystalline structure similar to the crystalline layer of *C. reinhardtii*, suggesting a common evolutionary origin. Indeed, Kirk’s notes, “*C. reinhardtii* and V. carteri, when stripped of their own crystalline layers, can nucleate the assembly of each other’s crystalline-layer glycoproteins in a normal crystal lattice, whereas *C. reinhardtii* and *C. eugametos* are incapable of such cross-nucleation” (Kirk 1988, p. 125).

During the asexual life cycle, the gonidia within a spheroid undergo a series of rapid divisions (approximately every 35 min). New cleavage events, generating all the cells within the spheroid. Isolated, each gonidion will be present when they hatch from the parent spheroid (Fig. 11.7 and 11.8A). Cleavages are stereotyped and extremely precise. To date, all known exceptions to this rule will follow a regular pattern displayed in response to close attention (Fig. 11.8B). However, we have discovered some exceptions (Kirk 1998, pp. 137–139). These exceptions, the cells seem to retain their assignment to a specific quadrant as divisions proceed on so prove wrong cells will yield to each other to preserve positioning.

# Fig. 11.8 Emission during embryogenesis. Schematic diagram of the axial Volvocan carter life cycle (A). Embryogenesis (B), showing the 22-cell stage where all cells are similar in size (a), the first set of asymmetric cells after the sixth division 

(b), the phialopore (c) and inversion (e). Reproduced with permission from D. Kirk, A twelve-step program for evolving multicellularity and the division of labor. *BioEssays* 27:39-210, 2005. © 2005 Wiley Interdisciplinary Inc.

During the rounds of asymmetric cleavage in *P. phialopora* it produces the embryonic new spheroids, incomplete cytokinesis results in cytoplasmic bridges between nearby cells. These bridges form a network that plays a critical role in the gonidial maturation process, because during the cleavage stage, new gonidia form on the outside of the growing embryonic spheroid, and new somatic cells on the inside. An inversion process must occur in order for the closely spheroid to be able to swim free from their parents after hatching. This inversion process (see Fig. 11.8b) is accomplished by successive waves of cell shape change; somatic cells initially have a spindle shape, but those closest to an open region called the phialopore take on a flask-like configuration.  Prolongating at one end.  As cells adjacent to the open region slide perpendicular to the cytoplasmic bridges, until they are attached to the bridge at one end rather than along their midsection. This causes the edge of the phialopore to fold over like a lip. As a result, the region of maximum curvature moves back toward the posterior of the spheroid, and the cells at the maximum curvature undergo the spindle-to-flask shape change, while cells over the edge of the lip relax to their spindle configuration. Finally, the lip regions 

nearly surround the inverted posterior hemisphere. At that point, the posterior hemisphere “snaps” through the opening at the equator, and eventually the phialopore lips come together once again at what will be the posterior pole of the adult. The flagellar ends of all somatic cells are on the exterior, and the gonidia, which protruded from the surface of the pre-inversion embryo, have been moved to the interior. (Kirk 1998, pp. 152–153)

The anterior-posterior axis is thus reversed during the inversion process. 

Embryogenesis typically takes place in the dark (Kirk & Collins 2004), although observations made by V. carter in 1927 can be completed in 48-h conditions, albeit with cells that are coming out of their initial response to light during a 44-h dark/4-h light cycle, the cells in that embryo appear to divide too rapidly. The life cycle can be completed in constant conditions. Kirk’s detailed drawings of *P. phialopora* embryogenesis (Kirk 1932a, 1932b, 1939) provide a visual record of the morphological changes that take place during the process. 

> **Figure:** A schematic diagram illustrating the life cycle of *Volvocan carter*. (A) Shows the axial life cycle, depicting the progression from a single cell to a multicellular spheroid. (B) Details the embryogenesis process, showcasing stages from the 22-cell stage (a) with cells of similar size, to the development of asymmetric cells (b), the formation of the phialopore (c), and the final inversion stage (e). The diagram highlights the changes in cell shape and arrangement during embryogenesis, and the formation of cytoplasmic bridges between cells.

In the gonidial maturation process, the gonidia become coated with a thick, gelatinous matrix (Kirk 1998, p. 153).  The matrix is composed of glycoproteins and is thought to provide protection for the developing gonidia, as well as a means of attachment to the substratum.  The mature gonidia are released from the parent colony and settle to the bottom of the culture vessel, where they undergo meiosis and develop into new vegetative cells.  The entire life cycle of *P. phialopora* takes approximately 24–48 h under optimal conditions.

The unicellular Volvocales, such as *Chlamydomonas*, exhibit phototaxis, and the multicellular *Volvox* species are also capable of phototactic responses (Kirk 1998, p. 154).  However, *P. phialopora* does not exhibit a clear phototactic response.  This may be due to the fact that *P. phialopora* is typically found in shaded habitats, where light is not a reliable cue for orientation.  Alternatively, the lack of phototaxis may be a consequence of the colonial lifestyle of *P. phialopora*, where the collective behavior of the colony is more important than the individual behavior of the cells.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

However, which cells secrete this protease. A range of questions remain unanswered, such as how the juvenile spheroids protect themselves from the protease, and why the protease has an effect only on the somatic cells of the adult spheroid that lie above the juveniles, so that these hatch through the “ceiling” while leaving the “floor” and “walls” around them intact (e.g. Kirk 1998, pp. 179–180).

After hatching, somatic cells in the parental “ghost” undergo programmed cell death, releasing nutrients into the water. Meanwhile, the new spheroids execute phototaxis in a manner generally similar to that used by *Chlamydomonas*, including threshold effects in order to remain in optimal light intensity. Now, however, it is clear that a question of flagellar pairs changing their coordinated beat frequency due to light exposure. Rather than differential responses of two flagella within a single pair. The role of calcium channels in transducing the phototactic response in *V. carteri*, compared to *Chlamydomonas* and other flagellates, has not yet been fully elucidated. Most recently, *V. carteri* and *Chlamydomonas* (Drescher et al. 2010) and *V. rouxiellii* (Ueki et al. 2010) have been the subject of extensive studies as models of biological fluid dynamics (Drescher and colleagues “A hydrodynamic bound state” in which nearby volvocine spheroids are drawn toward each other. A recent experimental study suggests that hydrodynamic interactions aid the synchronous beating of flagellar ensembles in *V. carteri* (Brumley et al. 2014). In a recent review, Goldstein (2013) summarizes some of this recent work and places it within the broad context of biological “microswimmers”.

> **Figure:** A series of microscopic images showing the development of *Volvox carteri*. (a) A newly formed spheroid with visible somatic cells and gonidia. (b) A more mature spheroid with a defined hollow interior. (c) A spheroid undergoing asexual reproduction, with daughter spheroids visible within the parent. (d) A close-up of flagellar movement on the surface of a spheroid. The images are black and white, with scale bars indicating the size of the spheroids.

As described earlier, *V. carteri* exhibits mutant forms with distinct developmental phenotypes. Studies of *Volvox* mutants are primarily due to the work of three laboratories – those of Richard Starr, at Indiana University and then at the University of Texas at Austin, Robert Huskey at the University of Virginia, and David Kirk at Washington University in St. Louis, whose seminal text has been our guide for much of the present chapter. These laboratories identified a plethora of mutants – *Mu1*, *Mu2*, *Mu3*, *Mu4*, *Meg4*, *R-1*, *Rad4*, *doughnut*, *round*, *posterior*, *S16*, *Pin*, *Dis*, *Pel*, *Rgl*, *Rot*, and many others. As we noted earlier, each of these mutants results in identifiable pathologies in structure and development.

The *Mu1* mutants are known as pattern-switching mutants, and cause asexual spheroids to develop as irregular clumps of cells. *Mu1* is the gene encoding a photoprotein, gonidia stimulatory factor 1 (gsf1). The *Mu2* mutants are also pattern-switching mutants, but in a female specific manner: mutant females do not undergo the normal divisions that generate eggs, and instead develop into amorphous aggregates. The *Mu3* mutants fail to secrete the extracellular matrix, and as a result, the spheroid falls apart. The *Mu4* mutants are unable to complete meiosis. The *Meg4* mutants have an enlarged cellular dimension. The *R-1* mutants are defective in the formation of the reproductive cells. The *Rad4* mutants are defective in DNA replication. The *doughnut* mutants form spheroids with a hole in the middle. The *round* mutants form spheroids that are not round. The *posterior* mutants have a defect in the posterior region of the spheroid. The *S16* mutants are defective in the formation of the flagella. The *Pin* mutants are defective in the formation of the eyespots. The *Dis* mutants are defective in the formation of the cell walls. The *Pel* mutants are defective in the formation of the cell plates. The *Rgl* mutants are defective in the formation of the cell regulation. The *Rot* mutants are defective in the formation of the cell rotation.

The genetic architecture of *Volvox* is also unusual. *Volvox* is not a typical haploid/diploid organism. Rather, it exhibits a complex life cycle involving both haploid and diploid phases, as well as a phenomenon known as “somaclonal variation”. Somaclonal variation refers to the genetic changes that occur in plant cells during tissue culture. In *Volvox*, somaclonal variation occurs during asexual reproduction, and can lead to the formation of new mutants. The genome size of *V. carteri* is approximately 700 Mb, which is about twice the size of the human genome. The genome is organized into 16 chromosomes. The genome encodes approximately 18,000 genes. The genome of *V. carteri* has been sequenced, and the sequence is available in the public domain.

> **Table:** *Volvox carteri* mutant phenotypes and associated genes.
>

> |---|---|---|
> | *Mu1* | Pattern-switching | *gsf1* |
> | *Mu2* | Female pattern-switching | N/A |
> | *Mu3* | Extracellular matrix defect | N/A |
> | *Mu4* | Meiosis defect | N/A |
> | *Meg4* | Enlarged cells | N/A |
> | *R-1* | Reproductive cell defect | N/A |
> | *Rad4* | DNA replication defect | N/A |
> | *doughnut* | Hole in spheroid | N/A |
> | *round* | Non-round spheroid | N/A |

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

The typical male pattern of cleavage, but produce eggs rather than sperm packets. As Kirk explains, "[t]hese eggs are then capable of being fertilized by sperm produced by the result of a single mutation within the mating-type locus of the *V. carteri* genome" (Kirk 1949, p. 244). This also implies that male *V. carteri*, which are haploid, contain the genetic information needed to follow at least some of the female developmental program. 

Perhaps the most fascinating mutants are those that affect the normal germ-soma dichotomy. These affect the genes that are essential for the division of labor. The first of these, at a locus known as *regA* (for "regenerator") phenotype) was studied first by Starr's laboratory, and then by Huskey's and Kirk's. *regA* behaving like normal somatic cells for a time, *regA* somatic cells retract their flagella and reorientate as gonidia. These gonidia develop normally, except that, upon maturity, somatic cells in their daughter spheroids express the regenerator phenotype themselves. Several *regA* variants have been identified, varying in the number and location of somatic cells that redifferentiate as gonidia. Experiments with a temperature-sensitive mutant show that all these different variants result from a mutation at the same locus, the different spatial patterns of regenerating somatic cells (throughout the spheroid, just at one of the poles, etc.) depend on the timing of the critical window of embryogenesis when the mutant *regA* is expressed.

The protein coded for by the gene at the *regA* locus is a transcriptional repressor that targets genes for chloroplast proteins (Meissner et al. 1999); there is no orthologous gene in *C. reinhardtii* (Umen and Olson 2012). There is a homologous *regA* gene, however, in *C. reinhardtii*, called *rdg1* (Niederkruger 2009), orthologous to a different gene in *V. carteri* (Kirk and Hallmann 2011). These results suggest that *regA* might have arisen in *V. carteri* by duplication of *rdg1* followed by mutation (Hallmann 2010). Niederkruger and Michel have suggested that

the evolution of soma in multicellular lineages involved the co-option of life-history genes whose expression in their ancestral unicellular was conditioned on environmental cues (as adaptive strategy to enhance survival at an immediate cost to reproduction, through shifting their expression from a temporal (environmentally induced) into a spatial (developmental) context. (Niederkruger 2009)

Niederkruger et al. (2009) found an environmentally-cued gene, “generally induced under starvation conditions comprising a domain of phytotoxins in green algae,” that showed some correspondence to transcripts in those *V. carteri* cells that do not reproduce (i.e. somatic cells). A similar environmentally-cued gene, *regA*, is expressed in somatic cells of developing *V. carteri* spheroids, except that its expression becomes developmentally arrested in reproducing cells. The expression pattern of a third gene, *midas*, is the reverse: expressed in reproducing cells, repressed in somatic cells. The authors propose that the co-option of environmentally-cued genes to control the germ-soma division of labor was a crucial step in the evolution of multicellularity. 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the proposed evolutionary pathway of the *regA* gene. The diagram shows a phylogenetic tree with *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii* and *Volvox carteri* branches. The *C. reinhardtii* branch has a gene labeled *rdg1*. The *V. carteri* branch has a gene labeled *regA*, with an arrow indicating it arose from gene duplication of *rdg1* followed by mutation. The diagram also includes text boxes explaining the function of each gene: *rdg1* is involved in chloroplast protein regulation, while *regA* regulates the germ-soma division of labor in *V. carteri*.

The argument that the evolution of multicellularity involved the co-option of existing genes is not new (e.g. Bonner 1998; Maynard Smith and Szathmary 1995). What is new is the identification of specific genes that may have been co-opted in this way. The fact that *regA* is a transcriptional repressor that targets genes for chloroplast proteins is also intriguing, given the importance of chloroplasts in the life of *Volvox*. The authors suggest that the co-option of *regA* may have allowed *Volvox* to regulate the expression of chloroplast genes in a way that is beneficial for the entire colony. 

The recent work on the evolution of the germ-soma division of labor in *Volvox* has provided new insights into the evolution of multicellularity. The identification of specific genes that may have been co-opted in this process is a major step forward. Further research will be needed to confirm these findings and to understand the full extent of the role that these genes played in the evolution of multicellularity.

# Kirk’s hypothesis for the genetic program underlying germ-soma differentiation in *Volvox*

Fig. 11.9 Kirk’s hypothesis for the genetic program underlying germ-soma differentiation in *Volvox* carteri. Kirk notes that “underlying this hypothesis is the assumption that the ancestral program of volvocinean differentiation 

(“first vegetative and then reproductive”) is also the default program in *V. carteri*” (Kirk, 1998, p. 256). Figure adapted by the author from Kirk et al., 1999.

Kirk’s hypothesis leads to a number of predictions that can be tested when the genomes of other species in the volvocinean lineage are sequenced.

First of all, we can predict that the closest “homotypic” relative of *V. carteri*, such as some isolate of *Eudorina*, will be found to possess genes homologous to many of the early-somatric and gonidial genes of *V. carteri* and will express these genes simultaneously, in a pattern similar to that seen in the *Glc/Reg* mutant of *V. carteri*. Second, we can predict that the isolate of *Pleodorina* that appears to be the closest living relative of *V. carteri* will possess a homologue of the *V. carteri* regA and regB genes and will express this gene selectively in those cells that are destined to remain small, flagellated, and incapable of reproduction…

But we predict that *Pleodorina* will not have functional equivalents of the gls or log genes, because *Pleodorina* species neither divide somatically nor have cells that fail to differentiate as biflagellate motile cells before differentiating as gonidia. The most distant relative in which we would expect to find a functional equivalent of the log genes of *V. carteri* is some species of *Volvox*, such as *V. tertius*, in which there are no asymmetric cleavage divisions, but in which nevertheless a discrete set of cells begin to enlarge and differentiate as gonidia immediately after the end of embryogenesis, without first passing through the biflagellate, quasi-somatric condition. Correspondingly, the most distant relative in which we would expect to see functional equivalents of the gls loci of *V. carteri* would be *V. obversus*, the only *Volvox* species that exhibits asymmetric division (albeit in a very different spatial pattern). In short, a specific set of predictions to be tested in an analysis would be that the three types of genetic functions that are now believed to play central roles in germ-soma specification in *V. carteri* were added to the volvocacean genetic repertoire in the sequence first regA, then log, and then gls (Kirk, 1998, pp. 256–271).

Furthermore, since V. rousseletti does not undergo asymmetric cell division, one would expect it to lack genes homologous to the gls genes in *V. carteri*. These predictions can compare with the phylogenetic history provided by Herron et al. (2009) and the twelve-step progression suggested by Kirk (Fig. 11.9). 

While the developmental program proposed by Kirk (see Kirk, 1998) posits that changes at three loci are sufficient to account for the evolution of complex, asymmetric reproduction, for example, as seen in *V. carteri*, recent comparative genomic data from the volvocinean lineage suggest that changes at these three loci may not be the whole story. For example, as demonstrated by De Hoff et al. (2011), the *V. carteri* regA gene is itself the product of a whole-genome duplication event and that regA-like genes are also present in the genomes of other volvocinean species. 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating Kirk’s hypothesis of germ-soma differentiation in *Volvox*. The diagram shows a phylogenetic tree of volvocinean species (*Chlamydomonas*, *Gonium*, *Pandorina*, *Eudorina*, *Pleodorina*, *Volvox tertius*, *Volvox carteri*, *Volvox obversus*).  Next to each species, boxes indicate the presence or absence of genes involved in germ-soma differentiation: *regA/regB* (regulation), *log* (large cell), and *gls* (gonidial specification). The diagram suggests that *regA/regB* genes were the first to evolve, followed by *log* genes, and finally *gls* genes, leading to the complex germ-soma differentiation seen in *V. carteri* and *V. obversus*.  The diagram also indicates the type of reproduction in each species (isogamy, oogamy, asymmetric reproduction).

# Footnotes

1. The eyespot gradient becomes more dramatic in either related species. Indeed, the posterior cells in *N. monoculus* lack eyespots entirely, appearing to be “blind” (Ueki et al. 2010).

2. A general term for a colonial mass of algae.

3. The role of the eyespot here provides an easy answer to the standard “creationist” question, “What use is ½ of an eye?” Clearly, it is of great use for visual cases where an organism needs to respond to light, but not actually form an image. For brilliant model of the simplicity of the entryway by which an image-forming eye might evolve from a directionally sensitive eyespot, see the classic paper by Nilsson and Pelger (1994), and also Richard Dawkins’s discussion of the topic in *Climbing Mount Improbable* (1996).

4. The structure of the eyespot itself provides additional directory (see Kirk 1988, p. 72, for more details).

5. The steps are: (1) Incomplete cyclokinesis; (2) Incomplete inversion of the embryo; (3) Rotation of the basal bodies; (4) Establishment of organismal polarity; (5) Transformation of cell walls into an extracellular matrix; (6) Genetic modulation of cell number; (7) Complete inversion of the embryo; (8) Increased volume of extracellular matrix; (9) Partial gem-sma division of labor; (10) Complete gem-sma division of labor; (11) Asymmetric division; (12) Bifurcation of the cell division program. More recently, Herron and Michel (2008) have suggested that the order of the first six steps may need to be revised, and that embryo inversion may have evolved in a single step (see also Mihi and Miller 2010). See Fig. 1.6 for how Herron et al. (2009) fit their proposed evolutionary lineage together with Kirk’s twelve steps.

6. In fact, Volvox does list around one side as it swims, since all the flagella beat with a slight bias to the right, so that the spheroid rotates counterclockwise when viewed from behind, giving rise to the “mere roller” (Kirk 1998, p. 180).

7. The sexual life cycle is induced when Volvox is exposed to a stimulating procedure. As Kirk notes, the temporal program of *V. carteri* is the most thoroughly molecularly known, capable of inducing full sexual development in a type-species manner as a consequence of an external stimulus (Kirk 1998, p. 182–183). A similar response, though the environmental cue and the precise molecular details, differs, has been documented in several additional Volvox species. Recent observations indicate that a specific photoreceptor protein, channelrhodopsin, may mediate the response to light, triggering the cascade of events that lead to the formation of sexual cells (Kadota et al. 2009).

8. For a detailed discussion of the evidence for the origin of multicellularity in Volvox, and the generalized model of the “somatic” route to multicellularity, see Kirk (1998, pp. 125–130).

9.  The gene is expressed in a pattern that is reminiscent of the expression of the *hox* genes during animal development (Matsuda et al. 2008).

> **Figure:** Figure 1.6. A proposed evolutionary lineage for the Volvox life cycle, integrating Kirk’s twelve steps with the proposed modifications of Herron et al. (2009). The numbers refer to the twelve steps outlined in footnote 5. The solid lines represent the proposed evolutionary relationships, while the dashed lines indicate areas of uncertainty. The figure shows a progression from a unicellular ancestor to a multicellular Volvox, with various intermediate stages representing key evolutionary innovations.

## THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

Orthologous genes share a common descent by speciation from a common ancestor and typically retain a similar function in the extant species. Homologous genes constitute a more broadly defined group, covering any set of genes that share a common ancestor; orthologous genes are a type of homologous genes, but so are paralogous genes, which are related by gene duplication.

# 12. Experimental Evolution

Sonya Bahar<sup>(1)</sup>

Department of Physics & Astronomy and Center for Neurodynamics, University of Missouri at St Louis, MO, USA

Keep your eyes peeled for a small black iron door.

LONG BEFORE it was given such a name, experimental evolution took place during the serial passages of pathogenic viruses and bacteria necessary to live attenuated vaccines (Kawasaki et al. 2012). The field of experimental evolution as we know it now, however, has developed rapidly and dramatically during the past three decades. Probably the best known experimental evolution study is Richard Lenski’s long-term evolution experiment (LTEE) at Michigan State University. Starting with twelve replicate *E. coli* cultures in February 1988, the experiment reached an astonishing 66,000 generations in November 2016, and (of course) continues. Using a strain that lacks a mechanism for genetic exchange, any changes seen in the twelve lines are results of mutation alone, under the action of selection. 

When the experiment was first started, Lenski envisioned it lasting only 2000 generations. “I’d already had success with some shorter duration, more traditionally designed experiments,” Lenski explained in a recent interview with Jeremy Fox for *Plus Biology*.

So it wasn’t a total shot in the dark – I knew the LTEE would yield data, I also knew, though, it was an unusually abstract, open-ended, and nontraditional experiment… Maybe I was overly confident, but I was pretty sure the outcome – whatever the might be – would be cool. I knew enough about what would happen – based on the experiments I had already done – that I was confident the data and analyses would be informative with respect to at least some of my questions (Fox and Lenski 2015).

The outcome was far more than he could have dreamed of in 1988. The study has continued for decades, resulting in a wealth of publications on the role of historical contingency in the development of novel phenotypes and a host of surprising results regarding the tempo and mode of evolutionary change. One particular advantage of the LTEE (and other experimental evolution studies inspired by it) is that samples from any generation can be frozen and stored, creating a living fossil record. An organism can then be revived in competition with a resurrected ancestor – allowing the experimenter to rate the evolutionary predicament of “replacing the tape”, imagined by Gould (1989) in his essay on the re-running of the Burgess Shale fossil record. Woodruff, Rosenbluth and Lenski (2014) did precisely this, with the evolutionary performance (as measured by the rate of growth) of the LTEE lines in 2006 compared to that of their ancestors at an early time point. The results are shown in Figure 12.1. The peak in the fitness of the LTEE lines is at 5000 generations, with a gradual plateauing thereafter. The experimenters also compared the fitness of the LTEE lines to that of a frozen stock of the original strain at 1000 generations. This had been kept frozen from the time it was isolated. A key finding was that the LTEE lines had not continued to evolve after 5000 generations, but had instead plateaued. 

> **Figure 12.1:** A graph showing the relative fitness of LTEE lines over time. The x-axis represents time in generations, ranging from 0 to 50,000. The y-axis represents relative fitness, with values ranging from 0 to 1.2. There are two lines on the graph: one representing the fitness of the LTEE lines, which increases rapidly from 0 to around 5,000 generations, then plateaus; and another representing the fitness of the original strain, which remains relatively constant at around 1. The graph demonstrates that the LTEE lines experienced significant evolutionary change in the early stages of the experiment, but then reached a plateau, suggesting that they had reached a fitness peak.

The experimenters also investigated the genetic basis of the adaptation. They found that the adaptation was due to a small number of mutations, and that these mutations were not specific to any particular line. This suggests that the adaptation was due to a general principle of evolution, rather than to a specific set of circumstances. The LTEE has also been used to study the evolution of other traits, such as antibiotic resistance and virulence.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

> **Figure:** A line graph titled "Divergence of cell volume in the first 10,000 generations of the LTEE." The x-axis is labeled "TIME (generations)" and ranges from 0 to 10000. The y-axis is labeled "CELL VOLUME (f1)" and ranges from 0.2 to 1.2. The graph shows multiple lines, each representing a different replicate population. The lines generally start around 0.6 and initially increase, then plateau, and some show slight fluctuations. The graph is labeled "Fig 12.1" and credits R.E. Lenski and M. Travisano, *Dynamics of adaptation and diversification: a 10,000-generation experiment with bacterial populations*. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 89:6814–6814, 1994. (1994) National Academy of Sciences, USA.

Though it fluctuated more than the cell size data, fitness increased rapidly during the initial 2000 generations, and then seemed to plateau. As with the cell size data, the fitness trajectories of the different populations diverged, though there was no clear trend in the standard deviation data for fitness as there had been for cell size. Either the populations had drifted apart and eventually come to occupy different adaptive peaks or were “climbing slowly along different ridges of unequal elevation toward the same peak.” (Lenski and Travisano 1994). The results were indicative of “macroevolutionary” trends toward both divergence and stasis. 

Lenski and Travisano next investigated the relationship between fitness and cell size. Both measures showed initial increases followed by plateaus, and a plot of cell size against relative fitness could be roughly fit by a line with positive slope. However, the relation between fitness and size within a single population over time (longitudinal regression), and among all populations at any given time point (cross-sectional regression), told a more complex story.





---

<!-- page 196 | Page 386 of 619 | 990ms -->

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

Within any given lineage, cell size and fitness increased together, though the slope of this increase differed between lineages. The cross-sectional regressions, however, suggest a divergence in the relationship between fitness and cell size *among* the populations. Despite the hypothesis that the functional relationship between size and fitness is causal and rigidly fixed, the authors concluded, in fact, the results suggest a divergence in Lenski and Travisiano suggest that this parallelism might be a result of the identical experimental environments, as well as inevitable mutational redundancies, given the number of population replications (~7.5 x 10<sup>11</sup>) and the baseline mutation rate (~2.5 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mutations per genome replication). They noted that a researcher stumbling upon the observed variability in their data but unfamiliar with the experimental conditions (essentially, the situation in which a paleontologist might find herself when comparing two fossil beds).

<br>

might attribute this diversity to environmental heterogeneity or phylogenetic constraints, but any such “just-so story” would clearly be misguided in this case. Instead, our experiment demonstrates the crucial role of chance events (historical accidents) in adaptive evolution. (Lenski and Travisiano 1994)

<br>

Broadly, they interpreted their results as indicative of a strong historical contingency.

<br>

Sustained divergence in mean fitness supports a Wrightian model of evolution in which replicate populations found their way onto different fitness peaks. Although the experimental populations were so large that the same mutations occurred in all of them, the order in which various mutations arose would have been different. As a consequence, some populations may have incorporated mutations that were beneficial over the short-term but led to evolutionary dead-ends (Lenski and Travisiano 1994). 

<br>

They noted the difficulty of moving to a higher adaptive peak in the traditional Wrightian fitness landscape model, since this would be hindered by selection against mutations that led to transient drops in fitness. “In this respect,” they wrote, “it is important, in our experiment, populations were not on one adaptive peak and asked to jump to another; instead, they were thrown into an arbitrary environment and asked to climb an accessible peak.” The behavior of the LTEE exhibited rapid diversification into a new environment.

<br>

The initial rapid evolution was presumably due to the intense selection triggered by the sudden environmental changes imposed at the start of our experiment. Although the ancestors of the founding bacterium used in this study had been “in captivity” for several decades, they were not necessarily systematically apportioned the experimental conditions we imposed (serial dilution in glucose-minimal medium). The experimental regime was therefore unusual, in several senses. The most remarkable characteristic was the open-ended nature of the environment—populations were grown in a continuous culture, and the environment never reached an equilibrium state. 

<br>

We saw an initial response to the new environment, and then a subsequent period of sustained diversification. The 12 populations exhibited a remarkable degree of repeatability in their evolutionary trajectories, yet also showed substantial idiosyncratic responses. In all populations, fitness increased substantially during the first 2000 generations, and then leveled off, but the rate of fitness increase varied considerably among the populations (Figure 1). (Lenski and Travisiano 1994)

<br>

> **Figure 1:** A graph showing the relative fitness of each of the 12 populations over time (generations). The x-axis represents generations (0 to 50,000), and the y-axis represents relative fitness, normalized to the ancestral strain. Each of the 12 populations is represented by a different colored line. The lines generally show an initial period of rapid fitness increase, followed by a plateau. There is variation in the rate and extent of fitness increase among the populations, and some lines show more fluctuations than others. The figure illustrates the repeatability of fitness increases across populations, as well as the idiosyncratic responses of each population.

<br>

In several populations, fitness continued to increase slowly for tens of thousands of generations, but in others, fitness remained constant or even declined. The populations also differed in the timing of their responses; some increased in fitness rapidly, while others were slower to respond. The most striking idiosyncratic response was the evolution of a subpopulation in population Ara-3 that was capable of growing on citrate, a novel carbon source not present in the original growth medium (Figure 2). (Lenski and Travisiano 1994)

<br>

> **Figure 2:** A graph showing the growth of the Ara-3 population in media containing citrate. The x-axis represents time (hours), and the y-axis represents cell density (optical density). Two lines are shown: one representing the growth of the ancestral strain in citrate media (which shows no growth), and one representing the growth of the Ara-3 population in citrate media (which shows exponential growth). The figure demonstrates the evolution of a novel trait (citrate utilization) in one of the experimental populations.

<br>

The evolution of citrate utilization was a particularly striking example of the power of experimental evolution to reveal novel adaptations. Citrate is a relatively complex molecule, and its utilization requires a series of enzymatic steps that were not present in the ancestral strain. The evolution of citrate utilization in Ara-3 was therefore a major evolutionary innovation.

<br>

# THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

> **Figure:** A line graph depicting cell size (f) over time (generations). The x-axis ranges from 0 to 3000 generations, with increments of 500. The y-axis ranges from 0.30 to 0.70, representing cell size (f), with increments of 0.05. The line fluctuates, starting at approximately 0.32 at generation 0 and reaching a peak of around 0.68 at approximately 800 generations. It then declines and oscillates between approximately 0.45 and 0.60 for the remainder of the graph. Error bars are shown at each data point, indicating the 95% confidence interval. The graph is labeled "Fig. 12.2 A punctuated pattern in *E. coli* cell size in the LTEE. Change in average cell size (f) in 10 – 15 over 3000 generations. Data points show the mean of 10 replicate assays, and error bars show 95% confidence intervals. The data is fit with a step function model. From S. F. Elena, V. S. Cooper, and R. E. Lenski, Punctuationed evolution caused by selection of rare beneficial mutations, *Science* 272: 1802–1804, 1996. Reprinted with permission from AAAS".

A follow-up study at 50,000 generations (Wiser et al. 2013) provides an interesting epilogue to this aspect of the LTEE story. Measurements of relative fitness over an additional 40,000 generations revealed a surprising trend. Instead of leveling off, fitness continued to increase, though at a far slower rate than in the early years of the experiment. Moreover, 6 of the 12 populations had acquired a “hypermutator” phenotype—their point-mutation rates had increased by a factor of about 100. Comparison of the hypermutators to the other populations showed that the former had a faster rate of fitness increase (Fig. 12.3).

The black circles represent ancestral mutation rates and show a generally increasing trend with a steep initial rise, leveling off around 30,000 generations. The green triangles represent hypermutators and show a more consistent, linear increase in relative fitness over time. # THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

Fig. 12.3. Fitness continues to increase. (Wiser et al. 2013) found that mean fitness of the twelve ancestral E. coli populations in the LTEE continued to increase over 50,000 generations. Six of the populations (black circles) attained fitness of one with the ancestral strain rate, while the other six (grey triangles) showed a hypermutator phenotype. Curves show the theoretical predictions of dynamical models; the mean show with the grey curve a mutation rate 100 times that of the one with black curve. From M.J. Wiser, R.E. Lenski, Long-term dynamics of adaptation in asexual populations, Science 332: 1364–1367, 2013. Reprinted with permission from AAAS.

Consistent with the lack of a plateau, hyperbolic functions did not fit the data well over this extended period of time. Not only was the data much better fit by a power law, but a power law fit to the first 10,000 generations predicted the future growth curve far better than did the hyperbolic fit used in 1994. A theoretical model accounting for “clonal interference” and diminishing-returns epistasis provided a similar result. (Miser & Lenski et al. 2013).

As of the date of Lenski and his colleagues could conclude that “[b]oth our empirical and theoretical analyses imply that adaptation can continue for a long time for sexual organisms, in a constant environment” (Wiser et al. 2013).

Among the many fascinating results of the LTEE, one of the most dramatic was the evolution of a novel phenotype that enabled the bacteria to grow aerobically using citrate as a nutrient source (Blount et al. 2008, 2012). Under normal conditions, *E. coli* cannot metabolize citrate. Indeed, the “inability to use citrate as an energy source under non-citrate conditions has long been a defining characteristic of *E. coli* as a species”; it lacks a citrate transporter that can import citrate under those conditions (Blount et al. 2008). However, one case of spontaneous mutation to a *citT* phenotype was observed in the 1980s, and the *E. coli* genome does encode a citrate-succinate exchanger, though this appears to only be induced under microoxic conditions. *E. coli* do not need citrate since they use a ferroic dicarboxylate transport system in order to facilitate influx of iron. Since the standard DM25 medium does not for the LTEE contained 700 μM citrate as a chelating agent, cells have the opportunity to develop mutations that would enable them to utilize citrate as an carbon source; after all, by the 30,000th generation of the LTEE, each of the dozens populations had undergone billions of mutations (Blount et al. 2008).

> **Figure:** A line graph depicting the increase in fitness over time for twelve *E. coli* populations. The x-axis is labeled “Time (generations)” and ranges from 0 to 50,000+. The y-axis is labeled “Relative fitness” and ranges from 0 to 1.2. Six populations are represented by black circles, and six are represented by grey triangles. A grey curve represents the predicted fitness increase based on a model with a high mutation rate, and a black curve represents the predicted fitness increase based on a model with a low mutation rate. The graph shows a continuous increase in fitness for all populations over the observed time period.

Populations 33, 27, and 19, however, a citrate-specific mutation that was responsible for enabling them to grow on citrate had arisen (Blount et al. 2008). Subsequently, fitness increases had been observed before, but had previously been transient (Gadkar et al. 2005; Miralles & Johnson 1998). The citrate adaptation, however, persisted for >30,000 generations. All other lines, to our knowledge, have failed to display a similar adaptation.

Cit’ clones could be readily isolated from the frozen sample of population Ara-3 taken at generation 33,500. To estimate the time of origin of the Cit’ trait, we screened 1,280 clones randomly chosen from generations 30,000, 30,500, 31,000, 31,500, 32,000, 32,500, and 33,000 for the capacity to produce a positive reaction on Christensen’s citrate agar, which provides a sensitive means to detect even weakly citrate-using cells. No Cit’ cells were found in the samples taken at 30,000, 30,500, or 31,000 generations. Cit’ cells constituted ≈0% of the population at generation 31,500, then 15% and the next two samples, but only ≈1% at generation 33,000. It appears that the first Cit’ variant emerged between 31,000 and 31,500 generations, although we cannot exclude an earlier origin. The precipitous decline in the frequency of Cit’ cells just before the massive population expansion suggests clonal interference—whereby the Cit’ subpopulation produced a beneficial trait that outcompeted the emerging Cit’ subpopulation until the latter evolved some other beneficial mutation that finally ensured its persistence. The hypothesis of clonal interference implies that the early Cit’ cells were very poor at using citrate, such that the mutation that improved competition for glucose could have provided a greater advantage than did marginal exploitation of the unused citrate. (Blount et al. 2008)

In the context of the LTEE’s potential to shed light on macroevolutionary trends, the new Cit’ variant was potentially revelatory. Was it simply the result of a rare mutation? *Finally* making its appearance? Or was facilitated by the background of prior chance mutations, and thus contingent on the particular history of the Ara-3 population? In so would provide a singular experimental example of how random determinism processes become intertwined over time such that future alternatives may be historically contingent manner (Blount et al. 2008).

In order to test whether the Cit’ phenotype had arisen in a historically contingent manner, Lenski and his colleagues resurrected a series of clonal ancestors to Ara-3 at 10,000 generation intervals. If the ability to metabolize citrate was contingent on the presence of a particular background of previous mutations, then did the repeated exploitation of the fresh habitat—in periodically subcultured populations—then threshold criteria would arise for a necessary accompanying background of previous mutations. At each 10,000 generation interval, the experimenters isolated the genetic makeup of an ancestral clone, then founded a fresh laboratory tap water population from that clone. Ara-3 was passaged periodically, resulting in a lineage of Ara-3 populations evolving in parallel with a Cit’ phenotype. To their surprise, a Cit’ phenotype arose independently in each of the 12 parallel lines, and in each case, the Cit’ mutations were identical. This compelling demonstration that a beneficial trait can evolve repeatedly under the same selective conditions—a phenomenon known as parallel evolution—was a landmark result. The fact that the same mutation arose in multiple independent lineages provided strong evidence that the mutation conferred a substantial fitness advantage. (Barrick et al. 2009)

> **Figure:** A graph depicting the frequency of Cit+ cells over time in the LTEE and in the resurrected ancestral lines. The x-axis represents generation number, ranging from 0 to 50,000. The y-axis represents the frequency of Cit+ cells, ranging from 0 to 1. The LTEE line shows a gradual increase in Cit+ frequency, peaking around generation 33,500 and then declining. The resurrected ancestral lines show a similar pattern of increase in Cit+ frequency, but the timing and magnitude of the increase vary slightly between lines. The graph demonstrates that the Cit+ phenotype can evolve repeatedly under the same selective conditions, providing evidence for parallel evolution.

The experimenters subsequently sequenced the genomes of the Cit’ mutants from each of the 12 parallel lines and identified the same two mutations in all of them. One mutation was in the *gcd* gene, which encodes a glucose/galactose permease, and the other was in the *rpoS* gene, which encodes a sigma factor involved in the regulation of stress responses. The *gcd* mutation increased the expression of the citrate transporter, while the *rpoS* mutation increased the expression of genes involved in citrate metabolism. The fact that the same two mutations arose repeatedly in all 12 parallel lines provided further evidence that these mutations conferred a substantial fitness advantage. (Tournier et al. 2009)

The LTEE and the parallel evolution experiments provided compelling evidence that adaptation can be both predictable and contingent. The fact that the same mutations arose repeatedly in the parallel evolution experiments demonstrated that adaptation can be predictable under certain conditions. However, the fact that the Cit’ phenotype did not arise until late in the LTEE demonstrated that adaptation can also be contingent on the particular history of a population. The LTEE and the parallel evolution experiments have provided valuable insights into the dynamics of adaptation and have helped to bridge the gap between microevolutionary and macroevolutionary processes.
