# Genomic Analysis of *Cit* and *rna* Genes

One particularly interesting result from the genetic analysis was that *Cit* clones after generation 36,000 had an SNP in the *mutS* gene, which codes for a protein involved in DNA mismatch repair. No evidence of this SNP was found in generations before 36,000, indicating that the mutation had arisen after the first cells began to express the *Cit* phenotype. Once it arose, this SNP facilitated further mutations, so that *Cit* cells after generation 36,000 accumulated mutations much faster than their *Cit-* cousins and their *Cit-* ancestors (see inset in Fig. 12.5). Recall that Ana-3 was not one of the lineages that had previously developed a hypermutation phenotype! 

What mutations caused the “actualization” of the *Cit* trait, enabling the cells to metabolize citrate under aerobic conditions? A prime suspect was identified when all nine sequenced *Cit* genomes were found to contain tandem copies of part of the *cit* operon, which controls citrate-transmembrane. The amplified segment included *citA*, which encodes the citrate-succinate exchanger, a protein typically inactive except under anaerobic conditions. The segment was not present in the ancestor or any of the sequenced *Cit-* genomes and it is only found in citrate samples after the evolution of the *Cit* lineage. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) screens also failed to detect this segment in 27 *Cit-* clones from generations 33,000 through 40,000, whereas it was found in all 33 *Cit* clones from the same generations. (Blount et al. 2012)

Southern blot and PCR studies from 13 isolates from a generation 33,000 clone had revealed to *Cit* showed no evidence of the segment. 

The repeated segment contained *citA* and another gene, *rna*, which codes for RNase II, as well as fragments of genes from either end of the *cit* operon. When the segment was repeated, this produced a hybrid sequence containing a promoter region for *citA*, aligned adjacent to *citT* in the next tandem copy (Fig. 12.6). If the mutated promoter region functioned under aerobic conditions, Blount et al. hypothesized, “the new *rna-citT* regulatory module might allow *Cit* expression during aerobic, and thereby confer a *Cit+* phenotype.”

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

While these cells were barely able to utilize citrate, they were able to out-compete Z830 cells lacking the mutant promoter. Evidence suggested that actualization and potentiation act epistatically, since expression of *mkt-cit* in the ancestor and in clones from *cl* and *C1* exhibited much weaker *Cit⁺* phenotypes than expression in potentiated clones from *C1*. Potentiation of *Cit⁺* lineages that exhibit an increased propensity to evolve into *Cit⁺* may be due to a mutation in *arc*, which codes for a histidine kinase whose disruption upregulates the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Expression of the *mkt-cit* segment from early *Cit⁺* clones produced very weak *Cit⁺* phenotypes, able to metabolize citrate, but at low efficiency. Blount et al. next set about investigating how this phenotype was “refined,” growing stronger and more competitive in subsequent generations. Later generations had increased copy numbers of the *mkt-cit* segment, up to nine copies cloned generation 33,000. Later clones went down to four copies, however, a drop in the ability to metabolize citrate, suggesting that other “stabilizing” mutations might have occurred in the interim, and that refinement itself is a multi-step process.

The *cit* region appears to be quite labile in *Ara-3*. Nineteen of the “evolved” *Cit⁺* strains from the “replaying the tape” experiments showed duplicated portions of the *cit* region, though none of these duplications are spliced at exactly the same sites. In one strain, a large portion of the *cit* operon moved to a location downstream of the promoter for a different gene entirely. The mutations that might have potentiated this lability, and other factors controlling the evolution of the *Cit⁺* phenotype, are currently being explored by a number of research groups (Leiby et al. 2012; Lebby and Marla 2014; Quandt et al. 2015; Turner et al. 2015).

One of the most exciting areas of experimental evolution – and the area most relevant for the theme of this book – is the evolution of multicellularity. These studies have consistently shown how it is for multicellularity to arise under straightforward selective conditions and of term reminiscent with a minimum of genetic change. One striking example of this is provided by the bacterial swimming study published by Velicer and You (2003). Wild-type *Myxococcus xanthus* can form swarms and fruiting bodies in a manner reminiscent of *Dictyostelium*. In order to swarm on soft agar, *M. xanthus* uses a mechanism known as S-motility, which is mediated by extracellular fibrous extensions called type IV pili. *M. xanthus* can employ a major structural component of these fibers, is coded for by the *pilA* gene. Velicer and You studied eight populations of *M. xanthus* in which they had deleted a large portion of the *pilA* so that the bacteria were unable to swarm. Interestingly, they performed series of transfer experiments in which the deleted *pilA* strains were placed on soft agar, and those that were able to swarm were transferred to fresh soft agar, repeating this process 30 times. In all eight populations, the bacteria rapidly evolved the ability to swarm again, and in five of the eight populations, this was due to the reinsertion of a functional copy of the *pilA* gene. However, the reinserted *pilA* genes were not identical to the original *pilA* gene. In two populations, the reinserted *pilA* gene had acquired a 20 kb insertion, and in one population, it had acquired a 60 kb insertion. In the remaining population, the reinserted *pilA* gene was a mosaic of the original *pilA* gene and a different *pilA* gene found elsewhere in the *M. xanthus* genome. 

> **Figure:** A graph depicting the results of the *Myxococcus xanthus* evolution experiment. The x-axis represents time in transfers (0-30). The y-axis represents the proportion of the population that is able to swarm. There are eight lines on the graph, each representing a different population. All eight lines start at 0 and increase over time, indicating that the ability to swarm evolved in all populations. The lines vary in their rate of increase and their final proportion of swarmers. Some lines reach a plateau, while others continue to increase throughout the experiment. The graph demonstrates the rapid and repeatable evolution of swarming ability in *M. xanthus*.

# THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

“These results” Velicer and You concluded, “show that fundamental transitions to primitive cooperation can readily occur in bacteria.” This cooperation did not come without a cost, however. Inhibition of the production of the fibrils necessary for this new mechanism of swarming increased the growth rate of strains ET and EB in liquid culture (by 5.3% and 4.6%, respectively); these growth increases were statistically significant. “Thus,” Velicer and You concluded, evolved fibril production slows individual reproductive rate under unstructured, social conditions, but appears to be favoured by selection at the kin-group level in a structured habitat by its mediation of enhanced group migration.” Superior migration allowed clustered groups of related cooperative to move into territory and consume resources that were unavailable to non-cooperative, poorly swimming competitors (Velicer and Yu 2003).

In the same September 2003 issue of *Nature* in which Velicer and Yu published their M. xanthus study, Rainey and Rainey demonstrated the evolution of multicellularity using *Pseudomonas fluorescens*. *P. fluorescens* is a rod-shaped bacterium that grows under aerobic conditions. Rainey and Rainey observed the evolution of a heterogeneous bacteria adapted to take advantage of various niches in a heterogeneous broth environment. Most interesting was the “wrinkly spreader” (WS) phenotype, so named in contrast to its smooth (SM) ancestor. The wrinkly spreaders formed a biofilm at the air-broth interface. “Colonization of this niche,” wrote Rainey and Rainey, “enables cells to avoid the anoxic conditions that rapidly build up in unshaken broth culture.” 

Rainey and Rainey found that the cooperating groups of *P. fluorescens* were potent potentiators by mutations in one ten genes. Was the competition. These mutations resulted in overproduction of a cell adhesive cellulose polymer that provides a structural matrix for the biofilm (Spier et al., 2002, 2003). Group adaptation comes at an individual cost, however. Competition experiments pitting individual WS cells against SM genotype under abundant resource conditions showed that the WS cells only 60% the fitness of their ancestor” (Despite a much reduced doubling time,” the authors reported, “WS readily invaded clumps (from a single mutant cell populations dominated by the ancestral genotype to reach population densities that exceed those of the originally dominant type” (Rainey and Rainey 2003). 

A genotype useful for a group of related organisms, but costly for individuals on their own, provides a ripe breeding ground for cheaters looking for a free ride. In this case, cheater strains were discovered to consist of cells lacking the gene(s) necessary to produce cellulose. They spread within the WS population, converting it into a fast-growing, but non-structured, SM population. Despite the detrimental impact of the cheaters on the group, the authors found that the cheaters themselves had a selective advantage in spatially structured environments. “The results,” Rainey and Rainey concluded, “demonstrate that the evolution of altruistic behaviour is contingent on spatial structure.”

> **Figure:** A graph depicting the relative fitness of smooth (SM) and wrinkly spreader (WS) *Pseudomonas fluorescens* strains in different environments. The x-axis represents time in generations, and the y-axis represents the population density of each strain. The graph shows that SM strains initially grow faster but are eventually outcompeted by WS strains in structured environments (represented by a solid line for WS and a dashed line for SM). In unstructured environments (represented by different lines), SM strains maintain a higher population density. The graph illustrates the trade-off between individual and group fitness and the importance of spatial structure in the evolution of cooperation.

“The evolution of cooperation,” Rainey and Rainey wrote, “is therefore not simply a matter of selecting for traits that benefit the group, but also of suppressing the proliferation of cheaters who exploit the cooperative system.” This theme is echoed in the work of Gregor Doetsch and colleagues on the evolution of multicellularity in yeast.

# 12.8 Spreading of *Fluorescens* Strains: The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

> **Figure 12.8:** A Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. 

The D phenotype resulted from a two-nucleotide deletion in a gene involved in the production of cyclic di-GMP (c-di-GMP), a second-messenger protein that regulates motility and induces a wrinkly phenotype. Further experiments showed that the D phenotype could evolve against a background of M cells easily. Different instances involved different mutations, but all showed mutations in the locus regulating c-di-GMP production (Kim et al. 2016).

The evolution of D cells against an M cell background was mirrored by the evolution of M-type cells in a population of D cells. A proportion of D cells consistently exhibited mutations disabling c-di-GMP production. When these newly evolved M cells were grown alone, they too allowed for the evolution of a new D phenotype in their midst. The phenotype could arise, even in the absence of a functional c-di-GMP production system. Kim et al. concluded that “robust bidirectional evolution…reliably generates whichever partner is missing for collective spreading.” The necessary mutations arose with ease, so that “the robustness and organization of the collective phenotype contrasts with the simplicity of its origin”; all the mutations involved the activation or deactivation of a single intracellular messenger which controls the transition from a motile to a sessile state (Kim et al. 2016).

Experimental studies of the evolution of multicellularity have been pioneered by Michael Travisano, who, after training at Michigan State with Richard Lenski, now runs his own laboratory at the University of Minnesota. Travisano and colleagues, working with both yeast (*S. cerevisiae*) and *Chlamydomonas*, have laid out some sets of conditions under which multicellularity and division of labor can arise under selection. In the first of these studies, Travisano and his group set out to investigate the conditions under which a transition to multicellularity might take place (Ratcliff et al. 2012). Does such a transition occur more readily by “aggregation of genetically distinct cells, or by mother-daughter adhesion after division?” Under what conditions would selection on multiple cell clusters come to dominate over selection on individual cells? Would the answers to these questions depend on the particular mechanism of cluster formation?

Previous studies showed how ecological conditions could favor the formation of multicellular clusters: the work of Boras et al. (1989) had demonstrated that “predation” by a small-motored culture results in the evolution of cluster-induced traits in the previously single-celled green alga *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii*. Travisano et al. (2013) took a different approach: they created “predators” by using beads to physically disrupt cell clusters, and showed that this too could select for cluster-induced traits. Ratcliff et al. (2012) set up a system in which cell decomposition was the selective pressure, and showed that this too could favor the evolution of multicellularity. 

To do so, they began with a population of *S. cerevisiae* cells that were capable of budding, but did not adhere to each other. They imposed a selective pressure by repeatedly washing away smaller clusters of cells, leaving only those with at least four cells. This imposed a selective pressure for cells to remain attached to each other after division. After 20 days of this treatment, the population had evolved a strong tendency to adhere, and to form clusters.

> **Table 12.1:** A Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

| Trait | Ancestral | Evolved | *P*-value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cluster size (cells) | 1.4 | 14.2 | <0.001 |
| Proportion of cells in clusters | 0.08 | 0.94 | <0.001 |
| Budding rate (buds/cell/hr) | 0.31 | 0.18 | 0.003 |
| Cell size (µm<sup>3</sup>) | 340 | 580 | <0.001 |

The evolved cells were not only more likely to adhere, but they also grew larger, and budded at a slower rate. This is consistent with the idea that the evolution of multicellularity is often associated with a trade-off between cell proliferation and cell size. The researchers also found that the evolved cells were more resistant to predation by a small, motile predator. This suggests that the evolution of multicellularity can provide a defense against predation.

# 12.9 Rapid, convergent evolution of the “snowflake” in the yeast *S. cerevisiae*. Replicate population number is shown in the lower right. All right. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 109:51–1500, 2012.

After budding. Reprinted with permission from W.C. Ratcliff, R.F. Denison, M. Borrello, and N. Travisano, Experimental evolution of multicellularity. *Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A.* 109:51–1500, 2012.

In the next stage of the experiment, the investigators set up a protocol that allowed selection for rapidly transferring. They took nine replicates from a population in which the snowflake phenotype had already evolved, and exposed three replicates to a series of transfers with 5 min allowed for gravitational settling, another three to transfers with 15 min for settling, and the last three to transfers with 25 min for settling. As before, each transfer was performed with a sample from the bottom of each aliquot. “With mutation as the only source of within-cluster genetic variants,” they wrote, “selection among clusters was expected to dominate within-cluster selection, leading to adaptation in multicellular ‘traits’” (Ratcliff et al. 2012). In other words, they had experimentally established the conditions for group selection. 

As expected, the stronger selection conditions (reduced time to settle) selected for snowflakes that settled faster; these clusters were larger and broke into larger propagule clusters, than the original snowflake ancestor population. Larger cluster size at the time of reproduction (i.e., when a snowflake split into propagule clusters) represented a “longer juvenile phase.” Most importantly, this was an emergent multicellular trait. “Because the response to selection changed the multicellular phenotype,” they wrote, “we conclude that selection was acting on the reproduction and survival of individual clusters rather than on their component cells” (Ratcliff et al. 2012). 

The snowflake experiments showed the division of labor as well as the evolution of simple multicellularity. Snowflake yeast experienced a tradeoff between settling rate and growth rate. Larger clusters settled faster and were thus selected for, but these grew more slowly, likely because cells in the interior of the cluster were starved for access to resources. An adaptive strategy to compensate for this “self-sacrifice” of a percentage of cells by apoptosis.

Snowflake yeast that produce smaller propagules can make more of them, increasing a cluster’s fecundity, and smaller propagules will be relatively faster growing than larger propagules… To generate proportionally smaller propagules, each reproductive event must be asymmetric, with propagules having less than half the biomass of the mother cluster. The investigators found that snowflakes allow all small propagules to escape from larger clusters (Ratcliff et al. 2012).

Observably and experimentally, asymmetric reproduction event must be asymmetric, with propagules having less than half the biomass of the mother cluster. The investigators found that snowflakes allow all small propagules to escape from larger clusters (Ratcliff et al. 2012). A model for the evolution of asymmetric reproduction in the snowflake yeast is shown in *Figure 12.11*. In this model, a cluster that produces a small propagule has a higher net reproductive rate than a cluster that produces a large propagule. 

> **Figure 12.11:** A model for the evolution of asymmetric reproduction in the snowflake yeast. (A) A cluster that produces a small propagule has a higher net reproductive rate than a cluster that produces a large propagule. (B) The model predicts that the frequency of asymmetric reproduction will increase as the cost of cluster size increases. The solid and dashed lines represent the predicted frequencies of symmetric and asymmetric reproduction, respectively. The inset shows the relationship between the cost of cluster size and the frequency of asymmetric reproduction.

The model predicts that the frequency of asymmetric reproduction will increase as the cost of cluster size increases. The investigators tested this prediction by growing snowflake yeast in a range of glucose concentrations. As the glucose concentration decreased (i.e., as the cost of cluster size increased), the frequency of asymmetric reproduction increased. This result supports the hypothesis that asymmetric reproduction evolved as a means of increasing the net reproductive rate of clusters in resource-limited environments.

The snowflake yeast experiments provide a compelling example of how multicellularity can evolve rapidly in response to selection. The experiments also demonstrate the importance of emergent traits in the evolution of multicellularity. Emergent traits are traits that are not present in individual cells but arise from the interactions among cells. In the case of snowflake yeast, the emergent trait is the ability to form large, rapidly settling clusters. This trait is not present in individual yeast cells, but it arises from the interactions among cells within a cluster. The snowflake yeast experiments show that emergent traits can be powerful drivers of evolution.

The machinery for the emergence of collective ensembles of cells does not arise by any mysterious means; it is right there in the zinc-finger-binding motif of a single protein. 

The genetic results just described clearly show that the yeast snowflake phenotype arose by incomplete division rather than by aggregation. As Stephen Jay Gould would have hastened to point out, however, by this point the dominant focus of selection has shifted to the multicellular collective, not the cell, and even less the individual gene.

Panel b shows a multicellular cluster, with arrows indicating the extracellular matrix. Rosenberg, and N. Travisano, Experimental evolution of an alternating uni- and multicellular life cycle in *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii*. *Nat. Commun.* 4:2742, 2013, copyright 2013.

Did the *C. reinhardtii* clusters originated via a unidirectional genetic bottleneck, like the yeast snowflakes? To test this, the investigators took isolates from the population that had evolved multicellularity. Portions of the genomes of these isolates were sequenced, and found to be identical at five unlinked loci, implying that the isolates shared a common ancestor. The initial genetic variation in the strain that evolved multicellularity had thus been whittled down to a single lineage. 

After 24 h in culture, investigators observed, individually, swimming cells in each of the ten isolates. In order to observe the life cycle in more detail, they transferred the cultures to fresh medium and imaged them using time-lapse microscopy. For the first 4 h, no single cells detached from the parent clusters. Then, after about 4 h, something remarkable began to happen. “Cells in clusters began to activate their flagella, causing the cluster to convulse rapidly,” they recounted. “This change in state, from stasis to full movement, took 3 min. Six minutes after the onset of flagellar activity, the first motile individual cells broke free from the cluster” (Ratcliff et al. 2013b). After about a day of observation, individually swimming cells were no longer observed, as all the individual cells had undergone fission and formed clusters. Two days after the culture was started, clusters had nearly tripled their volume. “Together,” the investigators concluded, “these observations demonstrate that experimentally evolved *C. reinhardtii* possess a novel multicellular life cycle consisting of alternating phases: a dispersal phase in which clusters reproduce via motile unicellular propagules and do not grow larger, and a growth phase in which clusters produce few propagules and instead increase cell number” (Ratcliff et al. 2013b).

Ratcliff and colleagues noted the contrast between the clusters they observed and the naturally forming clusters of *C. reinhardtii* that form when a single generation of cells is taken from the mother cell wall. The clusters that result from selection were much larger—typically 20–50 cells—and more spherical in shape. Additionally, whereas naturally formed clusters do not move, the evolved clusters were highly motile. The investigators then examined if cells within a cluster are genetically identical or if the multicellularity arose from a random mix of cells. They found that all cells within a cluster were genetically identical, indicating that clusters arise via cell division, not cell aggregation. Finally, genetic analysis of the evolved *C. reinhardtii* revealed a common genetic basis for the evolved multicellularity and the naturally occurring multicellularity in *C. reinhardtii*. The five loci identified as shared by all the multicellular isolates were also found to be associated with multicellularity in naturally occurring strains of *C. reinhardtii* (Ratcliff et al. 2013b).

> **Figure:** Fig. 12.10 shows a series of microscopic images documenting the evolution of multicellularity in *C. reinhardtii*. Panel a depicts tubes containing *C. reinhardtii* after 20 minutes of settling, with the left tube showing multicellular algae. Panel b is a close-up of a multicellular cluster, with arrows pointing to the extracellular matrix. Panel c illustrates mobile propagules released from a cluster, and panel d shows the ancestral, single-celled form which is phenotypically identical to the propagules. Panel e demonstrates the formation of a cluster originating from a single parent cell. A scale bar indicates 25 μm for all images. The figure highlights the transition from single cells to multicellular clusters and the subsequent release of mobile propagules, illustrating the alternating uni- and multicellular life cycle.

The authors propose that the evolution of multicellularity in *C. reinhardtii* involved a genetic bottleneck, where a single lineage acquired the necessary genetic changes. This lineage then underwent a series of cell divisions, forming larger, motile clusters. The genetic basis for this multicellularity is shared with naturally occurring multicellular strains of *C. reinhardtii*, suggesting that the experimental evolution recapitulated a natural evolutionary pathway. The ability to alternate between unicellular and multicellular life cycles provides *C. reinhardtii* with a flexible strategy for adapting to changing environmental conditions.

# PF

As organisms adapt to changing environments, change in gene regulatory networks can have decade and cascading effects. Recent studies have focused on the evolution of gene regulatory networks. The group headed by Gábor Balázi (formerly at the M. D. Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, and now at the State University of New York at Stony Brook) has studied a synthetic gene circuit integrated into the genome of *S. cerevisiae* (González et al. 2015). Balázi’s group used a synthetic gene circuit consisting of two genes—a transcriptional regulator (rTA) and an antibiotic-resistance gene fused to a fluorescence reporter (*yEGFP-zeoR*), shown schematically in Fig. 1.11. In the presence of the inducer doxycycline (an antibacterial compound that does not harm yeast), the rTA protein enhances transcription of its own gene in a positive feedback loop, and also enhances the expression of *yEGFP-zeoR*, which confers resistance to the antibiotic zeocin (Nevochaev et al. 2012). But rTA is toxic under some conditions, and thus antibiotic resistance can come at a steep cost. Since expression levels vary, each cell will have a different balance between antibiotic resistance and rTA toxicity.

*S. cerevisiae* is unaffected by doxycycline, which enabled the researchers to stress the cells (zeocin, an antibiotic which causes DNA double-strand breaks), ultimately arming the cell cycle and causing cell death) with the inducer of the stress response (doxycycline). Treatment with doxycycline alone, in the absence of zeocin, led the synthetic gene circuit to “respond gratuitously to a harmless environmental change,” leading to toxicity without any accompanying benefit. In contrast, cells treated with zeocin alone were unable to respond to a harmful stress. A more complicated scenario resulted in complex cost-benefit tradeoffs: treatment with a combination of doxycycline and zeocin resulted the cells to respond suboptimally to stress. 

Using two computational models, the research plot the fitness landscape with fitness measure as the rate of cell division (a function of the concentrations of inducer and antibiotic) [12,11]. They predicted that, in the doxycycline-only condition, mutations that decrease rTA toxicity would increase fitness, while in the zeocin-only condition mutations would be beneficial if they increased zeocin resistance, either enhancing rTA/ZEP2 expression or up-regulating native stress responses. When both doxycycline and zeocin were present, the situation became more complex, since no single mutation of the above types would be optimal (Goncalves et al. 2015). 

Based on the computational models, Balázsi’s team predicted that, when doxycycline and zeocin were both present in relatively high concentrations, “tweaking” (“T”) mutations, which weakened rTA toxicity, would predominate. In contrast, when the concentration of doxycycline was significantly lowered (from 2 to 0.2 µg/mL), both “mutations” and mutations that affect the response to zeocin (“genetic” or “G,” “mutational” would occur. The team further suggested that only 9 mutations would be favored in the zeocin-only case, while in the doxycycline-only case, “T” or “knockout” mutations, which abolished rTA toxicity, should be favored.

The team tested their predictions in yeast populations under the various conditions. In the doxycycline-only condition, with a high (2 µg/mL) concentration of doxycycline, fluorescence quickly increased and remained high during the first 40 generations, indicating unnecessary expression of rTA/ZEP2-toxin, and the appearance of “knockout” mutations (mutations that completely abolished rTA toxicity, as predicted at 2015). In the rTA/ZEP2-zeocin exposure. As predicted, zeocin-treated populations showed the exclusive toxicity of the “mutational” class, the initial cost of rTA toxicity was overcome (Goncalves et al. 2015). When both doxycycline and zeocin were present, “T” mutations predominated, and the population evolved to utilize the circuit, but at a minimal cost. 

To confirm these results, the researchers constructed a series of yeast strains with specific mutations and measured their fitness under different conditions. The results confirmed their predictions: “knockout” mutations were favored under doxycycline-only conditions, “mutational” mutations were favored under zeocin-only conditions, and “tweaking” mutations were favored under combined conditions (Goncalves et al. 2015). 

These results demonstrate that the fitness landscape of a synthetic gene circuit is complex and depends on the environmental conditions. The researchers showed that different mutations can be favored under different conditions, and that the optimal mutation depends on the trade-off between different costs and benefits. This work has important implications for the design of synthetic gene circuits, as it highlights the need to consider the environmental context in which the circuit will be used.

| Condition | Predominant Mutation | Fitness Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Doxycycline only | “Knockout” | Abolishes rTA toxicity, increases fitness |
| Zeocin only | “Mutational” | Increases zeocin resistance, increases fitness |
| Doxycycline + Zeocin | “Tweaking” | Reduces rTA toxicity, balances costs and benefits |

The researchers also investigated the evolutionary dynamics of the circuit over longer timescales. They found that the population could evolve to adapt to the combined doxycycline and zeocin conditions, but that this adaptation was often slow and unpredictable. This suggests that the fitness landscape of the circuit is not static, but can change over time as the population evolves.

These findings have important implications for the use of synthetic gene circuits in biotechnology and medicine. They suggest that it is important to carefully consider the environmental context in which the circuit will be used, and to design the circuit in a way that is robust to changes in the environment. They also suggest that it may be necessary to monitor the evolution of the circuit over time, and to adjust the design as needed to maintain its desired function.

# 12. Zachary Blount (left) and Richard Lenski with just a few of the plates used for their citrate experiments. Reproduced from Fox and Lenski (2015) under a C.C. BY 4.0 Creative Commons Attribution License

Some of the most striking in silico evolution studies have been performed by Chris Ofria and colleagues at Michigan State University, using the Avida platform in which populations of computer programs compete and reproduce, with their fitness determined by their ability to perform certain tasks (Ofria and Wilke 2004). In Avida, populations of individual organisms (computer programs with a fixed-length “genome” of instructional) compose colonies also referred to as multicells or groups. As organisms execute tasks contained in their genome (and are rewarded if they evolve to execute the Boolean logical functions NOT, NAND, ORNOT, OR, ANDNOT, NOR and EQU), they acquire resources for their colony. Different logical functions may be associated with different amounts of resources. The total amount of resources in the ecosystem is limited, with a continual resource flow into and out of the system – a digital “chemotaxis.” When a colony has acquired a certain amount of resources, it reproduces clonally, generating offspring colonies seeded by organisms from the parent colony. New colonies can displace older ones, which are then removed from the simulation. 

Avida has been used to investigate topics like adaptive radiation as a result of resource competition (Chow et al. 2004). Some of the most dramatic recent Avida studies have focused on the evolutionary origins of the division of labor and the factors that maintain a balance between levels of selection. In 2012, Ofria, along with Heather Goldby, Ben Kerr, and University of Arizona art researcher Anna Dornhaus, used Avida to investigate the role of task-switching costs in promoting the evolution of the division of labor (Goldby et al. 2012). From Adam Smith’s *Wealth of Nations* to Dornhaus’s own studies of ant behavior, the cost (in time, energy, and/or learning) of an individual switching between tasks has been found to favor the division of labor; it has even been suggested that the division of labor is impossible in the absence of task-switching costs. A classic example of this is the division of volvo somatic and germ-line cells, driven by requirement of decoupling the female from the basal order bodies in an organism to perform mitosis (See 11). 

Avida’s team set up replicate “worlds” containing 400 colonies of computer program organisms, each containing up to 25 identical (clonal) organisms. Mutations were allowed to occur only during colony reproduction. Since each function executed by an organism provides a bit of a limited resource, mutualism is favored. Importantly, organisms can only “trade” for greater than unit amounts of any function. To model cooperative resource exchange, a role will gain a reproductive advantage by collecting a variety of resources. This could be done in several ways. A colony could evolve to upend organisms, which then release their corresponding resource to the colony. A colony could evolve to “eat” organisms, which then release their corresponding resource to the colony. A colony could evolve to upend specific organisms, which then release only one type of resource to the colony. A colony could evolve to “eat” specific organisms, which then release only one type of resource to the colony. A colony could evolve to be a passive filter, collecting any resource that drifts by. A colony could evolve to be a “parasite,” which steals resources from other colonies, thereby increasing its own resource base, but decreasing the resource base of others. 

> **Figure:** A screenshot from the Avida simulation showing a population of digital organisms. The screen displays a grid-like environment populated by colored squares, each representing a digital organism. The organisms are arranged in colonies, and their colors indicate their genetic makeup or function. The simulation interface includes various controls and displays for monitoring the population's evolution, resource levels, and other parameters. The x and y axes represent the spatial coordinates within the simulation environment. The color intensity of each square may represent the organism's fitness or resource consumption rate. The simulation is used to study evolutionary processes such as adaptation, competition, and the emergence of complexity.

The results were striking. Colonies that evolved to specialize in collecting different resources outperformed those that did not. Moreover, the division of labor was not simply a matter of colonies becoming specialized in different tasks; it was also a matter of colonies becoming specialized in *different ways* of performing the same task. For example, some colonies evolved to collect resource A by upending organisms, while others evolved to collect resource A by eating organisms. This suggests that the division of labor is not simply a matter of colonies becoming specialized in different tasks; it is also a matter of colonies becoming specialized in different *strategies* for performing the same task. 

Interestingly, the division of labor was not always stable. Colonies that were initially successful at specializing in different resources often found themselves outcompeted by colonies that were more generalist. This suggests that the division of labor is not always the optimal strategy, and that the optimal strategy may depend on the specific environment.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

The evolution of cells that are both metabolically and propagule-eligible (i.e., *soma* ) faces two seemingly insurmountable challenges: First, any cell that performs mutagenic functions will damage its genome. Second, if a cell becomes ineligible to be used as a propagule, it removes itself from the reproductive line of the multicell. For the multicell to thrive, it appears that a subset of cells must perform both damaging actions, while the genetic material that encodes these actions must persist, unexpressed, in other cells (Goldsby et al. 2014a).

Mutations posed another problem still: by decreasing the similarity between cells within the colony, they increased intra-colony competition, shifting selection toward the individual, rather than the colony, level. 

Simulations were performed over a range of FML values, with populations in which every cell was initially propagule-eligible. For intermediate values, colonies evolved with a significant proportion of propagule-ineligible cells which performed “disproportionately large fractions of functions associated with mutagenic consequences” (Goldsby et al. 2014a). For one FML value, for example, propagule-ineligible cells performed an average of 64.17 mutagenic functions, while propagule-eligible cells performed an average of 0.59!

Such division of labor was favored because somatic cells, which had removed themselves from consideration as propagule cells, performed the mutagenic functions necessary for the digital multicell to replicate, while the germ cells maintained the genetic/s genetic information in pristine condition. (Goldsby et al. 2014a)

How did the germ-soma division emerge? Did a population of propagule-ineligible arise first, and then take on a range of mutagenic functions? Or did the cells shoulder the workload first? The second of these options “has some immediate benefits for the reproductive rate of the multicell but at the cost of putting the genetic information of the multicell in peril” (Goldsby et al. 2014a). On the first option provides no initial selective benefit, and could presumably arise only via genetic drift. In fact, the lineages at an intermediate FML value “followed an unanticipated pattern” on the dirty-work-first option.

The multicell first split the workload naturally among the propagule-eligible cells, where some propagule-eligible cells which we’ll call “pseudo-soma” performed more mutagenic functions than others. This innovation protected the genetic material in some of the propagule-eligible cells while the pseudo-soma dramatically increased the multicell’s replication rate. Next, the multicell evolved to make these pseudo-somatic cells into actual somatic cells by blocking their ability to be selected as a propagule and thus guaranteeing that only high-fidelity germ cells were used to produce the next generation of offspring. (Goldsby et al. 2014a)

As the propagule-ineligible cells multiplied, the workload of the dirty work shifted to them. The researchers found that this evolutionary trajectory was the only one that consistently evolved across the many replicator dynamics they investigated. Further, the researchers discovered that the ability to evolve the germ-soma division was contingent on the intermediate FML values. At low FML values, the replicator dynamics were too slow to allow for the evolution of the division of labor, and at high FML values, the replicator dynamics were too fast, and the population collapsed before the division of labor could evolve. (Goldsby et al. 2014a)

> **Figure:** A series of six graphs depicting the evolution of the proportion of propagule-ineligible cells and the average number of mutagenic functions performed by propagule-eligible and propagule-ineligible cells over time. The x-axis of each graph represents time (generations), and the y-axis varies depending on the graph. The first graph shows the proportion of propagule-ineligible cells, with the y-axis ranging from 0 to 1. The second and third graphs show the average number of mutagenic functions performed by propagule-eligible and propagule-ineligible cells, respectively, with the y-axis ranging from 0 to 70. The fourth, fifth, and sixth graphs are similar to the first three, but for a different set of conditions. The graphs demonstrate that as time progresses, the proportion of propagule-ineligible cells increases, and the average number of mutagenic functions performed by propagule-ineligible cells also increases, while the average number of mutagenic functions performed by propagule-eligible cells remains low.

These researchers also investigated the role of mutation rate in the evolution of the germ-soma division. They found that increasing the mutation rate increased the rate at which the germ-soma division evolved. This is because a higher mutation rate increases the likelihood that a cell will acquire a mutation that makes it propagule-ineligible. (Goldsby et al. 2014a)

The graph shows the strength of selection, measured as the percentage of tasks performed by each colony, decreased with the length of time between tournaments. Longer inter-tournament periods would allow the system more time to accommodate changing conditions, weakening group-selection. As expected, an increase in the inter-tournament period decreased the mean number of unique tasks performed by each colony, though this effect was qualitatively small. In another set of studies, group selection was weakened by allowing individuals from one group to migrate into another during the replication process. Changing the migration rate from 0 to 5% caused a drop from ~5 tasks, raising the migration rate to 20% decreased the tasks to 2 by a bottlenecked rate (Gokhale et al. 2014b). Variation in propagule size showed that, as the number of organisms in a propagule increased, so did the number of tasks performed by the evolved colony. In this case, division of labor was not favored by a bottlenecked life cycle. Successful colonies exhibited a variety of lineage structures. Despite the propagule size result just mentioned, some colonies evolved from single lineages, engaging in a range of tasks by phenotypic plasticity (for example, having a range of possible functions in an organism’s code that could be expressed depending on the conditions and interactions with other organisms). Other colonies contained a range of genetic lineages; some of these genetically diverse colonies also maintained phenotypic diversity. Knockout studies of phenotypically diverse colonies, in which individual lines of core were excised, showed that passage of epigenetic information from parent to offspring played a significant role in the “differentiation” of organisms within the colony. Within genetically diverse colonies, lineages were found to modulate their rate of replication in order to avoid “replicating” other lineages. If between-group pressure was removed from these colonies, however, the lineages within them no longer modulated their replication rate. The *Avida* experiments highlight the problem of balancing cooperation and competition, and how the tension between these complementary drives affects the levels at which collectives can emerge. We have encountered this pair of complementary factors repeatedly throughout the preceding pages. Now we must explore competition and cooperation in more depth and specificity.

A similar process appears to be at work in higher-level collectivities. In eusocial insects, there can be several orders of magnitude difference in the lifetime of workers compared to queens, and this has been suggested to result from oxidative stress on the workers’ metabolism (Correa et al. 2005; Remolina and Hughes 2008; Goldsby et al. 2014a). # 13. Cooperation and Competition: One Level Sitting on Another

Sonya Bahar

(1) Department of Physics & Astronomy and Center for Neurodynamics, University of Missouri at St. Louis, MO, USA

I will right down, feeling for the gift of sound and vision

*David Bowie*

THE EVOLUTION of multicellularity demonstrates the operation of selection at various levels; so does the evolution of eukaryotic cells themselves, suggested by Lynn Margulis to have resulted from the symbiosis of prokaryotes (Margulis 1981). In the chapters above, we have also considered situations where looser affiliations have functioned – or been classified – as a group. We have seen evidence suggesting that a delicate balance of competition and cooperation units at one level into a higher collective. In this chapter we will explore specific examples of this “essential tension,” and investigate how a shift of dominance between cooperation and competition can solidify a level of selection. Central to this process is a transition between two different types of multi-level selection: multi-level selection 1 (MLS1) and multi-level selection 2 (MLS2) in the terminology used by Okasha (2006). MLS1 involves selection on a group trait that derives from an average of individuals (for example, average height in a population). MLS2 traits are properties of the group itself, such as geographic range or overall phenotypic diversity. Method and other have argued that the transition from one level of selection to another involves a transition from selection predominantly at the MLS1 level to selection predominantly at the MLS2 level. This can be viewed as a shift from competition to conflict suppression. 

Before we explore the transition between MLS1 and MLS2, however, we must return to selection at the level of groups of organisms. While the action of natural selection on any sort of group could called “group selection,” the term is typically applied to selection on groups of individual organisms, either at the population or species level. It is here that the balance between competition and cooperation is most easy to spot, but it is also here that the idea of group selection has been most controversial. 

Researchers have searched for many decades for a central problem presented by the cooperation/competition balance at the evolution of altruism. Should altruism be explained on selection groups entities in their own right, or by a gene-level interpretation of kin selection? We have seen arguments between Allen (who was an early advocate of group selection) and Lack, Hamilton, and Williams, who favored gene-centric views. More recently, several authors have suggested that the debate may have been based on a misunderstanding, or at least a lack of precision in defining “group” and “altruism.”  Typically, group selection is defined as a process in which cooperation among individuals within a group enhances the group’s competitive ability against other groups. A common example is the cooperative hunting of predators or the cooperative defense of a territory.  However, Maynard Smith (1964) demonstrated that cooperation can evolve even in the absence of group selection, if the benefits of cooperation to the individual outweigh the costs.  This is the basis of reciprocal altruism, in which individuals cooperate because they expect to receive benefits in return.  The key distinction, therefore, is whether the primary beneficiary of the cooperation is the individual or the group. 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the two levels of multi-level selection. The top panel shows MLS1, with individual organisms competing within a group. The bottom panel shows MLS2, with groups competing against each other. Arrows indicate the direction of selection. The text "MLS1" and "MLS2" are prominently displayed. The diagram also includes labels for "individuals," "groups," and "selection." The overall message is that selection can operate at different levels, and the balance between these levels can influence the evolution of cooperation and competition.

> **Figure 13.1:** Schematic diagram of tradeoffs in the Prisoner’s Dilemma. The diagram consists of four circular nodes, arranged in a 2x2 grid. The rows represent Prisoner A’s choices: “Betray” or “Stay Silent”. The columns represent Prisoner B’s choices: “Stay Silent” or “Betray”. Each node contains two values, representing the time (in months or years) each prisoner receives if they choose the corresponding actions. For example, if Prisoner A chooses “Stay Silent” and Prisoner B chooses “Stay Silent”, both receive 1 month. The diagram illustrates the potential payoffs for each combination of choices, highlighting the tension between cooperation and defection.

Experimental studies have demonstrated that the use of evolutionarily stable strategies in actual biological systems. Milinski (1987) found sticklebacks using a “tit for tat” strategy in the presence of a predator, and interpreted his results as “support [for] the hypothesis that cooperation can evolve among egoists.” More recently, Brandl and Bellwood (2015) found evidence of direct reciprocity in pairs of rabbitfish living in coral reefs, in which one fish remained alert for predators while the other foraged.

Compared to solitary individuals, fishes in pairs exhibit longer vigilance bouts, suggesting that the help provided to the partner is costly, in turn. Fishes in pairs take more consecutive bites and penetrate deeper into crevices than solitary individuals, suggesting that the safety provided by a vigilant partner may outweigh initial costs by increasing foraging efficiency. Thus, the described system appears to meet all of the requirements for direct reciprocity. We argue that the nature of rabbitfish pairs provides favourable conditions for the establishment of direct reciprocity (Brandl and Bellwood 2015).

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

Likewise, Kramer et al (2012) demonstrated, in a paper delightfully entitled “You mob my mob, I’ll mob yours: play it-for-tat game,” that breeding pairs of pied flycatchers exhibit reciprocity in mobbing a predator. 

The prisoner’s dilemma model and other aspects of game theory continue to be used in a wide range of studies of cooperation. For example, Zagorsky et al (2013) considered situations in which a strategy of forgiveness can be advantageous in the long term. A recent study by Press and Dyson (2012), however, suggested the startling conclusion that strategy optimization can lead to extortion rather than cooperation. Stewart and Plotkin, after writing an initial commentary on the Press and Dyson work in 2012, dug more deeply into the model, and found that under some circumstances, cooperation remains an optimal strategy, but the outcome depends sensitively on the system’s parameters (Stewart and Plotkin 2013, 2014). In the words of science journalist Emily Singer, “generosity and selfishness walk a precarious line. In some cases, cooperation triumphs. But shift just one variable, and extortion takes over once again”!

Szőkeoli and Perc (2009) have suggested that multilevel selection can arise from a prisoner’s dilemma game on conveying random networks. However, Boyd and Richerson (1992) argue that reciprocal strategies are insufficient to drive the evolution of prosocial behavior (as proposed by Trivers in 1971) and that punishment is necessary in order for cooperation to evolve. Other critiques of the game theory approach point out that the “pair interaction” focus of the prisoner’s dilemma is not always realistic in biological settings. Johnson et al (2002) showed that when different individual differences, as when different individuals receive different payoffs for the same strategic choice, could destroy the expected outcome of the prisoner’s dilemma game. The debate remains, especially in the field of sociobiology.

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the results of a simulation of the prisoner's dilemma game. The x-axis represents the proportion of cooperators in a population, ranging from 0 to 1. The y-axis represents the average payoff to individuals in the population. Two curves are shown: one for a population with a high cost of cooperation (solid line) and one for a population with a low cost of cooperation (dashed line). The curve for the high cost of cooperation shows a peak at a low proportion of cooperators, indicating that cooperation is only favored when it is rare. The curve for the low cost of cooperation shows a peak at a high proportion of cooperators, indicating that cooperation is favored even when it is common.

Group selection remains such a controversial issue in large part because groups of organisms are looser affiliations than genes within a genome, or cells within an organism. As a result, it is harder for scientists to “see” them as a single unit, and thus it appears (and perhaps *is*) harder for natural selection to “see” them this way as well. This, however, does not mean that selection never sees them as such. Elliot Sober and David Wilson have cited a range of examples in which selection can be shown to act at the group or population level (Sober and Wilson 1998). But a prejudice remains against the very idea of group selection in the minds of many researchers, leading them to dismiss the idea out of hand, based on outdated arguments. 

David Sloan Wilson and his graduate student O. T. Edkar surveyed a number of songbird groups in Michigan, testing whether group selection in fact really existed, in terms of territory defense, and in an attempt to spare troublesome focal individuals from eviction. Edkar and Wilson (2006) found that groups in which individuals cooperated more effectively were more likely to survive. Zagorsky (2011) has shown that well-connected groups are more likely to survive. 

However, as previously noted, the issue is complicated. In a fascinating study, Robert Ackermann et al (2008) showed that cooperation can evolve even in the absence of group selection, through a process called “indirect reciprocity,” whereby individuals are more likely to cooperate with those who have cooperated with others. In addition, the evolution of cooperation can be facilitated by other mechanisms, such as kin selection (Hamilton 1964), whereby individuals are more likely to cooperate with their relatives. The relative importance of these different mechanisms remains a matter of debate. The point is that cooperation is not necessarily altruistic; it can be selfishly motivated, and it can evolve even in the absence of any conscious awareness of the benefits to others. As Robert Kurzban (2010) has argued, “Morality is a system of behavioral guidelines that evolved to facilitate cooperation.” It is not necessarily a set of universal principles, but rather a set of evolved adaptations that help us to navigate the complex social world.

> **Table:** A comparison of different theories of cooperation.
>
> | Theory | Mechanism | Level of Selection | Example |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Kin Selection | Helping relatives | Individual/Gene | Alarm calls in prairie dogs |
> | Reciprocal Altruism | Helping those who help you | Individual | Vampire bats sharing blood meals |
> | Indirect Reciprocity | Helping those who are helped by others | Individual | Reputation-based cooperation in humans |
> | Group Selection | Helping your group | Group | Cooperative hunting in lions |
> | Multilevel Selection | Combination of individual and group selection | Multiple | Evolution of eusociality in insects |

The essential tension, then, is between individual self-interest and the benefits of cooperation. This tension is at the heart of many of the most important challenges facing humanity, from climate change to global pandemics. Understanding this tension is crucial if we are to find solutions to these challenges. As Frans de Waal (2009) has eloquently argued, “We are biological creatures with a long history of cooperation, and we cannot afford to ignore this fact.”

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

I don’t know what’s gotten into E. O. Wilson. He’s certainly the most famous evolutionary biologist, and has gone from strength to strength over the years, winning two Pulitzer Prizes, writing great general books on not only ants but (also) conservation and social behavior. And he’s kept his health in the work, producing any number of technical papers and monographs. He’s even written a novel! Frankly, I don’t know how he does it. I haven’t always agreed with what he says—I think he’s overreached with the sociobiology stuff, for instance—but you have to admire the guy’s knowledge, breadth of conservation, and sheer workaholism. But now along Wilson, along with some collaborators like David Nowak and Martin Nowak, is definitely heading off on the wrong track. They’re attacking kin selection, maintaining not only that it has nothing to do with the evolution of social insects, but that it’s also a bad way to look at evolution in general. And they’re wrong—dead wrong. I’m baffled not only by Nowak et al.’s apparent wilful ignorance of the literature, but by statements that are just wrong. They flatly assert, for instance, that “inclusive fitness theory” is something different from “natural selection theory.” But it’s not! It’s simply a natural extension of population genetics to the situation in which one’s behavior affects related individuals. I could go on, but a little bird has told me that the big guns in the field will, soon and en masse, answer Nowak et al.’s arguments about both theory and *data*. I can’t fathom any motive, either psychological or scientific, for Wilson and Company to repeatedly denigrate the importance of inclusive-fitness theory. It’s just a shame that, this late in his career, Wilson has chosen to fight the wrong battle.

Have concluded by awarding a “ripe raspberry” to the *folks* at Nature who decided to publish such a strange paper in the interest of stirring up controversy, if they’d gotten decent reviews, and followed their advice, it never would have seen print.*

Richard Dawkins argued “writing that the Nowak, Tamalia and Wilson paper was “no surprise” since Edward Wilson’s misunderstanding kin selection as far back as [his seminal 1975] *Sociology*. David Sloan Wilson leapt into the writing on “an open letter to Richard Dawkins,” titled “Why Are You Still in Denial About Group Selection?” Mutual allegations of ignorance of the literature appear as a common motif. “Your view is essentially pre-1975 Wilson,” wrote Wilson, “a date that is notable not only for the publication of *Sociology* but also a paper by W.D. Hamilton, one of your heroes, who correctly saw the relationship between kin selection and group selection—which is to the work of George Price.”*

The trigger for this wave of professional hostility was the suggestion by Nowak, Tamlia and Wilson that inclusive fitness theory kin selection was not sufficient to explain the evolution of altruism. This was particularly striking since the work of W.D. Hamilton, one of the most important evolutionary biologists of the twentieth century, had shown precisely that. They proposed instead a model of “multilevel selection,” in which groups could be selected for altruistic behavior, even if individuals within those groups were not. 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the contrasting viewpoints of inclusive fitness (kin selection) and multilevel selection. The inclusive fitness model is depicted with individuals connected by lines representing kinship, with arrows indicating the flow of altruistic acts benefiting relatives. The multilevel selection model shows groups as distinct entities, with arrows indicating selection pressures acting on the groups themselves. The diagram highlights the differing focus: inclusive fitness emphasizes individual genes and their propagation through relatives, while multilevel selection emphasizes the group as the unit of selection. The text labels indicate "Inclusive Fitness" and "Multilevel Selection" with brief explanations of each concept.

Nowak et al. presented their arguments in a paper in *Nature* in July 2010. The paper was immediately controversial, and it attracted a great deal of attention from evolutionary biologists. Many biologists were critical of the paper, arguing that it misrepresented the inclusive fitness theory and that its multilevel selection model was not well supported by evidence. In a response, Dawkins accused Nowak et al. of “fundamental misunderstandings” of kin selection and of ignoring a vast body of evidence supporting it. He went on to say that their paper was “a triumph of mathematical modeling over biological understanding.”

The debate over inclusive fitness and multilevel selection is not simply an academic one. It has implications for our understanding of the evolution of social behavior, including human behavior. If inclusive fitness theory is correct, then altruism is likely to evolve when individuals are helping their relatives. If multilevel selection is correct, then altruism may evolve even when individuals are not related. 

The controversy over inclusive fitness and multilevel selection is likely to continue for some time. It is a complex issue, and there are strong arguments on both sides. But one thing is clear: the debate has highlighted the importance of rigorous scientific inquiry and the need to be open to new ideas. It also serves as a reminder that even the most established scientific theories are always subject to revision in light of new evidence.

# The ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

> **Figure 13.2:** The colony as superorganism. A mound constructed by the aptly named termite cathedral, *Nasutitermes triodiae*, in the Northern Territory of Australia. Photography by Yevgeny, reproduced under a CC BY-SA 3.0 Creative Commons License. [https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nasutitermes_triodiae-66958](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nasutitermes_triodiae-66958)

Relatedness is better explained as the consequence rather than the cause of eusociality. Grouping by family can hasten the spread of eusocial alleles, but it is not a causative agent. The causative agent is the advantage of a defensible nest, especially one both expensive to make and within reach of adequate food. (Nowak et al. 2010)

They second stage in Nowak, Tarnita and Wilson’s proposed model involves the development of traits conducive to eusociality. These arise by selection at the individual level (though, rather obscurely, Nowak and colleagues also describe them as the adaptive result of radiation, in which species split into different niches “where some (species) are more likely than others” to develop such eusocial phenotypes). Nowak et al. refer to these traits as “spring-loaded” pre-adaptations, as we will see in Chap. 15 below. Gould and Vrba suggest that this term should be discarded in favor of “preadaptations.” These traits include the tendency for solitary bees to behave eusocially when placed in a crowded partnership, Nowak et al. cite among others, a study from Jennifer’s lab at Arizona State University that followed forced pairings of bees from solitary and communal species (Jeanson et al. 2003). Strikingly, pairs of solitary bees were found to exhibit greater division of labor in tasks such as nest excavation than pairs of communal bees. Such studies suggest that 

division of labour appears to be the result of a pre-existing behavioral ground plan, in which solitary individuals tend to move from one task to another only after the first is completed. In eusocial species, the algorithm is readily transferred to the avoidance of a job already being filled by another colony member. (Nowak et al. 2010)

This is consistent with the “mixed threshold” model of the division of labor developed by Bombaert et al. (1996), according to which individuals have different thresholds for undertaking certain behaviors; once an individual begins to perform a certain task it inhibits other individuals from partaking in the behavior, leaving them available to perform other tasks, potentially even those for which they have a comparatively high threshold.

The third step in the process hypothesized by Nowak, Tarnita and Wilson is the development of “eusocial alleles.” While these “have not yet been identified,” the authors speculate that they might arise by a single mutation; the description of *Volvox* above shows that this speculation is far from pure fantasy. Indeed, the wireless store in social insects is to encode the recognition of relatedness. The authors argue that by bending their investment rules, such as the number of colonies built through uniparental reproduction in the wasp *Polistes versicolor* (Foster et al. 2004), a gene can tip the balance in favor of a specific reproductive strategy. Finally, the fourth stage concerns the cloud of other under particular influence of the same or similar reproductive logic. To fully appreciate this, it is essential to grasp the core of a gene’s eye point of view: to identify its fitness benefits and to recognize that these are not always best served by individual reproductive success. (Nowak et al. 2010)

The conventional wisdom, A. Kennedy has shown, is that workers control the queen, and not vice versa (Kennedy 1982). However, recent research suggests that the queen may actually be the primary regulator of worker behavior, and that the workers are merely responding to her pheromonal signals. 

> **Table 13.1:** Reproductive skew in social insects and the predicted effects of relatedness and ecological factors.

| Group | Relatedness (r) | Ecological Factors | Reproductive Skew |
|---|---|---|---|
| Haplodiploid Hymenoptera | 0.75 | High | Extreme (one or few reproduce) |
| Haplodiploid Hymenoptera | 0.75 | Low | Moderate (several reproduce) |
| Diploid Hymenoptera | 0.5 | High | Moderate (several reproduce) |
| Diploid Hymenoptera | 0.5 | Low | Low (many reproduce) |
| Termites | ~0.5 | High | Moderate (several reproduce) |
| Termites | ~0.5 | Low | Low (many reproduce) |

The table shows the relationship between relatedness (r), ecological factors, and reproductive skew in social insects. Haplodiploid Hymenoptera (ants, bees, wasps) have a relatedness of 0.75, while diploid Hymenoptera and termites have a relatedness of approximately 0.5. When ecological factors are high (e.g., limited resources, high predation risk), reproductive skew is more extreme, with only one or a few individuals reproducing. When ecological factors are low, reproductive skew is less pronounced, with several or many individuals reproducing.

The queen’s control is exerted through a complex interplay of pheromones, which regulate worker behavior in a variety of ways. For example, queen pheromones can inhibit worker ovary development, preventing them from reproducing. They can also stimulate worker foraging behavior, ensuring that the colony has a constant supply of food. And they can even influence worker aggression levels, helping to defend the colony against intruders. (Ratnieks & Visscher 1989)

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

we believe that Nowak et al. give the incorrect (and potentially dangerous) impression that evolutionary branching has been a powerful force in the development of this paradigm and a likely reply to have a continued role in the evolutionary theory of behaviour interactions (Pemière and Michod 2011).

Here and Wosie (2011) accused Nowak, Tarnita and Wilson of setting up a false dichotomy, arguing that their proposed mathematical model contained assumptions quite as stringent as those they accused inclusive fitness of. 

A particularly salient critique came from Bourke (2011), who wrote that Nowak and colleagues mistakenly assumed that the interests of eusocial insect workers were subordinate to those of the queen. This revealed a fundamental problem with the “stringent” conditions they required as the basis of a supposedly general theory. In their Supplementary Information, Nowak et al. wrote that “there is no paradoxical altruism that needs to be explained” because “the eusocial gene is [at the center of evolutionary analysis”, which makes “the epicycles of kin selection and inclusive fitness disappear” (Nowak et al. 2010). Paradoxically, they claimed to be taking the gene’s eye view in contrast to the kin selection approach, even though the gene’s eye interpretation of kin selection was one of its major selling points for proponents of gene selectionism.

We propose that kin selection among social insects is an apparent phenomenon which arises only when you put the worker into the center of evolutionary analysis. Kin selectionists have argued that a worker who behaves altruistically by raising the offspring of another individual, requires an explanation other than natural selection, and this other explanation is kin selection. (Nowak et al. 2010)

A first problem with this argument is the false opposition between natural selection and kin selection, the standard interpretation of kin selection is natural selection acting at the gene level. 
The second problem, Bourke argued, lay in Nowak et al.’s radical new suggestions for research on eusociality “that 

[t]he queen and her workers are not engaged in a standard cooperative dilemma. The reason is that the workers are not independent agents. Their properties are determined by the alleles that are present in the queen (both in her own genome and in that of the sperms she stored). The workers can be ‘robots’ that are built by the queen. They are part of the queen’s strategy for reproduction.” (Nowak et al. 2010)

Yet there are many ways in which the workers do not simply play a robotic role. First, the “inclusive fitness theories that Nowak et al. dismiss… focus on correlations between the genes of different individuals to group fitness” (Bourke 2011). Second, the queen does not control all aspects of worker behaviour. The workers respond to environmental cues, and their behaviour affects the queen’s success—for example, workers can decide whether or not to raise a new queen. Third, the assumption that the queen’s “blueprint” determines all worker traits is unsupported. “Worker policing” – the destruction of rival reproductive attempts by workers – is a widespread phenomenon (Ratnieks and Veller 2002). This behaviour cannot be explained by the queen controlling worker behaviour. 

Finally, and most importantly, Nowak et al. appear to have fundamentally misunderstood the logic of inclusive fitness theory. Inclusive fitness theory does not claim that workers necessarily experience a conscious motivation to help their relatives. Rather, it explains how natural selection can lead to behaviours that benefit relatives, even if the actor does not understand the genetic relatedness or the ultimate consequences of its actions. The key insight of inclusive fitness theory is that natural selection favours genes that increase their own propagation, regardless of whether this occurs through direct reproduction or by helping relatives who carry the same genes. 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the relationship between inclusive fitness and kin selection. The diagram shows a family tree with individuals connected by lines representing genetic relatedness. The thickness of the lines indicates the degree of relatedness (e.g., thicker lines for closer relatives). Arrows point from individuals to their relatives, with the length of the arrow representing the benefit conferred upon the recipient. The diagram also includes a mathematical equation representing Hamilton's rule (rB > C), where r is the coefficient of relatedness, B is the benefit to the recipient, and C is the cost to the actor. The diagram emphasizes that kin selection is a specific case of inclusive fitness, where the benefit to relatives is weighted by their genetic relatedness.

In short, Nowak et al.’s attempt to replace inclusive fitness theory with a new “gene-centric” approach is based on a misunderstanding of both inclusive fitness theory and the evolutionary logic of social insect behaviour. Their arguments are not supported by the evidence, and their proposals for future research are unlikely to lead to new insights.
