# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

Whether [scientists] stress the importance of one over the other will depend on the question they are asking. For example, relatedness has proved crucial to understanding conflicts between the queen and her workers over the production of male versus female offspring in ants, bees and wasps. For questions about how tasks are allocated to the workers in any colony or why the size of colonies differs across species, ecological factors are probably more relevant. (Okasha 2010)

In some cases, both processes may be at work, albeit possibly at different levels of selection. Further, Okasha argued, in many cases mathematical models of kin selection and multi-level selection provide identical results, and can serve as alternative interpretations, rather than alternative explanations, for the same phenomenon. One example of this is provided by Lehmann et al. (2007), who took a group selection result and showed that it could be reproduced exactly by a kin selection argument; see also Trailism (2010), Marshall (2011), and Lehtinen (2016). Of course, such demonstrations do not lay bare the evolutionary history of the trait, and therefore do not resolve underlying questions of causality. 

A broader demonstration of equivalence between multilevel selection and kin selection was provided by Wade (1980), who showed that Hamilton’s rule can be derived as a special case of the Price equation. Wade expressed the change in gene frequency under kin selection as the sum of two terms: the change within groups and the change between groups, analogous to the two covariance terms in the Price equation. Hamilton’s rule obtained when the change in gene frequency between groups was positive, and exceeded the absolute value of the change in gene frequency within groups. Thus a gene selection argument could be interpreted as a tension between selection at the individual and group level.

Okasha noted that alternative interpretations in other fields of science, such as Lagrangian vs. Hamiltonian formulations of classical mechanics, or matrix vs. wave approaches to quantum mechanics, have not given rise to the level of misgiving seen in evolutionary theory. (This may partly be a result of the rule of causality in the alternative physics models. Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics do not assume different underlying causes of the phenomena they describe, and in quantum mechanics causality is a total mystery to begin with, so hey). Political implications lie closer to the surface in evolutionary theory as well, as particularly evident in the critique of Gould’s ideas regarding adaptations and spandrels (see Chap. 15). This is also likely to raise the temperature of the debate.

It should come as no surprise that experimental studies purporting to show evidence for group selection, such as those of Pruitt and Goodnight (2014) on cooperation for group composition in a species of spider, have sparked heated exchanges (e.g. Rice 2014; Cornwallis et al. 2015). Experimental evolution is a powerful tool, but the interpretation of its results is often contentious. For example, Pruitt and Goodnight (2014) found that female spiders in groups with low numbers of cooperative alleles were more likely to disperse to new groups, which increased the frequency of cooperative alleles in the population. Rice (2014) argued that this result could be explained by individual selection acting on the tendency of spiders to avoid competition with related individuals. 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the debate between kin and group selection. The top portion shows a spider web with spiders, representing a group selection scenario where groups with more cooperative spiders are more successful. The bottom portion shows individual spiders dispersing, representing individual selection. The text highlights the controversy surrounding experimental studies on group selection, specifically the work of Pruitt and Goodnight (2014) and the critique by Rice (2014). The diagram visually represents the opposing viewpoints in the debate.

The ensuing exchange involved a large number of researchers (e.g. Cornwallis et al. 2015; Pruitt et al. 2016; Rice 2016), and highlighted the difficulties in distinguishing between different levels of selection in experimental settings. The problem is not simply a matter of terminology, but rather of understanding the underlying evolutionary processes. As Okasha (2010) put it, “the debate between kin selection and group selection is not merely a semantic one, but reflects genuine disagreement about how evolution works.” 

The tension between individual and group selection is not simply an academic debate. It has important implications for our understanding of social behavior, including the evolution of cooperation, altruism, and conflict. For example, if group selection is an important force in evolution, then we might expect to see more cooperation and altruism than would be predicted by individual selection alone. Conversely, if individual selection is the dominant force, then we might expect to see more conflict and selfishness.

**Table: Comparison of Kin and Group Selection**

| Feature | Kin Selection | Group Selection |
|---|---|---|
| **Focus** | Relatedness between individuals | Effects on group fitness |
| **Mechanism** | Inclusive fitness | Differential survival and reproduction of groups |
| **Level of Selection** | Gene/Individual | Group |
| **Hamilton’s Rule** | *rB > C* |  Groups with beneficial traits increase in frequency |
| **Example** | Alarm calling in ground squirrels | Cooperation in bacterial biofilms |

The resolution of this debate may require a more nuanced understanding of the interplay between different levels of selection. It is likely that both kin selection and group selection play a role in evolution, and that their relative importance varies depending on the specific context. As Gardner and Grafen (2009) have argued, the distinction between kin and group selection may be less important than the underlying mathematical principles that govern the evolution of social behavior. The essential tension between individual and group selection, therefore, may not be a false dichotomy, but rather a reflection of the complex and multifaceted nature of evolution itself.

Other recent empirical investigations have provided evidence for group selection, such as the studies by Emlen et al. (2012a, b). Emlen et al. (2012a, b) grew two different strains of the harvester bee *Pogonomyrmex barbatus* under conditions where their result easily result in overexploitation and the collapse of a common within an area for the foraging site. For example, in Emlen et al.’s (2012a) second to last experiment, bees had access to a common resource. This could easily result in overexploitation and the collapse of a common. Emlen et al. compared the foraging behavior of two strains, which differ in their individual seed harvest rate—a “high-graine” and a “low-graine” strain. When these two strains were mixed, the high-graine bees quickly exhausted the local seed supply, causing the collapse of the patch, whereas the low-graine bees were more conservative in their harvesting. 

> **Figure:** A graph depicting the results of Emlen et al.’s (2012a) experiment. The x-axis represents time in days, ranging from 0 to 10. The y-axis represents the number of seeds remaining, ranging from 0 to 1000. Two lines are plotted: a blue line representing the mixed strain (high-graine and low-graine bees) and a red line representing the high-graine strain alone. The blue line starts at 1000 seeds and declines rapidly, reaching 0 seeds around day 6. The red line also starts at 1000 seeds and declines, but at a slower rate, reaching around 200 seeds by day 10. The graph demonstrates that the mixed strain leads to faster seed depletion compared to the high-graine strain alone, indicating overexploitation.

Emlen et al. (2012a) found that when the two strains were mixed, the overall yield of seeds was lower than when only the low-graine bees were present, demonstrating that the high-graine bees were driving the system to collapse. This result was interpreted as evidence for group selection, as the high-graine bees’ selfish behavior (maximizing individual harvest rate) led to the detriment of the group (the collapse of the seed patch). Emlen et al. (2012b) performed a similar experiment with a different species of harvester bee, *Pogonomyrmex rugosus*, and obtained similar results. 

These experiments, along with others (e.g., Ratnieks et al. 2006; Wild et al. 2015), have been interpreted as providing evidence for the existence of group selection in nature. However, the debate over the relative importance of individual and group selection remains ongoing. Some researchers argue that most of the observed effects attributed to group selection can be explained by individual selection acting on kin (Hamilton 1964; Nowak 2006). Others maintain that group selection can be a powerful force in evolution, especially in cases where there is strong competition between groups (Travers et al. 2011). 

The question of whether group selection is a significant evolutionary force is not merely of academic interest. It has important implications for our understanding of the evolution of social behavior, including cooperation, altruism, and conflict. If group selection is important, then we might expect to see more instances of behaviors that benefit the group at the expense of the individual. Conversely, if individual selection is the dominant force, then we might expect to see behaviors that maximize individual fitness, even if they are detrimental to the group.

For each experiment, Bashey and Lively infected a number of hosts, and then counted the numbers of nematodes that emerged. After accounting for the mass of the host, they selected nematodes from the smallest and largest emerging populations, and used these to infect another set of four hosts. Four “high treatment” and four “low treatment” passages were carried out in five replicates, for each of the three nematode stocks. For two of the stocks, the nematode population gradually declined over the course of the four passages. In the third stock, a statistically significant difference was observed between the high and low treatment nematode population sizes in the first passage, and this difference was maintained – though it did not increase – in the subsequent 11 passages. Bashey and Lively speculated that the differences between the three experiments may have been exacerbated by the fact that the third stock had only undergone eight passages through wax moth larvae before the start of the experiment, while the other two had undergone 21 passages. This might have left the third stock with a larger store of genetic variability.

In the third nematode population, other traits appeared to evolve “correlated responses to selection on population size” (Bashey and Lively 2009). Populations selected for large numbers emerged faster from their host, likely because they more quickly depleted their host’s resources. Populations selected for small numbers emerged later and were larger in a natural environment, the “high treatment” nematodes would likely experience an individual fitness cost, since “[s]maller nematodes may have fewer energy reserves and thus may have lower survival when they are free-living in the soil…” Moreover, once exposed to a host, smaller nematodes have been found to be less successful at colonizing and surviving to reproductive maturity. Bashey and Lively noted, however, that “in the current study, we saw no differences across treatments in number of nematodes successfully colonizing to, we saw a nonsignificant trend toward greater parasite success (i.e., probability of nematode emergence) in the high treatment”. 

The studies in nematodes, water striders, and spiders in some only some of the most recent experimental studies of group selection. Many of the seminal studies in the field are reviewed in a 1997 paper by Goodnight and Stevens entitled “Experimental studies of group selection: what do they us tell about group selection in natural life?” (Goodnight and Stevens 1997). Presaging the work of Bashey and Lively, the work on water striders, carried out by Richard Taylor and his collaborators, demonstrated that group selection could operate on the water striders at a 37-day laboratory timescale. The water striders used in Taylor’s experiments came from a single population. The populations that generated the most adults after a 37-day laboratory timescale were allowed to reproduce, and this was repeated several times. In which Taylor demonstrated that group selection could operate on water striders at a 37-day laboratory timescale. Wade elaborated on these experiments, carrying out a concurrent comparison in the field to the next generation. Wade found that the field experiments did not necessarily mirror the laboratory experiments. Wade also noted that some spider populations were initially small, and the contribution to the next generation derived from larger groups was favored.

The y-axis represents the average nematode population size. Three lines are plotted, each representing a different nematode stock. The first two stocks show a decline in nematode population size over time. Wade’s (2007) recent work on the guppy *Poecilia reticulata* has also provided evidence for group selection. Wade and his collaborators established 28 replicate populations of guppies in outdoor streams, each of which was founded by a single female. The streams were divided into “high-density” and “low-density” treatments, with the high-density treatments having a higher initial population size. After 18 months, the guppy populations in the high-density treatments had a higher average body size than those in the low-density treatments. This result is consistent with the prediction that group selection would favor larger body sizes in high-density populations, as larger guppies are better able to compete for resources. 

The work of Bashey and Lively, Taylor and Wade, and others has demonstrated that group selection can be a powerful evolutionary force. However, the relative importance of group selection compared to individual selection is still a matter of debate. Some evolutionary biologists argue that group selection is rarely important in natural populations, while others argue that it can play a significant role, especially in certain circumstances. The debate over group selection is likely to continue for many years to come, as researchers continue to investigate the complex interplay between individual and group-level selection.

The snowdrift game has been suggested to be a better model for the evolution of human cooperation than the prisoner’s dilemma (Kimmleri et al. 2007). Using game theory, Gore et al. (2009) identified the ranges of inverse correlation cost and efficiency of cheaters where capture will occur which coerces cooperation and cheaters will take over. With a modulation of the efficiency term based on the observed nonlinear relation between glucose concentration and growth rate, the model fit the experimental data quite well. Further experimental studies showed that glucose concentration also affected the outcome. With more glucose present, cheaters had less need to rely on cooperation, and cooperators experienced a rising metabolic cost of inverse production. At a sufficiently high glucose concentration, their ability to produce inverse was inhibited completely. Their only option for survival was to adopt a cheater strategy. “We therefore see,” the authors concluded, 

that the wild-type inverse production strategy is exactly what might be expected in a snowdrift game. wild-type cells pursue the strategy opposite to that of their opponents. It is possible that glucose repression of invertase is partly determined by these social considerations, helping to make a population of wild-type cells relatively immune to invasion by strains with alternate strategies. (Gore et al. 2009)

A few years later, Gore’s team laboratory investigated the interaction between population dynamics and cooperation (Sanchez and Gore 2013; see also Allen and Nowak 2013). Evolutionary changes (such as allele frequency within a population) typically do not take place on the same timescale as changes in population dynamics, and therefore the study of “eco-evolutionary” feedback is comparatively rare. However, Sanchez and Gore noted, such feedback has been predicted to be very strong in species exhibiting cooperative growth and producing common goods. In the presence of sucrose, S. cerevisiae provided an ideal system in which to test this experimentally: it produced a good, its population dynamics and evolutionary dynamics remain on a similar timescale, and the breakdown of sucrose by invertase led 

to a cooperative transformation of the environment by the cells at low population density, the cells are too dilute to effectively transform the sucrose environment into a glucose environment, so the cells grow slowly on what little glucose they retain following sucrose hydrolysis. At high population density, however, the cells are able to produce enough glucose for the population to grow rapidly! (Sanchez and Gore 2013)

Consistent with these expectations, populations of any inverse-producing cells either grew to a stable size, or collapsed, depending on the initial population density. A mixed population of cooperators and SUC2-deficient cheaters, however, showed much more complex metabolic feedback. Plotting the system’s behavior in phase space, the population density on one axis and the frequency of the SUC2 gene in the population on the other, the system was shown to exhibit a multiplicity of attractors, a dynamic which is associated with evolutionary instability (Sanchez and Gore 2013). The authors found that at low population densities, the system was evolutionarily unstable, and the frequency of the SUC2 gene would increase over time. However, at high population densities, the system was evolutionarily stable, and the frequency of the SUC2 gene would decrease over time. This finding suggested that the evolution of cooperation in S. cerevisiae is contingent on population density. Interestingly, the authors also showed that the qualitative behavior of the system was sensitive to the relative cost of inverse production and the efficiency with which cells are able to transport glucose. 

> **Figure:** A phase-plane portrait of the dynamics of cooperators and cheaters in *S. cerevisiae*. The x-axis represents population density, and the y-axis represents the frequency of the *SUC2* gene. The solid lines represent stable equilibria, the dashed lines represent unstable equilibria, and the arrows indicate the direction of flow. The inset shows a schematic of the experimental setup, with cooperators (black circles) and cheaters (white circles) growing in a medium containing sucrose. The figure demonstrates that the system exhibits multiple attractors, and that the evolution of cooperation is contingent on population density.

These results are consistent with the idea that the snowdrift game is a good model for the evolution of cooperation in *S. cerevisiae*. In the snowdrift game, individuals are better off cooperating if they are rare, but they are better off cheating if they are common. This is because cooperators can benefit from the efforts of others, but cheaters can exploit the efforts of cooperators without contributing themselves. In the case of *S. cerevisiae*, cooperators can benefit from the glucose produced by others, but cheaters can exploit the glucose produced by cooperators without producing their own.

As in the 2009 study, it was found that only a small percentage of cooperators are needed to sustain the population. However, this does not mean that the presence of cheaters has no detrimental effects. Sanchez and Gore found, both theoretically and experimentally, that the presence of cheaters made the population less able to recover from an environmental shock, such as a dilution (analogous to killing a large percentage of the population). Cooperators alone could survive the shock, while a mixed population under similar conditions would fail to extinction. Sanchez and Gore elegantly showed that this could be explained by the relative proximity of the equilibrium points in the cooperators-only vs. the mixed population case to the separatrix between the regimes of collapse and stability in the phase space.

<br>

In the same year, Gore’s group also investigated the effect of range expansion on the relation between cooperators and defectors. Using the same S. *cerevisiae* model, they set-up a “stepping-stone” model for short-range population dispersal. A given well-mixed population was allowed to expand within a “habitat” of 12 wells on a 96-well plate. The population “spread” via the transfer (“migration”) of a fraction to its nearest neighbor wells (Datta *et al*. 2013). With a population of pure cooperators, the population expanded as a travelling wave with a characteristic profile in space consisting of a high-density bulk and a low-density front. Mixed populations also advanced as travelling waves, but more slowly. Most interestingly, they “observed spatial significant plate heterogeneity in allele frequencies within the mixed population” (Datta *et al*. 2013). Under the appropriate conditions, the wave of cooperators would be “stranded” by the wave of cheaters, leading to a spatial segregation of the two morphs. In essence, the cheaters were able to exploit the cooperators’ altruism to expand their range, ultimately leading to their dominance in the population.

While the cooperators led the wave front, the cheaters rushed to catch up with them. Their “invasion velocity”, however, did not equal the velocity of the cooperators. “We were intrigued,” wrote Data et al., “by this comparison, because it suggested that a population of cooperators continued to migrate as if it was invaded, the two populations might never completely mix.” To explore this, they thus tried the “severity” of the environment by changing the bulk dilution of the population<sup>16</sup>. Higher dilution factors would effectively subject the cooperator-dependent growth rate to a greater stress. All velocities (the cooperator wave front velocity, the cheater invasion velocity, and the velocity of the daily increased (decreased) concentration growth rate, the curves crossed one another. For lower dilution factors, the cooperators were able to “outrun” the cheaters, likely as a result of their growth advantage at low population densities. Fig. 13, for larger dilution factors, however, the cooperators were able to overtake them. This might seem counterintuitive, (since cooperators have high “intensity”, yet as Data remarked, “defectors spread into wells that are already occupied by cooperators, in which population densities are low and growth conditions favor defections”).  Moreover, as observed in all concentrations, “cooperators could not quickly enough to completely split off from the population of cheaters.” The outrunning, even in under limited conditions and without splitting, off mix, for a plausible mechanism through which cooperation could maintain in population environments (a completely split off mix of cooperators and cheaters).

# Fig 13.6. Schematic (top) and experimental observation (bottom) depicting the case in which cooperators can outrun detectors, in which the cooperators increase over time, even as the detectors invade. Reprinted with permission from M.S. Datta et al., Range expansion promotes cooperation in an experimental microbial metapopulation. *Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A.* 110(18): 7359–7363, 2013.

<br>

Cellker and Gore (2012) identified another ecological factor that promoted cooperation: interspecies competition. Cooperator and cheater strains of *S. cerevisiae* were co-cultured with an *E. coli* strain DH5α (that could not metabolize sucrose). Instead, DH5α survived on arabinose, which was present in the culture medium but not utilized by the yeast. After 10 day in co-culture, the yeast population had risen from 15 to 49% of the population. But were the *E. coli* simply out-cheating the yeast cheaters?

<br>

A possible explanation for this increase in cooperator fraction within the yeast population is that bacteria behave as a “superior” cheater strain by assimilating available free glucose, thus depriving cheater yeast cells of any sugar. In such a scenario, cooperator cells would do better than cheaters as they have at least some preferential access to the produced glucose. To test this, we competed yeast against a mutant strain of *E. coli* (JM110) that has much reduced glucose and fructose uptake rates… We found a somewhat smaller albeit still significant increase in the cooperator fraction within the yeast population under the same conditions… Bacterial competition for the public good may therefore be a contributing factor toward increasing cooperator frequency in the yeast population, but there is another mechanism at work.

<br>

The other mechanism, they soon identified, was cell density. The co-cultures exhibited a clear two-phase population pattern, in which the bacteria initially grew faster, before being overtaken by the yeast. This resulted in large part from the acidification of the medium caused by yeast sugar fermentation. *E. coli* do not thrive well in an acid environment. The investigators explored this further by using a VIPs (lipare-N/N’-bis(ethane sulfonic acid) buffer to adjust the acidity of the medium, essentially tuning the intensity of the competition. At higher PIPES concentration (and therefore higher pH i.e. *E. coli* population density), this simultaneously increasing the selection pressure on the yeast and decreasing the yeast density. As we have seen from previous experiments, cooperator cells do better in low density, since they can preferentially retain a portion of the monosaccharide they produce. As expected, as the PIPES concentration was increased, the cooperator fraction from the yeast population increased as well in a few words, interspecific competition drove selection for cooperators in one of the two yeasts. It is worth noting that, course, while cooperators were being selected for, the overall yeast population density decreased. Importantly, the investigators also showed that this acidity-dependent selection for cooperators extended beyond *S. cerevisiae*, rather, cooperators from *S. pombe* and *K. marxianus* also benefited from lower pH. Moreover, exogenous addition of acetic acid, a common yeast catabolite, drove an equivalent decrease in the cheater fraction. Together, these experiments suggested that bacterial competition, exacerbated by yeast-mediated acidification, can drive the evolution of cooperation in yeast.

<br>

> **Figure:** A two-panel figure illustrating the relationship between cooperator frequency and time under different conditions. The top panel is a schematic diagram showing a scenario where cooperators outrun detectors. The x-axis is labeled "Time" and the y-axis is labeled "Cooperator Frequency." Two curves are shown: one representing the cooperator frequency increasing over time, and another representing the detector frequency decreasing over time. The bottom panel is a graph showing experimental data. The x-axis is labeled "Time (days)" and the y-axis is labeled "Cooperator Frequency." Three curves are shown, each representing a different experimental condition: "No *E. coli*," "*E. coli*," and "PIPES." The "No *E. coli*" curve shows a relatively stable cooperator frequency. The "*E. coli*" curve shows an increase in cooperator frequency over time. The "PIPES" curve shows a further increase in cooperator frequency, indicating that increasing the pH (through PIPES addition) favors cooperators. Error bars are present on the data points, indicating the standard error of the mean.

<br>

Interestingly, the effect of acidification on the yeast population was not limited to the cooperator/cheater dynamic. The investigators also found that acidification increased yeast flocculation, a process in which yeast cells stick together to form larger aggregates. Flocculation is known to provide protection against predation by bacteria and other microorganisms, and it can also enhance yeast survival in stressful conditions. Thus, the yeast-mediated acidification of the medium may have provided a double benefit to cooperators: it reduced competition from bacteria and it enhanced yeast survival.

<br>

These experiments, together with those described earlier, suggest that the evolution of cooperation in yeast is a complex process that is influenced by a variety of ecological factors, including resource competition, interspecies interactions, and environmental stress. It is important to note that these factors are not mutually exclusive; rather, they can interact with each other to create a complex web of selective pressures that shape the evolution of cooperation.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

we would like an evolutionary theory which explains how the biological hierarchy came into existence, rather than treating it as a given. From this perspective, the levels of selection question is not simply about identifying the hierarchical level(s) at which selection acts, which it is how it was traditionally conceived, but about identifying the mechanisms which led the various hierarchical levels to evolve in the first place… This new ‘diachronic’ perspective gives the levels-of-selection question a renewed sense of urgency. Some biologists were inclined to dismiss the traditional debate as a storm in a teacup – arguing that in practice, selection on individual organisms is the only important selective force in evolution, other theoretical possibilities notwithstanding. But as Michod (1999) stresses, multicelled organisms did not come from nowhere, and a complete evolutionary theory must surely try to explain how they evolved, rather than just taking their existence for granted. So levels of selection other than that of the individual organism must have existed in the past, whether or not they still operate today. From this expanded point of view, the argument that individual selection is all that matters in practice is clearly unsustainable. (Okasha 2006, pp. 16–17)

To that end, Okasha devotes a large portion of his 2006 book, as well as other works (Okasha 2004a, b, Okasha and Patemotte 2012) to using the Price equation, which, as we have seen, can be applied to selection at any level, to characterize the simultaneous operation of selection at multiple levels. Such ‘causal decomposition’ of the levels of selection can be used to analyze the shifting of dominance of selection from dominance at one level to dominance at another. While Okasha has been criticized for a less than transparent use of the concept of covariance (Waters 2011), he has reasonably successful analysis of Michod’s model of the transition between levels of selection as a shift from MLS1 to MLS2.

The idea of parsing multi-level selection into MLS1 and MLS2 was originally proposed by Heisler and Damuth (1989). (see also Damuth and Heisler 1988). While we have briefly summarized the distinction between these two types of selection relating to fitness of a group defined based on the average traits of the individual group members (MLS1) and selection relating to fitness defined with respect to a property or properties of a group as a whole, and thus irreducible to an average organismal fitness (MLS2), their more correct definitions are somewhat subtler. MLS1 properties can be thought of as aggregative characteristics, and MLS2 properties as emergent ones (Okasha 2006, p. 48). More precisely, consider the definition of fitness itself. This is typically taken to be the number of surviving offspring produced. Consider a hierarchy of levels, with each unit a container of smaller units (Okasha 2006, p. 49). This could be a number of cells within an individual, a number of individuals within a group, a number of groups within a metapopulation, and so on. Fitness at the lowest level is the number of offspring produced by an individual. Fitness at the next level is the average number of offspring produced per group. But fitness at MLS2 is a property of the group that cannot be reduced to the average fitness of its members. 

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the different levels of selection. The diagram shows a hierarchy with four levels: genes, cells, individuals, and groups. At each level, there are arrows indicating the direction of selection. The arrows at the gene level point towards genes that increase the fitness of the cell. The arrows at the cell level point towards cells that increase the fitness of the individual. The arrows at the individual level point towards individuals that increase the fitness of the group. The arrows at the group level point towards groups that increase their own fitness, independent of the fitness of the individuals within them. The diagram also includes labels for each level, as well as a brief description of the type of selection that occurs at each level.

For example, the rate of reproduction of a group might be a MLS2 property. Alternatively, the ability of a group to resist invasion by other groups might be an MLS2 property. The key point is that MLS2 fitness is not simply the average fitness of the individuals within the group. It is a property of the group as a whole. Heisler and Damuth (1989) argued that the transition from MLS1 to MLS2 selection was a key step in the evolution of biological complexity. They suggested that MLS2 selection favored groups that were more cohesive and cooperative, and that this led to the evolution of multicellularity.

The distinction between MLS1 and MLS2 selection has been further refined by Godfrey-Smith (2000), who proposed a third type of selection, MLS3, which operates on the level of lineages or species. MLS3 selection favors lineages that are more successful at diversifying and producing new species. Godfrey-Smith argues that MLS3 selection is an important force in the evolution of biodiversity. He also points out that the distinction between MLS1, MLS2, and MLS3 selection is not always clear-cut. In some cases, selection may operate at multiple levels simultaneously.

The levels of selection debate has important implications for our understanding of altruism and cooperation. If selection operates only at the level of the individual, then altruistic behavior is difficult to explain. After all, why would an individual sacrifice its own fitness to benefit another individual? However, if selection can also operate at the level of the group, then altruistic behavior can be favored. For example, if groups with more altruistic individuals are more successful than groups with fewer altruistic individuals, then altruism can evolve. This is the basis of kin selection theory (Hamilton 1964), which argues that altruism can evolve if individuals are more likely to help their relatives, who share their genes.

# THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

In precise terms, the problem is to quantify how character or trait, (if you prefer?) 2 particle affects character Z of the collective to which particle belongs. Certainly, the collective character Z can be an average of the individual characters Z<sub>i</sub>. Okasha gives the average frequency of a gene in a population as an example of such an aggregate collective character. Other characters of the collective can be better described as emergent; they depend on, or relate to, the properties of the individual particle, but not in a simple manner. Okasha cites “the degree of morphological differentiation between castes, or the number of cell divisions before germ-line sequestration” as examples of such emergent characters. Another example would be the geographic range of a population. Okasha suggests that “aggregate and emergent are really opposite ends of a continuum… rather than dichotomous alternatives” (Okasha 2005, pp. 48–49).

A further point to be considered is the relative reproductive timescales of the particle and the collective life cycles. Biologically, there are examples of particles that reproduce simultaneously with their collectives (chromosomes within the cell and others that do not (mitochondria within the cell; cells within metazoan organisms). The timescales involved can affect the definition of fitness, a mitochondrion may reproduce copies, but along a smaller number of copies to the progeny of the collective (the cell) within which it resides. 

For the purposes of his argument, Okasha assumes that these two timescales will be equal, so that the definition of particle fitness will be straightforward: the number of offspring particles a parent particle leaves, unaffected by the relative reproductive timescale of the particle and the collective. The fitness of the collective is harder to define. It could be defined as an aggregate property, in terms of the average for total fitness of the particles within the collective. Alternatively, it could be defined as the number of offspring collectives. Okasha calls these possible definitions “collective fitness,” and “collective property,” respectively (Fig. 13.7). Collective fitness, is itself an aggregate trait of the type defined above, while collective fitness, is an emergent trait.<sup>2</sup>

> **Figure 13.7:** Two diagrams illustrating different modes of reproduction. Both diagrams are composed of circles representing particles. **A** shows a scenario where particles reproduce independently, with each particle splitting into two. The diagram shows one initial particle splitting into two, then each of those splitting into two again, resulting in four particles. Arrows indicate the direction of reproduction. **B** shows a scenario where particles reproduce as part of a collective. The diagram shows one collective (a larger circle containing smaller circles representing particles) splitting into two collectives, each containing the same number of particles as the original. Arrows indicate the direction of collective reproduction. The text below the diagrams indicates that A represents "collective fitness" and B represents "collective property".

# Fig 13.7. Collectives A and B have the same collective fitness. (same number of offspring particles), but different collective fitness. (different numbers of offspring collectives.) Drawing adapted by the author from Figure 2.7 in Okasha (2006)

Is the focal level of selection the particles (and the relative frequencies of their various characters?) In this case, the collectives can be viewed as “part of the environment,” and we are dealing with what Darhuth and Heider (1988) and Okasha refer to as multi-level selection 1 (MLS1). “Alternatively, we may be interested in the collectives as evolving units in their own right, not just as part of the particles’ environment.” If so, we will wish to track the changing frequency of different particles types and collective-types” (Okasha 2006, p. 56). Here, we have multi-level selection 2 (MLS2). Importantly, the collectives do not need to be anything more than transient groups for sorting individual particles. “The role of the collectives in MLS 1 is to generate population structure for the particles, which affects their fitness. For MLS 1 to produce sustained evolutionary consequences, collectives must reappear regularly down the generations, but there is no reason why collectives themselves must persist in stand-offspring relations.” (Okasha 2006, p. 58)

In order to demonstrate how the relation between MLS1 and MLS2 maps onto that between collective fitness, and collective fitness, Okasha turns to D. S. Wilson’s idea of trait groups in the context of the evolution of altruism. 

Organisms are of two types in this model: selfish and altruistic. They assert in groups for part of their life cycle, during which fitness-affecting interactions take place, before blending into the global population and reproducing. Within each group, altruists have lower fitness than selfish types. But groups containing a high proportion of altruists have a higher group fitness, that is, contribute more individual offspring to the global population. Within each group containing a lower proportion. So within-group selection favors selfishness, while between-group selection favors altruism; the overall outcome depends on the balance between the two selective forces. Wilson’s model is thus designed to explain the frequency of an individual trait – altruism – in the overall population. Although the explanation makes essential appeal to group structure, and treats groups as fitness-bearing entities, it permits no inference about the frequency of different types of both. Both levels of selection contribute to a change in a single evolutionary parameter (Okasha 2006, pp. 56–57).

As an example of the “downdating of collective fitness, and MLS2, Okasha cites Jablonka’s (1987) studies of “epigenetic systems,” which deal with the transmission of non-genetic information across generations. “The key claim is that epigenetic systems represent a form of heredity that operates at a level above that of the gene, and that the evolution of epigenetic systems is governed by selection at that level.” (Okasha 2006, p. 59). “Epigenetic systems are not simply a means of transmitting information, but are themselves subject to selection.” The point is that the fitness of an epigenetic system is not simply the fitness of the organism that carries it, but the fitness of the entire epigenetic network. “The evolution of epigenetic systems is therefore a case of multi-level selection, with selection operating at both the level of the gene and the level of the epigenetic system.” (Okasha 2006, p. 60).

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the concept of multi-level selection. Two panels are shown. The top panel, labeled "MLS1," depicts a population of particles, some shaded and some unshaded. Arrows indicate the flow of reproduction, with more offspring resulting from shaded particles. The bottom panel, labeled "MLS2," depicts a population of collectives, some shaded and some unshaded. Arrows indicate the flow of reproduction, with more offspring resulting from shaded collectives. The text indicates that both MLS1 and MLS2 can result in the same number of offspring particles, but different numbers of offspring collectives. The figure is adapted from Okasha (2006).

Okasha concludes that “the concept of ‘collective fitness’ is therefore somewhat misleading, because it suggests that collectives are the kinds of entities that have fitness in the same way that organisms do.” (Okasha 2006, p. 61). “Collectives are simply patterns in the distribution of individual organisms, and their ‘fitness’ is simply a way of describing the effect of those patterns on the fitness of the organisms that compose them.” The key point is that collectives are not independent entities, but are simply emergent properties of the underlying population of organisms. “The evolution of collectives is therefore not a matter of selection at the level of the collective, but simply a consequence of selection at the level of the individual.” (Okasha 2006, p. 62).

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

begin with, as with parasitic theories for the origin of the eukaryotic cell, or conflict may arise as a result of the evolution of selfish mutants, as can occur during the origin of multicellular groups. Furthermore, the
nature of the subsequent interactions may differ among transitions; for example, kin selection may operate as a conflict mediator during the origin of multicellularity but not during the origin of the eukaryotic
cell. In spite of these and other differences, a common framework involving cooperation, conflict and fitness reorganization can be understood. (*Michod 2005*).

From a formal perspective, Michod and colleagues use a population genetic model in which individual cells possess a single genetic locus, which can exist as one of two alleles, cooperators or defect. Cell growth rates may differ
depending on whether the cell is a cooperator or a defector. Organisms are ensembles of individual cells, and reproduce by generating N-cell propagules. The fitness of an organism is the number of propagules it produces, while the
fitness of an individual cell within the organism is determined by its individual cell replication rate. Thus, “an organism’s fitness is not equal to the mean fitness of the cells within it, although these two quantities may be proportional
to each other. This is the defining mark of an MLS2 theory.” (*Okasha 2006, p. 231*).

Michod and Nedelcu (2003) argued that the essence of an evolutionary transition involves the decoupling of fitness at the level of the individual cell from that of the larger organism (or between the fitnesses at any two levels in
a similar mutual relation).

> **Figure:** A schematic diagram illustrating the MLS2 framework. The top panel shows individual cells replicating independently. The middle panel shows cells aggregating to form a multicellular organism. The bottom panel shows the organism reproducing by cell division. Arrows indicate the direction of replication and reproduction. The text labels indicate the levels of selection: individual cell, organism, and group.

Group fitness is, initially, taken to be the average of the lower-level individual fitnesses, but as the evolutionary transition proceeds, group fitness becomes decoupled from the fitness of its lower-level
components. Indeed, the essence of an evolutionary transition in individuality is that the lower-level individuals must “ relinquish” their claim to individual fitness in favor of and reproduction of
the higher-level entity. The lower-level units still survive and multiply, but in so doing they contribute to the fitness of the fitness of the higher-level unit. This translated and reorganized fitness components
from lower to higher levels occurs through the evolution of cooperation and mediates of conflict that restrict the opportunity for within-group change and enhance the opportunity for between-group change.
(*Michod and Nedelcu 2003*).

While Michod and Nedelcu do not explicitly use the MLS1–MLS2 terminology in their 2003 paper, Okasha notes that their argument “bears heavily on the MLS1 versus MLS2 issue for in effect, Michod and Nedelcu are saying that in
the early stages of a collective transition fitness is defined in the MLS1 way, but as the transition proceeds fitness defines occurring, collective fitness in the MLS2 sense become relevant.” (*Okasha 2006, p. 232*, my italics).
To parse how such decoupling occurs, Okasha follows Wilson’s lead, adopting the population genetics models used by Michod and Nedelcu (2003) in their paper “Fitness components and evolutionary specialization”
(*Michod and Nedelcu 2003*). Consider a population of unicellular organisms, each composed of N cells, and suppose that cells can exist in one of two states: a cooperators state (C) or a defectors state (D). Cooperators
pay a cost to provide a public good, conferring a benefit to all cells in the group, while defectors do not pay the cost but still enjoy the benefit. The fitness of a cell is determined by its replication rate, which depends on
the cell’s state and the composition of the group. Michod and Nedelcu (2003) showed that under certain conditions, natural selection can favor the evolution of cooperation, even though defectors have a higher fitness than
cooperators within a group. This is because groups with a higher proportion of cooperators have a higher overall fitness than groups with a lower proportion of cooperators.

> **Table:** Fitness matrix showing the fitness of cooperators (C) and defectors (D) in different group compositions. The table shows the fitness of a cell as a function of its own state (row) and the proportion of cooperators in the group (column). The fitness values are arbitrary, but they are chosen to illustrate the key features of the model.

|             | Proportion of Cooperators = 0 | Proportion of Cooperators = 0.5 | Proportion of Cooperators = 1 |
|-------------|------------------------------|---------------------------------|------------------------------|
| **Cooperator** | 1                            | 1.5                             | 2                            |
| **Defector**   | 1.2                          | 1.7                             | 2                            |

As Okasha (2006, p. 233) explains, the key to understanding the MLS2 framework is to recognize that fitness is not an intrinsic property of individuals, but rather a contextual property that depends on the level of
selection. In the early stages of a collective transition, fitness is defined at the level of the individual cell (MLS1), but as the transition proceeds, fitness becomes defined at the level of the group (MLS2). This shift in the
level of fitness can lead to the evolution of cooperation and other forms of altruism, even though these traits may be disadvantageous at the individual level.

The MLS2 perspective has important implications for our understanding of the evolution of complex social systems, including the origin of multicellularity, the evolution of eusociality in insects, and the emergence of
human culture. By recognizing that fitness is not always aligned with individual interests, we can begin to understand how cooperation and altruism can evolve and persist in the face of conflict and competition.

The spatial structure of a population is known to affect the outcome of competition between cooperators and cheaters (Greig and Travisano 2004; Hauert and Doebeli 2004).

19

In all these *S. cerevisiae* experiments, populations undergo daily dilution and regrowth, see Gore et al. (2009), Sanchez and Gore (2013), and Datta et al. (2013) for details of the experimental protocol.

20

These studies can be compared with those of Popat et al. (2012) on cheater strains in biofilms, discussed in Chap. 9 above.

21

Other studies include, for example, the role of the rate of host evolution in symbiotic interactions (Damore and Gore 2011); theoretical investigations of the application of Price’s equation and Hamilton’s rule to the problem of microbial cooperation (Damore and Gore 2012); the role of tipping points in pushing a “producer/freeloader” yeast ecosystem to the brink of collapse (Chen et al. 2014); the role of clustering in driving the structure of multispecies bacterial communities (Celiker and Gore 2014); computational modeling of the effect of slow switching between environments in small populations (Tan and Gore 2012).

22

As Osaka points out, McGhee (1996, 2001a, b) argues that interaction among parts is necessary for a part-whole solution. Sober and Wilson (1998) specify that these interactions must affect fitness.

23

Typically, collective fitness, is most naturally applicable to situations where reproduction of the levels occurs on a synchronous timescale, and collective fitness, is more applicable to the case the generation times of collectives and particles are asynchronous. However, these correspondences are not inevitable (Osaka 2006, p. 58).

24

I would argue that this grey area could be more broadly defined to include the case where only a portion of collective fitness was proportional to cellular fitness, and thus only a portion of the collective character fitness covariance was driven by cross-level-byproducts from cellular fitness.

# 14. Evol = {f(evol)

Sonya Bahar

(1) Department of Physics & Astronomy and Center for Neurodynamics, University of Missouri at St Louis, MO, USA

...with a wild surmise. 

—Keats

DESPITE THE CLAIMS of Darwin, evolution is far more complex than “the survival of the fittest.” In order for any evolutionary change to occur at all, in order for the vast landscape of possible forms, variations is essential. Perhaps we are lucky this so, since in our imperfect world mistakes are inevitable, however accurate a proofreading enzyme might be. The inevitability of variation coupled with its “value” as a source of new evolutionary possibilities, provided Arthur H. Sturtevant with the answer to a question he posed in an influential 1937 article in the *Quarterly Review of Biology*. Sturtevant, who had assembled the first genetic linkage map of a chromosome (the *Drosophila* X chromosome) in 1913, asked why mutations do not evolve to zero. His paper laid the groundwork for the study of what is now called the evolution of evolution, or, somewhat less poetically, second-order selection (Tenailon et al. 2001).

> **Figure:** A black and white photograph of Arthur H. Sturtevant. He is a middle-aged man with short hair, wearing a suit and tie. The background is a simple, neutral tone.

Importantly, not only for an understanding of evolution itself, but also for more practical concerns like dealing with invasive species (Gilchrist and Lee 2007; Wagner and Drahí 2010), Massimo Pigliucci (2008) has suggested that evolution itself (and the evolution thereof) “may constitute one of several pillars on which an extended evolutionary synthesis will take shape during the next few years.” Wagner and Drahí (2010) state flatly that arguments against the evolution of evolvability “have not been rigorously examined by their proponents and are thus a self-fulfilling blind spot in evolutionary biology.”

One of the primary reasons for resistance to the idea of the evolution of evolvability is that ability is a trait at the population-level or above, and thus an unnatural concept for those opposed to the very notion of group selection. Moreover, the evolution of evolvability’ seems at first glance to require the paradox of evolutionary forethought: something selected for its future benefits. The paradox vanishes when evolvability is seen to result from the unintended consequences of traits evolved in response to other selection pressures, before becoming exploited as a selection trait at a later higher than the immediate selection pressure. Liu, Long, and Luyssaert (2006) provide an elegant example of this, demonstrating that the evolution of bet-hedging in *Arabidopsis thaliana* (a plant that produces a diversity of seed dormancy levels in order to maximize fitness in fluctuating environments) had the unintended consequence of increasing the rate of adaptation to new stressful environments. 

The evolution of evolvability therefore is not an anticipation of future needs, but rather a byproduct of past adaptations. This idea is not new; it was articulated most powerfully by Sewall Wright in the 1930s, as part of his “shifting balance theory” (Wright 1932). Wright’s vision, however, was largely ignored for 40 years, until it was resurrected in the context of quantitative genetics by Templeton (1982) and Levin (1983). The reemergence of Wright’s ideas, coupled with the growing realization that many evolutionary processes are not well captured by the standard neo-Darwinian paradigm, has fueled the current interest in the evolution of evolvability. 

> **Table:** A table titled "Evolvability and the evolution thereof." The table has two columns: "Evolvability" and "Evolution thereof." The rows list different aspects of evolvability and their corresponding evolution.
>
> | Evolvability | Evolution thereof |
> |---|---|
> | Mutation rate | Selection for DNA repair mechanisms, transposable element activity |
> | Recombination rate | Selection for chromosome stability, resolution of double-strand breaks |
> | Genome size | Selection for metabolic efficiency, resistance to viruses |
> | Gene duplication | Selection for functional redundancy, raw material for innovation |
> | Phenotypic plasticity | Selection for bet-hedging, canalization |

# THE ESSENTIAL TENSION (THE FRONTIERS COLLECTION)

Sturtevant suggested that artificial laboratory conditions seemed to raise the mutation rate, and wondered whether “all mutations so far determined experimentally [are] too high to be applicable for natural populations.” It was 
clear that mutation rate generally tunable, though the mutation rate is still unknown. Probably they act in various ways, but it remains possible that they have something in common, such for example as an influence on 
the relative duration in time of specific stages of mitosis or some other general property. In this case it might well be that such effects would have greater selective value through other results than their effects 
on mutation rate. (Sturtevant 1937)

Despite being less prevalent than deleterious mutations, favorable mutations occur, and Sturtevant wondered how selection might act in their favor.

—it seems at first glance that there should be a counter-selection, due to the occurrence of favorable mutations. It is true that favorable mutations furnish the only basis for the improvement of the race, and must 
be credited with being the only raw material for evolution. It would evidently be fatal for a species, in the long run, if its mutation rate fell to zero, for adjustments to changing conditions would then not long 
remain possible. While this counter-selection effect may occur, it is difficult to imagine its operation. It is clear that the vast majority of mutations are unfavorable, and Fisher (1930) has shown that the rate of 
favorable ones must, in general, be [in] gene with slight effects. In other words, for every favorable mutation, the preservation of which will tend to increase the number of genes in the population that raise the 
mutation rate, there are hundreds of unfavorable mutations that will tend to lower it. Further, the unfavorable mutations are mostly highly unfavorable, and will be more effective in influencing the rate than 
will the relatively slight improvements that can be attributed to the rare favorable mutations. (Sturtevant 1937)

Sturtevant was left, then, with a conundrum:

This raises the question – why does the mutation rate not become reduced to zero? No answers seem possible at present, other than the surmise that the nature of genes does not permit such a reduction. In 
short, mutations are accidents, and happen. (Sturtevant 1937)

As Sturtevant concluded from the evidence available to him at the time, deleterious mutations are known today to be far more prevalent than beneficial mutations. Denamur and Moolk (2006) cite values of up to 8 x 10⁻⁶ 
deleterious mutations per genome per replication in *E. coli*, in contrast to 2 x 10⁻⁸ beneficial mutations. Recent arguments from biochemistry and bioenergetics are consistent with Sturtevant’s suggestion of a lower bound on 
mutation rates (Sniegowski et al. 2000). Another factor that may set such a lower limit is the cost of fidelity. Optimization of transcription fidelity is likely not only an economical cost, but also a somewhat coarse 
process corresponding to transcriptional error rates of approximately one mistake every 10⁴–10⁵ base pairs (Hodgkinson et al. 1989; Kunkel 1992; Johnson 2003). With higher fidelity come more elaborate repair 
systems. The limits on fidelity and repair are reviewed by Fry and Loeb (1999). Furthermore, detailed analysis of genome damage in relation to nucleotide composition has demonstrated that the biochemical costs 
of maintaining a very low mutation rate in any given genome may be prohibitive (Lande 1979; Crow and Lande 1992). These considerations suggest that there may be an irreducible level of mutation rate, and that this rate is 
not necessarily a consequence of a failure to optimize fidelity.

Other studies suggest that observed mutation rates, whether optimal or not, are certainly not minimal. Perhaps more importantly, mutation rates are variable. Evidence now suggests that mutation rate not only evolved, but is continually adjustable. Experiments in organisms as diverse as bacteriophage T4 (Drake et al. 1969; Schaper 1988), *E. coli* (Schaper 1988) and *Drosophila melanogaster* (Nothke 1987) have succeeded in driving mutation rates below the wild type under selection pressure. Other experimental evolution studies, from Lenski’s group at Michigan State, have shown that selection pressure can drive mutation rates in *E. coli* above wild type. Sniegowski et al. (1997)

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

subject that 12 populations of *E. coli* derived from the same ancestral clone to a low-glucose environment. Three of these 12 populations developed a mutator phenotype, with mutation rates between one and two orders of magnitude higher than that of their ancestor. 

Antibiotics provide an obvious source of selection pressure on bacteria. A number of studies show that “mutator” bacterial strains, with high mutation rates compared to wild type, have greater antibiotic resistance than wild type, and thus have a clear selective edge in the presence of an antibiotic (Dramur and Matic 2006). Experimental evolution studies demonstrated the induction of mutator strains as a response to antibiotics. Mac et al. (1997) applied a sequence of antibiotic treatments to an experimental *E. coli* population with an initial population of one mutator cell (deficient in mismatch-repair mechanisms) in 100,000. After only four selective cycles, all surviving cells exhibited at mutator phenotype. An analogous process may be at work in metazoans such as *Daphnia*, which undergo sexual reproduction during times of increasing result genetic diversity.

Despite the bacterial studies just cited, there is no simple correlation between high mutation rate and antibiotic resistance. For example, Denamur et al. (2005) found that strains of naturally occurring *E. coli* with intermediate mutation rates survived exposure to multiple antibiotics better than those with high or low mutation rates. This is consistent with a computational study suggesting that, even though they spread more slowly through the population, weak mutator strains are more stable than strong mutators (Taddei et al. 1997). Weak mutator strains might be more robust with respect to environmental change, occupying a broad fitness plateau rather than a narrow peak. The value of such broad fitness peaks has been dubbed “survival of the flattest” (Wilke et al. 2001).

Mutator strains occur even in the absence of an identifiable selective drive. Strains having higher mutation rates than the norm are also commonly within a isolates of wild types of bacteria. Naturally occurring mutator strains have been identified in *Salmonella enterica*, *Neisseria meningitidis*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *E. coli*, among others (Dramur and Matic 2006). 

In some bacterial mutator strains, the source of the increased mutation rate has been identified. Often, mutator strains from inactivation of *mutS* or *mutM* genes in the DNA mismatch repair system. This can result from a range of mutations, including insertions, deletions, premature stop codons and shifts in the reading frame (Matic and Matic 2006). The protein coded by *mutS* recognizes all but one of the eight possible base pair mismatches; it can also bind small groups of unpaired bases that may occur as a result of insertions or deletions. The protein coded by *mutH* helps to link *mutS* with other repair components (Dramur and Matic 2006). Recent experimental studies suggest that Mut traps, MutS at the mismatch site to repair a weaker grip the paired DNA (Qi et al. 2006). 

Not all changes in mutation rate are mediated by the mismatch repair machinery. Recent work has shown that compensatory, or “suppressor” mutations can rapidly arise in mutator strains to restore mutation rates to normal levels. For example, in a population of *E. coli* with a *mutator* phenotype, Greene et al. (2005) found that suppressor mutations frequently arose in genes involved in the regulation of DNA replication, recombination, and DNA repair. These suppressor mutations often reverted the high mutation rate to wild-type levels.

> **Figure:** A graph depicting mutation rate versus time for different *E. coli* strains. The x-axis represents time in generations, ranging from 0 to 500. The y-axis represents mutation rate, measured in mutations per genome per generation, ranging from 0 to 1 x 10^-8. Three lines are plotted: a "wild type" strain (relatively flat line around 1 x 10^-10), a "mutator" strain (initially high, around 1 x 10^-8, then decreasing over time), and a "suppressor" strain (starts high like the mutator, but rapidly declines to a level similar to the wild type). The graph illustrates how mutator strains can initially have high mutation rates, but these rates can be reduced over time by suppressor mutations.

The evolution of mutation rates is therefore not a simple, unidirectional process. Rather, it is a dynamic interplay between mutator mutations that increase mutation rates and suppressor mutations that decrease them. This dynamic can lead to fluctuations in mutation rates over time, and can also result in the maintenance of intermediate mutation rates. The relative fitness effects of mutator and suppressor mutations will depend on the specific environmental conditions, and on the genetic background of the organism.

The question of whether mutation rates can evolve in response to environmental stress has important implications for our understanding of adaptation. If mutation rates can evolve, then organisms may be able to accelerate their rate of adaptation in response to changing conditions. However, the evolution of mutation rates is also constrained by the potential costs of high mutation rates, such as the accumulation of deleterious mutations. The optimal mutation rate will therefore depend on the balance between the benefits of increased adaptability and the costs of increased genetic load.

Sniegowski et al. (1997) suggested that the development of the three mutator state is another, seemingly contradictory property; they have a “hyper-recombination” phenotype, promoting genetic recombination. As suggested by Denamur and Matic (2006), “When selective pressure for increased genetic variability is no longer present, the hyper-recombination phenotype of mismatch repair-deficient strains might facilitate the reacquisition of the functional mismatch repair genes via horizontal gene transfer.” This can save the adapted mutator genome from being overburdened with deleterious mutations, and perhaps save it from losing beneficial mutations gained during the period of hypermutability.

Prokaryotic cells have one more reason to mutate: to follow mutators strains across the fitness landscape toward new heights: the robustness conferred by their large population sizes. While various definitions of the term robustness are still being debated, and the term continues, unfortunately, to be too often used as a buzzword, mutational robustness can be defined as “the ability to preserve a constant phenotype despite the genomic mutational load”, where this load is “the burden on the genome resulting from deleterious mutations” (Elena and Sanjutan 2005). 
In multicellular organisms, mutational robustness is most likely to derive from redundancy in the genome (Krakauer and Plotkin 2002) which can provide structural modularity and serve as a template for evolutionary experimentation. In addition to genetic modularity, sources of redundancy include:

alternative metabolic pathways, or chaperone proteins that buffer against mutation-induced proteins in other enzymes. In the presence of mutational load (…), these mechanisms would produce phenotypes similar or identical to that of the unmutated wild type, such that individuals would have similar chances for survival and reproductive success (Elena and Sanjutan 2005).

With large population sizes, bacteria and viruses possess robustness based on numbers alone. Minimal redundancy renders bacterial cells highly susceptible to deleterious mutations. But if they die, there is a swarm of other bacterial cells waiting in the wings, and at least some of these are likely to have beneficial mutations. Importantly, this is an example of robustness – and, as a result, the ability to take advantage of mutator phenotypes – at the population, rather than the individual, level (Elena and Sanjutan 2005). 
The differential role of population size and the ability of the cell to buffer against mutation have recently been recognized by biologists. The differential may have been overlooked previously, promoting erroneous phylogenetic and ecologic interpretations. Recent studies by Tenaillon et al. (2001) and Chao et al. (2006) have shown that *E. coli* populations can rapidly evolve robustness to deleterious mutations. As a result, the rate of adaptation to new environments is increased. Furthermore, the evolution of robustness is often associated with the irreversible loss of mismatch repair. The observation that robustness is often associated with the loss of mismatch repair is not necessarily paradoxical. In fact, it is consistent with the idea that robustness and mismatch repair represent alternative strategies for dealing with deleterious mutations. 

> **Figure:** A schematic diagram illustrating the relationship between mutation rate, population size, and robustness. The x-axis represents mutation rate (from low to high), and the y-axis represents population size (from small to large). The diagram shows that robustness increases with both increasing mutation rate and increasing population size. There is a shaded area representing the region of high robustness. The diagram also includes labels for "low robustness," "high robustness," and "mutation rate."

The relative importance of these two strategies depends on the environment. In stable environments, mismatch repair is favored because it prevents the accumulation of deleterious mutations. In variable environments, robustness is favored because it allows the population to adapt to new conditions more quickly. The evolution of robustness is also influenced by the genetic architecture of the organism. Organisms with high levels of genetic redundancy are more likely to evolve robustness than organisms with low levels of genetic redundancy. In conclusion, the evolution of robustness is a complex process that is influenced by a variety of factors, including mutation rate, population size, environmental variability, and genetic architecture.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

Many amphibian and reptile taxa experience dramatic shifts in their environment during development, essentially having to function in different niches. For instance, the komodo dragon (*Varanus komodoensis*) begins life as an arboreal predator of small insects, progressively moves onto larger insects, small vertebrates and eggs, then larger vertebrates and eventually falls a terrestrial large predator/scavenger niche… Mutations providing a continuum may advantage at any point along this continuum may be deleterious somewhere else during growth. This effect is less in mammals and birds because they typically feed their young until they can occupy the adult niche. Compared with other vertebrates, mammals and birds are also notable for an increased emphasis on homeostatic, particularly endothermy… Both effects, reducing the range of niches during development and stabilizing internal conditions, should enhance morphological evolvability. Indeed, while mammals and birds have diversified into widely different niches and morphologies from their ancestors that shared the planet with dinosaurs 65 million years ago, amphibians, turtles, lepidosaurs (snakes and lizards) and crocodilians typically have not… (Pôle et al. 2003)

Kirschner and Gerhart (1998) argue that metazoan evolvability derives from cellular and developmental processes conserved at least since the Cambrian explosion. In other words, some of the most rigidly conserved aspects of metazoan biology are precisely those that enable the unique characteristics of metazoan evolvability. “How,” they asked, “can all this commonality serve as the platform for the immense diversification of metazoa?” Redundancy in the eukaryotic genome is crucial, since “[f]unction is frequently conserved even when sequences differ substantially.” Genetic variation is often not matched by an equal functional variation. “This protects proteins that can easily be co-opted into other functions, while retaining their original role; the crystalline’s provide a dramatic example of this.” Likewise, the opposite also holds, and small changes in gene sequence can produce large changes in functionality. 

Kirschner and Gerhart point out, that, while many cellular processes are highly conserved, the regulatory mechanisms that control them are quite diverse. Much of the regulation in biochemical pathways takes place by inhibition (and by activation resulting from the inhibition of an inhibitor). Regulatory molecules are quite versatile and “sticky,” able to bind to a range of substrates. Calmodulin is a prime example of such versatility, being “effective without having to be highly specific” (Kirschner and Gerhart, 1998). Small mutational changes can trigger unique—and possibly advantageous—new interactions. 

Like gene regulatory networks, biochemical pathways possess what Kirschner and Gerhart call “weak linkage”, in contrast to the strong linkage present in metabolic networks, where “[s]ystemic consequences are high, and the complementary fit of surfaces of interacting components is precise.” Systems with weak linkage “can be molded in any one of a large set of ways.” Such regulatory networks, facilitates… the evolution of novelty, because the network’s components can be co-opted for different functions. Essentially, this means that regulatory networks are “robust” and “plastic,” facilitating experimentation, and the evolution of novel traits. The Hox genes provide a classic example of this principle. These genes encode transcription factors that regulate the development of body plan in animals, and small changes in their expression can lead to major changes in morphology.

> **Figure:** A diagram illustrating the concept of "weak linkage" in gene regulatory networks versus strong linkage in metabolic networks. The diagram shows two networks: one labeled "Metabolic Network" with tightly connected nodes and arrows indicating strong, specific interactions, and another labeled "Regulatory Network" with loosely connected nodes and arrows indicating versatile, less specific interactions. The metabolic network is depicted as a rigid structure, while the regulatory network is shown as more flexible and adaptable. Text boxes highlight the key differences: metabolic networks have "systemic consequences" and "precise fit," while regulatory networks allow for "experimentation" and "co-option of components."

The concept of “deep homology” (Gehart and Kirschner, 1997) is also central to their argument. Deep homology refers to the idea that seemingly different structures in different organisms may share a common underlying genetic and developmental basis. For example, the eyes of vertebrates and cephalopods (squid and octopuses) appear very different superficially, but they both develop using the *Pax6* gene, suggesting that they share a common evolutionary origin. This implies that evolution does not always create new structures *de novo*, but rather modifies existing ones. 

The concept of “facilitated variation” (Conrad, 1988) is also relevant here. Facilitated variation refers to the idea that certain types of variation are more likely to occur than others, and that these variations are often those that are most likely to be adaptive. For example, changes in the number of vertebrae are common in snakes, and these changes are often associated with adaptations to different lifestyles. This suggests that the genetic and developmental architecture of snakes facilitates variation in vertebral number.

# The Essential Tension (The Frontiers Collection)

In regulatory networks is also seen in the segmentation of body plans within any given phylum, and the compatible stability of the phytotypic* stage across a wide range of families, genera and species. A similar hierarchy was identified in *compactional* by He and Dem (2010), who suggested that “the slow evolution of the top components and fast evolution of the bottom components of the hierarchy is a universal phenomenon in evolution”. One reason for this, Kirschner and Gerhart argue, is that the “top” components are extremely robust, as a result of compartmentalization and patterns that can be easily triggered by self-activating signalling cascades. In *Drosophila* development, for example, initial egg polarity is determined only by four gene products, but *quickly* “elaborates into the 50 or 60 different spatial compartments of the body plan” (Kirschner and Gerhart 1998). The same compartmentalization that allows experimentation at the branches imposes rigidity at the root. Kirschner and Gerhart sketch out a hypothetical process of evolution by at the clade’ level. 

In each round of variation, selection, and fixation, it appears that during the fixation period there was a selection for properties of robustness and versatility of the new found processes. These properties then facilitated the generation of phenotypic variation used in the next round, and, we think, ensured the conservation of the flexible robust process itself, which was further selected with those new variations. Organisms with processes lacking robustness and versatility presumably lost out in the next round because of their inability to retain as much genetic variation and to generate selectable phenotypic novelty with as few mutational changes. Added to this is the preemptive argument that a clade of organisms still perfecting its body plan at a time when others (with perhaps less perfect plans) had already started originating appendages and mouthparts was now at a selective disadvantage… (Kirschner and Gerhart 1998).

It has been argued that mutator genes can only play a limited role in metazoan evolution due to the difficulty of hitchhiking in genomes extensive recombination during meiosis. Nevertheless, experimental evidence for evolvability in eukaryotes has been obtained. Not surprisingly, these claims for evolvability in the eukaryotic genome have been highly controversial. Susannah Rutherford and Susan Lindquist made the first experimental demonstration of eukaryotic evolvability in 1998. They showed that the gene for *Hsp90* encoding the *Drosophila* heat shock protein Hsp90 (Fig. 14.2) was mutated by even a single base substitution, such a system for an arginine, the flies exhibited a wide array of phenotypic disturbances, as shown in Fig. 14.3 (Rutherford and Lindquist 1998).
